Hosterwith bei Dresden December 17. 1891

Mary L. Ware, Boston Mass.

Dear Lady,

We received your very kind letter with great pleasure and are very glad to hear that you are pleased with the models of the last assignment. In a few days we shall finish again a series of 60 species of plants this time all Thamerogamnia and a great many analytical details. We are all very glad to see the time drawn near by which the journey to America by the younger of us will be carried out, it being rendered possible by this renewed act of kindness and generosity of you and Mrs. Ware. The is most happy by the thought soon to have the honour of seeing you and others. We are in person and he is looking forward with delight and pleasant hopes to the analyzing and collecting of those important forms of American plants which have been hitherto inaccessible to us. For all your kindness and interest that we and our work have been favoured with us, we express our sincerest thanks to you and we beg to send to you and others. We are at the occasion of the new year our hearty wishes, that your coming year be full of health and pleasure. We beg to ask you to remember us most kindly to Mrs. Ware and beg to send to you the kindest regards of all of us and we remain

Yours very truly

Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka

Boston, March 1st, 1892

Mrs. Loyland Law Boston DEAR

With many thanks for the kind interest shown in the work of the Howard Benevolent Society in the past we take the liberty of asking you whether it will be your pleasure to contribute to the support of the Society for the present year. If so, any sum that you may be pleased to forward will be gratefully acknowledged by the Treasurer.

We have expended during the past year about $8,000 in aiding The American Poor in the purchase of Coal, Wood, Groceries, Medicine, Flannels and Clothing for the sick.

We have no agents; we have no rent to pay and our money goes direct to the Poor. We have experienced visitors who give their time, to investigate each applicant for aid, who is aided at once if found worthy.

Our work is chiefly among the aged American poor and those who have seen better days, especially widows and orphans, most of whom desire to retain their little homes and self-respect, and to be saved from becoming paupers.

We are in need of more money for the coming winter and summer work. Money sent to Mr. Chas. F. Wyman, Treasurer, 58 India Square, or Mr. Edward MacDonald, 17 Monument Avenue, member of the Standing Committee, will be greatfully acknowledged. Also Cast-off Clothing and Flannels will be very acceptable and, on notifying Mr. Edward MacDonald as above, will at once be sent for.

Respectfully yours,

SAMUEL B. CRUFT, President.

ANDREW CUSHING,

JOHN CODMAN ROPES,

Vice-Presidents.

GEO. F. BIGELOW, M. D.,

Secretary.

CHAS. F. WYMAN, Treasurer,

Professor Goodale, ladies and gentlemen: On behalf of the President and Fellows of Harvard College I have the honor to accept in your favoring presence this

unique collection, in which I see at once an object of singular beauty, a durable means of instruction, and a memorial of a useful and honorable life. It is

a pleasure to call to mind the patience, skill and accurate knowledge manifested

by the artists who have made these models of flowers. Their work is done with a

fidelity and thoroughness worthy of the highest admiration. I am also authorized

to testify before you all that the givers of this collection, and the University

as well, feel greatly indebted to Professor Goodale, through whose energy, zeal,

sympathy, and tact, the memorial purpose of the givers has been happily accomplished. What more appropriate memorial could there be of the beneficent life

of a wise, modest, pure, and devoted physician?

An endowed university is full of memorials. This building recalls the prophetic enthusiasm and inspiring energy of the founder of the Museum of Comparative Zoology. This room is itself a memorial prepared by filial piety for an honored father. The very stones in the University's buildings, the books in its libraries, the pictures on its walls, and many of the objects in its collections recall the names of graduates, teachers, or benefactors who in their day loved and served this University, or believed that through it they could foster intelligence, piety and righteousness. As the generations pass, these memorials may fail to bring before the minds of the living true pictures of the persons whom they commemorate; but they will never fail to commend to the passing generations the high qualities of mind or heart which made the persons commemorated serviceable and beloved. We commemorate good deeds or good lives, not in the effort to keep fresh names, forms, or lineaments which must fade, but to inspire each successive generation to admire and imitate beneficence, piety, and heroism. The person fades from view; his act or life commemorated, brings forth like acts or lives; his generous spirit transmitted and multiplied, fires unimaginable trains of helpful influence. So may it be with the beautiful gift and the good life which we celebrate to-day!

Dear Badam

We take again the liberty of sending you these lines on purpose to express our best wishes and most respectful compliment of the new year season, asking you and others. We are to accept them as the sincere expression of our loyal feelings. We are getting on very well with the finishing work for January-consignment which will be composed of 50 species, exclusively flowers and their details, they are made with only exception of two marsh plants and Parmacia with the help of the material and studies of Jamaica and the West. We enjoy very much in our being able to illustrate the economic plant as of which a good deal will be represented in the January-consignment form the can\|_{n} Aucardium, star-apple Erynophyllium, the pencil-pedar Bedrela, Coca, Eucalyptus ete. Things that we never had found in bloom in a garden of Europe, same is the case with the western desert plants which are also represented in the consignment. We made also this time the curious Darlinglonia californica. We finished a good deal of the models and hope to be able to forward them earlier than in former consignments.

L. & R. Blaschka

## HARVARD'S GLASS FLOWERS.

A Lecture on the Interesting Ware Collection

of Blaschka Models.

Prof. George L. Goodale of Harvard gave a most interesting account last night in the hall of the Boston Society of Natural History of the Ware collection of Blaschka glass models of flowers in the Harvard University museum. A large audience was present.

After describing the general scope of museums of natural history and explaining that such museums have two ends in view, namely, the accumulation of material for research and the exhibition of selected specimens for the instruction of the public, Prof. Goodale described that part of the Harvard University museum which is devoted to botany.

The most attractive part of the collection which is open to visitors is that which contains the Blaschka glass models of flowers. These models are the sole product of the artistic work of two Germans, a father and son. The father had made a few flowers in glass as early as 1862, but these were destroyed in a fire in Belgium. From 1863 to 1886 the Blaschkas constructed only glass models of marine invertebrate animals, but in the latter year they were induced to begin the preparation of a series of models illustrating American species of plants. These models are constructed wholly of glass, part of which is colored before and part after the completion of the specimens. All the parts of the plant are reproduced with absolute fidelity, the minuter parts being enlarged under the microscope as occasion requires.

The artists are provided with plants for study by specimens sent from America and cultivated in their own garden or in the large garden at Pilnitz. Some of the models of tropical plants and of those from the far West have been based on studies made by the younger Blaschke during recent journeys.

Up to the present time more than 100 orders, 300 genera and 500 species have been thus fully illustrated, the total number of glass specimens, including the analytical details, being more than 2500. The existing contract between the Blaschkas and the university calls for about 100 complete specimens annually for the next six years. These specimens are arranged to illustrate the systematic relations and the economic uses of the species, and in every case the principal peculiarities of the plant, especially its relations to its surroundings, are clearly brought out. All of the time of the artists is devoted to the preparation of specimens for the university.

Prof. Goodale exhibited the method of packing by which these extremely fragile specimens are prepared for transportation. Three of the models received in the last importation were unpacked before the audience. These specimens, like all of those in the collection, seem like fresh plants just taken from the field and have no suggestion of glass about them.

Dear Professor Goodale,

I recall very well, indeed, the pleasure of meeting you quite a number of years ago, and I am happy to be able to give you the information which you are in quest of.

This past Summer I spent about three months abroad, and among other things I visited Dresden for the purpose of disposing of my father's estate there. One afternoon Mrs. Jenkins and I motored out to see Mr. Blaschka at Hosterwitz and spent part of the afternoon with him. He showed us the work which he had been doing of late, and as I have seen the collection of his work at Harvard and, also, many of the specimens made by him in years gone by before they were shipped to America, I think I can say that the work he now has on hand is without question the most beautiful that he has ever produced. The way he has worked out the fertilization of flowers by bees is really remarkable. The man, it seems to me, is at the present time at the very height of his productive ability, and I hope he may continue to be of still further service to Harvard. During our conversation I asked him if I could be of any help or assistance to him in any way, and I got him to talk of his own affairs.

Of course, during the war, he had a very hard time, and I think his financial resources have been strained unduly. He spoke very feelingly of the Xmas gift which you sent him a year ago, and which I think was of enormous help to him. He, as you know, is a man with an extremely sensitive nature. I am not sure whether it was thru yourself or someone else that he received a report of a many in America who was engaged in glass production of flowers, etc. It was a clipping out from one of the American Daily papers, and somehow

it got into his mind that perhaps his work was not being appreciated in America as it should be, and that the time would come for him to be shelved. I tried to disabuse his mind of this, but he has a feeling that his work for Harvard is complete now, and that he must do something else to support himself. I asked him whether I could be of any service in putting myself into communication with you and find out for him what the situation was because he is such a blessed, impractical man when it comes to a question of finance, or looking out for his own bread and water. But he felt that he did not wish to intrude upon you thru me, and so I naturally have not communicated with you. I know that if you have any further work to be done he would be extremely grateful for it, and it would relieve his mind immensely.

I found that his old mother was still alive, but she was confined to her bed the day I was there. His wife is a very suitable companion for him, and I believe is proving a decided help to him.

For his own peace of mind I think it would be a great relief if you could give him any definite news as to whether he is to be further employed in the work he has done in the past, or whether it is actually the end of his connection. Also, he is so buoyed up by words of kindness and due appreciation of his work that any comments along that line would be balm to his aching heart. He has a very high regard for you, but with his extreme sensitiveness feels that something must have come up; that he has either hurt you or that you have lost interest in him. Dear friend Professor Dr. Goodale,-

These weks have been continued, very busy and so I am late in my reply to your letter of September 23. The glass-work for the Gramineae began regularly by the beginning of October and I first took at hand some species in the models of the natural size made from life, which later will be followed by the enlarged ones. The sprays are in certain cases a work of patience, but I have well established. My studies from the microscope were very attractive.

Lately I had a letter from Mr. Deane. He is suggesting again to undertake also models of Carex in fruit and kindly offering material for this. If you approve of it I can try a sample, provided I can insert it among this half year's work for the Gramineae. Years ago I had studied Carex in flower, but we filled to get specimens in fruit, and owing to this the species, also the models I had done, were undeterminable. The accuracy, demanded for the copying of grasses, is awful, but I do what possibly can be done with the unaided eye.

Indeed it is a pity how the value of the German Mark is getting down. Yesterday the Dollar was 300 Marks, so your draft of August would be worth today more than three times as much in paper Marks. Yes, our profiteers are very busily at work to use the situation. The prices of everything are jumping higher every day. In September I wanted to secure some hundred weights of Paraffin at the price of 750 Marks the hundred weight (100 pounds) (in the late times of peace 50 Marks) Last week I received only one, because, as the dealers said, it is scarce and much risen in price, 1000 Marks the hundred weight. This is the general practice, they retain the ware on purpose to profit more later. The Mark is considered only in value of some German pennies and it is wicked how the profiteers push the prices also of such inland matters that are not touched in any way by the rate of exchange, f.i. potatoes. My dear Miss Ware:

On the assumption that you have returned from your trip to Europe, I am sending this letter to your home-address.

Your letter of June twenty-first has been ofetn in my mind because of your suggestions regarding the very problematical status of my future relations to the Museum. I would have answered that letter long ago, if I had not been deterred from doing so by the length at which I should have had to write. It seemed wiser to await your return when a conference, should you desire one, would be a much better means than a lengthy letter of making my position clear.

The Museum has also been much in my mind because there seem to be many points of view regarding its future development. Aside from final detail details there is the very serious question of the policy to be adopted if you have any influence in shaping it. The financial details are truly elastic. At this time if only sufficient income is available to pay salaries, the question crops up, 'What will salaries purchase in the way of constructive progress? There is nothing really constructive in shifting the collections about to make them more attractive. But I imagine many changes might be suggested to somebody who found himself confronted by the necessity to make a show of activity.

Personally, I hope that the new Curator will be a museum-man with a strong leaning 60-ward economic botany, or shall we say, plants in the service of man? At heart Dr. Goodale was an economic botanist. A reading of his reports on the departments under his direction will prove this beyond any cloud of doubt. In fact, he expressed himself significantly for us in that report to President Eliot in which he wrote: It seems no longer wise to withhold a declaration of the policy which I advocate in regard to the

Museum of Economic Botany. It is my wish to make the collection an authoritative cabinet of type specimens to be described in an illustrated series of studies. Goodale did not live in good health long enough to make this ambitions project take definite shape. Perhaps his enthusiasm and optimism prompted the declaration of a hope before he had reached that point in the requirement of knowledge which made economic bot-any seem to great a subject for one man to handle.

As I think of the Museum I am a bit pleased by the thought that some young man might begin to carry through the task which Goodale hoped to begin. I would be pleased to co-operate with any candidate for the work, unofficially if neceassary, if my aid or advice were regarded worthy of consideration.

Just at present I do not believe that the question of a large endowment is very pressing. To me it seems that the policy for future research is important. To be perfectly frank with you, I am not sure that there is anybody in sight who would satisfy my tastes in the matter of the policy that should prevail.

This letter will give you, at last, my matured views regarding the Museum. To pick up in a few words what I have tried to say:

I. Salaries for a Curator and one or more assistants.

II. A policy that will carry through Dr. Goodales' strong interest in economic botany.

and I would add, lectures that should make the Museum of vital importance in the instruction offered to classes in botany in Harvard College.

Yours faithfully.

Odeus Compass.

## REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE TO VISIT THE BOTANICAL MUSEUM

To THE BOARD OF OVERSEERS OF HARVARD COLLEGE:—

The Committee appointed to visit the Botanical Museum have the honor of submitting herewith the following report:

It is with a very great sense of personal loss as well as with a realization of the great loss to the Museum that they have to announce the death of Professor Goodale.

From the very beginnings of the Museum he has been its manager and director. To him the late Alexander Agassiz gave permission to erect a central section of the University Museum for the use of the Botanical Department, provided the funds could be raised within a reasonable time. This he accomplished by his own efforts, and in the building thus provided in 1889 have been housed the Botanical laboratories, Museum and class-rooms.

Originally consisting of a few selected specimens, illustrating economic plants and their products with some morphological material, it now comprises the wonderful Ware collection of glass flowers, to which arrangements have recently been made to add some of the grasses and sedges of America, as well as a large and beautifully mounted collection illustrating the economic uses of plants.

This idea of illustrating flowers by glass models was entirely original with Professor Goodale, and was always regarded by him one of his most important contributions to the facilities for their study and appreciation provided by the Botanical Department.

These collections have all been obtained and arranged by Professor Goodale, and have had for many years his constant care and attention, assisted only by his faithful and devoted helper, Mr. Bierweiler. All of this work has been done through the personal efforts and friends of Professor Goodale without any financial aid from the University. There are few instances of more unselfish devotion to the College than his, and we believe that he would ask no greater monument than the continued growth and development of the work to which so much of his life was given.

The responsibility for the continued support of the Museum now rests with the University, and your Committee believe it of sufficient importance to receive your favorable consideration.

The Ware collection of glass models above referred to, which will be completed on the delivery of the grasses and sedges, has always been one of the most interesting exhibits that the University Museum has had to offer, and has attracted a large number of visitors every year to Cambridge.

There is, besides the collection of the economic products of plants now made readily and permanently accessible and capable of much greater use for teaching purposes than it has been given credit for, the Agassiz collection of fossil plants and a printing plant in which the labels and pamphlets of the Department are prepared.

The Farlow collection of cryptogams is another important department of the Museum, but for the sake of better accommodations it has recently been transferred to the old Divinity School Library, where it is under the direction of Professor Roland Thaxter, Emeritus Professor of Cryptogamic Botany.

The Museum is not only a valuable department in itself, but if properly coordinated with the other Botanical Department, your Committee believe that its value would be materially enhanced.

Your Committee hope that the valuable and poorly paid services of Mr. Bierweiler may be given some recognition by the University, and that in the selection of a Curator the Corporation will try to secure some one who will not only carry out the general policies which Professor Goodale has inaugurated, but will further be able to increase the influence of the Museum by bringing it into closer relations with the other Botanical departments of the University.

My dear Miss Ware:

Although substantial endowment is necessary to assure the proper and dignified maintenance of the Botanical Museum, the question arises, is the development of the Museum beyond its present scope, sufficiently desirable to warrant our efforts being turned toward the amassing of a truly influential endowment? The answer to this question is found to be forcefully in the affirmative if we admit that research in economic botany is well worth while and if we discover that its importance will become greater and greater as civilization advances. We may take the view that Harvard University owes to the community opportunities for research in that branch of botany which is sufficient to important in our daily life to take up nine tenths of the advertising space in the street-cars. From Cadun ointment to Quinley cigars, economic botany flashes its importance from advertisements, everywhere. And yet, in Harvard University we are not giving to the matter that attention which it deserves. To develop this branch of botany properly, we need a large endowment.

I remember well, my feelings of despair when a student came to my laboratory at the Bussey Institution, to carry on research work in economic botany for the Doctor of Science degrees. There were many interesting problems to attack, but to begin on any of them meant the expenditure of money. I advised this student to make a comprehensive survey at Caffeine from the 1980s.

My dear Miss Ware:

Although substantial endowment is necessary to assure the proper and dignified maintenance of the Botanical Museum, the question arises, is the development of the Museum beyond its present scope, sufficiently desirable to warrant our efforts being turned toward the amassing of a truly influential endowment? The answer to this question is found to be forcefully in the affirmative if we admit that research in economic botany is well worth while and if we discover that its importance will become greater and greater as civilization advances. We may take the view that Harvard University owes to the community opportunities for research in that branch of botany which is sufficiently important in our daily life to take up nine tenths of the advertising space in the street-cars. From Cadum ointment to Quinacy cigars, economic botany flashes its importance from advertisements, everywhere. And yet, in Harvard University we are not giving to the matter that attention which it deserves. To develop this branch of botany properly, we need a large endowment.

I remember well, my feelings of despair when a student came to my laboratory at the Bussey Institution, to carry on research work in economic botany for the Doctor of Science degree. There were many interesting problems to attack, but to begin on any of them meant the expenditure of money. I advised this student to make a comprehensive survey of coffee from the botanical, historical and economic sides. He amassed a valuable

collection of data; wrote a creditable dissertation and passed the oral examination held by the Faculty of Applied Biology. On the strength of his Doctor's Degree he obtained, at once, a position in a western university. To-day he informed me that the MacMillan Company would publish the dissertation in book form, (some five hundred pages), and that as a result of this publication, he was in line for an assistant-professorship in a New York university at an attractive salary.

My understanding is, that there was no other laboratory in the United States where this young man could have obtained the data for his work and obtained the Doctor of Science degree in economic botany.

I think this one example will make clear to you that our Museum should expand beyond its present scope and offer attractive advantages to students who may wish to enrich the literature devoted to the plants that make the world go round, or get away for a while from the counting of chromosomes.

I realize that in my time there is little hope of seeing the Botanical Museum properly endowed, and in submitting the enclosed prospectus, I do so with the feeling that we will do well if only a small beginning is made. I have arranged under seven headings in the order of their pressing importance the needs of the Museum.

Yours faithfully,

Oakes Ames.

THE PRESSING NEEDS OF THE BOTANICAL MUSEUM.

1. It is proposed to use room 21a, for the library of economic botany and for the office and laboratory of the Curator. Before the books and furniture which are now at the Bussey Institution are transferred to Cambridge, it will be necessary to freshen the room with paint and to install electric lights. At present this room is without lights. The plumbing should be improved. The preparation of room 21a for the purposes described is, perhaps, the most pressing need at the present time.

2. There is now a large accumulation of unbound periodicals and pamphlets in room 20. This accumulation should be catalogued, bound and given shelf room.

3. Room 20 should be painted and supplied with electric lights.

It is proposed to use this room for research work in economic botany and for the students in Botany 15. This room should be ready for use not later than September, 1924.

4. It is proposed to use the balcony on the fourth floor of the Museum for the exhibition, and preservation of the economic collections. If it proves possible to move the cases from the entry hall on the third floor to the balcony, then the glass models now in the balcony will be combined with the main collection on the third floor. This change will free for the exhibits and working collection of economic products, a large space and will bring the library, laboratories and collections of economic products in juxtaposition.

5. It will be necessary in the near future to increase the Museum staff. The work of labelling, caring for models and the routine duties connected with the exhibits, require the entire time of one assistant. When students are admitted to the Museum for the

course in economic botany, a research assistant should be added

to the staff, to keep the current literature of economic botany

extracted and catalogued, and to act as botanical assistant to

the Curator.

and the labor of all kinds that a museum creates, and at the same

Exploration is as necessary for the understanding of ethnobotany as it is for the understanding of ethnology. We still depend on exploration for the elucidation of economic botany. D. Cases. My Dear Miss Ware:

At last the red-tape has been measured to the end and I come to you with a set of figures. I propose to limit the painting job to the 3d floor hallway because a more extensive undertaking would necessitate the aid of the U.S. Treasury or some other well-nigh inexhaustible source of money. The first figures received were beyond reason. Then I called for the cost of the different items. I give them here: Walls, $175. Coiling $150. Metal stair rails and risors $150. (The complete stairway covering all floors, $275.)

The ceiling is really very good.

I think the beams are attractive in their natural color. The stairs need not be done now, although in the future it will add greatly to the appearance of the Museum if they are painted in metallic green. If we attempt to include the stairs, then I think the Mineralogical Museum should pay the cost as the stairs are of importance to the exhibition-rooms to which one gains access by passing through the Bot-anical Museum hallway on the third and fourth floors. If we attempt to paint the stairs in any other color than the painful one they now exhibit, Mr. Henshaw may object on the ground that certain types of improvement in one department of the Museum cheapens the other parts. This is one reason why Mr. Henshaw is not sure that he wants us to paint the doors of the exhibition room to resombe aged metal. I agree with Mr. Henshaw, of course, but I hope to win him over to my point of view.

I think you will agree with me that we can go ahead with the painting of the walls at $175. The Museum can pay half of this, if you care to assume the other half. As to the ceiling, you may not agree with me. If you feel that the ceiling and walls should be painted, then it will be best to paint

the ceiling first. Mr. Burk is insistent as to this. The stairs can be delayed until we find out what the Mineralogical Museum and Mr. Henshaw think wise.

Rooms 20 and 21a are nearly completed. I am sure that you will be pleased at the results. Next week I hope to begin to move some of my laboratory furniture from Forest Hills to Cambridge. I am so much interested in this part of the game that I am mentally comparable to a child.

Louis has repaired all of the models except the Asclepias with the gargantuan bees. He did the best work possible on this, but I stopped him in the middle of his task, because the results would not warrant the labor. I am afraid that this model must be regarded a total loss.

Yours faithfully,

My dear Miss Ware:

I have received a most satisfactory letter

from Blaschka. He understands the situation perfectly and seems interested in the new proposals. When we meet again I shall show you his letter.

Work at the Museum is progressing after a fashion, which means in simple terms that one mess gives rise to another. The recent past has not been a bed of roses for the Curator. But details should be held for a talk.

The metal cases from the Bussey have arrived and are nearly in readiness to be arranged. I wish I could have kept a record of the number of tons of material I have moved from one place to another in the short time that I have been attempting to swing my new job.

At last I have matured my plans for the future development of the Museum. The fossils will occupy the second floor coming just above the cryptogams. Then will come the higher plants, now living, arranged systematically or in their relation to the environment. Then on the fifth floor the economic application of plants will receive attention. The present economic room on the third floor will be the precolumbian room,

with the products of the eastern hemisphere on one side, and the

products of the western hemisphere on the other side. In the small

central section, plants of doubtful geographical origin such as the

coco-nut and a few others will hold sway. I think this undertaking

will be most instructive, and be useful for the teachers of the schools

who make constant use of the Museum. To complete the program may

take years, but the beginnings are in hand.

Yours faithfully,

My dear Miss Ware:

John Waugh has arrived with material for the construction of the new cases. His promptness rather took my breath away, as I had been led to believe that he would need much time in which to secure the necessary stock. I am afraid that you are not ready to go on with the new cases at this time. If my understanding is right, undoubtedly I can weather the storm in some way. Please be very frank about this, and if you wish me to do so, I shall attempt to raise funds to meet Wauh's bill when it is presented.

We are about ready to start on the distribution of the models. In fact, I think the autumn will see the collection properly named and distributed.

Biology 1 students are making daily use of the Museum and my economic library seems to be doing good work at last. This is what I hoped for and I am very well satisfied.

To-day a great strangling fig arrived from Horticultural Hall. This specimen was brought from Florida by Mr. Burrage for the great Orchid Show.

Attendance at the Museum is on the increase. About five thousand for May so far.

I lectured for half an hour to a class from one of the high schools. This experiment led me to believe that we might arrange for such lectures as a regular service of the Museum. It is a simple matter to arrange an attractive exhibit on one of the tables and then touch the high-spots of economic botany. We might make friends for the Museum in this way if we could from time to time get small groups of interested people to come to the laboratory lecture-room. Parents and children might come together in small groups.

# Three hundred and fifty-five Commonwealth Avenue

Prof. Wheeler is making use of the insect models in connection with his course on entomology. This course is given on the fifth floor, in the laboratories assigned to the Bussgy Institution.

A vacancy is about to be made by the removal of Mr. Webster from the Visiting Committee. Mr. Webster is no longer eligible for reappointment. I think Victor M. Cutter, Vice President of the United Fruit Company might be a good man for the Committee. If you have any suggestions as to other candidates, I wish you would give them to me.

I saw Dr. Gage on Monday. He did not think that another meeting of the Committee would be necessary until next year.

I have already had enquiries about my course in economic botany. It would seem that the Biology 1 students who come to my laboratory to read economic subjects in connection with their written reports have their interest stimulated in the broader significance of Botany and wish to go farther in the subject.

Please excuse this very scrappy and badly written letter. I find that my mind becomes weary by night time.

My last orchid book was awarded a gold medal.

Yours faithfully,

Qakes Amess

My dear Miss Ware:

I realized when I wrote to you last, that the news of John Waugh's activities would disturb your equanimity. When I gave the order for the new cases, I was under the impression that John would be busy in Philadelphia for the greater part of the summer. What I thought, however, has nothing to do with the present situation. It is before me and I intend to master it. I have studied my budget carefully and I think I can see money enough to pay John's bill without having Mr. Mead take me to task. So much for that. It is the very least of my burdens.

The heaviosy burden in sight for me to carry is one that will

fill your soul with pure joy. I have just passed what might be termed an exclamatory morning. Something like witnessing a show of fireworks that begins with a

few Roman candles, and erds with bombs that explode in succession and make the

most stical onlooker give audible expression to his feelings. At eleven o'clock

I not Professor Weston by appointment and together we went through the models of

the cryptogams. For the first time I saw this collection as a whole. The experience

both for Weston and myself was not only delightful but overwhelming. We agreed

that the necessity for exhibiting these models is a pressing one and we both felt

impatience for the day to arrive when the collection can be made available for

students and the public. But here comes the burden. A burden that is best expressed

in terms of space. We have not the cases in which to exhibit the cryptogams. Even

with the addition that Waugh is now making to our case equipment, we shall fall

far short of space enough for them. Then again, we must do some experimenting

with tablets, because Weston agrees with me that the delicate cell structures

constructed of white glass must be contrasted with black. It will take our combined

ingenuity to make the best of a beautiful collection. Weston gave vent to his

feelings by saying, "And these have been rotting here all these years!"

Our meeting this morning was for the purpose of weeding out

the poorer models. I think we came to the end of our task with less than four models in the discard. To exhibit the models that were accepted would take more case-room than is now given over to the insect-models. Yes, much more. And that is a serious discovery. It may mean a row of tower cases along the wall to the left of the stairs on the third floor where the ferns are now in position. If we are able to mass the cryptogams as a unit, I am sure that we shall have an exhibit that will call for three stars in Baedoker.

I agree with you as to Dr. Cage's attitude toward another meeting this year. My impression is that he not aware of the importance of the work the Museum is doing for the University and for the public. How to awaken the interest of the Committee is a matter for serious consideration. I have enough faith in the Museum to give my time to it, and it seems to me that my efforts should meet with something more substantial than thanks or praise. I have reached that point in life where thanks and praise mean very little. I am more interested in results of a substantial and helpful kind. You and Miss Minne have made me very happy, but I am not willing to impose on you good people.

I find that the glass models are regarded by a captious critic of by gone days, as one of the really great achievements of Dr. Goodale's administration. This man has come to see that a museum must first attract and then educate. As Dr. Moore of the Missouri Botanic Garden put it to me at the Orchid Show on May 10th, "The glass models are the most attractive bait that exists anywhere against which to build a botanical museum." This change of front on the part of both artists makes no anxious to have the whole collection of models tell its story at last. I expect to leave for North Easton by the end of next week. Through the summer I shall make trippin' to the Museum to keep the work moving smoothly.

Yours with best wishes,

355 Commonwealth Avenue, Boston, Mass.

My dear Dr. Gage:

I have made a rough estimate of the additional funds necessary to meet the cost of the work to be done at the Museum in 1924-25, if we are to continue to make progress.

Painting and lighting are really pressing needs as the Museum is now visited by over one hundred thousand visitors during the year. The need for paint is apparent to anybody who cares about the impression Harvard University makes on students and the public.

We have in storage a magnificent collection of models which should be made available at once for students of cryptogamic botany. Therefore, I urge you to consider means by which we can build new cases this summer.

Our unbound volumes of botanical periodicals

that should be within the reach of students' represent the accumulation of many years. Books of reference in paper covers soon become seriously damaged and parts of volumes are easily lost if left unbound.

In winter afternoons the halls of the Museum are dangerously dark. It is surely necessary to have halls lighted if students are to use the Museum after four o'clock in December and

January.

Book-shelves should be built for Room 20 to take care of volumes that are now in storage in the basement.

The catalogue of trade-names of economic plants

and the catalogue of extracts from current literature of economic

betany has fallen far behind the times through the lack of clerical

assistance. A library assistant for the year 1924-25 will be necessary

if we are not to fall hopelessly behind in a most important part

of the routine work of the Museum.

For two months I have given the services of one of my assistants; I have installed electric lights in my laboratories; I have renewed the plumbing and painted the walls and ceilings of rooms 20 and 21a; at great expense for moving and installation I have placed my library of economic botany at the command of students. But, unaided, I cannot keep abreast work that remains to done or meet the demands of students and the public.

My dear Miss Ware:

This morning Dr. Wheeler and I were discussing some means of illustrating with models, the relations of insects to plants other than for pollination. This led to the suggestion that we ought to have a model maker on the spot. Of course, under the present conditions this is impossible, and the suggestion is only interesting. Then, Dr. Wheeler referred to the models at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and remarked that the man who makes the models for that museum is, in his estimation, more skilful than Blaschka. I find it hard to believe this, but I shall go to the New York Museum in the near future to check up. Perhaps, if you are in New York in the near future, it might be well for you to take the time to examine the models there from a comparative point of view.

Just at this time I am rendered unsettled in my mind by an invitation to go with Ham Rice and Dr. Strong to the Amazon this summer. Dr. Strong wishes to have me along to study poisonous plants. #### THE BOTANICAL MUSEUM

To the President of the University:

Sir, - As Curator, I have the honor to submit the following report on the progress and condition of the Botanical Museum. This report covers the academic year beginning July 1, 1923, but my appointment as Curator was not

made until October 29, 1923.

The Botanical Museum since its foundation in 1888, has been entirely dependent on annual gifts to meet expenses of maintenance. On January 30, 1924, this undesirable situation was changed by a gift of fifty thousand dollars, received from an anonymous donor, to establish the George Lincoln Goodale Fund. In April, 1924, an additional gift of fifty thousand dollars was received from Miss Susan Minns, to establish the Mary Hancock Fund, the income to be used for economic botany and the purchase of books for the library of the Museum.

As it seemed advisable to ascertain what use is made of the Botanical Museum by the public, a record of the number of visitors who enter the exhibition rooms was begun toward the middle of February. This record falls short by about seven months of covering the year included in this report. It indicates that over one hundred thousand visitors come to the Museum annually and that the maximum exceeds twenty-two thousand with a daily maximum of one thousand seven hundred and eighty-seven.

$ ^{*} $ From February 14 - October 31, the record showed 114,338 visitors.

I take this opportunity to direct your attention to the use of the collections by neighboring colleges and schools. Supervised classes come to us for the purpose of studying plant relationships by means of the glass models. We welcome this evidence of the value of the models in education and offer to visiting teachers every facility at our command.

Early in 1924, preparations were made to bring the Museum into closer contact with students in the University, through a course of study in economic botany. This course will be offered next year, as Botany 15, by the Department of Biology. It will emphasize the influence that plants have had on human history and social progress. Two rooms on the fourth floor have been thoroughly renovated; supplied with electric lights and made ready for classes. To facilitate the work of instruction, the Curator transferred his library of economic botany from the Bussey Institution to the Museum and installed it in Room 21A, where it is now available for use.

By a rearrangement of the exhibition cases and with the addition of new cases presented by Miss Mary Lee, it became possible to concentrate the collection of Blaschka glass models on the third floor and to convert the gallery on the fourth floor into a repository for our large representation of botanical raw products. This change has many advantages and brings the working material close to the research laboratories and library.

The Ware collection of Blaschka glass models is being thoroughly reorganized as a systematic unit. Because of limited

space in the main exhibition room, recently acquired

models had been placed on temporary deposit in different parts of the building, far distant from their proper position in botanical sequence. It is hoped that before the end of next year all of the models will be brought

together and the purpose fulfilled for which they were

originally acquired.

Dr. Goodale, in his last report on the Botanical Museum (1920-21) directed attention to the completion of the contract under which the Ware Collection of glass models of plants had been made. Miss Mary Lee Ware, who had generously borne the entire financial burden of this contract for many years, gave her consent to a plan for continuing to secure for the Museum, the product of Mr. Blaschka's studio, provided this could be done without any additional expense being imposed on her. Dr. Goodale with the financial aid of several friends of the Museum, entered into a new contract with Mr. Blaschka. It was agreed that any models made under the new contract should constitute a distinct unit that might be exhibited apart from the Ware Collection in a special room on the fourth floor of the Museum. After careful consideration, it was agreed that Mr. Blaschka should devote his scientific knowledge and artistic skill to the preparation of a series of grasses and sedges. In October, 1923, the first shipment arrived. In the opinion of the Curator, the new models although remarkable for their beauty and extraordinary accuracy, seemed to repeat the monotonous habit of grasses in a

way that would fail to appeal to the public, while for

specialists the collection if completed could hardly

take the place of herbarium specimens. After a conference

with the Museum Committee and with the friends of the

Museum who had helped to secure Mr. Blaschka's services, it

was agreed that the remaining years of the new contract

should be devoted to special models that would be serviceable in the study and teaching of economic botany. Miss

Ware then made known her desire to resume business relations with Mr. Blaschka and to take over the new contract.

This was made possible by conference with everybody interested. Miss Ware then consented to add the models of grasses to the collection given to Harvard University as a

memorial to her father. By this very satisfactory arrangement, the Ware Collection will contain all of Mr. Blaschka's models of plants and the necessity for segregating any

part of his product will be eliminated.

On the reasonable assumption that a museum must attract before it can educate, our museum is in a fortunate position. We possess, in the Blaschka mobs what is regarded as the most attractive botanical exhibit to be found in any museum. Around these models which draw to us over one hundred thousand visitors annually, we are able to reflect exhibits that indicate the broad influence of botany and emphasize the importance of plants in the past history of mankind and in the life of the modern community. In the final analysis the models constitute the best means we have to attract and stimulate the attention of the public and to awaken a substantial interest in botanical science.

During the year numerous additions were made to the representation of botanical raw products. Some of these additions were secured by the Curator in Yucatan, Hon. duras, Costa Rica and Panama. Many specimens sent in for identification by travellers and business houses have been added to the permanent collection. A fragment of the Washington Elm, presented to the University by the City of Cambridge, has been placed on exhibition in the economic room on the third floor among the species of woods. From the Canton Christian College a well-come series of botanical raw products and dried plants has been received. In this series are many species new to science, some of them being of extraordinary importance in connection with Chinese ethnobotany.

Museum exhibits should be erected against a background of facts, therefore a large part of the work done in a museum should be in the realm of research. As it is undesirable, however, to label every specimen with a complete record of its history, or with exhaustive data regarding its scientific or commercial importance, all of the evidence secured through research, should be accessibly filed in catalogues that are always open to students and properly qualified investigators.

A beginning has been made toward a permanent record of every specimen in the Museum. By a file number it is proposed to indicate the whereabouts of data connected with each specimen so that students will be enabled to obtain the information they need. When the task of building up

this record is well under way, it will be possible to find prompt answers to many of the questions that are put to us and to direct attention to sources of useful knowledge. In other words, the Museum will become a treasury of classified facts illustrated by an extensive series of properly identified specimens and accurate models.

A vast amount of labor confronts the Curator. This is true, because a mass of material awaits determination and systematic distribution. The necessity for prompt attention to this work is pressing. Valuable specimens now on temporary deposit in storage cases are exposed to deterioration influences. In spite of constant vigilance, inroads of insects and mice are reducing the value of these specimens and are tending to render them useless. It is dis-couraging to live with the thought that this condition is to be long lasting. A research assistant, a man qualified to do museum work of a highly technical type, is urgently needed on the Museum staff, and funds from which to pay an attractive salary should be provided as soon as possible.

In the reorganization of the collections and in administrative work, the services of Louis Bierweiler, have been of immeasurable value. Mr. Bierweiler's long training in the handling of the glass models, his knowledge of the technique of mounting models on plaster tablets and his familiarity with the traditions of the Museum have made the work of the Curator delightfully simple.

GEORGE LINCOLN GOODALE (1839-1923).

Fellow in Class II, Section 2, 1874.

George Lincoln Goodale, Fisher Professor Emeritus of Natural History and Honorary Curator of the Botanical Museum of Harvard University, died in Cambridge on April 12, 1923, in the eighty-fourth year of his age. He was born in Saco, Maine, on August 3, 1839, the son of Stephen Lincoln Goodale and Prudence Aiken (Nourse) Goodale.

From Amherst College he received the A.B. degree in 1860 and six years later the honorary degree of Master of Arts. From 1863 to 1866 he practised medicine in Portland, Maine, having received, in 1863, the M.D. degree from Harvard.

At the age of thirty-three he began his active connection with Harvard University, having come there from Bowdoin College, where he had held a professorship in the natural sciences from 1868 to 1872. At Harvard he began his term of service as lecturer on vegetable physiology and instructor in botany. In 1873 he was appointed assistant professor and five years later was made full professor.

From October 6, 1879 to July 31, 1909 he was Director of the Botanic Garden of Harvard University, a position which brought him in close contact with influential men of Boston and afforded an opportunity for the development of his administrative powers. The Botanic Garden in the early days of Goodale's directorship was the botanical center of the University. Until the classes became too large for the lecture room, which had a capacity of about eighty students, it was at the Botanic Garden that laboratory work was done and instruction in botany was given. It was at the Garden, also, that the collections of botanical specimens, which were later transferred to the University Museum, were assembled, treasured and exhibited. Shortly after his appointment to the directorship of the Garden, Goodale found that the growth and progress of his department depended on substantial additions to the sources of income. He immediately set about the task of enlisting the sympathies of men who were interested in horticulture and who would help him with advice or money. Soon delapidated structures were giving place to new buildings and the invested funds of the Garden were being increased by

gifts. So that in addition to the eminent services rendered as an inspiring teacher through thirty-seven years, Goodale was stimulating that development of botany which will always make his term of office memorable in the annals of Harvard University.

During these years, Goodale built up a strong department in the botanical sciences. Early in his career he foresaw the necessity for a well-equipped botanical museum which would arouse the interest of the public and serve as a valuable aid in the courses offered to students. With untiring energy he labored toward the fulfillment of an ideal. His reports to the President of the University emphasized again and again the need of additional space for the rapidly growing classes and for the collections of specimens that were crowding the limited accommodations at the Garden. With the museum in his mind and before its erection was assured, he visited Leopold and Rudolph Blaschka at their home in Dresden for the purpose of inducing them to make models in glass of plants and parts of flowers. Only after repeated refusals did the Blaschkas consent to construct the desired models and enter into the contract which resulted in the now famous collection of glass flowers that is one of the most popular and instructive attractions of the museums maintained by Harvard University.

In 1890–91 he went round the world, visiting the leading botanical establishments of Ceylon, Java, Straits Settlements, Australia and Japan, forming valuable contracts with scientific men and enriching his store of scientific knowledge. The influence of this trip to the tropics was far-reaching. As a result of his observations of the vast importance of botany in the commercial enterprises of the tropics, he determined to make the exhibitions of the new museum reveal the part that plants have played in the service of man.

Of the two great interests of Goodale's life, the museum which he built and a proposed work on economic botany for which he had assembled many critical specimens, the second was interrupted by administrative duties and by failing health. His interest in economic botany was very deep. He was convinced that this branch of his subject was one of the most important for modern times. In his report to the president of the University, for the years 1889-90, he set forth his plan as follows: "It seems no longer wise to withhold a declaration of the policy which I advocate in regard to the Museum of

Economic Botany. It is my wish to make the collection an authoritative cabinet of type specimens to be described in an illustrated series of studies." To those of us who knew the scope of the project and who recognized Goodale's exceptional capacity for its fulfillment, it must ever be a source of disappointment that he did not live to carry it through and fill a gap in botanical literature that still exists.

Although Goodale was the author of many papers on plant physiology and economic botany, and brought out in 1882 his Wild Flowers of America for which Isaac Sprague prepared the colored plates, it is his Physiological Botany, published in 1885, which stands as his most significant contribution to his subject. This work was prepared for the series of university textbooks which Asa Gray had planned as a complete course of botanical study. Goodale's textbook of Physiological Botany was a painstaking production which abounds in helpful citations and is characterized by straightforward exposition. This textbook was the result of profound knowledge and crystallized, as it were, the experiences he had gained in opening up for American students the subject of plant physiology as understood at the time by leaders in botanical thought. L. H. Bailey, in a biographical sketch of Goodale published in the twenty-fifth volume of Rhodora, writes of this work as follows: "It is a solid substantial book that students of the present day would do well to understand." It was only in the last two decades of the nineteenth century that physiological botany began to take its place in the development of science in America. Goodale was among the leaders in this field and his textbook stands as a creditable monument to the part he took in the introduction of physiological botany to American colleges. He hoped to issue a second edition of this textbook. With this aim in view he accumulated a vast amount of material, but he became so much occupied with other work that a second edition never appeared.

His desire to increase the influence of Harvard University in the realm of science led to the establishment of a tropical garden and experiment station in Cuba, near the city of Cienfuegos. He succeeded in interesting Mr. E. F. Atkins of Boston in this enterprise, which is now one of the important branches of Harvard's establishments for research in applied biology and a repository of an extensive collection of economic plants. In this garden originated the first seedlings of the sugar cane to be raised in Cuba. Toward the end of

his life he had the satisfaction of knowing that a liberal endowment had been secured to perpetuate the work he had started.

It was my good fortune to accompany Goodale to Cuba when in 1899 he made his first visit to the proposed site of the new garden. It was on this trip that I began to know the sterling character of the man and to form that deep affection for him which increased with the passing of time. As I think back through the years in which it was my privilege, both as student and colleague, to know Goodale, the outstanding characteristics of his personality were delightful courtesy toward all who had dealings with him; consummate tact in handling the delicate situations which confronted him as head of a university department, and punctilious integrity in his business transactions with the many good friends who helped him to bear the burdens of building up the Botanic Garden and the Botanical Museum.

It was as a charming and finished lecturer, I think, that Goodale stands out most prominently in the memory of those who attended his courses in Harvard College. As a teacher he was forceful and concise. His demonstrations were fascinating and skillful. Combined with unique gifts of clear thinking and careful exposition were a commanding presence and a convincing manner. If, putting aside Goodale's achievements which stand as concrete evidence of his capacity, we judge him simply through his influential contacts with students during a long life as an inspiring teacher, we must arrive at the conclusion that his position among scientific men is a commanding one and that he made an indelible impression on the history of botany and botanical thought in America.

From 1888 to 1909 Goodale was Fisher Professor of Natural History. In 1909, when he retired from active teaching, he was made Fisher Professor Emeritus and Honorary Curator of the Botanical Museum. After his retirement he lived quietly at his home at 5 Berkeley Street, Cambridge. Here he converted a room into a laboratory and carried on his researches in museum technique. His visits to the Museum grew less and less frequent as his bodily strength waned, but to the end the Museum was uppermost in his daily thoughts and what might be its future was the only disturbing question in his mind.

Beyond the University his work was well known. In 1889 he was vice-president of the Biological Section of the Association for the

Advancement of Science. In 1890–91 he was president of the Association. In 1890 he received the LL.D. degree from Amherst College. In 1894 Bowdoin and in 1896 Princeton University honored him with similar degrees. He was an honorary fellow of the New York Academy of Sciences and of the Royal Society of New Zealand, and member of the Philosophical Society and National Academy of Sciences. He held membership in many botanical societies and was in attendance at the International Botanical Congress held in Brussels in 1910.

In 1866 he married Henrietta Juel Hobson who survives him, as do his two sons, Dr. Joseph Lincoln Goodale of Boston and Francis G. Goodale of Weston, Mass.

My dear Miss Ware,

I am off for Ormond, Florida, tomorrow night, urged to go by the Family. I shall be away until April 1st, unless something hastens my return. Work at the Museum is progressing slowly, but there is nothing amiss and with Louis faithfully plodding along with Hubbard's assistance one day a week, the routine work will not need my guidance.

At a dinner of the Committee on botany, it was agreed that any drive for biology should include an attempt to raise substantial funds for the Botanical Museum. A big drive is in prospect, as new laboratories are needed. I directed the attention of the Committee to the folly of building more space for biological laboratories if that meant the removal from the Museum of the men who now use the second and fifth floors. This would mean that value-able space would become wasted as the Botanical Museum cannot develop additional space without a substantial increase in endowment. It was agreed that the Botanical Museum must develop in the future and that the entire Botanical section should be made available for museum purposes. I was de-lighted with this decision as it really seems probable that our interests will be merged with the interests of general biology in any effort to secure funds. Of course it will take time to accomplish definitive results, but that the Museum is to be considered as a beneficiary of any drive, we have much to cheer our souls.

Yours faithfully,

(signed) Oakes Ames.

# Botany 15. Outlines of Economic Botany. Laboratory work. (September 29 - November 15).

##### THE SEED

“He discovered that wild plants could be grown at will, and herds of wild animals could be tamed and kept in a state of captivity. From hunter he became shepherd and farmer, abandoned his roaming hand-to-mouth mode of life, and, assured of ample means of subsistence, became attached to the soil; settled communities thus arose, organized societies became possible, and all the advantages which accrue from subdivision of labor” Sollas, ANCIENT HUNTERS p. 117.

1. Examine the seeds of twenty economic plants; after arranging them in botanical sequence, sketch and describe the seeds examined. Study internal structure. In connection with your studies, read and understand, Chapter VIII, A TEXT-BOOK OF BOTANY FOR COLLEGES (Ganong); Chapters V & VI, BOTANY FOR AGRICULTURAL STUDENTS (Martin); Chapters I & II, THE ORIGIN OF CULTIVATED PLANTS (DeCandolle).

2. Examine the contents of the trays in the collection of economic plants and study the products of the Gramineae.

a. Make notes on the origin of wheat, maize, rice, oats, barley and rye. (Cf. THE ORIGIN OF CULTIVATED PLANTS).

3. Write a thesis (1,000 words) on the economic significance of the seed in the development of civilization. Treat the subject so that the above quotation from Sollas, ANCIENT HUNTERS will be explained in full detail.

Reading: THE CHILDREN OF THE SUN, Chapters II, III, XXV, & XXVI (Perry); Chapter IV & pp. 567-571 in Sollas, ANCIENT HUNTERS; THE GOLDEN BOUGH, (Frazer), abridged edition, with the aid of the Index read passages that treat of ceremonies connected with wheat, maize, rice, barley and oats.

“The acquisition of farinaceous food by cultivation must be regarded as one of the greatest events in human experience.”

# BIOLOGY 1 (Botany)

Suggestions for Study. No. 2.

December 1925.

1. Secondary thickening takes place in stems and roots. Explain what is meant by secondary thickening.

2. Just as the terminal meristem is carried out by the growing root or stem tip, so the cambium ring is carried farther and farther away from the center of the stem by the growing wood. Explain.

3. The cambium adds cells on both sides. In what way does this type of growth differ from that of the growing tip of the stem?

4. What are the products of the division of cambial cells?

5. The cambium is that layer which gives rise to the timbers of commerce. Explain.

6. In a growing stem the youngest layers of wood are outermost and the youngest layers of phloem are innermost. Explain.

7. What relation does the cambium bear to the art of grafting and to the healing of wounds in woody plants?

8. Study carefully the cross section of a typical dicotyledonous stem (cf. textbook), paying attention to the epidermis, cork, cork-cambium, cortex, pith, phloem (bast), xylem, cambium, medullary rays (wood rays). What part does cambial tissue take in the formation of these tissues? What is the function of the tissues named? Can you draw from memory a cross section of a typical dicotyledonous stem? You should be able to do this.

9. How does a typical monocotyledonous stem differ from a typical dicotyledonous stem?

10. What do you understand by the terms: open bundle, closed bundle?

11. Why is the chestnut-bark disease which attacks only the outer bark, cortex and bast, so fatal to chestnut trees?

12. Why does girdling result in the death of a tree?

13. Explain the formation of annual rings in the wood of an oak tree.

14. If a nail is driven into a tree five feet above the ground, will the nail be carried higher as growth of the stem continues?

15. How does the fibro-vascular system of a typical stem differ from the fibro-vascular system of a typical root?

16. Study carefully the functions of phloem, xylem and medullary rays.

17. Read the chapter on the root in one of the textbooks.

18. Study the different theories regarding the ascent of sap.

19. What is the economic significance of alkaloids and glucosides? Read the articles on these substances in the Encyclopædia Britannica.

20. Pages 23-35 in Sinnott should be read carefully. (Study figs. 13 and 19.)

Study carefully the models that show the relation of insects to flowers. Make notes regarding the different types of floral mechanism associated with pollination. The models are in the cases to the left of the stairway on the third floor of the Botanical Museum.

My dear Miss Ware:

Your welcome letter of the 11th, December came in this morning. Aside from the references to your continued depression of health your letter was most gratifying. Mr. Blaschka's letter gave me the assurances I have so much wanted.

I have been at the Museum today to make plans for the changes that are to be made in the Economic Room. If I can find the money, I am going to alter the objectionable tower cases and free the middle of the room from obstructions to the view. John Waugh was with me for an hour estimating costs and as he feels sure that he can do the work for about one thousand dollars, I am inclined to push ahead with my plans. My reason for hurrying developments are found in my desire to co-operate with Barbour. Substantial changes are being made in the zoological division and it is necessary that the transition between our rooms and the zoological rooms shall be made psychologically attractive. At present there is no call to the visitor to leave our restful exhibition rooms and pass into the dark, for-bidding precincts of zoology. If the Economic Room is made enticing, the step to Zoology will come naturally and the Museum will be made more influential.

On the mineralogogical side, vast changes are being made. So, with my neighbors working to excel my quarters, it is natural that I should feel an irresistable inclination to keep a step in the lead.

I wrote a long letter to you some time ago. I am afraid you failed to receive it.

The University has started work to floor over the open space in the gallery. When this work is finished I shall have a delightful and spacious laboratory, informal lecture room, and students' collection for my museum work in Botany 15. The models have been protected from threats of injury by means of a temporary floor and special coverings.

Really, things are moving rapidly. And each change means greater efficiency and more happiness.

It is needless to tell you that I am giving most of my time to administrative work. But I have many irons in the fire and I hope to get down to productive work again before the winterreends.

Blanche joins me in sending to you the best wishes we have, not only for your health, but for your happiness in the attractive surroundings you have chosen for your winter rest.

Faithfully yours,

Qakes Cannes

My dear Miss Ware.

It seems ages ago since my last letter to you was written, but there has been very little to write about except my own troubles. In February I went on a trip to the West Indies, planning to spend some time in Jamaica with Blanche for the purpose of assembling material for the Museum. When we reached Havana, word came that Pauline was very ill and needed her mother. There was nothing to do except obey the calls of home. Blanche made a quick get away and I went on with the baggage making the round trip via the Canal Zone and Costa Rica. The day I reached home I came down with grip and had to remain in bed for days. Recovery was slow after I got up and to make myself fit for duty, I went to Arizona and remained there among desert things until the first of May was coming along. Then I returned to Boston and began to pick up my work at the Museum and elsewhere. I have been busy almost every hour of the day since May first and while I have thought of you and the things that are of interest to you, I have really had no time in which to write, unless I used my stenographer, and that is not according to Hoyle.

Work on the Economic Room is progressing slowoy. It takes time to prepare the exhibits and to arrange them after they are prepared. But I am sure that the new arrangement will please you and be more useful.

Your letter about amber thrilled me of course, because I have a

dee, interest in this material and have a strong desire to assemble as many examples

as possible of the different types including the rare Sicilian variety. What we already have makes a brave showing, but it is chiefly Baltic and a bit monotonous

from the point of view of a Museum collection. If you have succeeded in picking up some additions, your efforts will bring joy to my soul.

You have a very wrong idea of the book I have had prepared for the elucidation of the glass models. This book has very little to do with the Blaschkas and the history of the collection. It is rather a catalogue raisonné and not only deals with every species represented but uses each species as an excuse for bringing in allied species that are of economic importance. It is a book which will appeal to the student and will be a distinct addition to botanical literature. Once published it will make the Ware Collection a basis for the wider study of plants in the service of man. I am in no hurry to issue the book as I want first to receive the fruit models and include them. This is a wise delay.

You wrote that you would be willing to help the Museum in its 1927-28 budget. Of course you have done more than your share already and it seems unkind to look to you for additional funds. If you feel that you want to help, any assistance received before June 30th will be pure gold. I want the Committee to help this year as I have been far too liberal in running up bills against our slender and dadly inadequate income. I am afraid however that the members of the Committee, excepting the ever kind and interested Miss Minne, will not contribute very generously.

The collection of fossils displayed on the third floor landing, has been the source of much favorable comment and the palaeontologists from the other side of the Museum are coming to us for opportunities to study fossil plants. Each fossil has been provided with a lacquer red stand and the bright color helps the general appearance vastly.

We have nearly arrived at the million mark for the Arboretum Fund. I have added one full professor to the staff with the title of Professor of Forest Pathology and now I am after a first rank plant breeder. Mr. Lowell is standing back of my enthusiasm and my one hope is that my efforts will please him.

Miss Waro/3. May 22, '28.

Rockefeller Foundation, has its meeting this week and will consider whether or not to grant three or four millions for Harvard Biology. With several million dollars we could make a brave showing in matters biological. And I should have a feeling that I had had my finger in the pie.

Louis informed me a day or so ago that there was a rumor about that you might not return home this summer. I sincerely hope that there is no foundation for such a situation. Vacation is coming along, and when it arrives, I can settle down to a little research and turn out some of the long delayed papers I have had in mind.

My dear Miss Ware:

I was lingering in the Museum this afternoon, after everybody else had gone, when your delightful cablegram arrived with the news about Sicilian amber. It seemed almost as if some kind fate had held me at my post after hours to be on hand to receive your communication. As I am working assidually among the resins in preparation for the reopening of the Museum on June 18th, the news about the work you have done fitted in delightfully with the trend of my thoughts.

Perhaps I should explain that the extensive operations in the M.C.Z. to repaint the cases and walls, to improve the lighting and to rearrange the collections, resulted in a closing of the doors to the public. I took advantage of this situation to refinish the Economic Room and to install a more creditable collection of specimens than the old one was. Louis and I have been busy with the mounting and preparation of specimens and now we are hurrying to have the room ready for the formal opening of the Museum on the 18th. The research that goes into such an undertaking is astounding. If you want to find out how little you know about common things, try to arrange a collection of economic

plant products with the loud pedal on accuracy. Nothing must be taken on faith. Every bit of information must be checked and every specimen must be correctly identified.

You will be interested in the Blaschka models of sea animals that have been brought to light and placed on exhibition in the M.C.Z. They are really delightful.

It seems unkind to burden you with another letter so soon after my last one was written, but the arrival of your cablegram explains my industry.

Blanche desires to be remembered to you and I

join in her good wishes.

Faithfully yours,

Oakes Arnes

Miss Mary Lee Ware, Florence, Italy.
