My dear Miss Ware:

The summer is drawing to an end and there are rumblings in the air that indicate the approach of university drudgery. The storm breaks on the 24th and from that date on I shall be at the mercy of students and at the beck and call of University Hall. Always at this time of year when the country begins to take on an attractive aspect and there is a feeling of cosiness in the library by the autumn fireside, I wonder why I allow myself to be submerged in work that calls me to the city and to the duties of a college professor. Is such a life worth while for a fellow who has reached the age of fifty-four years and has thirty years of service to his credit?

This is about the first opportunity I have had to write a letter as

since August 4th. On that day I went to the poid to swim. It was/hot as some famous

place is supposed to be and Blanche and I wanted a cooling experience. There is a

concrete dam at the pond and into the concrete(when I built the dam) I let in a large

ringbolt to serve as means of holding boats. Grasping this ringbolt in my right

hand I jumped into the water from a sitting position. Everything came free except the

terminal phalange of my middle finger. I was held by that, the finger being jammed

between the ring and the concrete. At trip to the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital followed and for four weeks I have been nursing a very sad looking finger.

Painters have been busy in the Museum this summer painting the walls, ceilings and doors of all the stair landings, You would hardly recognize the place. And all this is at no expense to the Museum. We are getting a little attention at last without begging for it or paying for it.

Mr. Sussmann has not put in an appearance yet, but I am looking for a letter from him almost any day now in which news of his return will be mentioned. I am most anxious to have the Sicilian amber in hand when I begin my lectures on the resinous exudations of plants.

The Museum has been very much crowded this summer. I have never before seen so many people enter the doors. In August the sight-seeing busses seemed to arrive hourly throughout the day.

Your letter of August third reached me in good time. My failure to reply to it promptly has been accounted for. Please send to me a long letter regarding your visit to Dresden in September. I shall be anxious for news of Blaschka's work and eager to know just when the next shipment will be sent away.

Very faithfully yours,

Oakie Amus

Miss Mary Lee Ware,

Dear Professor Ames,

It seemed easiest in this very long letter to separate the de-scription of the glass work itself from the more personal part, so I have done this and now will tell you the rest to the best of my ability. I have been out alone, half an hour by auto, three of the four times that I have been to Hosterwitz and have passed the whole afternoon, a long one, looking first at the models, it took two afternoons to see them, then looking over the work room and its contents, being shown all the great improvements made by them in the house since his marriage, and finally accepting their hospitality of tea and delicious cakes, a far better arrangement than the old time one of a whole day and two solid meals! Both Mr. and Mrs. Blaschka received me most cordially at the little garden gate and we looked at each other to see what time had done, and that first day I was daunted to see what seemed a little old man, with not strong legs, very rounded, stooping shoulders and a very white face. He must have dropped nearly two inches in height, his hands are somewhat out of shape from rheumatism and were very trembling. However, to at once correct that impression, I came to the conclusion that it was partly or largely excitement at seeing me again and anxiety as to what I should say to the models. When I was ready to leave and said aufwidersehn he drew himself up with quiet dignity and said, "Well, Miss Ware, are you satisfied?" I said, "Yes, Mr. Blaschka, I am more than satisfied and I do not see how anyone could feel otherwise." He looked intensely relieved at once, and the next time I went out his colour had returned and Miss Niklason thought he looked well and strong, barring the stoop which I suppose is inevitable with such sedentary work.

His eyes are simply marvelous, piercing, and yesterday in painting the leaf he worked most of the time without glasses, and he is seventy-one! He speaks freely of his age, of the work which can possibly still

be accomplished and that he is the only one in the world who can do

it, which I think is true. You would never find another man who combined the scientific knowledge of many years' study in plant and animal

life; the study of glass, its component parts and its possibilities,

not merely book knowledge but derived from experiment as well, together

with the power of concentration, mental and moral, the artistic ideal

as a load-star which has enabled him to forego everything called pleasure except his wife. She is sweet and devoted to his ideal too, has

softened and broadened him, and so humanized him that he is much better

fitted to come in contact with the world than the Rudolph Blaschka who

came to America in 1896. He is just as modest and absolutely honorable

as he ever was, but he has a sense of his own worth, his own unusual

force of intellect and character, and there is everything to justify

that. I asked him one day whether he was still applied to for models to

be kept in Germany and he said, "Oh, yes"; the Prof. Neymann, to whom he

went for something at your suggestion, asked why he would not give them

some of his work? I asked what he replied? "Oh," he said, "I told him

that I worked for Harvard University, that I was a man of absolute

honor, I made no change and was satisfied."

I found that Sunday was his one day of rest and suspecting, from previous knowledge, that he was not taking time for air and exercise and perhaps working late in the evening, I extracted the information that lately he had taken little or no time for fresh air and had been working evenings, sometimes till midnight. I remonstrated vigorously and told him he must not do so, but he only said Prof. Ames wanted the models and tho't him very slow--that it was impossible for him to do such work any faster, that no man could. It had evidently worried him much and I had to work hard to reassure him that you would not feel so if you knew him and could see him at work, that I would explain to you and that he

absolutely must stop evening work and get the necessary air and relaxation to keep himself in good condition. I told him also that you

were only impatient to complete the exhibition cases in the half, and

that even if the finished models were not completed in group form

as yet, that he had so many finished, that he better send those at once

before the bad weather of winter. It will be quite enough for you to

take care of at once, he only regrets that each group of fungus, etc.

is not complete, but he has had to do them as he could and when he could

get the specimens, etc. Dependent more or less on seasons, weather

etc. He hopes to send off by the middle of the month, I think it will

be nearer the end, but perhaps not, some twenty-five models, sprays or

plants with their sections, etc. I think this includes all the pears except the blossoms, and strawberries, whether more I do not know. Apples,

plums, apricots, peaches, cherries, are largely finished ready for the

sprays, and the leaves largely ready to paint, exquisite fruit blossoms

ready for the branches (that part of the pears too will not come). He

thinks the rest will be ready for shipment in the spring, some thirty

more. The fruits are not so beautiful to look at as the flowers are,

but they are marvellous and how our man can do it hour after hour, putting in the gossamer veinlets, or all the myriad little brown dots and

irregular brown patches to the Beurres, passes my understanding,

you would say that years could not do it, or a lifetime. If he hurried

or worked quickly he would be insane.

I sat and watched his movements as he worked, the table is covered not only with implements but with trays of leaves, formed but not colored, bottles in which he could stand the glass stems with leaves while drying or cooling, specimens of fungus covered fruit or dried leaves for use as guides (for the most part he could study them without glasses) bottles with powdered glass as needed, and saucers for the enamel paints of

powdered glass. In spite of the slightly unsteady hand his movements were quiet, deft, soft in laying down or taking up where speed or a miscalculated movement might ruin the work of hours. It is breathless to watch.

The first afternoon I saw the pears in every stage of disease, sometimes the fruit only, sometimes leaves and branch too. The moulds were wonderful and I think you will be delighted with them all, but, of course, I know nothing of fungus, etc. He had magnified 250 times a section of mould which comes on bread--remarkable. The strawberries were fascinating, plants, fruit and moulds, also the result of frosts on the developing fruit. The apples etc. were good, the peaches in their present stage of development seemed to me less so, but the final varnish was not yet on and they all looked rather glassy. It all leaves you breathless that anyone can and will do such work. Mr. B's head and bearing are very expressive and I wished I could catch a photograph of his profile as he stood for a few moments, a plaque with a model lying on it held in both hands, and his whole expression of absorbed, concentrated study was worth keeping, had it been possible. His own garden is small but full of fruit trees from which he gets some of his material for work and more he gets from large fruit orchards near by. He also has books on the fungus, mushrooms, and is looking forward eagerly to the work for Prof. Weston. He says the lamellae will be very difficult but that he can make them. In view of his advancing years and the uncertainty of health, I would suggest that Professor Weston makes a list of those subjects which he wants most, which are most important, although on account of weather, season, and materials it may be impossible for Mr. Blaschka to follow the sequence exactly, still it would be a guide.

It troubles me very much that he and his wife cannot come over to see his life's work now that you have them so beautifully arranged and he looks so eager and pathetic when I describe the misuse of scene. They are very simple and unaffected, dignified, and I hope sometime that I can manage it if I can only keep well when I come home. It seems cruel not to but of course they could not travel on what they have in our country. I find that he did not lose all his investments in real estate or mortgages, etc. but all government investments. One change in the character of his work and consequently in the time necessary to accomplish results since I was last here is very noteworthy. Then he bought most of his glass and was beginning to make some, and his finish was in paint. Now he makes himself a large part of the glass and all the enamels, which he powders himself to use as paint, which he considers practically indestructible except by force--that if we could come back in a thousand years we should find form and color as today. He has dozens and dozens of little bottles with colored powders and little boxes labeled with colored enamels which he makes himself and powders for paint. The colored enamels are beautiful and fascinating. Some pieces he exposed on his roof or under the eaves for over a year, winter and summer, and it had not changed in any way!

I have been housed for two days with a slight cold but otherwise am feeling so much stronger. Tomorrow I go out for my last visit and stay to supper. I will keep this open for any last items. I am dreadfully sorry that you hurt your finger so badly and hope that it is well before you begin work. I had no idea that you were fifty-five and as to lectures, if I could do it as well as you can, I should adore hearing myself speak! You really ought to have a gallery for ladies, exempt from exams! I have had much bad news from home this summer, the death of my cousin, Miss Morse, came very close; notwithstanding I have been

I have been showing the results of the year and a half of Dr. Gigholi's work. He has been patient and I have tried to be. Now when the rheumatism is finished off, I hope to return to my native land. Alas, I have had to give up the poultry plant. Too many grain bills to carry, I could not send at once to Bucharest, but have done so now and asked them to send you a colored drawing of the big piece in case some generous soul should feel inspired. I have not heard from them, post connections there are slow, but you will doubtless receive it like the other by Government pouch. I hope Sussman turns up duly and shall be most anxious to hear what you think of the pieces of amber.

October 6 - My last visit to Hosterwitz was made most happily, Miss Niklason went with me and enjoys it as much as I do. Supper was excellent and informal and pleasant, and I regaled them with all the Museum gossip that I could think up. Mr. Blaschka did some leaf work again and Miss N. felt just as I do, that it is a great experience to watch that man at work, his whole head and hands are a study and he worked until it was almost dark without turning his electric light on. She also felt that the work was enough to wear anyone's nerves to madness. The confined position and closed room being a part of it.

I told him that he must stop evening work with late hours, and must get out for air and exercise for a time every day, that it was not fair to his wife or himself and that it made no difference how long it took to complete the models and that I should tell you I had said so. She is 45 only and perfectly devoted to him but nobody can keep fresh without a little fun. She said they used to come in sometimes when first married but it was long since. I tried to get them in to supper and the opera but unfortunately had to give it up on account of a cold. I know it has given him a fresh start and fresh courage to see me, and I am sure that I accomplished what I came for in the five times that I have been out there.

I wish I could run in oftener, for so few realize what he is doing and their lives are necessarily secluded tho' evidently on friendly terms with their neighbors. I shall be very anxious to know if you receive this safely but please do not feel obliged to write when you are tired and busy--much as I always enjoy your letters.

The Ontario apple is superb! Please remember me to Louis and with always most cordial greetings to you and Mrs. Ames

Very sincerely yrs.

Signed - Mary Lee Ware

This is strictly speaking a "long letter." I did not dare to have it typed so near Kosterwitz.

The painting of one peach leaf affected by fungus:

Each leaf is formed of clear white glass, pulled and worked by simple instruments in the flame, and each point on the margin must be pulled out separately from the hot glass, to make the crenate edge to the degree characteristic of the species.

The leaf remains attached to the long stem of glass, 12 inches

perhaps, from which it has sprung, until the cloring is completed and

annealed, when it is separated and the fine wire, necessary for the

permanent stem, is attached, coated with glass and the leaf is ready

to be attached to the branch; this last I could not see as it took from

about three till half after five to color three leaves and put in ribs

and veins to one, then anneal it.

A green leaf would be made of green glass, the method of coloring would be the same for both.

The colors are made in powdered glass mixed (moistened) with a few drops of turpentine or ..... carefully administered to the powder in little china saucers and mixed with a fine camel's hair brush, which, finely pointed in the moist paint, administers the color to the leaf also.

The undulations of the leaf have already been made in the white glass so the buff or yellow paint is brushed on perfectly smooth, several times and before it has wholly dried, a strip of pointed whale bone marks the main vein down the centre, and the pointed quill of one of the camel's hair brushes is used to mark each rib. Then a little of the powdered glass is dusted on by a camel's hair brush, shaken off and dusted on again in spots. If the leaf is partially healthy faintly colored green glass is applied to the healthy parts. The camel's hair brushes, larger of finer, then are drawn down the vein and the ribs over and over and again to give the necessary strength to the vein of size and color and to emphasize, as needed, the ribs. Many, many times the delicate tip of

the brush only would touch tiny spots on the lines which needed a thought more of color.

Then with the most delicate touch of the finest pointed brush the cob-web veins were drawn in to the texture of the leaf, between and at the end of each rib, like fine etching perhaps, but almost more delicate, like a breath rather than a touch and absolutely exhausting to nerves and patience to continue, till the leaf was completed and ready to anneal.

Two wicks in two cups of parafine were started in front of him and the flames driven at each other horizontally, his face, nosé and mouth, protected by a piece of asbestos.

He took the glass stem in his left hand and inserted the leaf be-tween the flames, where they just met. The tip first, moving it constantly after it had become red hot till the whole leaf was finished. He keeps his right hand free to manipulate the apparatus or to handle, guide the leaf if necessary, as he turns and twists it in the flame. Not infrequently the annealing starts a flaw in the glass and the leaf breaks so that many are necessary to complete a branch. He says that there is far more nervous strain and it is far slower and more difficult to make a leaf than to make flowers. The use of annealing the powdered glass instead of simply pointing, makes the process slower and more dangerous, but the final result much more permanent, in fact, the color cannot change and nothing but violence can destroy the model. He can scratch and scrape a leaf with his penknife and it leaves not a mark.

There is additional labor which I did not see. Annealing leaves the glass glittering and shining, and that look he destroys by the application of a certain varnish, and he applies this to the flowers after stamens and pistils are set.

I think he said that he no longer paints at all except with the powdered colored glass which he can anneal, and another complication is that $ \underline{\text{only a certain kind of glass}} $ can be used for the foundation glass, as the others spring and destroy the coat of anneal. All this is new since I was here nearly twenty years ago. He told me then that he had not at all come to the end of the possibilities of glass work and these latest models show it to have been true.

The fruits are made over a fine but very strong wire and he says

in some of them there is as much as a $ 1/2 $ lb of glass. That process I

have not seen, most of the fruits I think are done and quantities of

leaves on their glass stems ready for painting are in drawers. Some

of the fruits are blown but very few, for he dislikes blowing glass

and the fruits are like eggshells, too perishable for transport. There

are one or two sprays however with fruit of both kinds on them and you

would never know the difference in their looks.

The large Beurre pears and large apples looked to me hopeless to transport for no wire could stay on them and no paper hold against their weight but he is confident that by pinning the stalk firmly above the fruit stem it will never move. He has ordered a very heavy weight for the card board boxes.

Wany Lee Ware

North Easton, Massachusetts, July 15th, 1929.

My dear Miss Ware:

You must have thought it strange that I should postpone so long a letter which you have had every right to expect would be written promptly, but the truth is I have been very idle since coming here for the summer. I found the let-down from University work very complete after I gave way to it and in a few short days I realized that I had had about enough of nagging duties. I don't mean to imply that a letter to you ever takes the form of anything nagging, that would be untrue and unkind. But once I felt myself beyond the reach of University Hall and the Laboratory and was conscious of the fact that a vacation was taking from Cambridge the people who make demands on an administrative officer, I felt a complete relief from the expectation of the usual crop of letters, application papers to be signed and requests for appointments. And then came the complete realization of the strain that goes hand in hand with a diversified task.

The models arrived in very good condition. There on or two minor injuries, but on the whole there was a welcome lack of damage. The shipment came through much better than the last one and Loitis soon had the broken pieces in place. For the present I have the collection in my large laboratory in the cases that have been empty for so long. There I can study them and begin the labor of preparing the labels. At first this seemed simple enough, that is the writing of names etc., but as I realized the vast difference between the new models and the old and became aware that they must justify themselves, I decided to make the labels reveal the fascinating historical

background of our north temperate fruits of the Rosaceae. Here is an opportunity to offer some valuable information and to impress the casual visitor with the romance of the origin and development of our cultivated plahts.

The strawberries are really charming and I think they equal the earlier work of Rudolph Blaschka, but there are indications that the finer touch has gone and that age is beginning to have its influence. What else can we expect? A man reaches his best long before the world is ready to cease to expect miracles from him and then, unless there is a recrudescence of genius, excellence gives way to mediocrity. There is a rise and fall in ability and in enthusiasm and an uneven quality in the product becomes painfully evident to those who must be critics. Don't take these remarks to mean that I am disappointed in the models of fruits. I am not disappointed. But some of the cross-sections of peaches (there are only two or three) are really below the standard of ten years ago.

There is one thing about the nature of the new models that will give a distinct addition to the educational value of the Ware collection. That one thing is that we can bring out in a separate unit the history of the introduction, improvement and value of the products of a single family of plants. It will take careful research and careful planning of labels to do this in a way that will be worthy of the Museum, but I intend to begin the preliminary work this summer. In any event I do not intend to place the new models on exhibition until the labels are completed and the scheme of arrangement definitely decided on.

The routine work at the Museum goes forward day

by day and I think we are making progress. Louis has been busy giving a number to every specimen in the collection and entering all in-forming data on cards. Unless some such system is adopted there is sure to be ambiguity prevalent for those who come after us. It is surprising how quickly the history of a specimen evaporates and how soon a valuable type becomes worthless because neglect has isolated it from its data. All of this means conscientious labor on the part of somebody and Louis is admirably conscientious.

We have been having a most extraordinary summer here. Very little rain and a series of nearly perfect days. It has been hot at times, but the average temperature must have been below normal. Cool nights have been the rule and an abundance of pure sunshine has attended us during the daylight hours. One strange thing is the good condition of the gardens. The crops seem to be perfectly adapted to the weather.

We remained in Boston later than usual this year, as Blanche had to finish two portaits of Dartmouth professors before Commencement. Now we are on vacation and spend much time at golf.

I am addressing this letter to your bankers as I am not sure that you will be in Florence at this season.

With all good wishes,

Faithfully yours,

Oaken Corner

Miss Mary Lee Ware.

Copy of letter to Mr. Blaschka.

My dear Mr. Blaschka:

It was a great pleasure to receive your good letter of March 1st yesterday, for except for the letter to Mr. Goodale, I had no means of knowing whether you had received my letter of early January. I was greatly interested to know from Mr. Goodale's letters just what was your financial status, as I know that you had Rosaceas sprays in hand, as also the completion of the diseases. I know that the work is what Prof. Ames desired and I had also in mind possible plant tissues for Prof. Weston, who is so delighted with the early cryptogams which you sent over. He told me recently that he sends the students to study them constantly. I am very thankful to say now, that my affairs are adjusting themselves and that I can and have sent to Mr. Goodale five hundred dollars, one half only of what was due to you on Jan. 1st. The remaining half I will pay when I can, dependent on my next quarter's income and on sickness here.

I hope to be able to continue at probably irregular intervals through the time, the two years, that you say you have intended to work, for I deeply appreciate all that you have done for Harvard University, and especially the spirit in which you have carried on the beautiful models. In this rushing material, mechanical world the idealist is hard to find, at least such an idealist as you have shown yourself to be, and it pained me to think that I had got to bring our work to an end.

The financial crisis through which we have just passed is the most valuable experience which could have shaken our people into realization of their folly and stupidity, we all feel that Roosevelt has taken the reins in hand with courage and apparent ability, though the reforms are in the main what Hoover tried to establish. His hands were tied but some credit is due to him and the fine spirit with which he has tried to cooperate with his successor.

We feel very hopeful that conditions here will gradually improve, but the help asked for unemployment is great and there has been a terrible amount of sickness among the ordinarily well-to-do people. Together with the drop in incomes has come old age and illness to some who must always be my first care, before any other pledge whatsoever, for this reason I cannot be absolutely definite in promises to others, but I do sincerely hope to be able to continue the regular payments to you, during the two years that you would like to work, then I think it must cease. You will have fully done your duty and Harvard will be fully satisfied. For the blossoms of the fruit-Rosaceae there is just at present full occasion to take up renewed studies direct from nature as the fruit-trees are now splendidly in bloom this year and I shall finish some sprays over this summer. generation of some Ascomycetes f.i. of Monilia and Fusicladicum, of which the first form of the disease, the Comidia-form is so amply represented. This is the plan I had taken into consideration in order to complete this remarkable fruit-series, and I am endeavoured to finish this last consignment to be able to send it over to the Museum next year. We live in a very interesting, tense period of history. The national revolution has got the victory in Germany, and they hope that the crisis shall be improved by this, I specially have followed eagerly the reports from America during April concerning the American standard. I had been much afraid of the consequences if America gives up the gold-standard, and now it has taken place. You have got inflation, but I hope America has also learned from our experience how far they dare go. I shall write him this week and request him to send me a draft for July of same amount as in March, to secure me during my working. Dear Cousin Mary:

Thank you for your use of June 19th enclosing check to my order as agent for $1000. to cover the semi-annual payment for Mr. Blaschka.

A serious complication has arisen with reference to Mr. Blaschka's funds in my hands. I have hoped for weeks that I could come to see you and discuss this with you. I have been unable to do so, however, partly by reason of the death of Robert Homans and the consequent additional work which fell to my lot at the office, and partly because I have been suffering from a carbuncle. I am fairly well now but am going off with Margaret for the greater part of next week to get a little rest and change. When I return I ought to be really on my feet again and I shall hope that you will find it convenient to let me drive up to Rindge and call on you, or even invite myself to luncheon. I will write or telephone and find out whether it would be all right for you to have me do so.

In brief, the complication regarding Mr. Blaschka is

this: The Hitler Government has passed a law which can be translated as the "Fatherland-Betrayal-Statute". It forbids Germans to invest money in foreign countries. Mr. Blaschka dutifully reported the investments in my hands, and is now confronted by threats of severe

Miss Mary L. Ware.

penalties unless the funds are immediately converted into German

Marks and transmitted to the Reichsbank. They will be placed to

his credit there and he will not lose his savings altogether, but

he has had to pay back-taxes, fines, etc. amounting to about $1000.

and the present ruinous rate of exchange will mean the shrinkage of

perhaps one-third in the savings which he had relied on for his old

age and that of Mrs. Blaschka.

Mr. Blaschka's very guarded letter seems to me to contain a hint that he would like to have me refuse to comply, on the ground that you and Harvard University are interested in this fund as a provision for his old age, and that I cannot transmit it to him without your consent. I do not dare to write freely to him for fear of getting him into trouble, but I have not yet sold his investments and am waiting for a reply to a carefully worded letter which I sent him recently, which I hope will elicit his true wishes in the light of the situation which confronts him.

On further reflection I am going to deposit your present check for $1000. in a special account in the name of Hill, Barlow & Homans, Attorneys, instead of in Mr. Blaschka's account. Perhaps in this way it can be saved as an emergency fund in this country for his use in time of need, even if all the rest of his funds have to be sent to Germany.

I will tell you more of this when I see you, which I hope will be soon.

Affectionately yours,

Taucus Tootala

##### My dear Parents!

Yesterday evening at 7:30, I arrived safely in Bremen. The trip was quite pleasant especially up until Hanover. During the trip I did not have to leave the wagon, which I boarded in Dresden, at all. On the last stretches between Hanover and Bremen our wagon shook worse than a stagecoach on a rocky country road, which according to some of my fellow travelers was supposedly because our wagon was one of the last. Despite the fact that one could hardly balance oneself on one's seat, I found the experience extraordinarily nerve-strengthening and fun. I spent the night very comfortable in the Central Hotel, a first rate hotel right across the street from the train station. In the house next door is the comptoir of our agent Ehrhorn, Emden & Mayer, which I just visited. These same men are providing me with all my travel issues (documents). So tomorrow morning I am traveling on the steamship "Saale" in the first cabin with a ticket priced at 400 Marks. I can stay in Bremen, and another night here, because the northern German Lloyd has contracted to send each passenger on each departing steamship by an extra train to the ship for free. This train, which I will also be using, departs tomorrow morning at 8:45 for Bremerhaven. In the past few days there supposedly have been severe storms in the north that are now calming down so we are hoping that the time of our trip is well-times. The weather here in Bremen (and during our whole trip) is mild and damp like in Hosterwitz: no sign of snow or ice, everywhere green fields and sown fields. It is now time dear parents to send you my last words of goodbye, with the repeated hope for a happy and healthy reunion, I remain with loving greetings and kisses.

Your loving son,

Rudolf

##### My dearest Parents!

Today I finally found the time to end and a chance to tell you more thoroughly about my experiences and it's my dearest wish and hope that these lines find you in the best of health. The two hour ride in the train to Nordenham was not very interesting. Just flat fisherman's huts around the coast along of the Weser, but it was an unusual singular feeling as the train stopped and right next to us was the huge hull of the Saale. The long hours transferring the passenger's luggage went quickly enough because we were taking a tour of the exterior and interior of the ship. The interior is amazingly luxuriously outfitted [ausgestattet]. Every comfort is there that anyone could ever wish for. The cabins are always arranged for two people with two beds, one over another, a sofa, a mirror, a washbasin and with tape electric lighting all night from 6 in the evening to 9 in the morning. Luckily I have gotten a very nice place, cabin #200, right next to the lounge and since there are many passengers, the bed above me is vacant. I have the whole cabin, a beautiful little room of 12' in length & 8' in width with every comfort all for myself. At exactly 2 o'clock yesterday afternoon we lifted anchor and the huge ship moved proudly toward the north. The hope that the southwesterly storm will have run itself out, was not completely fulfilled, because the closer we got to the North Sea the stronger the wind became. When I took a walk on the deck at 5 o'clock the sea was so high that the waves which had just recently been dwarfed by the ship almost reached the deck. Despite the heavy rocking of the ship the deck was full of passengers who thought they could escape seasickness by standing in the fresh air and wind. But you notice right away that nobody felt very good. I then immediately returned to the quiet lounge because I had made the acquaintance of an older American lady, Mrs. Perkins from Sioux City on the train and I wanted to practice my English conversation with her. The lady also seems to enjoy it. After 5 o'clock the wind kept blowing even harder and the rocking of the ship kept getting stronger. Because I was also starting to feel queasy and light-headed, I took father's advice and didn't participate in the 6 o'clock supper. And then in the 7th hour, a storm came upon us which made me worried all night. I lay as if in a swing, at first my head and then by legs over the other, on and on, I kept listening to the noise of the waves crash over the deck of the ship. I didn't sleep at all until the week hours of the morning. I didn't really get terribly seasick because I'm pretty used to the rocking, but the dizziness and the unusual in my throat haven't quite disappeared yet. Towards morning the storm quieted down a little bit so I could sleep for a few hours. And now, with Dover in sight, and as we're about to reach the canal, there is just a refreshing breeze blowing which really isn't too unpleasant. The other passengers didn't make it through the stormy night that well, only a very few came to breakfast. All in all there aren't very many passengers on the Saale. In the cabin there are a lot of Americans, and between the decks [steerage?] there are a lot of Russian Jews and Hungarian Slovaks as you can see from the enclosed passenger list. I'm going to send this letter from South Hampton, which we should reach this afternoon, and by the time you read it I should be on the ocean. The wakeful hours I spent last night, I sweetened with thoughts of you my sweet parents. Of

how you're doing and whether you are healthy and happy. It will be a long time before I can have the joy of receiving a letter from you. I will write to you again as soon as I arrive in America because the ship is just now beginning to rock violently again. I'm going to have to close my letter with the hope that everything will turn out for the best.

With the most heartfelt greetings and kisses

Your Rudolf.

On board "Saale" 12 Feb. 1892

My dear Parents,

I hope that my letter (and the box) from the third of the month both arrived in one piece. Since our arrival today in America will be soon, I decided to write about my other experiences on my trip. Just hours after I finished my last letter to you, the weather changed entirely. The wind became progressively weaker and the weather was so clear that the English coasts, which soon came into view, were significantly lit by the golden sun. Around three o'clock in the afternoon we past Dover; it was so close that one could see every house and the smallest details in the landscape. With that, our happy fog-free passage through the dreaded canal was guaranteed for the night. It was approximately 8 o'clock in the evening when we reached Southampton. Although we anchored at a significant distance from the coast, one could see the outline of the coast and the harbor by the starry night. The mail and passengers were quickly dropped off and picked up by a small steamboat so that we soon continued on our voyage. But the joy of a smooth and quiet trip to America was not granted to us. Already on the next morning a strong rocking of the ship informed us that we could expect stormy seas again. The farther out into the ocean we traveled the more violent the waves became. And then the days came which would make my memory of my first ocean trip unforgettable and highly interesting. On Thursday afternoon this ship began to sway and dip so much that it was hardly possible to stand, to sit or to lie down. The waves continually became wilder and battered the ship causing a terrible din (noise). Every 2 or 3 minutes continually a monstrously huge wave would crash over the ship in a thunderous boom so that it became dark in my room where I have a window, and the air pressure took my breath away. In these moments our ship seemed to be entirely crushed by the waves, but every time it lifted itself high above the water again, while each time the big box would shake itself out like a soaked poodle, which during the long duration of the storm did not by any means cause pleasant feelings. During the day the traffic on the upper promenade deck, despite some quiet moments, was almost impossible. But on the lower decks it was actually life threatening because there was every danger of being washed out to sea. At night I could barely sleep because I had to constantly hold on to the bed otherwise I would be thrown with vehemently thrown onto the sofa across the room. This stormy sea continued without interruption for four days - only Thursday until Monday. During this time I did not once lose my good mood, because I enjoy experiencing myself that which my dear father described so exactly and well. At the beginning, during the first stormy weather in the North Sea, I saw many sailing ships and small steamboats that were thrown under the waves like nutshells. At the time I would not have thought that the violence of the elements could also have such an effect on a huge box like our ship. The sea became quieter and since then we've had inconsistent but quite pleasant weather. We had fog only on one single morning on the whole trip during which the whole time the large steam (fog) horn was in use. The closer we come to America the brighter and fresher the weather becomes. During the whole trip my health was quite satisfactory. I was never really seasick. In the beginning my appetite was diminished which was caused by a strong dryness of the mouth and in the throat that I already had since my departure from home. Since using beverages also didn't help, I unfortunately put off using our old home remedy, sodium bicarbonate, and I had the ship's doctor give me a portion of it. The remedy helped wonderfully at the time and I developed a hearty appetite so that I was able to partake in every mealtime. It's probably also caused by unfamiliarity, having to acclimate to the unfamiliar times and foods. During the whole trip my thoughts were with you dear parents and whether you are doing well. At night I always dreamed about home. On

board there is a small (Doberman) pincher, the captain's dog whose appearance reminds me of my little Bella. As I am writing these lines, the coast of America is coming into view. The weather is most beautiful and bright, just a little cold. The (Lootse?) has come on board ship. Just now the lighthouse of Fire Island has come into view. In about an hour we will be at Sandy Hook, then a few more hours we will be in New York. I will take this letter to the post office when I arrive in New York. So dear parents, dearest greetings and kisses from America.

From your,

Rudolf

My dear Parents!

...already at Sandy Hook, as the officials came on board, a letter from Prof. Goodale was brought to me, wherein he informed me that I would be awaited at the exit of the customs house in Hoboken by Mr. Ganong, an Instructor and Assistant of Botany from Cambridge, the same gentleman we had to deal with in matters of our models.

While no attention to the clothes and everything else in the trunk, a higher official was summoned to whom I explained the purpose of everything. Finally I was shown to an office where the superintendent asked "are you Professor of Botany" which I affirmed. Finally it was "all right," and I signed a declaration and got everything in free [of customs tax]. I now met Mr. Ganong, a slim man of my height and about my age with a black mustache, who concerned himself about me in the most friendly manner and hired a hackney-carriage that brought us to Central Station in New York. The night train at 11 pm took us (in the sleeping car) to Boston, where we arrived at 7am in the morning....

...directly to Prof. Goodale's house, where I was welcomed in the most friendly manner by Mr. and Mrs. Goodale, who had received notice by telegraph about my arrival. Prof. Goodale assigned me a nice 2-windowed room with the remark that I should feel like at home, and I was introduced to the family with the highest "payment of respect." The house is on 67 Sparks Street and is a villa consisting of 3 houses (also called a corner-block) – all of Cambridge is built like villas – and Prof. Goodale has rented the whole house for himself alone. My room is on the 2nd floor with a wide free view...

The first walk yesterday morning led us to the Museum. Nearly all the buildings in Cambridge and Boston are the same, erected of red brick and making an extraordinary grand impression. Iron stairs [in the museum] lead to the Ware Collection of the Blaschka Glass Models on the 2 $ ^{nd} $ floor [American 3 $ ^{rd} $ floor]. With delight and emotion I saw all the old friends united here and I can report to you with joy, that everything, even the oldest things, are still nice in form and color, like we delivered them. Some trifles and some “half-broken” do not matter and I think about laying my hands on them [to fix them] before returning [home] in order so that everything is arranged honorable. My only regret while seeing the models was that you were not present to share my joy at this moment.

The whole is provisionally arranged in a side-hall in 16 large (table-like) cabinets. They are made of Mahogany-like American cherry wood about 8" deep and have mirror-glass on the top and the sides. Most items still stand on the same cardboard [palettes] on which we delivered them, experiments have only been made with a few items to determine the grayish, brown-gray, and black shades of the supports that best suits them, as the models are nice on all.

The larvae-model and the cacti species look nice on black. Cardboard is used for the supports and the models are placed upon it without fastening. Next to the long side hall where the models are, there is a large nearly square hall, the nicest in the whole museum building, with 9 windows towards outdoors (toward east), about 48' and 42' wide, that is empty momentarily (except for our models, no other botanical items are displayed). This hall is the ultimate destination of our models and with the arrangement will begin immediately when the current delivery has arrived. I have to insert her that I was very astonished to learn when arriving in New York that the Lloyd steamer "Elbe"

that has our 5 boxes on board, and had departed so many days earlier, arrived in New York only the same day as we did. (The later in the morning and us in the evening.)…

I have also seen the botanic garden, but could only visit the greenhouses, as the strongest winter weather reigns.

Everywhere there are electric illumination and electric street cars that I have traveled on several times. Tomorrow, Monday, Mrs. and Miss Ware wish to receive me for 5 hours in the morning. I am supposed to be introduced to the president of the university, Mr. Elliot. The journey to Jamaica will presumably be commencing at the end of the week. Prof. Goodale will not be traveling himself, but he has arranged an agreement with the director of the botanical gardens in Jamaica, and I saw from his letter, the gentleman is looking forward to seeing me and to support me with all matters....

From Cambridge, the Inspector of the Botanical Garden, Mr. [Robert] Cameron, a Scotsman, will accompany me on the journey and will take care of all matters for the preservation of the plants, etc. and will helm me in everything....

Various persons I have been introduced to, like Prof. Agassiz and others....

Dr. Watson lies badly ill with influenza....

My health ....[con't about customs appeals...]

15. Itinerary 1892

My dear Parents!

Only yesterday I wrote you a very long letter, but there remains so much left to tell you, which I will be glad, however, to report to you orally after my return. As for the museum I still have to note primarily that there is a place for our models that will be there for many years and that this institute is really a noble worthy showcase for our work. Today was an important day for me because this afternoon at 5 o'clock I was introduced to Miss & Mrs. Ware. The ladies received me in a very friendly and dear manner. Mrs. Ware is very strong and robust; Miss Ware is a large blond lady of very lively temperament. She regretted very much that it was not possible for her to visit us in Hosterwitz. The small brunette lady who visited us with Miss Kennedy was therefore not Miss Ware incognito as we had believed, but in fact, according to Prof Goodale's reckoning was a Miss Ingels. With the ladies today we made a decision, with which Prof Goodale was immediately agreeable to when I presented it to him, namely that we will not hold ourselves to the number of 60 species, but instead we will produce as many as we can comfortably make, and also the number 50 will be our minimum. When Prof Goodale presented it to the ladies they were immediately very much in agreement. Dr. Kennedy, the father of Miss Kennedy invited me with Mr. and Mrs. Goodale to a supper Tuesday evening at 6 o'clock as soon as he learned that I had arrived, and that Miss Ingels and other ladies would also be there. We will probably accept the invitation. If I had known that the unpleasant occurrence about which I wrote to you yesterday (the abscess behind my ear) would disappear so quickly as it has today, I would not have told you about it in order to spare you any concern. Today it is totally normal. It was just too scary to me to have a blister the size of a half of a greengage plum, near my ear, which also by the way, caused me pain. Prof Goodale's son, who already has been a practicing doctor for some time, examined me and immediately diagnosed that that kind of thing often occurs as a result of an influenza infection. He wanted to open the abscess the next day when it luckily had gone away by itself. So I believe that the issue is to be seen as settled and I am glad to appear completely in good condition. The trip to Jamaica is completely arranged. I will, around Saturday this week, depart on a Boston steamship in the company of Mr. Cameron. He will come along especially as an assistant that will take care of conserving the plants we collect. Even though I will write again before I depart, I will give you my address in Jamaica now and ask you to write me a couple of lines to that address as soon as you receive this letter and tell me if you are healthy and doing well. In all of Boston and Cambridge the weather is balmy which causes a fruitful mud [= sloppy wet], during which my gunboats (= boots) from Hosterwitz are serving me well, during this weather. In the family of Prof. Goodale where there is also a young lady who has come to visit, I am basking in the friendly attentive treatment. All evening I must play piano because the ladies are very interested in it. In Boston and Cambridge everything that I see is interesting and new for me and I am very glad about everything. With the wish that my letter finds you in the best of health, I remain with heartfelt greetings

Your

Rudolf

PS I ask you dear Father please write me a letter to the following address right away. I would like to learn as soon as possible how you are doing.

Mr. Rudolf Blaschka

Care of the Director of the Botanic Garden

Cambridge, Mass 19 Feb. 1892

My dear Parents!

First I can gladly share with you that I am in perfect health and constantly glad and happy. Everywhere everyone is most attentive towards me; it is amazing how the knowledge of the great value of our work is known in such wide circles. Just the mere mention of our name is enough to precipitate friendly handshakes and endless well- wishes from serious proper people. For example today I was introduced to one of the riches people in Boston the banker Peabody. The greatest honor that an Anglo American will present to a stranger is when he brings him into his family; this Mr. Prof Goodale does for me in the most complete manor, because in his family I'm treated as a family member. It did not surprise me particularly however, that on that day also Mr. Dr. Kennedy the father of Miss Kennedy took the opportunity to bring me into his family and invited me to lunch at 6 o'clock. On Tuesday I took advantage of the invitation and was accompanied by Prof. Goodale and was received with in the most friendly manor. Miss Kennedy sat next to me at the table and repeatedly expressed how gladdened she had been by her visit to us. Miss Kennedy and Miss Ingolssay hello. Miss Ingolssay the same lady who at the time we thought was Miss Ware, is the about 36 year old aunt the younger sister of the mother of Miss Kennedy. The house of Mr. Kennedy is an old building in the style of (landhaus) in Roxburgh [sic] a suburb of Boston. Mr. & Mrs. Kennedy have 2 grown daughters and sons. On Wednesday I had the pleasure of taking a field trip 3/4 hour away via train to southeastern Massachusetts to visit the orchid collections of Mr. Ames. Mr. Ganong gave me the pleasure of accompanying me with 6 ladies. The many flowering orchids among which there were specimens worth $2,000 were wonderfully beautiful. In the evening I attended at lecture of Prof Goodale's in the Natural History Society of Boston, aside from that I've already heard 2 lectures at the university by Prof. Goodale and Ganong. Yesterday afternoon Mrs. And Miss Ware came to the Museum and I had the honor of explaining our models to them. The ladies expressed their admiration about everything and especially Mrs. Ware is very compassionate regarding the strain it takes us to make the models. On Saturday evening or Sunday morning I will take the steamship "Bowden" of the Boston Fruit Company to Jamaica. The trip takes 6 days and we will land at the harbor of San Antonio on the northern coast. There are 3 botanic gardens in Jamaica that are to be found relatively high in the mountains. I at first sent you in my last letters an address to Castleton but immediately afterwards I was told by Prof Goodale to send a card with a better address of Hope Gardens, Kingston (post office). Please write to me soon and a lot so that I will soon learn if you're in good health. The letters are important to me at any rate. The stay [in Jamaica] will be limited to March after which I will return to Boston and will immediately set out for California. There the plan is to stay for a few months. And the return trip should lead us through Colorado, Texas, etc. So dear parents it will be over a week before, as I hope, will be able to write to you from Jamaica. Until then I send you my dearest greetings.

Yours truly, Rudolf

##### Dear Father!

I have sent you today as “sample without value” a number of (about 29 species) seeds from the Cambridge Botanic Garden and would like to explain some things in regard to the signs made about the treatment. The annuals are marked with W if the seeds are to be sown in pots and than transplanted, {ein f.} that is, if they are to be sown directly outdoors, if marked with both signs either can be tried. Some species are perennials. There seem to be nice species among them. Today at noon, 5 boxes with models arrived at the museum. They were lifted up to the $ 3^{rd} $ floor with the chairlift-elevator and all looked well-preserved. The porter and houseboy of the Botanical Museum, a negro, very skillfully uncovered the packing from the box, where after Professor Goodale, with his own hands, unscrewed the case and opened it. We took out the boxes with Datura arborea and Prof. Goodale showed me, how skillfully and carefully he handles the unpacking. The mode was well-preserved. The other must stay preliminarily until the customs inspector comes one of these days in order to have the boxes opened at his will and a matter of having inspected them. After everything will have been unpacked, the models will all be placed in the large designated hall, where they will make a beautiful figure. The present, provisional exhibition hall for our models is a long-stretched hall that measures 36 ordinary steps long and 12 wide. In the afternoon hours of these days, I had a pleasure of my own. The Museum was visited by numerous persons, I mingled amongst them as an ordinary visitor, and listened to what people said. They expressed joy when they met a plant they knew, and the “beautiful,” “nice,” and “wonderful” [exclaims] would not end. I’m just getting on a boat from Boston with Prof Goodale and it’s supposed to leave on Monday 22 February at 8 o’clock in the morning. (RB talks about) how the ship is equipped for passengers in the first class. The ride is quicker and passage is cheaper than the New York West Indian boat.

The next letter I hope to write to you already from the land of palms and bananas. The latter are supposed to be so abundant in Jamaica, that they are eaten instead of bread. They ate bananas (plantains) instead of bread. I have already got enough that I have got used to them because Prof Goodale eat them for lunch everyday, and they now taste good and I like eating them. So dear father I send you the heartfelt wishes of good health and ___ please kiss my dear good mother for me.

Your loyal Rudolf

Hope Garden Kingston 6 March 1892

##### My dear Parents!

I hope my writing from Annotto Bay on the 1st of March really made it to your hands. I wrote the letter after the departure from St. Antonio which occurred on Monday at midday. We were hoping that afternoon to reach Annotto Bay which was only 3 hours away by steamer. This was, however, impossible because the ship first had to visit a farther port on the northern coast in order to deliver bananas. On the way back from there we also visited Port Maria so that we didn't land into Annotto Bay until midnight. I found it very interesting to visit these different ports and the paradise-like landscapes, each one more beautiful than the last. In Annotto Bay, through the generosity of a employee of the Boston fruit company, we found a good hotel room where we paid 6 shillings (6 marks) which around here is cheap and where we found comfortable beds and a hearty breakfast with meat, fish, and Jamaican coffee served by the black (female) innkeeper. We were always concerned about how we were going to transport our very through (copious) luggage because the mail coach doesn't take any trunks. My companion Mr. Cameron had brought even more boxes with glass jars, etc. with him, so that we had a very big wagon load of stuff. Here the clerk in Annotto Bay, Mr. Kennedy, helped us again. He gave us two bananas and one was a donkeys in Castleton for 16 shillings so that we could easily bring everything with us. This ride through the romantic, wonderful, beautiful mountain valleys and up the mountains slopes will stay unforgettable for me. I saw the sugar beets, coco, banana, and coffee plantations, impressive forests with indescribably beautiful vegetation Philodendron trees, orchids, pineapple species, Tillansea, Promelia, Thunbergia, Ipomocas species covered the bushes completely. Under that were growing tons of Begonia floribunda, gold and silver colored, and many plants. Along the roads and all the fields there is a weed all over Jamaica called "sin-plant," Mimosapudica. The black farmers have their own name for "shame-my-darling." Also the coffee plantations are in the most beautiful bloom everything covered in the snow of white blossoms which emitted a wonderful fragrance. After about a 4 hour ride we reached the botanic garden in Castleton the layout of which is amazingly beautiful. Mr. Cameron met an acquaintance here who supplied us with a buggy in which we took our hand luggage my microscope and drawing materials. At 3:30 we left for Hope Garden where we arrived at 7:30 in the evening. The superintendent of the garden, Mr. Cradwick a friend of Mr. Cameron, took me graciously in and gave me a lovely bedroom and also further room for my studies which is very pleasant and comfortable for microscope work. Mr. Cradwick and his wife are friendly in every aspect, and they have already explained to us that they will provide us the whole month with food and lodging for which they will ask about 5 pounds sterling (100 Mark) per week (which considering the local situation is not too much). Wednesday at noon I could already start my studies and up to today, Sunday, I have already drawn and studied 20 species. Mr. Cameron provides the material and takes care of the preparation of the plants in white rum and water, and the drying for the herbaria. I was introduced to the director of the Royal Botanic Garden of Jamaica, Mr.

Fossett, at a visit to a meeting of the Garden Construction Society in Kingston (where Mr. Cradwick was giving a lecture.) the gentlemen had already heard through Prof. Goodale about my trip to Jamaica. He came yesterday to visit me and examine my work of which he approved very much. He is a very dear gentleman. He invited me for a visit to his land on the Royal cinchona plantation.

Hope Garden where I am now staying is still newly planted as just 4 years ago in this place was thick forest, but there are still many old trees and useful plants which greatly interest me. So I could study many flowers and fruits of tropical bananas, for example the coco tree, mango (Mangifer indica), the star apple (Chrysophyllum), both of the coffee varieties are grown in Jamaica, Coffee arabica and Liberica. Today I had the pleasure of seeing the flowers of the cinnamon tree, Cinnamomum officinale, which grow almost wild here. It is very interesting to see such plants, for us at home in the garden or in the greenhouse, which only get to be small trees or bushes while here they are massive trees, such as the Ricinus. The old tree with fiery red blossoms about which I wrote to you, when I saw the kolibris [check word!!], I have found here again in the garden. It is Erythrina corelladendron, and I have already inspected the flowers. There are any greenhouses here, and unlike our palms and orchids that we have as houseplants, they grow in their native air. In fact, as far as I now know I must say in our room at home it is not very warm as it is here in March. Here the evenings are humid, after the sun has barely even set it becomes suddenly night. The moon and stars shine so brightly, however, that one can differentiate everything clearly as if in a bright twilight. It is a great pleasure to stroll through this balmy evening air, when the "g_illen" birds chirp, glowing insects swarm, when the air is filled with the most wonderful blossom fragrances, all this will remain unforgettable for me. Hope Garden is in a very dry area, the air is therefore healthier than in the moist districts of the southern coast. The journey through the country from north to south from Annotto Bay to Hope Garden was very interesting for me, because I got to know the extraordinarily differences between the soils and vegetation of the land north and south of the mountains. North of the mountains the area around Annotto Bay to Castleton, the characteristic beauty and richness of the vegetation reminds one of the Amazon River in South America. But just after one has crossed the mountains and reaches the southern plain the landscape takes on a different character that is very similar to the vegetation of Mexico. Tree-like cacti, Cereus and Opuntia, cover the landscape and one finds huge Agavaseverywhere in the gardens and fields. The ground is dry and rocky. Most of the inhabitants of that land are black. On the trip from the northern coast to here, aside from the [Germans?] in Castleton, we didn't see a single white face. I'm now back in my old habits drawing to my heart's desire. It has become my great happiness to be able to study tropical plants in their homeland. I sit in my airy room at my quiet work just like at home, and I leave the pleasure of exploring the mountains and the terrible hot sun for collecting plants to Mr. Cameron. The house of Mr. Cradwick in which I'm staying is made of paxterre [type of clay?] and is one story and it's like all houses in Jamaica built very light and airy. Reckoning according to the number of plants that are blooming in March, and my productivity in examining those, if everything goes well, I will be able to bring together a collection of approximately 100 species. Today I am also sending you as an example some seeds which are not very valuable that Mr. Cameron and I collected here and in

Port Antonio. To grow these plants the climate will have to probably be very warm, but I think I will be able to draw some species that could be used as houseplants and in the garden. The only bad thing is that I don't know what exactly all the seeds are, but I'll be able to figure that out later. Of interest is a yellow blooming flower which is marked No 14. Convulvulous sp. that is common here and grows on the dry ground on rotten things [translation?]. Because I investigated that species, it would be interesting if you would try growing that indoors and outdoors. And you can also try the same thing with Thunbergia (a lovely white flower) No 7, Ipomoea, Cleome, white Phaseolus; Amaranthus; a species of Spanish pepper (Capsicum). When I was in Port Antonio I collected the seeds of a wonderful Solanum which was growing very much like a bush in a garden. The flowers smell like purple grapes, and in color and beauty, they are very similar to a Glycine. A shrubby cotton Gossypium religiosum is interesting because of its big beautiful flowers which are yellow with maroon flecks. Maybe we'll get a chance to grow these species in the greenhouse in Pillnitz. There will be many more seeds and bulbs to collect. Up next for instance is the Paneratum caribaeum which sat on the window of our study for years without blooming and which grows here wild in the mountains.

My dear Parents!

Friday the 18th of March was a holiday for me because I had the great joy of receiving the first letter from you. I'm overjoyed to learn that you are healthy.

Dear Mother should not worry too much about her teeth. It will be my happiest day when I can embrace and kiss you again. And everything will seem nicer than before. I'm very glad all the pets are still alive. I think of Bulla countless times, because wherever you go here people have lots of dogs. All the other news that you've written to me is most interesting. Franzen's daughter and Hickisch were certainly in a hurry to get married. Miss Ware asked me right away about the ladies, Mrs. and Miss Blake, who visited us which I had to deny at the time. I have to recommend from Dr. Goodalea Miss Desoto who may visit you. I am glad that you got my first letters, especially after you said you only had gotten my telegram and not that long letter that I wrote in sight of the American coast, which I sent as soon as I arrived in New York. Time is going so quickly with my work that I find it odd that yesterday was already my fourth Sunday in Jamaica. Saturday morning at 4 o'clock I rode with Mr. Cradwick in a buggy to Castleton Garden where we arrived at 7:30. Mr. Thompson, the inspector of the King's house garden, and Mr. Cameron followed us on horseback. I had the microscope and drawing materials with me and began my work in the apartment of the garden inspector (a colored family), which after 2 days (until Sunday afternoon) at 4 o'clock - despite many disturbances and annoyances and negro children, I produced 15 species. Of those plants were many economically useful plants, such as Jacaranda, cloves, nutmeg (which I collected some fruits myself) camphor, coconut, etc. whose trees are blooming right now. There are many more impressive plants with impressive flowers. Some of these plants are not American [missing words], and they are not economically useful so we can't use them. Castleton Garden is wonderfully beautiful. There can't be more amazing vegetation anywhere else in the world, but the climate there is not very healthful so that one can only visit for a little while like we did. At night time there is a moist fog that gets in everywhere, in the room where I was sleeping, my cloths got moist. Towards morning, the temperature gets cooler and the fog thicker. And the sun is hardly up before it becomes so steamy that you can barely stand it. We were all very glad to arrive in the healthy dry air of Hope Garden where the temperature night and day is more regular. We had a small storm and an hour of heavy rain that day which freshens the air and the vegetation very much. Today I worked on 5 species that I brought from Castleton and have reached the number 90. Because I draw 5 species on average a day, I hope the day after tomorrow to reach my goal of 100. It is most important that I study these things here in the tropics because it's mostly trees and shrubs that would not bloom in greenhouses. It's not worth it to collect seeds from here, at least not for our purposes. At most we could collect a few prairie plants. It would take years of care for them in greenhouse and grow some of the species I have been collecting here. A few days ago I went to visit a very rich family called White (so called English Creoles) where I played piano. It was also pleasant to seat on the

veranda which was surrounded by the wonderful blossoms of Datura arbora that balmy evening. I couldn't visit the cinchona plantation to which the director Mr. Fawcett invited me, because this place on the mountains can only be reached by horseback. Instead for the next few days I'm going to take a buggy to Spanishtown and Rio Cobra. Next Monday (8 days from today), we're thinking of making an early start for Annotta Bay in order to catch the Monday night steamship over to Port Antonio and then Boston. If I still have time and a chance to send news from Jamaica I will gladly do it. At any rate I will write as soon as I get to Cambridge. Please write me soon care of Prof. Goodale.

With loving greetings and kisses from your Rudolf.

##### My dear Parents!

Since this morning was especially beautiful and the weather was a bit cooler, I decided to spend another ½ day visiting Kingston. The city is about 2 hours away from Hope Garden and the buggy ride through the lovely tropical landscapes is very interesting. The wish to show you visually at least a little bit of the majesty of Jamaica made me buy some pictures in Kingston, which will be a nice souvenir for the rest of my life of my trip to the West Indies. Because in the United States you have to pay duty for photographs, I decided not to take the photographic pictures to Cambridge, instead I'm sending them directly from Jamaica to you. I would have liked to have brought them myself in order to explain everything in person about all the places I've been to, but I think it will run for you to see right now all the stuff I've seen in Jamaica. So I have sent from the main post office in Kingston a package with 11 photographs which you will not receive at the same time as this letter. As far as the description of the kind of vegetation of Jamaica, I have a little to add to my earlier description, which I've been planning on telling you to wear Father. Namely that the 3 tropical vegetation pictures you painted are excellently magnificent and accurate. While the picture of the American forest matches what we have here in the mountains, during my tour of Annota Bay to here I was often reminded of the picture of tropical Africa. The coloration and everything is amazing, and in addition to all the wonderful majesty of the forests here, there is the pleasant fact that in the West Indies there are hardly any dangerous predators. Of the poisonous snakes in Jamaica, there's only the rattlesnakes that are only extremely rare in the mountain wilderness, because the snake is prayed upon by the very common little quadruped, the mongoose. As to the photographs I would like to explain a little more. The picture with the label "On the road to Castleton" shows a bridge over a deep gorge with Wag River, which I passed myself one time, and in a few days on my trip to Annota Bay I will have passed it four times. Two further pictures show the amazing growth of the palms and other tropical trees growing under the care of the botanical gardens in Castleton. The cotton trees show the wild vegetation of the river bank with their abundance of orchids and "throwing plant" and ferns, etc. like I have seen countless times. "Feathery bamboo" depicts a pretty bamboo colony like they often grow along the street in Castleton. The picture "Orange Garden" was taken near Golden Spring where I went on Sunday for the third time. It is such a sight to see the orange plantings, to see how the reddish-gold fruits glow out from the dark foliage. The picture "Kings House" shows the Governor's house, the same one that is here in our neighborhood, which I was able to visit the Sunday before last, and where I was all already wrote during a fine supper had my first taste of real English pudding. Of the smaller pictures, the River Cobre shows the river landscape of Jamaica very well. While the pictures of Kingston ("View of Kingston from Harbor") show the prisoners and "Street Scene from Kingston" we see the life of this interesting city. The photograph "Public Garden ... or so-called Parade Garden shows [the life in the streets]... during my trip I didn't have time, and wasn't interested in taking

photographs myself. Prof Goodale wanted to loan me a very small camera from the institute and to teach me how to take photographs. But for various reasons, especially that I don't have the time, to waste my time in Jamaica I lost interest and decided not to pursue the issue. But Prof Goodale, who is not happy about that, taught Mr. Cameron how to use it and gave him the camera and told him to take pictures of flowers and landscapes for me. But the camera will no doubt return to Cambridge without having produced anything. I find that photographs are totally unnecessary to our studies. Since I would much rather draw than toll with boring photography. Tomorrow morning I will magnify the 100th species. I think I can be satisfied with the result with barely 3 weeks of work. By us at home it would be very difficult to find so many species in bloom at one time. So dear parents I hope that you are both healthy and doing well. I thank God that I am in perfect health. Hoping that the photographs bring you great joy, I remain with loving greetings and kisses.

Your Rudolf.

Garnishtown Jamaica

##### Dear Parents!

I can't forget to write to a couple of lines before I leave Jamaica to tell you that I have finished my work with 106 species, and also to say that I have returned successfully from my trip to Spanishtown and the Rio Cobra. Spanishtown is the hottest town in Jamaica. Everything there was extremely interesting especially the very romantic Rio Cobra River. In the street that runs into the plateau [plaza?] and also later on the Rio Cobra I saw several huge examples of the gaudy cotton tree, which is Bombax malebaricum of which I sent you a photograph. This morning I visited Gordon Town on the Hope River which is in the mountains not far away, where I had the great joy of seeing the stately ___ [akarden] that are blooming. Early tomorrow morning we're going to take the buggy over to Castelton to Annoto Bay where we will reach the Boston steamship. It's going to take another whole day to make this trip across Jamaica again. On the trip back, the steamship will visit Port Antonio again. I'm writing this quickly so that this evening still I can send you my greetings and kisses to you from Jamaica one last time. And hope that you are doing well and are healthy. Thank God my health is perfect. Please write me back soon in care of Prof. Goodale, Cambridge, Mass.

Your Rudolf who loves you very much.
