##### My dear Parents!

I arrived in good shape in the afternoon of the day before yesterday in Cambridge. This morning I was very glad to receive a letter from you from March 25th and to learn through that letter that you are both happy and healthy. I'm just sorry that you were so worried about me, which was probably aggravated by the exaggerated stories in the newspaper about the yellow fever in tropical America. I didn't notice any yellow ever in Jamaica, but it is true that the West Indian ports always have to watch out for that. I heard in Kingston about a case of fever that had the characteristic black vomit, but such cases are isolated and are always caused by either too much sun or too much drink, which is very common in the ports. The Hope Garden, where I spent much time in Jamaica, was a very healthy place. The people don't even think about yellow fever at all. In Jamaica the people don't differentiate between the different fevers. They just talk about one kind of fever, which comes up in mild and severe cases. The severe cases are most common in the humid areas of the northern districts. The most notorious place for that kind of fever, which I had to pass through twice, is on Annotto Bay, but thank God I got through healthy. The main thing is that I lead a reasonable lifestyle. So please don't worry about me I will always try to stay healthy. I wrote to you a lot from Jamaica as soon as I got there. I wrote a long letter from Annotto Bay, and since you got my postcards from Port Antonio, which I had sent on the 25th of March, but still have not received a letter from me, I'm afraid the letter from Annotto Bay must have gotten lost. Because the letters between Jamaica and Germany usually take 21-23 days. On Sunday, the 28th of February, we landed in Port Antonio when I wrote you the first postcard. Since then I found out that the connection to Kingston from Port Antonio goes over high mountains, which is inconvenient and costly. Because of that, we took the same steamboat "Bowden" on Monday afternoon to go to Annotto Bay. but because two more ports had to be visited in order to deliver bananas, and those are Port Maria and Rio Novo, the steam had not yet been reached and in a very adventurous way. The whole time during the afternoon on the steamboat I used to write a letter to you about the sea voyage and my impressions of Port Antonio. The first employee of the Boston Fruit Company in Annotto Bay, Mr. Kennedy, a very honorable gentleman whom we liked very much, volunteered the other morning to take my letter to the post office and he paid for it. It was very heavy and had to have two stamps put on it. Please let me know the next time you write whether you got that letter. I would really like to know. Then I wrote you the first letter from Hope Garden which didn't get sent until the 8th of March because that's when the next steamship left. My dear parents, it is my greatest joy to write to your regulars and often, but it was sometimes really tough in Jamaica to find the time, because during the day time, I had to do so much drawing that when I did write you, I sometimes had to stay up to 11:30 or 11:45. I hope that you receive all those letters in time. It's just a really long distance. Now from the States we should be able to correspond more quickly. I already got your second letter that you sent to Jamaica sent up to me here. Now my dear parents I have to continue telling you about my journey. On Monday on 28th of March we arrived to Annotto Bay at 10 in the evening on the

steamship on the "Albert Dumois" and there we were under the supervision of the same Mr. Kennedy. Travel between ships in Annotto Bay can only happen by boat so we also had to get into a boat pretty far off of the coast. The Boston Fruit Co owns a large proportion of banana plantations, from which, through the whole year, bananas are twice weekly sent away on ships of that company. These bananas are packed in groups of 150 bunches and are sent unripe from here and allowed to ripen in Boston. The steamship "Bowden" belongs to the company and they rent 4 steamships, one of those is the "Albert Dumois" for each of those the company pays $3,200 in rent. All the workers in Jamaica also cost a lot of money so everything has to be done through mass production. Last year 2 million bunches of bananas were ordered from Boston and our steamship had 19,200 bunch on board. In order to deliver this load of fruit, numerous ports have to be visited that's why we couldn't leave Jamaica right after we reached Annotto Bay. We had to go on a tour around the island towards the east, but there was a lot of interesting stuff to see. We sailed because of that on Tuesday morning to Hope Bay then to Margaret Bay and Port Antonio, where I last sent you a postcard from Jamaica. Then we stayed in Morant Bay in Port Morant from where on Wednesday at 6:30 in the morning we left Jamaica. At first it seems we would hit stormy weather because the ship was rocking drastically, but by afternoon things got better and it stayed beautiful until we got to Boston. This trip was my best of all my sea voyages so far. The ship was sailing under a Norwegian flag the Captain Rustad, a very likable nice decent man, and the rest of the crew aboard were Norwegians. The steam ship was only built last year, and it's very elegant, a little bigger than the Bowden with engines of 1,200 horsepower. The captain had a piano on board because his wife played a little, and so I had the opportunity many evenings to play piano, which was much fun. The 6 days went by quickly and pleasantly. As much as I like Jamaica and the nature there, I was glad to see the red houses of Boston appear through the fog. It was as if I was half way home. Prof Goodale and his wife had just left on a trip as I arrived, but I was immediately received by Mr. Ganong and led to his apartment where I stayed the night. It was handled in the most friendly way by him and his lovely wife. That same evening Mr. Ganong invited me to go with him to an American theater that was a great opportunity to get to know the American peculiarities. I went with some friends so we visited the Park Theater in Boston where they presented a new piece of the "Circus." After the introduction by a very comical skit, there appeared acrobats, tight-toped dancers of the first order, Japanese people with their own arts, an animal tamper with huge lions, and a man with 2 trained donkeys, horseback aerialists etc. It was all very fun. Yesterday morning I rode to the Arboretum in Forest Hills, a huge garden where I will go tomorrow and the day after in order to make studies. Today I drew and studied 5 types of plants in the Cambridge Botanical Garden. Yesterday afternoon Mr. Ganong showed me through Boston. I ascended the Bunker Hill Monument from where one can see all of Boston and all the surrounding area. I saw many other noteworthy things in Boston. That evening I sat in on a meeting of the Boston Natural History Society and had the pleasure of meeting Prof. Morse who visited us in Dresden a few years ago with a young lady Miss Abbot. The lady is, so he tells me, married to a chemist, and Prof. Morse gives her greetings. He was visibly glad to see me. Since yesterday evening, I stayed with Prof Goodale and was welcomed as hospitaly as the last time. He told me that you wrote to him. The main thing I have to tell you is that the models in the museum are exhibited.

in the big room. It's impressive to see everything there together. It looks beautiful. Almost all the models from the last shipments arrived in one piece. Even the breakable things are unharmed. I am staying another few days in Cambridge in order to draw the early flowers [early flowering plants]. In the beginning of the week, we are planning to go on another field trip, so I asked Prof Goodale to give me an opportunity to travel again soon so that I can take advantage of my time here and I can be reunited with you quickly. The biggest obstacle right now is that it's hard to find a companion for the trip, but it's pretty much set that I'm leaving for California in the middle of next week, and it's probable that Mr. Ganong will accompany me, which will be very nice. So while I'm here, my dear parents, I must take advantage of my time and get all my work done. I am longing to see you again and hug you and kiss you. That will be my happiest day. Just don't worry about me with God's help I will finish everything well. Please write back soon care of Prof. Goodale. I'm always so happy when I receive a letter from you. So at least in spirit I am embracing you. I remain with the dearest greetings.

##### Your loyal Rudolf

PS Mr. & Mrs. Goodale send their friendliest greetings. They were very glad to hear the news about the birds Bella etc. If you get the chance, say hello to Mr. Hofgärtner for me.

My dearest Parents!

When I got your letter on Thursday it gave me no comfort. I would like you to know as soon as possible that I got back from Jamaica in good shape & sent you a telegram from Boston which you should have received by now. Then I organized the seeds that I collected in Jamaica. There aren't very many different kinds, I put some in a packet as an example & sent them in the mail. Aside from the yellow papers [?] that you already know about, there are also some interesting things to which I would like to bring to your attention. A beautiful blue blooming [flinging plant = Shlingpflanze] Clitoria ternatea [ck if seed pods explode]. I had to leave it out [of his room] for a while. Cajanus indicus, the so called Congo Pea, is a medicinal plant (the peas are not edible.) There is an unusual Rizinus (genus) that has very small leaves. In the small packet with Cycar written on it, there are some palm seeds that I found in Castleton that, some big seeds...inside belong ... infrequently (probably a rare species of Cycar), maybe our acquaintances Pillnitz could try to germinate the seeds, the huge beans belong to another Shlingpflanze belonging to Enteda scandens, but I don't know if that is going to work. The things would all have to be grown in a warm environment. Gossypium barbadense is the most commonly grown cotton in the West Indies. I'm also sending you something that will definitely intrigue you. In Castleton where they have impressive coffee plantations I had the opportunity to pick the white berries of the best sort of Jamaican coffee Chofea liberia myself from the plant & I'm sending you the ones I picked. So that dear mother can make real Jamaican coffee. Then I'm sending you a bunch of pictures that I bought in Kingston that I brought back here with me. These are pictures taken from photos that show the landscape of the northern coast & the mountains. "Bog walk" is the name of the beautiful area of the coast in Rio Cobre in the south about which I wrote so much to you about. When you look at the picture you could almost imagine that you're looking at our mountainous area, if the bush [plant life] weren't bamboo and tropical. Gordon Town is very close to Hope Garden. In the area there are many of the [argaven = agave?] "maypoles" that the next picture shows that are in the same area of which there are many in that area. That huge group of "Dildo-Arch" cacti in the area around Kingston is the same group I've so often seen & admired. I cut off a piece of that same cactus species & brought it with me. If it's still alive when I get home we can plant it. "Beginning of a river" and in "the home of the filmies" are pictures of the huge mountain forest of Jamaica which I will never forget. The rest of the pictures are of the rivers in the northern part of the island. I didn't want to have these things around anymore and thought you would enjoy them as much as I do. Yesterday & the day before I was in the Arboretum at Forest Hills doing studies and among those I did 10 species of elms, American hazel nut, willows, etc. The head of the institute Mr. Watson gave me a nice room to work in & was very friendly and helpful. The inspector of the Arboretum Mr. Dawton, to whom we once wrote about the bushes, got the letter and says he wrote back but didn't have the species he wanted. And he was very nice to me. The Mr. Watson I just mentioned shouldn't be confused with Dr. Sereno Watson who was sick when I

$ 1^{st} $ arrive in Cambridge & died while I was in Jamaica. I am now getting ready for my further journey to the far west. It's all planned and arranged, The trip starts on Tuesday the $ 12^{th} $ which is the day after tomorrow, $ 1^{st} $ going directly to Chicago from there over to Missouri, Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico, and Arizona where I'll make a little stop, then on to San Diego, Los Angeles on the Pacific, the big ocean. After about 2 months I'll return going through San Francisco and Colorado (Denver) on the Northern Pacific train. My companion is Mr. Ganong whom I like very much. I will receive your letters if you keep sending them the same old way care of Prof. Goodale, Cambridge, because Prof. Goodale sends them to me without delay. Please write back soon. I will write as often as I can. Don't worry about me I'll get through this just fine. Stay healthy and take it easy. So that I don't worry too much about you. I greet and kiss your spirit lovingly.

##### Your loyal Rudolf

Friendly greetings from Mr. & Mrs. Goodale. While I was finishing this letter Miss Ware came to Prof. Goodale and complimented me in a friendly way about my work.

# Rudolf Blaschenka 2. Z. Tempe L. Phoenix Vision

Morning!

My dear Parents!

Finally mid-day on Easter Monday, I have reached my first destination in the west. I arrived healthy and in good shape in Tempe Arizona where we're hoping to stay a few days because there's a lot of good study material in this vegetation. It made me very happy to travel through the unbelievable stretches of land of North America to see the different interesting cities and landscapes and I've sent you a postcard from every station where I had the time - at least a ½ hour. I hope you get the cards eventually. It might be fun for you to watch my progress through the United States through the postcards you receive. The first night we went through the state of Massachusetts and New York through Albany Utica, Syracuse to Buffalo and I saw the last three towns in the daylight. All day Wednesday we were traveling along the coast of Lake Erie which offered many interesting views and landscapes while the vegetation was still in its winter state. The winters second night & a green-Thursday morning when my companion Mr. Ganong and I stopped in Chicago to spend the day in this metropolis, the next train to the west didn't leave until the evening. We explored Chicago in the street cars and the elevated line in every direction and looked at the buildings of the World Fair (Weltausstellung)¹, the Art Museum, the skyscrapers (Riesenhäuser = huge house), and all sorts of noteworthy [weird/unusual] stuff. Chicago is the center of the union where all the train lines converge, so we had to go from Boston first north to Lake Michigan in order to get the Atchinson Route, Topeka-Santa Fe train. After we found ourselves on a Friday morning on the fertile plains of Missouri & Kansas which have been cultivated for many years, all the way along the train tracks you see green crops that have just been seeded and mile-wide stretches of corn fields. On the way out of Chicago we were riding in first-class sleeping wagons which were so comfortable that they let us forget the stress of traveling. I'm now as used to the shaking as an old sailor is. The plains of Kansas seem endless. Not until Saturday did we get to the wild prairie in Colorado where we could go for hours without seeing a house. As far as the eye can see there is nothing but the plains full of dry grasses which immediately catch fire from the locomotive and sometimes keep burning along the train. The trip through the Rocky Mountains was amazingly beautiful, a piece of the big Indian Rocky Mountains that reminds you of Indian stories. Then came the prairies and endless savannas of Colorado and New Mexico where [buffalo] herds of thousands of animals are grazing, but in New Mexico there are stretches of hundreds of miles where nothing grows but one species of yucca, cacti & other desert plants. We also pass places where no vegetation grew at all. Sand-deserts where it had n't rained in years. On Easter Sunday we reached the Rio Grande which is the border between the United States and the Republic of Mexico. In the afternoon we arrive in the main border town of El Paso, Texas. We hung around there for a few hours and decided to take a tramway over the Rio Grande to Mexico. The Mexican city is called Ciudad Juarez or Paso Del Norte.

wanted to send you a Mexican postcard, but because it was Easter Sunday one couldn't do that because everything was closed. The difference between the two cites is that in El Paso everything is in American English and in Mexico everything is in Spanish. Many people did not understand us when we spoke to them in English. Because it was so dry there the vegetation was sparse we took the evening train to Maricopa in Arizona from where we took another train line to Phoenix. We're going to stay in Tempe for a little while before we got to California. The weather has been beautiful ever since we left Chicago. Spring is full-blown here in Arizona. You see blooming trees, bushes, flowers even desert plants all over the place. Tomorrow I'll start studying (illustrating). We rented two nice rooms in the hotel and are very satisfied with the modest prices. The rooms cost only $1.50 a day & the food is $1 per head daily which considering the prices in the west is not very much. In Arizona it was very interesting for me to see real Indians who make up a large proportion of the population here. I have so much more to tell you. But I'll leave that for my return home when I'll be overjoyed to share that with you. During the six nights that I spent in the train I dreamt of you my dear parents and of our familiar home which with God's help I hope to see before long. Now I have a lot of stuff to do. In all the places I will travel San Diego and San Francisco will be the farthest I'll be away from you. But my dear parents don't worry about me with God's help I'll get through this well. Take care of yourselves and we will be able to see each other in good health again. Prof Goodale will send the letters from you to San Diego & San Francisco for me & I'm already looking forward to receiving word from you to see how you're doing & how things are going. It is my dearest wish that these lines will find you in good health and happy. As soon as I find a little bit of time I'll write you another letter. With the most loving greetings.

Your Rudolf

NEW YORK N.Y. APR 27 7-18 1892

Tempe near Phoenix in Arizona

20 April 1892

My dear Parents!

This evening I'm really feeling the need to talk to you, but since right now its impossible because soon I'm going to be 1,500 miles from you, I'm taking the quill in hand and at least communicating with you this way. Yesterday I did a lot of drawing and through that work I now have 10 interesting species. There is really a huge richness of species of wild growing plants here. During the opportunity to make an excursion into the desert with Mr. Ganong in a carriage, I was very glad to realize that most of the plants here are different from our species and the whole vegetation has a foreign character to it. The desert is what people call a mile-wide stretch of land which has a rich vegetation despite the unusual dryness and stony ground. All over the place you find thousands of yellow blooming plants, Larrea mexicana, next to that are growing yellow & white flowered composite, cacti, white Lavia, & Lupines etc. I was very interested to see lots of tree like huge cacti, and today I've already drawn 2 other smaller species. Even though handling these poisonous prickly cacti is not particularly fun. It seems like all plants in this area have thorns. Arizona is the quintessential representative of Mexican vegetation. It is actually the real old Mexico in this area where you see lots of ruins of old towns which were founded by the original Mexicans and were where they still lived at the time of Montezuma during the Spanish invasion. The town Tempe (an Indian name) is only 15 years old and most of the houses are very cheaply-built and look brand new. The Indian huts which are spread around near there are pathetic poor caves where you can barely believe that people live, but otherwise there are great shops and a colorful combination of people like Yankees, Germans, Jews, Spaniards, Mexicans, and Chinese and mostly Indians. Watching the last group of people gives me a lot of pleasure. I see them going by all the time because they often gather by the dozens near the yard of the hotel. So these Indians are mostly of the tribe Maricopas & they have the typical strong build and copper-red coloring on the faces painted with bright red paint and dark tattoos and straight black hair which often grows past their shoulders. It was great joy for me to watch these people riding when their hair would blow by like a man. I'll still have a lot to tell you when I come home. In this hotel, we've found a good comfortable place that we like. The owner is an Englishman and his wife and her sisters are Germans from Bavaria, really pretty, friendly women. I'm unbelievably glad to be able to speak German again. Since there is so much plant material for me to find around here, we plan to stay in Tempe until Sunday then to travel to San Diego at the beginning of next week. The climate here is very mild, typical of the subtropical zone, no snow in the winter, amazing heat up to 180°F in the summer. It's very arid but in the town there are excellent canals that fill with the river. So that Tempe is a charming oasis with vineyards and orange orchards and pretty green gardens. So the leaves in the trees are a wonderful green and the roses bloom beautifully in the gardens, but I wouldn't want to live here forever. In the middle of all the beautiful and amazing things that I've seen in this wide world the image of our familiar home and Hosterwitz seems like a paradise where I have my only
Your loyal Rudolf.

22. April 1892

My dear Parents!

Today was a group excursion to the mountains & desert that are a few miles outside of Tempe and it went well. We rented a wagon and with that we rode early in the morning out into the wilderness. We were well-equipped with holders to keep the plants fresh. We found more than we expected because we found many very characteristic representatives of the Mexican desert vegetation. I had the opportunity to draw the flowers of about 4 cactus species and because of that I allowed myself to dig up a cute young example of all the species & took them with me. We didn't have to conserve these cacti in alcohol, instead I intend to send them this week from California to you which I'm sure we will make you very happy. Again today I saw tons of huge Cereus 30 feet high & higher, then I saw a tree like species called Jumping Cactus = Spring Cactus, which is the worst and most poisonous cactus and naturally which I did not want to collect. The prickles in this species have a very fine hook on the end so it's impossible to remove them from the skin using your hands. As soon as you touch 1 single prickle the rest of them seem to jump on you of their own volition that's why they're called the Jumping Cactus. On our first excursion I had a very very small opportunity to get to know this darling characteristic of this cactus. The desert floor where the cactus grow is very rocky and mixed with sandy loam. It's very pleasant for me to participate in the excursion like today and Tuesday because it's a very welcomed change from my regular studies and I have an opportunity to find some very interesting plants myself. So today I found on a tiny little spot on the desert an impressive Delphinium of which there were many individuals and which I drew as soon as we got back in the afternoon. A large proportion of the desert plants are very tiny species so we ignored most of them and we only pick out the most showiest and most characteristic plants, so that the number of plants that are useful for us is 25 species. This number is more than I expected to find here. The weather is very a little more than the desert this morning. The field was mowed this morning and yesterday in the hotel we had fresh strawberries from the country for lunch. In 3 weeks the peach harvest is expected and at the end of July are the grapes. It's a really wonderful place, except that the dust settles unpleasantly in your throat. Since we'll be done here tomorrow and I will have finished with all my sketches, we're first going to Maricopa tomorrow morning to spend the night there and then take the courier train Sunday morning to California. The trip will take us first to Los Angelus then to San Diego in southern California where I hope to find good material and will write to you again. I'm already looking forward to finding a letter from you in San Diego and to hear that your happy and comfortable. Alright then the dearest parents, dearest kisses & greetings

From your Rudolf

Maricopa / Arizona 24, April 1892.

My dear Parents!

At last I've reached one of the farthest destinations of my journey. This afternoon at 1 o'clock I arrived in the best condition in San Diego. I always tell you the hour in which I reach the mentioned places even though during the ride from Boston to here the clock had to be set back a few times. The sun rises about 10 hours later in San Diego than by you in Hosterwitz. As much as I've already seen in America the recent trip from Arizona to California was extremely interesting one which I enjoyed very much because I got to see new and interesting things. The trip through New Mexico, Texas, and Arizona peeked my interest especially because it offered the opposite of what I saw in the West Indies, namely the desert in all its forms. In New Mexico and old Mexico I first saw the Yucca desert where on the endless sandy plains there is nothing other than Yucca gloriosa, Y. philamentosa and other species. Then from Texas to Arizona was the mesquite dessert where only the mesquite, Prosapis juliflora is present. In Arizona, I had a lot of fun near Tempe and Maricopa when I discovered the chaparral desert which consists of millions of chaparral bushes and the species is Larrea mexicana, and also the cactus deserts. They [i.e. cactus desert] are real deserts that through the present of the flowers on millions of shrubs, and on the sand and rocky ground, but they could also be called flower gardens. Sometimes I think it unfair that such areas are such rich vegetation exists, despite the unfavorable soil conditions, terrible sun and dryness, are called desserts. These deserts are exactly like the areas in the Cape of Good Hope in Africa and New Holland where the Erica species, Epacris and the Australian legumes live. I was still hoping for a complete dessert like the Sahara and the other African deserts, and this wish was fulfilled yesterday. All the way thru Arizona to Yuma, the same landscape is in the background. There is a rocky mountain range and before that is the chaparral plain which switches off with the cute jumping cactus and the huge giant cactus. After we crossed the border of California near Zuma, the landscape showed a different character. The mountains are only visible in the distance and in front of that the sandy plain becomes wider and the vegetation more sparse. They say that along time ago a huge ocean reached all the way into present day California as a huge gulf which slowly retreated and dried out and left a huge salt desert behind. I have now seen this huge southern Californian desert. For about 2 hours you drive through an area where nothing grows on the cracked sandy and rocky ground, no shrubs no grass, and now I understand what the term "desert" really means. (By the way I also have to mention that the people in Arizona told us that later, in about 4 weeks, in the Arizona deserts the vegetation that I described also completely disappears - so we arrived at just the right time to observer the plant life.) The big California salt desert is also interesting because the same thing lies under the ocean. This is a unique instance that you can't find anywhere else on earth. The train tracks after Yuma to Salton are about 260 feet below sea level and it was exciting to see how much deeper the train kept going [words missing in the sentence]. After the depression, the train climbs quickly back up to 2,000 feet above sea level. We passed the San Jacinto whose peak is constantly

covered in snow and here the vegetation too is also of a different character. The chaparral brush disappears slowly and huge Yucca and interesting ___

[carmoisinrote] and blooming Oputias alternate with the charming violet heads of Abronia umbellata. We arrived in Los Angels at 10 and had to stay overnight because the train to San Diego didn't leave until 8:45. That trip was very picturesque, orange orchards with golden fruits and at the same time with huge blossoms changed the character of the landscape which becomes more rich with flowering plants. Wheat fields, vineyards, rose gardens, and everywhere the rich wild vegetation of blue lupines, delphinium, Mesembriantemum and a mass of yellow composites which often give entire hills a lively yellow color. That made my feeling even stronger as we reached the Pacific Ocean around 10 in the morning and that I'm so lucky to see this ocean so from here on to San Diego, the ocean remained in view. San Diego is an unusually spread out, developed city close to the sea, and very close to the border with Mexico. The temperature is the same all year long, never too warm. The air is always kept pleasantly cool by the sea breeze. The clean air here reminds me of Hosterwitz at the most lovely time of the year, May and June. In the gardens everywhere are beautiful flora, the voluptuous roses, climbing roses on the houses, pelargonium as trees and next to that lots of other opuntia and cacti. Several years ago this was still all desert and through clever irrigation and years of hard work was turned into this flower paradise. The ground is just poor sand. Because we are sure to find a lot of material here, we're going to rent rooms for about a week in the Bay View Hotel, a very large new hotel of the first rank. I asked at the post office and had the great joy of receiving 2 letter from you. One of the letters was from the 5th of March that you wrote as the second letter to Jamaica and the other was to Cambridge from the 30th of March. I was very glad to hear you were doing well. Everything you wrote made me ____. Please write again soon, I must close my letter now and will write back again soon.

With love Rudolf

My dear Parents!

Last night while I was writing this letter it got so late that I had to stop writing suddenly. All yesterday afternoon in San Diego and the surrounding area, we were traveling around to visit certain botanists who had been recommended to us, but we did not find any of the gentlemen at home. But it was a lot of fun to explore the wide streets where the houses often stand 15 minutes away from each other and also to see the wild plants that we found in the undisturbed areas and hills which are very different from our plants back home and at most are just grown as ornamental. We took a few things with us so that I could start with my work this morning at 9 o'clock at the hotel where in the meantime the trunk with the microscope had safely arrived. But I was very disturbed because the botanists with whom we had left our boxes came to the hotel while my friend Mr. Ganong was away so that I had to lead the proceedings myself. The first visitor was Mr. Orchutt, who is a seed and plant merchant from whom we once asked for a catalogue. He promised to do everything he could for us, to sell plants, onions (probably corms), and seeds, and to arrange excursions himself in order to show us the places of origin of these interesting plants. The later was immediately undertaken in that Mr. Orchutt and Mr. Ganong, from this afternoon to tomorrow afternoon, will make a trip to the mesa that is many miles away to gather material. I had to forgo participation on the excursion because I have to first work on a portion of the plants that grow here. I will have enough opportunity later to participate in excursions. Despite having been interrupted for an hour by a Mr. Meacon, who is a high official and private (amateur?) botanist, I was able to complete 5 species. I have finished these drawings. I can already draw 5 species pretty easily, but with a little more effort, I could probably work up to 8 species and increase that to more later. Now that I'm all alone in my room this evening, it gives me great joy to reread the 2 letters from you in which the parts about the masters of botany etc. always put me in a good mood. Now we have to have patience for a time until I have completely ended my task. Aside from our plans to make some excursions into the Californian wilderness and a possible second visit to nearby Mexico we plan on the following: in order to reach the giant conifer forests we will travel to San Bernadino, and from there to San Francisco where we will stop for a while. Then we are going to Utah and Nevada to Colorado (Denver and Colorado Springs) in order to study the very characteristic vegetation of that area. And then on the trip home, we will stop in St Louis and at Niagara Falls and then return to Cambridge. Prof Goodalere regrets that he could not accompany me on my trip and because of that is planning a short trip at the end to the Alleghany Mountains and Virginia and North Carolina to which Dr. Kennedy in Boston will accompany us. It's supposed to be the greatest importance for me that I see their Rhododendron flora and the gentlemen want to give me the opportunity to see Washington so that I really will have seen all of America. Then I won't be able to wait to come home to you. For now everyday I see new things which grab my interest. A few times I thought that I had been transported to China because we passed by some Chinese settlements where the yellow guys with their slanty eyes and long braids lived in great numbers. I had already

seen a lot of them in Jamaica but here in San Diego you encounter Chinese people all the time. Also I have to say that San Diego and Los Angeles and the other Californian places that I have visited all posses the comforts of electrical lighting, trolleys, etc. and one would be very wrong to say that this is a semi-wild country. While we were in Arizona there was a powerful earthquake in California, which for example in San Diego lasted 3 minutes and caused quite a bit of damage, but we did not notice any of that. Now I can tell you that the whole trip is bringing me a lot of pleasure. My companion Mr. Ganong is a complete gentleman whose charming behavior makes his society very pleasant, but he is also very good and responsible toward me and helps us in the interest of our job. He helps me with the conserving in alcohol and the herbarium without making too big a deal out of it. He generously gives me the seeds he collects and doesn't show the least bit of greed by that. All of this lets me enjoy my journey without the least bit of unpleasantness and I'm very glad that Mr. Ganong was my companion. The cacti that I personally collected for us in Arizona I have taken with me to San Diego and I want to buy some important bulbs for Mr. Orcutt in order to send all of those to you altogether. Purchases like this have to come out of our budget for the pharmaceuticals and it's very good that I have a little spending money. The ladies paid for the whole trip and the hotel costs, but there are always other little extra expenses which add up and that I could never ask anyone else to pay for. As for damage to clothing etc. I think that our noble friends consider my visit in America will handle the opportunity. [difficult sentence = they will probably take care of clothing expenses.] So I have again told you a lot and it's time to take a break. So stay healthy, write me back soon care of Prof Goodale and think of me often, who sends you again his heartfelt greetings from

Your loyal Rudolf.

San Diego, California

30. April 1892.

My dear Parents!

There is not much new to tell you today, except that everything here is great and I'm doing very well. My most precious wish is just that this letter meets you in good health, too. Yesterday afternoon we made a trip to a grand valley near San Diego, Old Mission Valley, named after the ruins of an old mission. The impressive vista over the wide valley and mountains and the wonderfully clean air reminded me of our own Hosterwitz, if not for the endless plane of the still ocean on my left side and the first look at the vegetation didn't remind me how far away I am here. It was a great pleasure to wander around the neighboring grounds and to boast of the time I found some plants growing wild in great numbers that we at home raise in the garden so carefully. Some examples are the violet Collinsia bicolor (which are like the vetch-like flowers ), and Castillaia species with their fiery red bracts. There are very interesting bulbs here, which congregate in huge groups along roadsides, in the city, on undeveloped hills very close to our hotel. For example: the Calochortus splendens, a large, pink tulip, Brodiaca, and others. The ground is so rock-hard, however, that it's impossible to pull the bulbs out. I tried a few times to dig some up, but only had limited success because they sometimes reached more than a foot down into the rocky ground. The botanists here tell us we came at just the right time, the richness of wild plants will disappear soon because the dry season is coming. The only bad thing about southern California, is that, like in neighboring Mexico it rains so infrequently. If there were enough irrigation, this land would rank among the richest and most fertile on Earth. Here it is not nearly as hot as Jamaica. I find the nights pretty cool and am comfortable in my woolen undergarments. The sun is amazingly bright, but there is always a cool wind from the ocean that keeps the temperature even. Aside from that, everything here seems like home in high summer. Fresh fruits of all species are everywhere. Among them are some unfamiliar tropical fruits that grow quite well in the moderate California climate. During the day I always draw and so far in San Diego I've finished 25 species. Since I take regular breaks, I don't think I'm putting myself under too much strain. After dinner at 6, I also take regular walks along the electric-lit city streets, where there are often interesting things to see. It is then that I enjoy watching the daily ceremonies of the Salvation Army, which makes itself known on the open street here. These peculiar religious zealots parade around in various groups in the lively streets. At the head is a flag bearer, and each participant has a musical instrument, large and small drums, trumpets, pipes. The women have a kind of tambourine with little bells. They play marches and sometimes sing and play pipes, then the whole group kneels in the street and prays Our Father and litanies. A few members preach to the public, some of whom take it seriously, some laugh and making fun. The day before yesterday I found some Chinese people in the audience, but unfortunately I couldn't understand what these people thought

of the Salvation Army. As for me, I couldn't help thinking of the Geißelbrüder from the middle ages. Since we find a good amount of plant material daily here, we believe we must stay another few days in San Diego. On Monday we're thinking about making a trip across the border to Mexico. I hope to write again soon, before I leave San Diego, and remain with heartfelt, loving greetings

##### Your loyal Rudolf

P.S. If you have the time, please say hi to all our good friends and acquaintances ...

Schaberschul and family as well as Uwnzl, Etc.

San Diego, California, 4. Mai 1892.

My dear parents,

I'm hurrying to quickly sending you a few lines from here before we leave San Diego this morning and leave for San Bernardino in the mountains. The past few days I've gotten to see still more new things because on Monday we made a long excursion on the train. I had the chance to see southern California's great water source, the Sweet Water Dam, then we went farther south toward Tia Juana, over the border to Mexico. Along the train tracks were always magnificent flower gardens, groves of oranges and figs. In a few fields they were cutting barley. A second field trip led me to Coronado, which is right across from San Diego and separated from it by the Bai, and where the largest hotel in the world is, the Coronado-Hotel. It is a fantastic complex, like a city all its own. There is also a large garden with many rare shrubs, which is called the botanic garden, and where we found a few useful things. This field trip was very fun and interesting. Botanically speaking our stay in San Diego was very favorable. The botanists there, particularly Mr. Orcutt were more than generous in the procurement of plant material, so that I completed 36 species in San Diego. We were also to obtain all the other kinds of plants from Mr. Orcutt cheaply/easily. The small box of cacti and some flowering bulbs was sent today with other things to Cambridge and I will ask Professor Goodale to send you them. I collected a large part of the cacti myself. I think it will all arrive unharmed except for maybe the piece of giant-cactus that was cut from a large individual and is rotting a little where it was cut. Yesterday we had very odd weather; a heavy rain storm all day, which is rare for this time of year in San Diego. Other than that we've had magnificent weather during our stay. So, dear parents I conclude my writing with best wishes and heartfelt greetings.

Your Rudolf

San Bernardino, California,

##### My dear parents!

This afternoon I arrived in the best of health in San Bernardino. After a brief look around the city, which has the same architecture as San Diego, just a more pleasant affect on account of richer plant life, we went to visit a famous botanist, Mr. Parrish. The gentleman lives on a country estate, three English miles away from the town, so that we had to take advantage of the opportunity. ... was very friendly, asked us to stay the evening and informed us of all the good spots to find plants in central California. After that we changed our plan to stay a week in San Bernardino. This evening still we are taking the night train to a town northwest of here called Hesperia (about four hours by train) where there are supposed to be some excellent sources of plants. We want to spend the entire day collecting there, and after my trunk with the microscope arrives tomorrow evening, I can start studying and drawing the day after tomorrow and, if necessary, into the following days. When we are done there, we are going back and southeast toward Arizona to Agua Caliantes, where we hope to find interesting stuff. From there we will return to San Bernardino, in order to capture their flora during a stay of some days. The heavy rain of yesterday and the day before stretched all across the west. According to this morning's news stories, the northern states such as Wisconsin, Illinois, etc. had snow storms. Here in California it softened the hard ground so much that the roads are sometimes bottomless. The nice thing about it during the trip was, though, that the dust that normally makes long trips here challenging was pretty much eliminated. Now I don't have much news left to report, except that everything I've seen on the journey so far – orange groves, olive gardens, wildernesses with forests of yellow and red blooming opuntias and other cacti, romantic valleys around the mountains, etc. – made me very glad. The air is very clean and pleasant everywhere. The temperature has gotten a little cool, so that I wear my coat over my summer things early in the evening. As soon as I get some more time, I'll write you again, and I remain....(illegible, but seems to be more greetings)

##### Your Rudolf

P.S. I am already looking forward to finding a letter from you in San Francisco, where I hope to be within the next 14 days. Please write me again soon care of Prof. G. Cambridge, Mass.

##### My Dear Parents!

I hope that my letter from San Bernardino as well as my cards from Hesperia and Banning reached you. And in addition to those, today I have even more news for you. We took the advice of Mr. Parrish in San Bernardino and took the night train to the northern town of Hesperia, in the mountains in the middle of the desert, which is a small settlement that consists of not many houses and where we arrived early at about 3 o'clock and then we found rooms at a hotel that was near the train station. We thought that through this trip we would find many new central Californian desert plants especially the characteristically Yucca Brevifolia. At day break I saw in the unbelievably wide desert plain, that is surrounded by mountains from which the snow topped summit of the San Bernardino Mountains majestically sticks out, a very different desert landscape than I've seen before. It's like a forest everywhere the tree-like yucca rising out of the desert sand. Lots of impressive examples of Yucca Brevifolia and we also saw some other yuccas like Yucca gloriosa and Whippels, Bucotta etc. which I also saw in New and old Mexico, Texas, etc. but these are different because they are tree-like and have many branches while the others just had a strong trunk. In the morning we took a pretty far excursion into the desert but we were disappointed when we saw that the yucca had already bloomed, because all of the plants had unripe fruits growing on them. The whole area had lots of different species [yet] so that we didn't find very much new material, but we did see very interesting things. Because there are many things about the hotel we didn't like, we decided not to stay any longer and took the afternoon train back to San Bernardino and then to Colton which is a ½ hour train ride away where we had to wait a few hours for the next train. We used that time to make an excursion to the nearby mountains and schluchten which are called "canyons," where we found very pretty things. The evening train didn't stop at the station that we wanted, which was Seven Palms, so we just rode another two hours from Colton to Banning where there's good hotels where we spent the night. Since the morning train doesn't arrive until 1 o'clock we spent the whole morning in the rocky gorges in the surrounding area and discovered a lot more pretty stuff, a very beautiful cactus species of Opuntia basalaris with fine big crimson-red flowers. It is very characteristic for southeastern California and is very common there. After about an hour ride, we reached the Station Seven Palms, a lonely train station in the middle of the desert where a vehicle was waiting for us which we arranged by telegraph and was to take us to Agua Caliente. The hour and half ride over a desert plateau, a place completely void of vegetation, was pretty adventurous but we finally safely reached this blessed place at the foot of the San Bernardino Mountains. But it is very lonely and remote which is why we [Americans] have the saying that the foxes say good night to each other. In this area three years ago they discovered a hot springs which the Indians had already known about since early times. The Mexicans named the small settlements in Spanish "Agua Caliente" hot water" a doctor, Dr. Murry opened a hotel, bath and spa and Agua Caliente became a "booming" place much like most Californian cities - booming, burning and full of noise. Sometimes they say the boom is over, like in San Diego, which despite all the business is in decline. Three years ago it had 35,000 inhabitants today there are 15,000, but we were very glad to find a nice place in the little town by the hot springs. The owner Dr. Murry took care of us in his hotel. Aside from us, it only holds ten people. I have every comfort

for my studies and we believe we will find much new material, to which our acquaintance with Dr. Murry, who is also a botanist, will also be useful. At any rate, I think we will stay here a couple of days. In the past few days I have had to spent a lot of time climbing around in the mountains so that I was very glad this afternoon at 3:30 to be able to back to my work. Mr. Ganong is taking care of holding the plants, which is very easy when done in glass containers with alcohol and water, and with dried specimens. From our trip so far, Mr. Ganong has already sent 2 boxes of material to Cambridge where they will stay until I am ready to return home. Now dear father since today is the 7th of May, and I recon the letters from here will take about 19 days, so that you will get this present of writing around the 6th of May, so I can't forget to wish you a Happy Birthday. God willing when we see each other again everyone's health will be fine. Last night in Banning I dreamt of you dear parents very realistically and unpleasantly so that when I woke up I was really surprised that I hadn't been at home with you. Before I leave this town I hope to be able to write you again. Before we go to San Francisco, we will probably visit another small town. These little towns are more profitable [economical] for us than the big cities which all have the same kind of character. So my dear parents greetings and kisses and

Your loyal Rudolf

##### My dear Parents!

As I told you about our plans in my letter the day before yesterday, we left Aqua Caliente (also called Palm Springs) yesterday morning and after about 4½ hour trip we reached Colton where we took rooms in the transcontinental hotel. The trip through the desert after the train station was like a trip over the African desert because a hot desert wind was blowing down from the mountains which blew the desert dust around in such masses that one automatically thought of “Art von Samum.” The whole trip went smoothly, however, and I again today studied comfortably a number of desert plants that I brought with me. I was alone at home almost all day because according to our plans, today Mr. Ganong went to nearby San Bernardino in order to visit Mr. Parrish again in order to gather a couple of new plants with that gentleman. And he really did bring 6 new species this evening, which I will work on tomorrow. Then he brought me something else which gave me endless joy, a letter from you from the 20th of April that had arrived through Mr. Orcutt to Mr. Parish, through San Diego, to which our correspondence had pointed my attention [to talk to Mr. Parish?]. I was in a good mood all day and thought constantly of you because the night before I also dreamt about you. And so that evening I heard from you really did bring me the joy of hearing something of you. I am happy to learn that you are doing well and are in good health. I'm glad that everything is going well at home and that the trees are blooming, when I come home I will see young fruits, that the “girl” Bella (his dog) and birds are behaving well, that you received all my letters and photographs. Regarding the last letter, I was thinking today that when Father has time and desire that he should paint a picture of the bridge, which is depicted on our colorized American landscape “On the Road to Castleton.” As a souvenir of my visit to Jamaica, because I have friendly memories attached to this bridge, which I passed 4 times. But there’s time for that later. I’m still advancing on my current trip since I have not reached the farthest point. Tomorrow evening we will depart for San Francisco. The arrival at which will require another 24 hour trip. Through correspondence with botanists and good recommendations, we have already made all of our arrangements in advance.

Most likely we will not take a room in the noise city of San Francisco, but in Oakland, which is only separated from the city by the bay and lies across from the later, like Cambridge is to Boston. Oakland is quieter and more conveniently located for plant hunting. In the same town lives a botanist, Mr. Lemmon, who specializes in the collection of Californian conifer seeds. Unfortunately the gentleman is beginning of traveling to Arizona and Texas. If we do indeed catch him at home, I won't forget to acquire some seeds for gardener Wenzel, whom I would like to ask you to say hi to me. I myself have not arrived at the conifer region in California. This starts only north of San Francisco. My exploration thus far has been mainly in the Mexican and southern Californian desert region where one finds very few conifers. I have collected various seeds of desert herbs. If I have the time soon I will send you some although it is already quite late to be sowing. I, thank God, am totally healthy except for a cactus prickle from Arizona.

that is irritating me a little bit in my left hand. For which the remedy that dear mother sent with me is working well. This spring cactus (Opuntia bigeloni) is truly the most infamous plant in the world that exists. On Monday during a field trip in Palm Valley, I accidentally brushed against one of these devilish fellows and I was impaled through my socks and lederhosen. And another one stuck Mr. Ganong through the boot. The cacti that I have sent to you are of a much more benevolent nature. Of course you always must be cautious with these spiny fellows, but I believe that because we need them it's better to receive them alive then in alcohol, because we can grow the flower ourselves. I also have to note that three of the cacti, the long snake cactus, a small Cereus from Kingston, and an Opuntia, were collected by me from Jamaica and therefore must always be grown in the house. Now I must end my writing as it is already late in the evening. Please write back soon. I will send my next letters from San Francisco – Oakland.

So stay in good healthy I greet and kiss you in spirit and remain

your loyal Rudolf

##### My dear Parents!

Today I can already tell you that my stay here is very fun. The two of us, me and Mr. Ganong who always enjoys a field trip with me, went on an excursion to the mountains nearby. The excursion and clean air and magnificent not-too-warm weather turned out to be really pleasant. Nearby there is a park much like our large garden in Dresden that we explored. Then the scenery became more wild, which was better for us because then we could find the plants that we needed. One of the main plants throughout central California is Eschscholzia californica. It grows very impressively and is a bright orange-red in color and is so common and grows so thickly that the mountains glow orange. Another plant is Orthacarpus, which gives the mountains a soft pink color in great masses. You see plantations of eucalyptus trees which have the tendency to dry out swampy land. Then there're also some interesting flowering shrubs and it was pleasant to see how the shiny green "kolibris" and it buzzes around the blooming shrubs. Because once in a while you see a palm tree, I am sometimes reminded of Jamaica, but the landscape is too much like the pictures of the temperate zone and the temperature in comparison is too cool. Truly amazingly beautiful is the view from the ocean to San Francisco. The green mountains, "the Golden Gate," south of that sprawling Oakland next to the city of San Francisco — all of it majestic and beautiful. It's just a weird thought that at this point in the west I am as far from you as I have been in my trip. So now, soon I will get on the train back. Yesterday afternoon just as I returned, I quickly drew 3 more species. Today, Sunday, I was not as productive I only finished 5 species. Tomorrow we will take a pretty long trip several hours by train. We want to see a forest made of the giant California conifer Sequoia sempervirens in redwood and hope to see this tree in bloom and to see other species that we may have already seen. It's getting hard to find new plants. Around here you mostly see just a few dominant species and they occur in huge numbers. We will soon be done with California for this season, and depending on how quickly we work through all our material and after we've visited Francisco (a well loved nickname for San Francisco), we hope to maybe continue on our journey at the end of the week. This scientific gypsy life is fun, but I will be very glad to exchange it for the quiet life I'm accustomed to. We hope to spend a lot of time in Colorado where the flora of the Rocky Mountains, the great rocky mountain range, will be full of new opportunities. My dear parents before I travel on I hope to write another time and I hope this letter finds you well. I am sending my heartfelt greetings

Your loyal Rudolf

##### My dear parents!

I've been wanting to write to you today, but I'm just getting to jot down these lines to you now. Our planed trip to see the giant trees on Monday went well. It took all day because the ride in the train to the forest near Santa Cruz is 4 hours. Many of the Sequoia are truly gigantic. I measured one of the average specimens and it had a 40 stride circumference and those are not small strides. In the woods we found quite a few new and interesting plants that will be useful for us. For example we found a yellow violet and a very small wild rose that looks almost exactly like the small wild roses we have in our garden. Every time it is a joy for me to see plants that we grow in our garden that grow wild here. Our hope to find the Sequoia sempervirens blooming was unfortunately not fulfilled because the flowering time of most conifers in central California is almost over, but through our acquaintances with local botanists we will be able to get local flowers sent to us later. The conifer botanist, Mr. Lemmon, about whom I wrote to you, was not at home and because there are no other collectors of conifer seeds here, I'm afraid I will not be able to fulfill Mr. Hofgartener Wenzel's wishes, unless I have time in Cambridge. The pine cones that I found in the woods myself appear to be empty and perhaps we will have another opportunity to visit more Californian forests. Before I left Prof. Goodale told me a lot about a plant called Darlingtonia californica, which is very close to his heart because it never blooms in greenhouses. This plant only grows in a valley 400 miles from here near a tall mountain which has the unusual name of Shasta. The trip there and back takes 4 days and costs $70. We couldn't decide what to do, so Mr. Ganong had the good idea of telegraphing Prof Goodale and we're still waiting for the reply. But today at any rate we will decide to go to Shasta or not. I've been in San Francisco 3 times and the bay between Oakland and here is like I thought. It will take 15 minutes for the ferry to cross. Otherwise the city has the same character of other big American cities, except that Chinatown transports you perfectly to the middle of the heavenly realm. Yesterday evening we went to the Chinese theater where the Chinese perform in Chinese. It was extraordinarily far from the home. Today we still have to make 1 visit because Miss Ware has 2 brothers in San Francisco and then early this evening or tomorrow morning we will leave Oakland for either Shasta or Colorado Springs. Now dear parents I greet and kiss you in spirit and remain hoping that you're in the best of health.

##### Your loyal Rudolf

##### My dear Parents!

As I already told you today on a postcard, this morning at 4:10, after an uninterrupted journey of 3 days and 3 nights, my companion and I reached our first destination of our return trip which is Colorado Springs in Colorado. Like our stay in Oakland and San Francisco, the weather during our entire trip was beautiful. The horrible storms and floods that have been attacking the north and middle states of the Union, and which you will have no doubt read about in the newspaper, didn't come to the far west at all. The long train ride brought me again rich variety and new experiences. Not long after we left the San Francisco station the entire train pulled into an enormous steam fairy which took us and a second long train over an extraordinary wide Sacramento River. That's the kind of thing you only get to see in America. Shortly thereafter, after we passed the capital of California, Sacramento, they attached a second locomotive to our train because it was required in order to cross the great California snow mountains the Sierra Nevada. The entire afternoon we rode through these snowy forests of long needled conifer species until we reached the summit of the (pass = "kames") "kamme"? which was 7,000 feet tall. Then we rode for hours along snow barriers which protect the train from avalanches, etc.. The other morning we found ourselves in the state of Nevada where the landscape is very different. The snow-topped mountains become ever farther away in the distance and after crossing the border of the state Utah, we returned to a very low lying desert through the huge northern salt desert of America. Then we went past the big salt lake which also was called the Dead Sea where the Mormons founded their big settlement New Jerusalem which is now called Great Salt Lake City. I sent you a postcard from Ogden on the Great Salt Lake. The interesting part began on the third morning because the boring deserts ended and we started climbing the Rocky Mountains, a huge American mountain range. All day long we saw the most amazing natural beauty: oddly shaped cliffs, clefs, scary narrow passes with waterfalls and mountain streams. There's also everywhere lots of conifer forests which is why a whole colony of coal makers makes this their home. I always image on the rocks the figure of Indians who lived here not to long ago. Near the smelting huts in Leadville where we reached our highest altitude at 10,200 feet. Colorado Springs is 6,000 feet above sea level. It got its name from the famous natural carbonated iron springs ("quelle" is a spring) which are close by in Manitou. This morning we took a little trip to Manitou in the gondola which took less than an hour. We tasted the famous water which tastes like Biliner water. The afternoon we dedicated to a further trip to Cheyenne Canyon, a wild romantic beautiful valley with a big waterfall. Because we felt like climbing, we decided to take another way back which was a steep rocky mountain that was about 20,000 feet high so that we reached an elevation of 8,000 feet above sea level over the lake. This climbing trip in the Rocky Mountains was very fun and gave me a lot of joy and will always remain unforgettable for me. Among the powerful mountain giants that surround Colorado Springs, one snow-topped peak stands out. It's taller than the rest of them. It's the Pikes' Peak and it is 14,200 feet high. As long as the gondola goes there we want to take the opportunity

during our stay to look around on the giant (mountain). The weather is unusually warm, the sun is burning like it does in southern California, so it's surprising that the vegetation is so far behind still. The fruit trees are just starting to bloom and we were actually a little disappointed to find so few wild plants in bloom. But there are a few plants that had already past (blooming) in the south. For example, the American cottonwood tree that's planted everywhere, a flowering time had already been passed in Arizona and California, while there they are just starting to flower. The same goes for conifers of which I have found a few nice species here. A botanical excursion that we have planned for Monday morning will determine whether we should stay here another week. We have rented rooms in the new Alamo Hotel, a first rate hotel with all comforts, electric light in all the rooms, etc. Towards the end, in Oakland, I didn't really like it anymore. I got an upset stomach there probably caused by the bad water and unhealthy foods that you get in the hotels. The problems consisted of loss of appetite and dryness of mouth, but they have improved and I'll be very glad when I can switch this food mishmash with the delicious healthy food by our dear good mother. As you can see from my excursion and mountain climbing, after which I am not tired at all, that I am otherwise in very good health. You also shouldn't be too worried that I sit too much at my work. I am very careful. I wait yearning daily since it always seems like such a long time since I have the well-known handwriting in my hands. I am coming ever closer to you until we become happily united. I hope that you are healthy and doing well. Please write back soon so that I will receive some letters in June during the last days of my stay in America and so that I will know that you are healthy. I always think of you in my field trips to the mountains, forests, and deserts while I'm working, you are always with me. I am always interacting and speaking with you in spirit. So dear parents the time when we will be reunited is coming closer. I will work hard to finish so that I can come home soon. With the most loving greetings and kissing you both in spirit, I remain

### Your loyal, Rudolf

PS I still have to tell you a little about the story of Shasta. We waited 36 hours in Oakland, but didn't get an answer from Dr. Goodale. I thought about Shasta: do we go to Colorado now and this thought was also thought through. Today I got the answer by telegraphic that we should not go to Shasta. I wouldn't have agreed with the telegram, if there hadn't heard so much by word and writing about the Darlingtonia. I think that Prof. Goodale couldn't get the vacation time for this trip from the university. His earlier assistant now his colleague of French Canadian extraction, Mr. Ganong, had to take over part of Prof. Goodale's class. Prof Goodale would have liked, as he told me himself, would have rather sent his favorite [Mr.] Cameron to participate, but I did everything in my power to not let our friend, the garden inspector who showed us every seed in Jamaica, come along. He is Prof Goodale's friend the garden inspector who showed us every seed in Jamaica. My trip is going very well and the small things are as they say in Saxony is a "sausage" [worscht = means "don't care" but RB uses a spelling indicating a dialect]. Just a little joke.

##### My dear Parents!

I hope that the letter I wrote the day before yesterday found you in the best of health and I wish the same for this letter I'm writing currently. My health is now back to normal, appetite and everything is back to the usual. I am doing well. The Colorado air helped with that. Today we're making another trip to the Cheyenne Pass this time to the so called North Canyon, to which a botanist who has been leaving here for a while, suggested we make a botanical excursion. It became an unusually hot day therefore we walked along the miles-long gorge without climbing any mountains. The botanical results were surprisingly rich. Through the gorge, between rock formations, there rushed a small river surrounded by various vegetations where we found a great deal of things in bloom, which were much prettier flowers than those in the desert. Upon arrival at home yesterday, I quickly drew 2 more species and today 5. Tomorrow I will have to study again because today we found several new things. I am now working in a very causal manner in order not to tax myself too much - as many species as I can get together in America, as much as the possibility exists, there the rest will figure itself out. Don't think that if only I could work more quickly we could collect much more, this time of year there isn't a big selection and in addition to that the people in Cambridge are picky, they don't want this or that species because it's already represented, etc. In order to accomplish 600 to 800 species, I would have to spend the whole year wondering around America and I really don't want to do that. Up till now I have drawn and studied 200 species and I think that when I leave America I will have collected 400. So anyway, we found so much good material here that we decided to stay until Saturday. The day after tomorrow we want to take the train up to Pike's Peak. Friday will be another work day and Saturday afternoon we will travel straight to St Louis, Missouri where the largest botanic garden in the United States is, in order to stay a few days there. We coincidentally met the director of the gardens, a Professor Trelease in San Diego. In a good botanic garden it is much easier for me to find material because the names and everything are at hand. On the entire trip so far there haven't been any botanical gardens. We had to get everything from the wild, because I myself could often take part in that myself, I found it extremely enjoyable. Also because I didn't always get the chance to thoroughly become acquainted with the habitats. After the great heat yesterday, we had a powerful thunderstorm. It was an amazing spectacle to watch the ascending and the depositing over the mountains and there was powerful lightening and thunder. Because of that the temperature has cooled of a little bit. Well dear parents, now I can say until later, and I'm also not forgetting little Bella and our other housemates, in that I say my dear parents that I kiss you in spirit and remain with heartfelt greetings

Your loyal Rudolf

My dear parents!

Yesterday evening I had the great joy of receiving a letter from you that I had been longing for so passionately. That letter, dated the 7^{th} of May, is the 6^{th} from you and with that I so far I have received all of your letters. I was sorry to hear, that dear mother should be somewhat careful that so that she doesn't get a cold and that she doesn't put to much stain on herself so that when I will return home I will meet her in the best of health. Just don't worry about me and the happy resolution of my journey with God's help and with my unwavering manly strength of will and endurance, will be carried out well and successfully.

The largest part of the weakness-spells, which is often not minor, are thankfully over. Regarding the mild illness about which I wrote to you that befell me in Oakland you do not have to take any further notice because there is no sign of it left. I only told you about it because I promised to write to you the exact details of my health, and you can see through that when I inform you that I am completely healthy. I have been rarely irritable on my trip and the worst is when I get very fatigued by my work or sometimes there's a special cause which spoils my regularly good mood. Otherwise I'm "at the core" always aware and ready to go "on the place" [on the ball]. I am monitoring myself in every regard about that you can count on. The people I encounter treat me with polite respect of my studies as far as I have come in contact with botanists in Californian etc. They're all of course always very curious about our models and would like to see them because they can't imagine what they are like. Outside of Cambridge there has been very little written about our work. After the end of my trip, the work should be publicized to botanist around the whole world through some sort of memoir. Sometimes a newspaper journalist will write something in a newspaper and will make silly generalizations. So during my return trip from Jamaica, the pilot or navigator of the ship bought a Boston newspaper in which there was a long article about our models. All very favorable, but with a big mistake, the Boston Advertisertells his readers that the only people in the whole world who know the secret and the art of making these models are two brothers named Blaschka in Germany, of which the younger brother is now traveling in America and will return from Jamaica in 6 weeks. I had to laugh heartily about that, in that, I automatically thought of the second [brother] on Cranach Street. Sprinkled with similar inaccuracies was in yesterday's Colorado Spring Gazette an article about botanical expedition of greatest importance the goal of which is carrying out the exploration for the flora of the Rocky Mountains this local city. Well dear parents, this exploration is giving me a lot of joy. Yesterday was a big expedition day. In the morning we made a trip thought Colorado City to Manitou in an electric train, and from there we took a cog-railway to Pike's Peak, which is about 12,000 feet high and at the snow line. On the trip back we experienced a magnificent vista from which one could see the entire area. That afternoon we visited the "Garden of Gods," which this example of this rock formation in Colorado gladdened me very much to see. There was a powerful thunderstorm, but we didn't become the least bit wet. Dear father you write to me about your work. Take it easy there will

be plenty of time when

Cambridge people correctly and

kisses, I remain

You loyal Rudolf

##### My dear parents!

Because in just a few hours this afternoon, I will have left this place and with that [be] entirely outside the territory of the wild west. I must hurry to write you a few lines. First I can tell you that my health is perfect and leaves nothing to desire. I have seen everything noteworthy of this friendly area and my stay in the Rocky Mountains, the old Indian rocky mountain ranges will always remain unforgettable for me. The past 2 days have been very stormy, which cooled off the temperature somewhat and as a result the stay here has been made very pleasant. Because we couldn't visit a relative of Prof. Goodale while we were in San Francisco, for various reasons, Prof Goodale sent a telegram to Mr. Gonang telling him to do everything he could to visit his cousin, President Slocum of the local university. Mr. Ganong had already been there and had acquired various information about plants etc. Yesterday evening we were both there but only his wife was home, a very corpulent lady who received us warmly and made a special point of saying how happy she was to see me. The two big [great] ladies, the wife of Capt Goodale and her sister who two years ago came to visit us in Hosterwitz with Prof. Goodale, his cousin and traveling companion, and with Mrs. Nuttall, are the sisters of Mrs. Slocum and they told her so much about us and our models. The wife of the president of the university repeatedly expressed her regret that I hadn't brought a couple of models with me on my trip. Also the acquaintances can only be useful for our purposes. Mrs. Slocum gave us the addresses of the local curiosity [natural history] merchant who specializes in collecting wild seeds of local plants. Early tomorrow we want to visit her in order to determine the value of her things [collection]. I have been looking everywhere for people who collect and sell seeds so that later we could grow a few things. Then we are traveling, as I already informed you, straight to St Louis, again we will have to spend 36 hours without interruption in a train car. After my arrival in St Louis, in Missouri I will write you right again. So dear parents I hope you are in the best of health and hearty greetings and kisses.

##### Your loyal Rudolf

PS Also the news in your dear writing about Cyperipidum made me very glad.

H. Louis (Missouri) 31. Mai 1894.

##### My dear Parents!

So after a 40 hour train ride I have happily reached the next goal on my journey. We left Colorado Springs under thunder and lighting and were accompanied by heavy storms throughout the trip. The Arkansas River was overflowing and wide stretches of the flat land right up to the train were underwater. Before I had taken my present journey to the States, I had always imagined that the states Kansas and Missouri were wild lands made of only prairies and where Indians lived. Now I know they are wonderful examples of agriculture, because their land with their excellent soil is among the vast land for growing grain in America. The true wild part of America I didn't see until I went west and south of the aforementioned states. So this morning at 7 o'clock we were happily dropped off in the neighborhood were the botanic garden is, and had the pleasure of being expected by Mr. Dewart, a friend of Mr. Ganong's and a former assistant to Prof. Goodale. It was the same here as during the entire trip, severe storms and rain. During our further ride in the electric street wagon it suddenly became night, so pitch black that the electric lamps had to be turned on everywhere. The people were afraid of a hurricane [probably means tornado] or an earthquake. It ended up being a rainstorm, however, which did not last long. The Mississippi has said to have reached an unusual height. Mr. Dewar already had accommodations for us at an inno on Grand Avenue where we didn't have to make any more arrangements and so we went to the botanic garden where I was graciously given a room for my work, (it's in the workroom of the assistant Mr. Dewart). The garden is really amazingly planted and immediately offered us interesting material. By the way, the oddity, Darlingtonia, because of which we traveled to the Shasta Mountains, was in bloom and today I have already made a sketch for the color and I have put a good specimen in alcohol. There's not much to the plant and the flower. It is very similar to Saracinia. Aside from that I have recorded an additional 3 species not a bad beginning. The goal of our stay here, which presumably will last until Saturday, will bring in about 18 plants species that I have set for myself for this trip of about 150 species. Achieving this goal is probably not going to be possible through the botanical garden, but through an excursion for wild plants which we will undertake tomorrow to a distant location. I had the endless joy through the help of Mr. Dewar of receiving your letter of the 15th of May, which made me extraordinarily happy. Everything you write to me makes me very glad, especially that you both are healthy and doing well. Oh dear parents how I would love that I were sitting next to you today under our old Linden tree and chatting with you about everything I've experienced. It will still be a little while before this wish is fulfilled, but time marches on. Also I can share with you that I am completely healthy. The water in Saint Louis is a terrible beverage, in a glass dirt of which one could not even keep a frog. I drink it only in it's cooked form, that is, when barley and hops have been cooked in it, when it has an excellent flavor. Today for lunch we are visiting a large park-restaurant close to the Botanic Gardens which belongs to a German. While the Americans weren't particularly impressed, I had an excellent sourdough cornbread and a glass of the most delicious beer, a long awaited pleasure that I alone prefer over
