My dear Parents,

Although the stay here is quite pleasant for me, I am still counting the hours until we can continue on, so that I will come closer to the point in time that I long for, when I will see you again. So this is the last place on our current trip where we will have a more lengthy stay. Then we're going to go straight to Cambridge, where we hope to arrive next Tuesday we hope to meet the F.D.M. [??] (excepting for a few hours in Chicago and the short jaunt away to Buffalo and Niagara Falls). So after that, I will see if the last big excursion to the Allegheny Mountains in Virginia etc. will start. But if this all gets dragged out too long, maybe I'll decide to just cancel the whole thing and journey home since I don't have the desire to stay too long in Cambridge. I will definitely visit Mr. Gillett in Southwick, who sent you the catalogues and sent us the pretty Cypripeds, etc. because it is not far from Boston, and then we can talk in person regarding the acquisition of seeds and plants. During the present trip I had little opportunity to collect seeds myself because the plants were generally in their spring state and the seeds don't usually start until July. I had a snapshot of the vegetation and the nature of the state of Missouri yesterday during an excursion to a town called Pacific which is about 1½ hours from here by train. We traveled through a string of low forested hills where we found a good number of interesting plants that grow very well in the moist good soil. Today I have finished working on 6 of those species. The botanic garden where I have my work room is in a suburb pretty far away from our hotel on Grand Avenue (36th Street in St Louis). Each time it's about 25 minutes in the street car. There are a noticeable number of Germans in St Louis. Among the businesses and streets one keeps finding German names. And then there's also the well-represented black element, at every step one sees Negros in all nuances. The weather has cooled off after the storms so that it is currently very pleasant. My health couldn't be better so I'm hoping to be able to complete the trip in the best shape. On [Pfingsten = a holiday] Saturday, the day after tomorrow, we want to leave this place and then on [Pfingsten] Sunday spend a few hours in Chicago. I will soon after reporting everything to you. In the hope that you are both quite healthy well in body and spirit. I kiss you in body and spirit. I remain

Your

Rudolf.

H. A. Leibniz (Missouri) 4. June 1892

##### My Dear Parents!

About an hour ago I arrived in Cambridge in the best of shape and found the friendliest reception at Prof. Goodale's new apartment at 10 Craige Street. After a brief discussion, we decided not to make a further trip to the south for this project, which sounds very good to me because I very much yearn to see you again, and because I'm very tired of all the train rides. The stay here will therefore not last more than a week or at most not past the end of next week. We were in Boston this afternoon, Prof Goodale and I, in order to inquire about a cabin space. We found out that the Bremen steamship "Spree" which is leaving next Tuesday (8 days from today) is so full that it's doubtful there will be a good place left. Therefore I will probably either come on the Bremen steamship "Aller" on Sunday the 18th of June or on the Hamburg one. Because it will be decided in the next few days, I will let you know immediately about it. So we have another trip to Southwick Massachusetts to visit the Gillett Garden and that won't last more than 1 to 2 days. Then I will need about 2 days in order to do some repairs in the museum for which I was very happy to receive the package with the paints etc. from home. The remaining days of my stay will be spent with studying and drawing the plants from the local gardens. Mrs. and Miss Ware are at their property in New Hampshire. As Prof Goodale informs me, I will not have another opportunity to see them in person again because the location is supposedly too far away. The trip home from St. Louis to Cambridge was happy and pleasant in every measure. The Mississippi had flooded the area around St. Louis for miles so that our train in some places was going through water and we also had to make detours on the tracks of completely different train lines to Chicago, which is why we arrived over 2 hours late. All over the place we could see traces of the flooding that had occurred during the recent storms along the train to Buffalo where on the morning of our arrival we found the city in great upheaval. On account of the retched events that had happened nearby through flooding and burning (of petroleum) in the town of Oil City and Titusville, about which you probably read a lot in the newspaper. In Chicago by the way, I again had the opportunity to see the buildings of the World's Fair [i.e. possibly the World's Columbian Exposition that opened in 1893], then the small jaunt to Niagara Falls gave me a lot of joy about which I will tell you when I come home. Thank God that this will happen soon. The long journey to the west is happily over, and I must admit that I am not in the least excited about a further trip to Washington, etc. I will be happiest once again when I am reunited with you, and when the familiar quiet and order return. For now I have seen an awful lot of the wide world, so dear parents my heartfelt greetings and kisses which will soon be reality.

I remain your ever loyal,

Rudolf

I am to impart very friendly greetings from Prof & Mrs. Goodale.

Cambridge Mass. 8. Juni 1892.

My Dear Parents!

Yesterday evening news came from the Bostonian agent that there is no room left on the Tuesday steamship. And on the steamship named “Aller” that is headed for Bremen from NY on Saturday the 18th of that month has only one spot for a $100 in the middle of the ship in the first cabin not far from the machine room. After briefly thinking it over, I decided to take this spot; so yesterday evening Prof. Goodale ordered the ticket. So if nothing unusual happens, I will depart on Saturday the 18th about which I am wildly happy. So much that I am already counting the days and hours when I will be again reunited with my dear parents, my only true friends. I am really very glad that everything turned out so that I can soon leave this country in order to see you and the familiar friendly home again. As pretty as the summer now is in Cambridge, I still don’t feel really at home. I am writing you these lines today quickly in order to let you know of my upcoming departure. And should anything get in the way of my plans, such as for example that in the meantime the vacancy was already sold yesterday, I will immediately inform you. But I believe everything is going to go just fine, so that God willing at the end of this month, I hope to be reunited with you. I will write again in the coming days and great and kiss you in spirit in the hope that you are in good health. I remain

Your loyal

Rudolf.

Cambridge Mass. 10. Juni 1892.

My dear Parents,

Today I had the joy of receiving your letter of May 29th which as always made me very happy, especially because I learn from it that you are both in good health. I also thank you from the bottom of my heart for my upcoming birthday wishes, the day before my departure. I believe that I will spend June 17th in New York because I'm very anxious to have a good look at this city before my journey home. My passage on June 18th on the Bremer steamship "Aller" is now set and I am endlessly glad, God willing, that I will soon be able to embrace you. I'm surprised that it was so hot in Hosterwitz. The weather here is very pleasant, only mildly warm; yesterday it rained all day in a storm, but today is very beautiful. Aside from the deserts of Arizona and southern California, my whole trip has not been overly warm. I am having a good time in the lovely countryside house of Prof Goodale because the Prof and Mrs. Goodale are very friendly to me. Yesterday during a short audience with the President of Harvard University, I was introduced to Mr. Eliot, who in a thoroughly and friendly manner asked me many questions and spoke admiringly about our models. I have had plenty of opportunities during my journey to observe that most of the public and scientific world possess the same admiration for our work. Yesterday and today I made repairs on the models undisturbed in the museum in a small room and it gave me joy to have the good old friends, which are still as beautiful as they were when we sent them, in my hands again. There were especially a lot of orchid flowers and pseudobulbs, etc. that were broken – I first worked on these, and yesterday and this morning, I made such short order of it that Professor Goodale and others were very glad. Today I saw a thing with leaves on it which almost frightened me. But I was able to fix it in the most critical places in a unique way that I'm very happy. I think I will be finished with all the repairs tomorrow, when the entire collection will stand flawlessly to be an honor and source of joy for our friends. It is a magnificent how highly we regard the treasure [i.e. models] here in Cambridge and all the people I meet here express their joy and admiration of it. Yesterday I received a large onion, a Crinum, from Mr. Orcutt in San Diego (California), which he sent me as an example sometime after a packet of seeds had arrived from the same gentleman. I plan to make an arrangement with Mr. Orcutt regarding the request for a large number of seeds and bulbs of such plants, the flowering time of which we were not able to wait for while we were in California. In this way we can gather a whole lot of material. Through my drawing and studying of what we collected, I was only able to acquire about three years of material, and I did my best given the few work days and the circumstances that nothing in flower was neglected, but everything – even to the smallest weed- was recorded. So my dear parents, stay healthy soon I will be able to press you to my heart again. I send greetings and kisses in spirit.

Your loyal

Rudolf

Cambridge, Mass. 16. Juni 1892.

My dear Parents!

Now I can already send a report. The first part of my journey was all over rather nice and lucky. The [horse driven] coach to Dresden was a rather racing "car." Quarter to eight [3/4 8], on time, we arrived at the railroad station. The bill was 5 Marks for the fare and 40 phenic (sp?) bridge toll. I paid the money including a tip for the coachman. I'm under the impression that the express train was faster than 3 years ago, because we arrived at Leipzig at quarter to 11am [3/4 11] & Hanover was a 2-hour stopover and I used the time from 4-6pm for sightseeing. At 8pm, I arrived at Bremen. Everything was nicely organized in regard to my luggage and my hotel. I stayed again in the Central Hotel & have in the first story a nice little room with a view to the garden. It is understood that we have had during the whole tour – very nice weather, all the time sunshine but not too warm. So it is today here in Bremen and the forecast from the North Sea predicts good weather. This morning I first arranged the ticket business. The people at the Lloyd office were very nice and no nit-pickers (penibel). Early tomorrow morning at 10 minutes to 8, the train will leave for Bremerhaven, which will bring all cabin passengers to the steamboat. The Fulda arrived already on Tuesday. It is supposed to be a very good ship with special comforts for the second [class] cabin. Now my dear parents, you can imagine that I have to think about you all the time and still the separation hurts. By the way, I am in a much better mood on this trip than 3 years ago. I think and I hope everything will turn out alright. Please both of you take care and do not have any unnecessary worries about me. Preferably think about me as "the travel uncle" (Reiseonkel). I will be alright. I made botanical studies yesterday from the railroad car. Unfortunately, rather superficial because the intense speed of the express train did not allow [me] to determine species. I was rather interested in a white flower in the swamp of the heath (Lüneburger). It grew there in such huge quantities, that the area glowed white. This flower should grow only in those peat swamps. This was told to me by one of my fellow travelers, they were a simple respectable couple. I think an elderly Pasteur and his wife who traveled from Hanover to Bremen. Again and again, I looked at the old gentleman with pleasure because strangely he had a resemblance [to my] beloved father. From Dresden to Hanover, I have had a young fine lady sitting opposite to me. She introduced herself as the daughter-in-law to the manufacturer Dietrich [pharmaceutical factory] in Helfenberg near Nieder-Poyritz. Now for today I have nothing more to report. All travel arrangements are under control. In Bremen hardly anything changed in those 3 years. The old Roland [a monument] still stands in front of the city hall. A short time ago I visited our agent Ehrhorn, Emden and Mayer, which the only present bookkeeper recognized me immediately. This time I did my affairs with tickets and luggage all by myself. Tomorrow, so God willing, we will go to sea and I will report my next adventures as soon as possible. Please stay healthy and receive [in mind] hearty greetings and kisses from your faithful,

Rudolf

An Bond der, Fulda, Kremerhaven

My Dear Parents,

Yesterday noon prior to the departure, there were only a few minutes left and therefore I could write only a short departure note. Due to the low tide, the Fulda stayed half-an-hour outside Bremerhaven. All passengers were brought out by 2 small steamboats. The magnificent ocean liner is designed differently as the "Saale" and "Aller" that I already know. The cabins are laid out for 4 persons. Those from the second-class are slightly smaller. I learned in the office at Bremen that I will have 2 cabin companions. Later I found out that this arrangement was not too bad; my 2 cabin mates are a fat Bavarian named Strasser from Eichstadt. Due to his furious dialect, often one cannot understand 1 word. The other is a 40 years young constable from Leese; near Bremen. He is the nephew of the 3rd helmsman of the Fulda. There are 2 bunks opposite the wall while I have a comfortable bed all to myself. It is located on the side of the hatch [like = porthole?]. With a fresh northerly breeze, soon we reached the outer Weser River. Then suddenly a very dense fog developed which stayed with us until sunset and therefore the voyage was interpreted for several hours. From approximately 4-6pm, the anchor was cast because the captain was very careful and he did not dare to enter the North Sea due to the dense fog. Probably between 6 and 7 we started with ½ steam, however, again and again we stopped because many fishing boats were around. In the 8-9 hours a little stronger wind came up and the horizon cleared totally. Now all night long we then had full steam. I felt no traces of seasickness. Just as a precaution, I held down with food [= didn't eat much] And I felt like a seaman with such a sea trip is routine one should not gloat, but it is really funny to see how strong courageous boasters turn quiet at the slightest breeze. By the way, there are only a few passengers – 22 in the first-class and 19 in the second-class, most people are emigration in the steerage [lower deck]. Then I slept rather comfortably and very well until this morning at 4am. The uninterrupted warnings of the fog horn indicated new fog. Right away we reduced to ½ steam and so we went on very slowly all Sunday because the fog did not disperse. Once said that we will reach Southampton this night, but I think that if we proceed as we do now – it will be Monday morning. Our steamboat does not move faster than a horse-driven wagon. But the precaution has to be praised, because it is of no concern whether we arrive 1 day later in America. The ship is really excellent and goes very smoothly also and we have rough sea. The Captain Meier is well-known as a very precautious man. Now when you have received this letter you have proof that we have passed the most dangerous part of the North Sea and the canal, because the mail will be posted in Southampton. By the way I like the second-class, there is no baggage difference to the first-class, where you find a bit more luxury. Otherwise the food and the accommodations are good. The next letter I will mail if God's willing, you will get from America and I will be glad to receive some news from you. I will read [that] you are in good health. Don't be afraid about me, I am in a very good mood and everything turns out well.

With hearty greetings I remain your faithful,

Rudolf

An Lond Dr, Fulda 17. Juni 1895.

My dear Parents!

Today I'm in the position to tell how the journey continued and I'm glad to tell you that I'm in the best of health and well-being was not bothered one moment. As it was predicted, the journey did not stay so comfortable as it was up to South Hampton. The old wrathful ocean insisted on his rights and was several days in a very bad mood, to such an extent that even the brave Fulda was brought extremely out of balance. Overall the journey was an average between two ocean journeys which I made previously and not as bad as the winter journey and not as nice as the return trip 3 years ago. All the time blew a violet northwesterly wind often accompanied with rain showers and once in a while alternating rain and sun. However, all the time rather cool on deck between 8 and 12°R. [Réaumur] Although the ship did not pitch and toss too badly, I experienced much worse situations; the majority of the passengers were seasick to such an extent that only 5 or 6 others could boast to be regular visitors of the dining room. Nothing could shake my well-being, not even the duets that could melt stones [which were] performed by my 2 cabin companions. Yesterday was the stormiest day that we had on the journey. Several times huge breakers went over the deck which forced all walkers down under deck. Early this morning, I made the observation that the ship was going much calmer and how was I surprised to see the smooth calm surface of the sea underneath a cloudless sky and a golden sun reflecting from the surface. A festive mood came over me that came to a high point when I became aware that today was my birthday. My good father and dear dear mother would certainly think about me. Now I hope God might bless me and the overall travel so sunny and lucky as the day is today. Due to the nice weather of today, the overall mood affected all the passengers and even the staff. This morning the first officer addressed me and told me if the weather continues we could already have breakfast tomorrow in New York. The trip in the second cabin did please me very much, there was no boasting (genierthat) and embarrassment like in the first cabin. The food is very good and plentiful and all in all one cannot complain. I made acquaintances with all other passengers, however, without intimate approaches [=no close friends] and I would be pleased to tell you 1 day more about interesting observations. In the saloon of the second cabin there is [by accident] no piano forte. However, I played twice already on the piano to which I was invited. This afternoon the tugboat captain is supposed to come on board. Therefore we will probably arrive in New York bay this coming night. I will post this letter in New York City. Now my dear parents, please write as soon as possible, because I like to know how you are doing and I trust that both of you are in good health and well. Please be careful to avoid a cold and heavy labor. Stay away from dust and heat that you will not fall ill. Don't worry about me and do not believe news media reports and diseases and accidents and other terrible things; I will bring this enterprise for our good and noble affair through with energy and wisdom, and will use all my strengths about this you can be sure. You really don't have to bother about me. About my further adventure I will write on a regular basis and remain with earnest greetings and kisses.

Yours faithfully,

Rudolf

My dear Parents!

I hope you received my yesterday's telegram on time and I am glad to send you today another report. Monday we had beautiful weather and therefore an excellent journey. In the early morning hours we passed Sandy Hook. The country houses near the coast are located with beautiful vegetation, which were lit by the morning sun. This presented an unbelievably beautiful view, after a short pause to do some government business [probably with customs], we arrived on the 8th morning hour [8am] happily at the pier of Hoboken. I was ready for a complicated customs procedures, however, the officer was a good man. He was interested only in small parcels and contents in my luggage. They did not contain anything liable to duty. On the other hand, he didn't even ask to see the microscope. The china vase he didn't take into his hand, he just asked if I pay for it. After he surveyed everything, he said "alright" and I passed everything duty-free. Next to the custom office was a big sign with the tariffs for passenger coaches, I found out that a horse-drawn carriage from the ship to New York Central station was about $5. Therefore I made a different arrangement. I received a receipt for my piece of luggage and handed in to an express company for fast delivery to my address at the Botanical Museum in Cambridge. Then I started walking in the direction to New York City, carrying my hand luggage. For 3¢, I crossed the Hudson with the ferry and then I proceeded conveniently to Broadway. There I asked a policeman for the best streetcar connection to the Central Station. This worked well because he pointed at a nearly carriage which brought me for 5¢ after a ½ hour drive at 10:30 am to the station. There I learned that an express train to Boston would leave at 11am – sharply. For $5, I bought a ticket and traveled through Connecticut to Boston having beautiful weather [the whole trip]. I arrived in Boston @ 5:30pm. After some investigation I heard that there are no hotels in Cambridge, only pensions for students, etc. This is amazing because Cambridge has 68,000 inhabitants. Therefore I decided to stay for the time being in Boston. I looked for a conveniently located hotel. There are two kinds of American hotels. The first category operates under the "American Plan," this means food and lodgings, the other hotels operate under the "European Plan," lodging only. One rents a room, but is not obligated to dine in the hotel. Since I was already sort of tired, I went with my two pieces of luggage to Park Square where the Cambridge streetcars stay. It was my intention to ask in a restaurant. There I saw a big sign, Thorndike Hotel – European Plan; I went to this place and got a room for $1 daily and I was safe. First I restored myself, took the little box with the vase and went with the electrical car to Cambridge. Punctually at 8pm, I stood in front of No 10 Craigie Street, the house of Professor Goodale. He received me amicably. Mrs. Goodale enjoyed very much the beautiful present from my mother. By accident I have had the opportunity to do something in Bremen for the little son (a number of old stamps). The son had great joy over this present. The Professor praised the choice of my hotel and expressed regret that I did not announce my arrival by a telegram and did not stay as a guest in his house. However I have no doubt that everybody was glad that I made my hotel arrangement. The Professor asked me to stay here for a couple of days to study the plants in Cambridge and Boston, as well as Massachusetts. Since the trip to Cambridge is only 5¢, I will decline any hospitalities and stay for the time being in my hotel in Boston. I believe this arrangement pleases my friends as well. Today I saw the Museum and everything is beautiful. There are upright standing boxes squeezed in and filling the hall to quite an

extent. However there is still sufficient space to place all models which we will prepare. My last things [models] arrived very well and pleased very much. So often discuss dirty stories about the travel escort I told today the Professor. Now he knows everything and agrees that we will not speak anymore about this affair. He has a young man, a poor student, named Blankinship who traveled extensively with great success in plant collecting. He will join me on my journeys and assist in collecting. However in all respects I stay independently and will travel on my own. The first tours we will do in Massachusetts. Today I was with Professor Goodale in the Arboretum of Harvard University where several beautiful bushes were in full bloom. Tomorrow I will start drawing and in a few days when we are through with local plants, we go to the Alleghenies where I will have the opportunity to study there – the flora all the way down to North Carolina. For today, I'm coming to an end, wishing that these lines will meet you in good health and hoping to receive from you a letter soon. In the near future I will write again. I feel very well with the summer weather.

Hearty greetings and kisses from your Rudolf

Boston, 21, June 1895.

My Dear Parents!

Already today I am able to tell you that I adapt myself to the New World very well and I'm fine in every regard. Professor Goodale and his family are treating me with great amiability and attention. Already I dinned twice in his house by his invitation and he made sure all my wishes were fulfilled and my stay in America agreeable as possible. Yesterday I started a little bit with my studies, however my luggage arrived not before the afternoon and therefore I could only finish a few things. I work at the Museum in the same room and at the same table as 3 years ago. This is very close to the model exhibition, but very quite (undisturbed). The building is open at 7 in the morning and it's closed in the afternoon at 5:30pm. In other words, this is my working time. Today I was already better arranged and in spite of critical items at the beginning, I studied 8 specimens. Today I was obliged to quit at 5pm because the Professor and I went to Boston to see a splendid exhibition of flowers, wild plants, roses, vegetables, giant strawberries, etc. which interested me very much. Splendid orchids were exhibited. Tomorrow I'm going to receive a number of wild plants from the mountains in New Hampshire from the exhibition for my studies, things that are less beautiful, but are very rare and for America - of great interest. Tomorrow I will diligently study those and in the evening I will leave with Mr. Blankinship to the swamps on the coast of Massachusetts, near Plymouth to collect plants there on Sunday. The Professor insists on joining me for my own safety and finally this rather agreeable young man, [who] made many experiences in his lifetime and seems to be of a different category than the other previous colleagues, although rather suitable and good-natured. Overall I will keep wisely my independence. What a difference from my earlier escorts [which] can be seen from his comments. Mr. Blankinship, in the presence of Dr. Goodale, where he was discussing my relationship [to Goodale] said: "Tell me whatever you need in regard to collecting and keeping plants. I am your assistant and will fulfill all your wishes and this will be confirmed by the Professor. Everything seems to be very well. Beautiful warm in America. I bought in Bremen for 40p a small but very functional thermometer which gives me great pleasure to read the temperature in Réaumur and Centigrade, because in America they all use great numbers in Fahrenheit. During our journey on the trip we have had 8-12°R when we arrived in New York on my trip to Boston. I found 22°R in the shade. Here in Boston and Cambridge 24° to 25°R, and in my sleeping room, I have had today 22°R. I will cancel my room in the Thorndike Hotel tomorrow morning and probably after my return from Plymouth, I will rent an apartment in Cambridge. Very soon I will write again and will remain with hearty greetings - Your Rudolf

My dear Parents!

Today only a few lines to tell you that I'm fine in every respect. I have no problems with my health. But now I'm waiting anxiously to receive a letter from you. I already spoke with Professor Goodale. He will send all letters to me wherever I might be. This afternoon, I will travel again, this time to Southwick to see Gillet's Nursery and some beautiful valleys in the neighborhood. Probably I will not return before tomorrow evening or Monday, otherwise I'm illustration and studying diligently and yesterday I made my 32 $ ^{nd} $ piece [drawing]. For a beginning, this is enough to do in 5 $ \frac{1}{2} $ working days. Yesterday I had a very enjoyable evening with Mr. Deane in Cambridge. This is the gentleman who wrote in such a nice way about our models after he checked them with a magnifying glass. I was treated with the greatest respect. Now I have to come to an end because the time is limited. I will write again in the near future. In the hope that both of you are very well and healthy and at home everything will be alright.

I remain with hearty greetings.

Your,

Rudolf

My dear Parents!

Although I cannot report much news, I am going to spend my free evening hours to be with you in my thoughts and to send you my greetings by letter. Still I have a lot of free time, from 7am I drew diligently in my quite laboratory in the museum. The only interpretations are the meals that I take in a student club, the so-called Foxcroft Club and in the nearest vicinity of the museum. This restaurant is managed by students and one gets the best food at half the price in comparison to other restaurants in Cambridge and Boston. The 3 meals are very fine food a /a carte costs less than 3 Marks (usually each one 80-90 p each). While I'm studying the time passes fast: before I realize it, at 5:00 comes the museum negro, James, who locks the rooms. Now the regulations are so strict that no one - not even the museums official should not stay longer. Until approximately 8pm, we have a bright daylight. When we have good weather I take the pleasure for a hike or I ride to Boston for a glass of beer. Certainly everything in a decent and reasonable manner. I have complete freedom to do as I like. I rarely visit Professor Goodale's house unless he expressly invites me for a supper. He continues to be very friendly with me and the separation of business and pleasure is right and I like it very much this way. And probably the people like it too. My Russian landlords are rather agreeable and friendly folks. They are either from Lithuania or Latvia. Probably more Slavic than German. They told me they emigrated because - as a result of a conflict with Russian officials who expelled him from his teaching job. How long time I will stay here in Cambridge is still uncertain. Travel plans are established everyday and postponed and changed quickly. The main reason is that I am supposed to study everything in the vicinity first. Today I studied the 41st pieces [drawings]. The tour to Southwick I told you about in my last letter has been postponed as well. The Professor reasoned it that the people in Connecticut - Thale are the strictest Sunday saints in America and therefore no one is allowed to enter. Yesterday we [land Mr. Blankinship] were on another tour in Cambridge country to see old historical places like Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. After ½ hour ride in the electric car we walked happily over 6 hours through fields and woods until a funny American thunderstorm ended our pleasure. We returned from Concord to Cambridge by train. Mr. Blankinship proved another time to be the right man which I need now very much. Besides different water lilies, 2 species of Utricularia, a very strange water plant which is very difficult to force into bloom, we found in full blossom. Mr. Blankinship undressed without any hesitation and pulled out these plants, although the water reached his hips. If I would have been alone, I never would have done this. I think in the future everything will turn out alright and I have no reason to complain. He is a poor devil and has no status here in Cambridge and does not dare speak up. I spoke frankly with Professor Goodale about my former companions and I made him understand that the arrogance, rudeness and gossip of my companions would damage the whole enterprise. The Professor knows and understands this totally and assured me that everything will be well-arranged. The companion is nothing but an aid for me - to serve me and to be for my protection. So far I did not see the local Botanical Garden, today I received a list from there with approximate 150 blooming plants. When I and the Professor went through the list together, we found out that at most only 4 would be usable. The Scottish inspector who still works in the same position at $100/month has been married for 1 year. I met him once at the Goodale's house and spoke to him briefly. Again I felt right away disgusted about him by the way, his character is known here by several people. My present companion once did a collecting trip with him and had a very bad experience as he told me frankly. It seems that Professor Goodale knows now the subject, however, that he is a good supervisor. Now dear parents, this is how the time is passing – passing very rapidly making many fine experiences and

getting impressions. In spite of yesterday's extended hike, today, I am not in the least tired and I am strong and healthy. For a week, the temperature is rather moderate and agreeable after a heavy thunderstorm, normally not more than $ 20^{\circ} $R. In Cambridge and Boston they prepare for the national holiday July $ 4^{th} $. Woodpiles for bond fires are erected, shooting guns are tested and more of those wild things. Maybe I will be here on Thursday and experience the whole spectacle in Cambridge. It is now for sure that we will go at the end of the week to North Carolina. I'm looking forward to it. The money situation has been arranged in such a way that the Professor gave me the surplus, which I returned in American currency without even counting it. I'm supposed to pay my rent in Cambridge with this amount as long as the money lasts. When the money is gone, fresh one will be delivered. I cannot ask for a better arrangement. However, in no way am I extravagant. Since I'm longing for a letter from you to learn how you are doing and whether you are alright. To my loving mother, I send hearty congratulations and a thousand kisses for her name-date. I hope that this letter will arrive in time for this date. Now I'm coming to an end.

Your faithful,

Rudolf

Dear Mr. Blaschka,

At your departure you entrusted me with the physical well-being of your loved ones. Unfortunately, I cannot give you good news regarding your father. Previously I had visited him several times and found him well. On Thursday, June 27 $ ^{th} $ at 11pm, I was called for him and diagnosed a stroke which left his left side paralyzed. I visited him daily and gave all the necessary instructions. Your good mother nursed him most faithfully day and night, not leaving his bedside. However, this morning, a second stroke followed which left his right side paralyzed as well. I arrived again at 1pm and while I was taking his pulse, a third stroke hit him – it is getting difficult for me to describe it – the end followed! Your good father is no longer with us! Quietly, and without pain, he went to our Father in heaven!

Naturally, your poor mother is heartbroken and confused today. I will do everything in my weak powers to consult you and her and to help you in every respect. This I can assure you. At the least, she is one treasure you have entrusted to me. With these lines, I express my hearty condolence, our infinitely good Father in heaven above, our master and savior, is the only one who can consul. I am asked to convey hearty greetings from your dear mother. I remain yours faithfully and most devotedly,

Your grieving doctor,

Dr. Hartung

My dear Parents,

Finally I bought the Southwick excursion (partie) to a lucky end and arrived yesterday evening safe and sound in Cambridge. I traveled again accompanied by my assistant Blankinship. In spite of my earlier aversion against companionship, this time I rather liked to have it in a foreign country a useful man with me. The day before yesterday at noon, we traveled via Springfield, there we had a 1 hour stopover, to Westfield Mass in order to stay there overnight. There in “whiptown” (Westfield has approximately 8,000 inhabitants and dealing mostly with whip fabrication.) I experienced a so-far unknown spectacle, the evening before July 4th, the national holiday. It was really a witch’s Sabbath, which was enjoyed by young and old and both sexes. From every house pistil shots burst past my ears; step by step, the streets were full of waves of people walking up and down that were dangerous due to burning firecrackers. Most of the young people, among them many young maidens with long trumpets, the national 4th of July “horns” with which they made an unbelievable noise and blew in everybody’s ears. Others have had bells or other noise making instruments that they pulled behind them with ropes. On top of all the blowing, ringing, and shooting, there are small firearms bursting small cannons, fireworks, rockets, and bond fires. One really could get scared because as usual in America the whole town was built of small wooden houses. On top of all, one heard national songs from a choir and different musical instruments. The turmoil lasted all night long, although I could not go to bed before midnight. All and all I’ve had a lot of fun. The next morning we drove to Southwick to botanize there and to visit the gardener Gillett. His nursery was not as big as one should expect due to his advertisement and his big catalogues. In fact not as big as the nursery of Müller in Striesen. The buildings there in the middle of the small village exists of a small shack & 1 barn (a small greenhouse). Gillett was at home and very friendly helpful. He showed us everything and has had different American plants which mostly he finds in the neighboring forest. Other ornamental plants he buys mostly in Europe. We took 3 or 4 plants with us. He didn’t ask for money, however, after we urged him to be asked for a half dollar. Then we walked more than 3 hours back to Westfield where we really found and collected some nice things in the forest. We arrived by train late in the afternoon in Boston, where the festival mood was due to rain, was rather reduced. The burning of firecrackers was mostly impossible, but the spectacle was similar to Westfield and in the apartment at the quiet University quarters in Cambridge, I heard the shooting and the noise nearby – all night long. Even today, having nice weather, the festivity continues. Today all newspapers are about accidents and the uproar. In Boston, a fight occurred that started at the parade yesterday afternoon. One man was shot, several wounded and others almost beaten to death by the police. From now on, I will always stay away from all such crowds. Today I continued my studies quietly and drew the 51st piece. Soon I hope I can report from the beginning [of fieldwork] to the southern mountains. We will decide about the organization as soon as Professor Goodale returns from a business trip in the next few days.

With hearty greetings, I remain your,

Rudolf

My dear Rudolf!

We have received all your letters and the telegram and we are very pleased that you survived the sea journey happily and healthy. The [Your] good father's intention was to write the first letter to America right away, but "Man proposes, God disposes" — everything else you have probably [learned] from Dr. Hartung's letter. The Almighty has hit us heavily. Now we hope He will give us the strength to carry the burden. We have had no notion that it would go this way. After the first stroke, the doctor gave us hope the old gentleman would recover within 6-8 weeks. However it went differently, it got worse and worse. The delirium became worse and I felt miserable and was in total despair. We never let him alone for one minute. Our maid was very helpful. She helped me in every act of nursing. I never left his bed, day and night, and none of the time was I in total despair, still hoping for improvement. Tuesday I was in total despair and he was very restless. In his delirium, his intention was to go to New York because there it would be much nicer than Hosterwitz and his Rudolf would be with him and he could work together with him [you]. His breathing became shorter until he began gasping. This went on the whole night until Wednesday at noontime. Then came the doctor and then the worst happened while he was taking his pulse, he fell asleep softly. Now imagine my despair. My heart could have broken in losing our good father and the only child in a foreign country. However, very soon good friends showed up and helped me in every respect. The doctor reported it right away to the governing authorities who came right away with Mr. Petzold and offered their help. In the same way that Mr. Kunert and [Mr.] Baumeister did, as well as the administrator of the post office of Pillnitz [and] furthermore, the Court Chaplain to Prince Georg. On Saturday afternoon at 4:00 we carried him to the grave. It was a very nice funeral with many wreaths and condolences. The priest made a long nice eulogy and everybody tried to express their sympathy to me. However, there is no comfort for me, maybe time will heal the heavy wound. I placed an announcement in the Anzeiger [the local newspaper]. A big laurel wreath with tea roses came from the Schaberschul family. And the Nachrichten [newspaper] gave a long obituary. Furthermore, in Aicher [Bohemia], I told both relatives about the loss. Then my sister came in time for the funeral. Probably she will stay here for a few days. For me, the maid is just right because it is so deserted in the house. Now my only beloved son, we both will be terribly afraid until we are together again. Now please write as soon as possible about what your plans will be. Now I'm so afraid for you and I pray to God that he protects you and brings you back happy and healthy to your homeland. I feel sorrow for you, but we have to console each other and God will strengthen you and me.

I hug you and kiss you with hearty greetings from your poor Mother.

Cambridge Mass, 8. Juli 1895.

My Dear Parents!

Yesterday, Sunday, I spent in an agreeable way. To obey the American laws in regard to Sunday rest, I did not work. Rather we made interesting excursions where all the time I see something new and have an opportunity to collect new plant material. For example, yesterday I went into another area of Massachusetts, northeast of Cambridge. First we went to Medford by the electric car [trolley] and then we walked through the Medford Park over small hills and through forests very rich with blueberries. After 3 hours, we walked to Melrose and then we proceeded to the coast via electric car up to Lynn. This place with about 4,000 inhabitants is a nice tourist area and well-known resort area. The main attraction however, is that this place is the biggest and most important shoe making town of the New England states. We walked on the beach and roamed through the big peninsula, Nahant. The resort areas at the beach [possibly separate areas for swimming, camping etc.], [held] probably more than a 1,000 people resting and strolling, mostly people on a Sunday outing to enjoy the clear sea air and to listen to the music of the “swimming?” bands on the sand dunes and salt marshes of the quiet peninsula we found a few strange beach plants. Then we visited a beautiful vantage point on the cliffs of Nahant and then we drove by steamboat back to Boston. We had had beautiful weather, maybe in the morning, rather warm. Altogether, I marched again in total of 6 – 7 hours. Today, I'm fine and without any trace of tiredness.

Today it was the hottest day during my stay. Now at 10pm the thermometer in my room still shows 24°R. After I illustrated the 58th piece today, Professor Goodale drove with me in a one-horse carriage to Belmont to visit to Mr. Atkins (millionaire and owner of a sugar plantation in Cuba and a great friend of our models). We were very cordially received and after the return to Cambridge, I had to take supper with Prof. Goodale. Now we are preparing for our departure to the southern states. Probably after tomorrow or Thursday we will start. Soon I will write about it. Otherwise I can tell you that I am fine in every respect. I did not receive one of your letters yet. I'm longing for it in order to learn how you are doing.

With hearty greetings and kisses,

I remain your,

Rudolf

Cambridge Mass. 10. Juli 1895.

My Dear Parents!

Today is an important day for me because the total plan of my journey in America has been finally fixed. I have studied [everything], every plant in the state of Massachusetts and Cambridge is growing this season. Altogether there are 61 species and now I have to try to find at least 300 new things. For this purpose, we organized the details of our travel plan, however, more changes might be necessary. Therefore, I'm in the position to tell you how our trip probably will go. This evening at 7pm (this is our time in Germany 12:75 [sic]) I'm traveling with my companion Mr. Blankinship – first to Washington [D.C.] to make a sightseeing tour in this important location. Then we will continue by steamboat to Norfolk where we will stay for a few days pending on the number of new [plant] material. Then we proceed from this Wilmington location to North Carolina, and then further to Marion in the high mountains. Probably there we will stay one week and afterwards we will travel to Chattanooga Tennessee. A roaming excursion to Georgia and Alabama is not impossible. Then we cross the Mississippi to Arkansas, and Missouri, and Oklahoma (Indian Territory). From there probably we take a direct train via Texas to the capital of Mexico where I will meet my second companion Mr. Pringle. We hope to find in this a rich plant species country, over 100 new things to study. Mr. Pringle is a beautiful and quiet man between 45-50 years old, who traveled for the last 20 years, annually to Mexico and the most important collector of Mexican plants. He has a great reputation in America. He just returned to his homeland in Vermont. Due to Dr. Goodale's telegram he showed up in the Museum today, therefore we were in a position to discuss everything in detail. He will return to Mexico at the end of August. He will be my companion-collector and assistant for several weeks and be reimbursed by Mrs. And Miss Ware. He said it is right now the best time for the vegetation there. Later rain in the mountains will impede the excursion. If God willing, I will return home to you, via Cambridge. Please do not worry, everything will be alright. Please write as soon as possible in order to receive news which I long from you. I will send you letters from every location where I will stay for some time. Now I have to close because the time for departure in coming.

With hearty greetings and kisses.

Your faithful,

Rudolf

My dear Parents!

As I reported yesterday by postcard, I arrived in good shape early yesterday. We passed the capitol of Washington, and also Philadelphia and Baltimore in the daytime so I had a general view of both cities, but the stay in Washington, I enjoyed most. The town is one of the most beautiful ones in which I have seen in the United States with the spacious straight construction, many gardens, parks, and magnificent buildings. First we visited the Capitol with the different state departments, the Congressional chambers of the House of Representatives, and mounted the copula to enjoy the beautiful view over the town and neighborhood. Next we went to the National Museum, the Botanical Garden, etc. and found friends in the botanical state departments from which we received advice for our future enterprises. With hesitation we parted at 7 in the evening from beautiful Washington to go by steamboat on the Potomac River down to Norfolk, which turned out to be a very nice pleasure trip. In Norfolk, we arrived in the morning, but we proceeded right away to Suffolk, a small town in southern Virginia. There we should have better chances for botanizing in the forest of this flatland. After we found a good private boarding house, we roamed all day long around the neighborhood and found some nice new things. The temperature here in the south is more moderate than I thought, probably reduced due to a thunderstorm [and is] not more than a few 20 degrees R in the shade. In the fields, one mostly finds corn, tobacco and cotton-wool. The potato fields are often destroyed by the Colorado beetle which appears here to the same extent as to the north. I collected this beetle besides many other species as a curiosity. The forests are often real jungles, full of lianas, Bignonia radicans, Passiflora, etc. ripe and very very tasty blackberries are now here by the million. The design of the town reminds me in several ways of Jamaica; a great deal of the inhabitants are Negros. Now tomorrow I will continue to study and illustrate again. We will not stay here for a long time because we do not have sufficient time for the plains and will soon continue to the Carolinas. Soon I will write again and remain with hearty greetings.

Yours,

Rudolf

Suffolk (Virginien) 15. Juli 1895.

##### My dear Parents!

Originally we [he and field companion William Blankinship] planned to stay here only a very short time, however, we added a few days. Therefore I write a few lines to you from Virginia. With my companion, we roamed through the neighborhood and botanized it. We again found some new species of plants. Yesterday, we almost reached the borderline of North Carolina, a country in which we will have our quarters soon. Today I drew diligently again and finished No. 70 [Carex spp.] For tomorrow another 4 or 5 species are in preparation. Tomorrow evening we plan to leave Suffolk and head in the direction of Southern Pines, a well-known very healthy forest in North Carolina. The change in studying and making excursions is rather healthy for me and I feel very well doing it. However, I wish the illustrating and studying would go much faster. But often I find totally strange species of plants in my hands that require a through study. Mostly I think it is good to investigate everything locally instead of hasty sketches. Because those are very hard to read later, it is my intention to finish as much as possible.

As I mentioned in my last letter, many things here remind me of Jamaica, negro faces all over, wild magnificent vegetation, but without Palms, huge quantities of lightening bugs and the chirping of grasshoppers. By the way it is rather warm here, the temperature at 10 pm is still 23° Réaumur.¹ Well in the Carolinian mountains there will be less heat. Whatever [there is] I get used to everything and right now I am enjoying the tremendous heat. I'm glad I do not have to travel to northern climates. That's all I can report for today. Through the days I often think about you. I'm pretty sure a letter is on it's way, but it will hardly arrive before next week. Since I requested that the first mail be sent to Marion in North Carolina when I was with Prof. Goodale, they might not be there for 5 – 6 days. Please send all your letters to the address we agreed upon, in care of Prof. Goodale. He will reroute everything to specific places. I will now close with hearty greetings and kisses.

Yours,

Rudolf

My dear Mother!

I am horribly devastated ("knocked to the ground") from the news of our good father's death. I received the letter only today and interrupted my studies immediately in order to return to you as soon as possible. What a terrible blow. In the beginning, [I was] stunned and couldn't grasp it all. Now I'm longing to comfort my dearest little mother. To see you at least healthy, I will manage to travel home as soon as possible. May God comfort both of us. We have to think it all was God's will. I write this in great haste because I have to leave this place in a few minutes. Please give my regards to Dr. Hartung and the other friends who helped so much by their friendship. Please give everyone my hearty thank you. Now my dear good little mother, please take good care about yourself so that you do not fall ill. I'm coming - so God willing, [I will] soon will be home.

With hearty greetings,

Your

Rudolf

My dear Professor Goodale; Your valued letter is at hand, and I perceive from it that you and Uliis Ware have thought much about the year 1897. I did not at all intend, through the mention of it, to quicken unpleasant memories, or indeed, to undertake a campaign against Uliis Ware's Portennonmanie. I think that the deficiency at that time may be attributed entirely to the insufficient arrangements of the contract, and to myself. I was so completely absorbed by the ideal interest in this work, that I completely forgot my practical interest in it. The shipment following that of January 1896 had lasted until the middle of October, in spite of strenuous exertions, and there was therefore very little new work under way, when in December 1896, I received your letter with the question as to how the payment stood, whether and how I wished to have it. I understood your question as a claim on the portion of models due after the July payment, 1896, which however, it was impossible for me to furnish in so short a time. I made you the proposal, or left it open to you, to pay according to the number of models, according to the shipments. You tacitly accepted this, as did

Miss Ware, to whom likewise, I had written at Newyear of the

My dear Mr. Blaschka:

Your letter of July 11th reached my office while I was absent from Boston. I did not return to Boston until this week, and now take the first opportunity to deal with the matters referred to in your letter.

I regret exceedingly that it has been impossible for you to induce the authorities of the Reichsbank to recognize the peculiar circumstances affecting your situation and your arrangement with Harvard University and with Miss Ware.

Under the circumstances I see no alternative except for me to submit to the representatives of Harvard University and Miss Ware the letter of the Reichsbank which you enclosed, together with your instructions that I immediately convert your securities into cash and deliver the proceeds to The First National Bank of Boston for the account specified in the letter of the Reichsbank. You will understand, of course, and I assume that the officials of the Reichsbank will equally understand, that this will take a little time, even if it is ultimately decided by the persons who must be consulted here, that it is legally possible to comply with the requirements of the Reichsbank. You

may assure the latter officials that I will give the matter my immediate attention and will proceed with all reasonable speed.

Please instruct me further on one point concerning which I am in doubt, by reason probably of my insufficient knowledge of German. Does the Reichsbank require the transmittal of those funds only which were received since July 12, 1931, or does the law apply also to the funds already on hand on that date which were accumulated during the preceding years? I will endeavor to take the necessary steps here which will enable me to follow your instructions in either alternative immediately on my receiving further word from you.

Much more even than by your disastrous financial experiences I am troubled by the news of your serious illness. I hope earnestly that the joy of complete recovery has by this time made up for your suffering and the anxiety of yourself and Mrs. Blaschka, and that you will have no recurrence of ill health.

I wish very much that I could repeat my happy experience of last summer in calling on you and Mrs. Blaschka. That, however, is a pleasure which I shall have to defer until some future time.

I have now recovered completely from my illness, and

Mother and all the rest of my family are in good health. Mother

in particular would join me in warmest greetings to you and Mrs. Blaschka if she knew of my writing to you.

Sincerely yours,

My daughter, Miss Mary L. Ware, and I, offer for your acceptance a collection of glass-models of plants, flowers, and analytical details of vegetable structure, now in process of construction by the well-known artists, Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka, of Germany.

A contract for the construction of the models was arranged and signed in Dresden, on April last, by L. and R. Blaschka, on the one part, and by Professor Goodale, on the other part, and meets our complete approval. We accept-- assume in full the responsibilities regarding payments of the sums mentioned in the contract, and we shall provide the necessary amounts on the dates specified. The collection was begun two years ago,and will require for its completion ten (10) years from July of the present year.

On the -84 24th. inst. Rudolf received at Chimney Rock, N.C. two letters forwarded from Cambridge. Both announced the death of his father. He telegraphed at once saying that he should arrive in Cambridge, on Friday, 26th., and asking me to secure passage for him in the next express steamer for Germany. He arrived at nine o'clock, Friday, he said that from the first of July, he had been overpowered by a dread of some impending calamity, and on his return from Westfield had a long talk with me about possible changes in the work. That was about the fifth of July; after a few days here, he went with Mt. Blankinship to Virginia and worked at Suffolk, and afterwards in N.C. at Sothern Pines. From this place they went to Chimney Rock. On approaching the letter town, Mr. Blaschka said to Blankinship that he could see two letters with black seals, and hardly had the Post Office been read before he had the bad news in his hand.

In talking with me at the Museum, he said he could hardly think of resuming his work with his father absent from the

studio, but "I must find consolation in work now". He asked me

what arrangement would be agreeable to me now that the contract had

expired with his father's death, and I answered that Mrs. and Miss

Ware had left too much responsibility to me. I felt unwilling to

complete any new arrangement until I had seen both of the patrons.

But I said that in a conversation not long since with Miss Ware,

I had asked her wishes in case of any disability of either of the

artists, and she had agreed with me that unless the number of models

fell far below fifty per annum, she and her mother would prefer to have

the original contract price stand, because they would both feel that

the artists were doing all they could. This seemed to please him so

greatly that I ventured to prepare a letter to him asking whether he

would be willing to continue the preparation of the models on the same

pecuniary basis, making all he could in the year without any injury to

his health. He then asked me to fill out a formal letter in the same

way, and to add a formal agreement for him to sign, subject to the

approval of Mrs. and Miss Ware. He then signed the contract.

At ten thirty we went over to the Steamship office and paid for the stateroom, and then went to the Albany station, from which place he went at eleven, to New York, to sail next day.

He gave me the letters from his doctor and his — he told me about his mother's letter, expressing what we all felt, that it was strangely they had not telegraphed.

His father was taken ill on the 28th. ultimo, and when the doctor arrived at midnight, he was found to have had a shock affecting the left side. From this he rallied, but on the 2d. inst. he had one on the right side, and he passed away in the doctor's arms in the afternoon, having been unconscious from the first. The funeral was conducted by the catholic priest, and was attended by large floral numbers of people from Dresden. The decorations sent were very remarkable. The notices in the German papers are very appreciative.

Rudolf learned also from the doctor that his mother was ill from the excitement, and urged him to hasten home.

Dear Madame,

My mother and I have been happy to receive your highest esteemed letter and beg to express to yourself and Mrs. Ware our most heartfelt thanks for your very kind sympathy. The comfort by so noble, sympathizing friends is like a sunblink to us in our sad time. It has been terrible indeed for both of us to be bereft so suddenly of the dear father and under such circumstances. When we planned my journey there was no idea to think even of the possibility of such an accident. We found that the material remaining from my journey should cover only two more shipments, and when, owing to your great generosity, the second journey was secured, my father often expressed the hope, he wished to be able to construct with me also the new models with good health till 1900. But man proposes, god disposes. I shall never forget the day when I received the ominous letter in North Carolina. Our friends had div�uated my mother from telegraphing to me, which was well meant as the effect should have been too fearful to me. Remarkable was a certain strange presentiment with me of some mischief menacing me. On the road to Chimney Rock, the place where I expected letters I was so dejected, thinking incessantly of the possibility of illness with father.

or mother, but the terrible blow on the next day came though unprepared. This misbelief I had not ventured to think of. Now it was dreadful to me to know my dear mother alone in this situation, The fright and grief on the unforeseen death of the father (he died while the Doctor felt his pulse and expressed all good hopes) had made her ill. To I returned in double anxiety and grief. But God had mercy with us. The had got better already when she had received my telegram from Washington that I come immediately, and today I am most happy to state that she has entirely recovered. Of course it will last for years before the wound in our hearts will be healed. Our family-life has been so most intimate and cordial and we shall never forget our good father. The resting now on the Hosterwith cemetery. A fine wall-monument of Pirna sandstone and Genite adorn his grave, and next spring I shall plant some American flowers there to the memory of his last work to which he devoted the last strength of his life. I have sought comfort in my study of nature again, nature with the eternal laws of coming and passing away, producing and perishing, to which all beings are subdued. SHORT SKETCH of the LIFE of L. & R. BLASCHKA.

Leopold Blaschka is born in 1822 (May 27) at Eohmisch-Aicha (town in the northern Bohemia) as the youngest son of Joseph Blaschka, a mechanician and artificer renowned as a specialist in electric apparatus, lightning-conductors, etc., as well as in glass-work (the workmanship in glass being herediantary in the family.)

L. B. found his first instruction at the grammar-school of his birth-town and was then introduced into the study of natural history (this becoming his favorite science) by the opportunity of libraries and classically educated teachers. Later on the academic painter Elsner who lived in his father's house gave him lessons in painting, and advised him earnestly to turn painter. But as his father decidedly liked him to turn a goldsmith he acquired the technical faculties in cutting and setting precious stones etc., gold, and silver work, by a some-years sojourn near Turnall (Bohemia). When returned at home he managed united with his father and after his father's death alone to mix the metal and glass-work in manufacturing fancy articles for export houses. However this monotonic business did not satisfy him, he was more and more occupied with the study of Natural History by collecting and painting objects of Nat. History. 1853 he undertook specially on account of his

health a trip to North America, and partially in the business of

the said Bohemian export-houses. What he saw during the long

voyage became later on of great importance to him. After his

return to Bohmisch-Kicha 1854 he followed his natural impulse and

made (whilst inspecting his own small metal-work-manufacture driven

on with several workmen) the first glass-models of plants. The

botanist Prince Camille de Rohan who owns a great garden and castle

in Schrood not far from Bohmisch-Aicha, saw the first of these

artificial plants and was so much pleased with their truth-to-nature that he ordered his gardener to give to L. B. all material,

complete flowers, even of the rarest Orchids gratis for his studies by which L. B. completed till 1862 a collection of about 60 species of Orchids modelled in glass that he first exhibited in Prince Rohan's palace in Prague and afterwards 1863 in the Botanic Gardens of Dresden. (Many of these specimens came afterwards into the possession of the (now burnt-off) Botanic collection of Liege).

1863 removed to Dresden, L. B. did not proceed to make such flowers in glass, but he made now exclusively other glasswork; artificial sea-anemones (by coincidence of suggestions from different sides) at first for the purpose to form artificial marine-aquariums for the Dresden Natural History Museum.

The Director Ludwin Reichenbach protected the young enterprise and prophesied always a great future success. By suggestions of L. Blaschka who had 1853 had the opportunity of drawing

some Medusae (Physalia, Pelagia Aequorea) during a some-weeks-calm

on the Atlantic the collection was increased by some models of

Medusae and the (already formerly made) land-mollusks. With

success he made these models for many museums and schools. In

1870 his only son Rudolph Blaschka (born 1857 June 17th (at Bohmisch-Aicha) educated in Dresden) entered the business as apprentice.

R. B. was bred from the early youth in natural-science

having all opportunities for study and he became the only assistant of his father (being the only pupil his father ever had

Dear Friend,

In answer to your questions about the origin of our family and my father's first flower-work I think it best giving you a sketch of all I know of our family. So you can use of it what you find suitable for your purpose, and perhaps you do not find it too tedious to look over this tale of the course of life of a whole family, though it contains many particulars not belonging to the mentioned points. I beg to tell these particulars to you as to our proved highly appreciated friend.

The presumption of the Venetian origin of our family and the knowledge of the eldest Blaschkas is based upon tradition, tales, transmitted by the father to the children since many centuries. A cousin of my grandfather's, the old city-major J. Blaschka of Liebenall in North-Bohemia, a wholesale-merchant and renowned manufacturer in Bohemia glass-stones has troubled himself a good deal in searching after the first origin of the family and he has pursued it back to the ancient Roman times. But my grandfather, a man, free of any pretension and pride of ancestry did not pay any attention to this search and told the history to my father just as I do it by these lines. In the first half of the fifteenth century a man was registered at Prague with the name Blasch-

ka as an artifician in decorative glass-work who was said to come

from Venice. The name Blaschka (Blazka) is a genuine Slavotshechish term and a translation of the Latin christian name Blasius. Probably this translation has taken place in those times

of extreme Slavismus but anything else about this point cannot be

proved; that is too long ago. The descendants of this Blashka

have carried on glass-working and glass-painting since further, but

the tradition says that often among several sons there was only one

who possessed the hereditary gift and succeeded in artificial work.

A chief specialty of the family was the painting of glass with

enamel-colors in which the picture is composed of annealed relievodots so that it looks like enamelled. We find such glasses

sometimes in Museums. The family was known also to possess secrets in fusing enamels of diverse colors and much skill in making

decorative objects from out of it. My grandfather knew of old

documents in the family from the 16th and 17th century, concerning

certain privileges. Another branch of family-members have

turned painters and copper-engravers, some living at Vienna.

On the end of the 17th century the glass-makers Blaschka undertook

it to establish glass-manufacturies. The manner of manufacturing at that time was quite different from that nowadays. They

hired a district of woods from the owners of large dominions and

established a glass-furnace with a number of workmen. As soon

as the fire-wood was worked up, they left the place and began anew

on another place. So the Blaschkas came into the province

Upper-Austria. My father's great-grandfather, manufacturing

near Ried in Upper-Austria, had 8 sons. The 4 eldest of them

were from his first marriage with a German-Austrian lady, and when

his wife had died he left Upper-Austria for Pribram in Bohemia

marrying again a native of Bohemia and increasing his family for 4

more sons. This latter branch, the descendants of the second

marriage have succeeded best in the struggle of life. They

turned wholesale-merchants and textiles-manufacturers, breaking

entirely with the traditional glass-relation. Their grandchildren are now the owners of the grand cotton and cloth-manufacturing establishments in North Bohemia, some of them known as

millionaires. The 4 sons of the German-Austrian mother were all

well instructed in glass-working. They went up to the 9 sermountains, near the bound of Silesia. The families of 3 of them

are extinct, long ago. Franz Blaschka, the 4th son, my greatgrandfather, was owner of a saw-mill, and in company with another,

of a glass-furnace. He was known as the most skilful among his

brothers and his own decorative glass-work was very highly appreciated. He had 4 sons, who were all initiated in the art of

the family. The eldest son went down to Venice where he died

without leaving family. The two youngest sons have got victims

of the military duty. They perished, both, in the battles

against Napoleon. Joseph, the second son my grandfather, went,

when his father died, to Saxony. He had always taken pleasure

in the study of mechanics and wished to turn mechanician. After

wards he studied Physics and Mechanics at Prague with Professor

Gerstner, who advised him to engage in electric practice. He

lived for many years in Teplitz till 1813, when the war disturbed

all advance. On purpose to improve his health he removed to his

wife's home, to Bohmisch Aicha, a town in the foot of the Jeschken

mountains. Here, on 27th May 1822, Leopold, my father, the

third and youngest son was born. He visited the grammar-school

and Latin-school of the town, and, perceiving his excellent memory,

the teachers advised his father to send him to the high-school.

But there was yet another high gift and inclination with Leopold.

When he was yet a little boy, he could draw and paint everybody in

town from memory with striking likeness, like a photograph, and

with rapidity. His elder brother Vincenz had the intention to

turn artist, and, though he had not the least natural gift for it,

he insisted on the study with obstinacy, probably incited by and

worried at Leopold's, natural success. The arrival of Elsner,

an academic artist of Vienna who was engaged for the renovation

of the decanal-church, ended the uncomfortable state between the

brothers. The 18 years old Vincenz had made a picture after a

biblical motive, working several months with assiduousness, and

Elsner, when he saw it, gave him the good advice to turn anything

but painter. Upon this, the 12 years old Leopold took his

brother's paints and painted the same motiv in two days. Elsner said, he, the artist himself, could not make it better and he

asked the father, to give Leopold entirely over to him, he should

take him to Vienna and Italy and guarantee the best success.

But the father was an experienced acute man who has had plenty opportunity of observing the distress among painting-artists, and so he did not agree. He said, the Genius should open the road in Leopold's life quite of itself and first he wished him to learn something for the practical life. So Leopold had first opportunity of studying one year the pleasure and sufferings of an apprentice in a merchants-store and was very glad to give it up. He went to a place near Turnan where his eldest brother lived, in order to get instruction in gold and silver-working and cutting of precious stones. He then returned to his father, faithfully working with him in metal and glass-work. His father instructed him in everything of the traditional art of the family in which Leopold with his high talents was the only of the 3 brothers. When 24 years old he married 1846 the daughter of an owner of mills Carolina Zimmermann and was happy during 4 years. In summer 1850, when a war against Prussia was in sight (which however later-on was settled by diplomacy) the Austrian government threw huge crowds of soldiers into the peaceful valleys near the Saxon and Prussian bounds and at the same time there the Cholera Asiatica appeared, as people said, brought in by the soldiers from Italy. The epidemic was one of the most terrible in this century, distributing over all Austria, Saxony etc., Bohmisch Aicha a great many people died within a few weeks. My father and his wife lived very carefully, but intended to go for

some time to her father's country-possession. On 10. of August,

same morning, when they intended to leave, Carolina got ill after a

cup of milk, and died same day in the afternoon. Yet in his

high age, my father got moved to tears when speaking of what he had

suffered that time. He lived now for 2 years very much retired. He had at the same time trouble with his health, suffering from an injury in the chest, and so he sought and found his

only comfort in the study of nature. In company with a friend,

a physician who possessed a fine natural-history-library he collected plants studied and painted them, and at last fortunately his

health had quite improved. But when 1852 his father had died

(78 years old), he wished to leave the country for some time.

He determined to journey to America and, provided with very good

letters of recommendation and orders by the houses Unger and Blasch

ka of Liebenath he sailed early in 1853 on a small old brigg, Pauline of Bremerhaven, crossing the ocean in 9 weeks. During a

calm of 2 weeks, not far from the Azores, he had opportunity of

fishing out and drawing some Hydromedusae and a Physalia. He

was interested in the glass-like appearance of these animals which

he had known before only from illustrations in Nat. History books

and here he first got the idea that these forms could be imitated

in glass. (I beg to enclose a report of one of my readings held

before the Dresden Natural Hist. society 15 years ago in which I

mentioned this.) In America he lived for some months in New

York, entering in some business in jewelry with some whole-sale

firms, and took a trip down to Pennsylvania and Virginia. Induced by over-apprehensive letters from his brother Vincenz and by

the request of the merchant Unger who was in embarrassment about a

kind of gilded and silvered tacks for glass-l.stres which my father

had exclusively manufactured he returned in Winter to Bohmisch

Aicha. 1854 he married Carolina Riegel, daughter of a citizen

of B. Aicha and established in the house of his father-in-law a

manufactury, chiefly for lustre-tacks, with a number of workmen.

He only needed to survey his workmen and got plenty time for Botanical studies which he liked so very much. When on 17 June

1857, I was born he got anxious to remove to a big city and engage

there only in artistic activity. He tried, only for his

pleasure, to make flowers from glass. A friend, the director

Mazek of Prince Rohan's garden at Sichrow, some miles east from

B. Aicha, supplied him with rare greenhouse-material. My father

was introduced to the prince himself, who took very much interest

in my father's studies. The prince ordered his director to supply my father with all species of Orchids that he wished to study,

entire inflorescences of the most precious varieties, gratis.

My father made now by and by during the years 1860-62 about 100

tropical plants of about 50 species, mostly Orchids, and composed

them on 2 artificial trunks of trees to a big group illustrating

the tropical vegetation in wild nature. It was a grand, marvellous work of art, and though I was very young when I saw it, I

remember it so clearly as if I had seen it only yesterday. This

work of art was ordered by nobody. My father made it on purpose

to show his ability, and perhaps he could find a purchaser for it.

Prince Camille de Rohan took over voluntarily the protection.

Unfortunately he, the owner of large dominions was just at that time in pecuniary embarrassment, caused by immense losses by the fraud of his chief-treasurer. At any time else, he said, this work of art had certainly got in his possession. He permitted my father to exhibit it in a room of his castle at Prague and he invited the Haute Volée of Prague and did all the best he could for drawing the attention of the old emperor Ferdinand to it. The artistical success was great, but there was no pecuniary success at all. When my father counted over lateron the expenses of the journey, he found a big deficit. It must be stated that Prince Rohan cannot be made answerable for this at all. My father es-teemed him always as a gentleman of noblest character. Prince Rohan advised my father to apply to the renowned botanist Professor Reichenbach of Dresden. Relying upon the prince's recommendation my father came to Dresden in summer 1863. Reichenbach was very much pleased with my father's work and arranged for the exhibiting in the pavilion of the Botanical garden. This fine and noble act of Reichenbach saved my father all trouble and expenses. Reichenbach wrote much in the papers praising my father's skill, and the success was great in all directions. Once a Russian prince offered my father a sum of about 600 Thaler (1800 Mark) for the group, but Reichenbach dissuaded from selling so quickly. For this amount, he said, we shall acquire it at any time for our Mu-

seum, and I shall see about it that this work of art shall not

leave our city. But when lateron my father took him at his

word, he was unable to do anything. In his enthusiasm he had

probably made the account without the ministry of the finances.
