You perhaps remember what I told you once of the parallel

he drew between the price of a natural and an artificial flower and

how my father beat him. About at the same time an Englishman

who lived in Dresden asked my father whether he would engage in

making artificial sea-anemones for Aquariums as those animals were

so perishable. My father told him of his ideas and observations

made on jelly-fishes on his voyage to America and was ready to try

it if there was a chance for selling them. The gentleman, whose

name my father never heard, neither Reichenbach ever mentioned, lent

the book of Gosse, Actinologia Britannica, to Reichenbach, who

eagerly took up the plan. A number of water-banks filled with

artificial sea-anemones made by my father after Gosse's drawings,

were exhibited in the Museum. Reichenbach invited the king and

the Haute-Volée and Scientific World, whereupon the minister of

public instruction permitted the purchase of all the original work

of my father in marine Zoology for the Natural History Museum.

My father broke off the exhibition in the Botanical Garden. He

had to work very assiduously at home in our lodging as he got plenty orders for artificial aquariums, also from abroad, for England,

Russia etc. One day, Reichenbach came with Professor Morren of

Lege, who selected the finest and largest inflorescences of the

Orchids asking my father, to forward them to Bridge. He promised to send the extremely low amount that my father had charged, at once after his return. Reichenbach had induced Morren to the purchase with warm recommendations. It was certainly his good intention to make good everything in the flower-matter, and to do the best for my father. But here is a point coming in, which I dare not pass over in silence. Though the proverb says: De mortius nil nisi bene"—Morren is dead since long ago—I must explain you why, on your first call, my father was not disposed to engage in Botanical work again. He forwarded the case with the glass-flowers to Morren, but did not hear anything of it for some months. On my father's question Morren replied that some of the orchids were broken but they could be mended if perhaps my father would come sometime to Belgium and repair them. Then he should pay for them. My father was compelled now, to write a dozen times to Morren stating the ridiculousness of the demand to travel to Belgium (at his own expense) on account of that trifle amount. He had charged the flowers at an under-price, I think it was about 400 Francs or so. Morren wrote also a dozen letters full of paltry pleas and offered at last payment of half of the contracted amount. Reichenbach, when he heard of it, was much afflicted but shrugged the shoulders, saying: "I am very sorry, I cannot do anything, Morren is a scientific man in a prominent position, whom I should not wish to get my enemy. It is too bad indeed."

sickening for my father. Morren seemed to have made up his

glass-flowers actually existed in good condition with Morren.

So this was the end of the undertaking, though so troublesome and

You find in these statements the response to your second question,

that my father neither made flowers for Prince Rohan nor for Reichenbach. He never has done Botanical work again till you engaged

us. 1864 my father experimented in Medusae and Mollusca, the

first for the Dresden Museum and copies for abroad. Owing to

the too cheap price the business did not pay very much. Though

the models were wonderfully constructed and generally acknowledged

of being excellent, there were also hair-splitters who vexed my

father. Reichenbach, who protected the work, had a great many

enemies especially among the young scientists. So my father

was compelled to take up also other sources of earning. A rich

undertaker and wholesale-merchant in Bijouterie-wares (of Dresden)

requested my father to invent some novelty for him, and undertook

on this a business in wares of the so-called violet-wood. My

father made charming miniature-boquets of small enamel-flowers in

Haut-Relief and Bas-Relief, mostly roses violets and forgetmenots

on brooches, fans, ear-rings etc. of violet-wood. The little

relievo-forgetmenots got my first study, when I commenced 1870.

This business was very lucrative for many years. The trade was

in the hands of the undertakers, and other merchants who earned

much money by charging huge prices for the little objects of art.

We were told that they often abused our modesty by putting the mark

on them, "made in Paris". It was disagreeable but we could not

make ado about this, - it is the fate of artists to get at last

indifferent against abuse and disregard. The funny part of it

was, when we stopped this work (about 1873) entirely, some merchants actually applied to Paris without getting anything. In

glass-blowing, in the sense of the word, my father has never engaged. Even for this term he had aversion. Once, when he

heard people complaining of the fragility of artificial eyes made

in Paris etc. he prepared some of such eyes from out of a very hard

solid glass-mass. Though he never offered or advertised them,

many people came and asked for such things and fame brought it thus

far that he was compelled to keep quite a collection of such eyes.

A society for charity in Dresden (the, Augenkrankenheilverein')

sent by and by many hundreds of poor people to my father and his

great skill in doing the Prosthesis was generally acknowledged by

the physicians and patients. However neither my father nor I

took pleasure in this activity. It was disturbing in our studies and we were both very glad to get rid of the whole matter by

our removal to Hosterwitz. As to the work in Zoological models

during the years 1866-74, so it never stopped entirely. My father got more or less orders every year. Reichenbach came now and then with an old book from the former century or with a snail that he caught on his excursions, wishing to get models of them for the Museum. My father has always made it possible though the cheapness as usually desired by Reichenbach did not pay the trouble. I remember that the bills for the Museum were not allowed to surmount 30 Mark.

I had visited the catholic chief-school of Dresden and

got Primes in the last class. Though I think that I never was

pious enough, but there was a priest (Jesuit) P. Schlegel Director

of schools in Dresden who tried to persuade my father to let him

be the guide of my further studies- for my education for the

priesthood- it should not cause expenses at all to us," he said.

But my father replied that he should care for my education only

himself, the expenses for my studying on high-schools being a

trifle matter, but chiefly he never should permit such a trade

against my will and against the liberal traditions of our family.

So I was most happy, to be free and to stay with my father.

Excuse me, that I am so particular to tell you also what we did

not like to turn, but it belongs to the history. My father instructed me in all branches of our art, in glass and enamel-modelling and painting of any kind. I visited some institutions of

Dresden for the study of ancient and recent languages, Mathematics

History etc. so that I easily got the qualification for the one-

year-volunteer-service in the army. 1874-75, I served as one-year-volunteer in the Emperor William Grenadier-Regiment in Dresden

In 1876 we had got a very honorable order for 2 complete collections of Zoolog. models by the South Kensington Museum of London.

I studied now very earnestly Zoology and anatomy with teachers and

with the help of the great Nat. Hist. library of the Imperial

academy Carol. Leopoldina which we had in Dresden that time.

My knowledge in Natural history had thriven thus far that I could

enter already 1880 in much scientific activity in the Dresden Nat.

History society (Jsis) of which I am yet corresponding member.

We paid visits to several German universities, everywhere kindly

received, and appreciated especially high Professor Haeckel's

(Jena) friendship. 1879 I took a trip to Italy and the Adriatic

for studies in marine Zoology. We had a room in our house in

Dresden filled with sea-water-tanks with living animals, sent to

us partly by the Imper. Austrian Zoolog. station of Triest partly

from England and the Northern coasts. In this way our work in

Zoological models had improved more and more and we got so many

orders that we often could not do justice to all wishes. It

was very pleasant to us to introduce our work in the Museums of

America, England, Germany, India, Australia, New Zealand and so on,

in all parts of the globe. One of the most pleasant and honorable orders was that by the Japanese department of public instruction, introducing our models of Invertebrata in 100 schools of

Japan and the Tokio Museum.

My dear Miss Ware,

Will you excuse my use of the type-writer, if

I write myself? It happens to be rather easier this morning. I

have just received a letter from Rudolf, which convinces me that

down with influenza of a bad type, and they are only just now

about again. He urges me not to come at present, for he says that

from experience he knows what it is to be away from home when the

last days have come for a dear friend. He would be happy to see

me in the winter or next spring. Both he and his mother send all

kind messages, but are anxious lest I should think them inhospitable in keeping me away now. Twenty models have been finished and

are ready for sending, and this in spite of the severe illness.

We returned safely home, the middle of last week, from our journey. We went as far as the Adriatic, and had beautiful weather all the time, while, as we learn, they had bad weather every day in Hoster-witz. The journey therefore was most agreeable and health-pro-ducing. I now feel perfectly well and endowed with great powers of endurance. Our great pleasure from our journey was still further heightened on our return by your valued letter for which we desire to send heartiest thanks. We were also pleased to learn that your father's health has improved, and that Mrs. and Miss Ware are in good health.

So far as the dates of payment are concerned, you will please adopt the course which suits you all best. I shall begin my work at once, and shall prosecute it under conditions which are full of joy to me: Joy produces health.

May I ask you to communicate to Mrs. and Miss Ware my sincerest thanks for the confidence they have shown in me, and will you also accept my good wishes. My Mother joins me in the expression of regards for you all and for Mrs. Goodale.

My dear Professor and friend,

Your good letter of March 17. has brought

us a most delightful surprise indeed. We look

forward with most pleasant anticipation to the

days that not only shall give us the great pleasure

of removing our personal acquaintance and friendship

but also the great honor of this Ware's visit to our

home. You all may feel sure that we will do all

in our power to make you a pleasant stay. It

is a delightful anticipation to think of this Ware

Mrs. Goodale, yourself and the dear Francis here in

our hermitage; and the fair season promises to

known the pleasure by good weather. Yesterday

I went down from on purpose to get the Reichskurzbuch, but we have yet to wait for some week

The new edition with the new summer-time table

appears only on the first of May, while the last

edition is sold everywhere, and I think, would not

be of any use for you. I shall promptly send the

news one as soon as it is to have. As to a pension

in Dresden I shall look out and make inquiries

for a recommendable place. As soon as you care

for a plain country-sojourn, be so good to use

our spacious house; we will always be at your

disposal with great pleasure. I fully agree with

Abies Ware's opinion, to avoid overcrowded places and reports. There is no enjoyment at all, to be justified in the throngs of tourists who run over all the most renowned and frequented places of mountain and valley, often only on purpose to prove by an illustrated postcard's that they have been there. For the trip with my mother two years ago I had chosen a route already well known to me as giving the most charming picture of beauty of nature connected with best accommodation. We went directly to Vienna where I bought a 40 days valid round-trip ticket Vienna-Triest-Venise-Verona-Tirol-Salzburg-Vienna - a very grateful and reasonable route. We stopped several places of Stiria which are usually neglected, especially by the international intercourse - the foreign tourists pass by as the good people there do not understand to beat the big drum of Reclame as it is done in other countries. Graz, Gilli and its surrounding and the whole valley of the river Sann are of fascinating beauty. In St. Peter, a village on the high-plateau of the Karst we stopped on purpose to take a separate trip down Tiume and Abbaxia and surroundings, some of the cosiest and most beautiful places in the world. After some days in Tiume and Abbaxia we sailed by steamer to Pola on the south end of Istria, the Austrian war-port, but a very cozy and interesting place with beautiful antique buildings from the ancient Roman times. From Pola we sailed, all with the wonderful weather which is the privilege of that country in late summer, up to Triest, visiting the grand Halactite grattons of St. Cantezian - again one of the less blazoned places, but deserving world's reputation. As far as this place we have been only enchanted at the beauty of nature. The slight oriental tint together with often subtropical beauty gives a remarkable charm to those countries. Venice was high interesting as ever though filled with strangers, that belong to the physiognomy of the place, and does not disturb. But homewards in Tirol we got a glimpse of the modern tourists pleasure, overcrowded trains, expensive places etc. till we reached Salzburg, a very interesting place but also usually much frequented. Well, Tagree with many people who travelled for pleasure, who say they prefer the Austrian South-East to all other routes. I am happy you found your visit to this place satisfactory, and for us it is something very sweet to remember it is with great delight that I look back at those lovely days of your dear visit, a pleasure that never can fade. You were so good to bring us cordial friendship and friendship in the most valuable thing in the world. Indeed there have been moments with me sometimes when I wished to have more intercourse with world, longing for more friends and so on. However this country has its peculiar social uses and circumstances, much different, I think from those in your country. How many a man well-bred and gifted, I have known, who was introduced into distinguished society, and felt lonelous there than in loneliness at home. Having no power or disdaining to Thrust forward obviously, he at last retired. The common way of getting acquainted here, used by people of all classes, is the regular visit

to Restaurants, but this has never been my pleasure neither my father's. It would be incompatible with my work, surely. This is an old experience. It is a peculiar circumstance how this scientific artistic work demands of the man to be entirely yielded to it, but this would always be observed. 36 years ago, when we removed to Dresden, my father longed for society and friends. By and by, in the 25 years we lived in the city and in the last years here, he got a perfect hermit, by his experience. To to myself, I think it perhaps can change sometime later, but at present circumstances demand of me to live on as my father did and to which I became adapted. However in case we yearn for society, we have always a mean at hand. I wished you to see the throng of hundreds of people in our quiet hermitage at times of exhibitions of models. The few invited people tell it their friends and families and the inundation is sometime quite frightening. The work could often be called a sacrifice indeed but it gives pleasure when finished, and this charm would explain much to those who wonder at a singular course of life which is so seldom understood.

I feel happy you appreciate our work very much, many sincere thanks for your good sentences which prove how acutely you understand it. I was very glad to learn you had such a pleasant time and feel so well in Switzerland. There is a great difference from here in the pure air of those alpine regions, I too prefer mountains to flat countries.

This work I was trying for the first time some flower-heads of a golden rod. It can be done, but it will demand much time, I think, about 6 weeks. I have made up my mind to do it within the next months.

To Goodale I have not heard from since his stay in Wureburg and so I directed an American letter arrived for him lately, also to Naring Nors. I was about to write him on account of Vanilla planifolia. This remarkable Orchid would certainly give a good model, interesting to students and to the many friends of Vanilla-flavour. I failed to get it in Jamaica and here in German gardens it gets very seldom in bloom. Some time ago I read in the newspaper of great nurseries exclusively of Vanilla, owned by the duke of Northumberland, but it was not told where

Dear Professor and dear friend!

I received your good letter and we are very glad, Mrs. Goodale and yourself have a good time. We often speak of the pleasant fourth of July, that, I can assume you, belongs with ourselves to those most pleasant moments in life that we never can forget. It gave us hearty delight to see our dear old friends again, and to get acquainted with Mr. Gallagher and his family. Please remember us occasionally kindly to them. We only regretted the absence of Miss Ware and Francis. I have written Miss Ware some time ago, telling her of my plans about the shipment. For, I have changed mind with regard to the planned finishing of the consignment by end of July, on purpose to fulfil my own wish to increase it to 20 specimens. The number suits me much better for packing, and I used the weeks since your visit for making some new plants. The last two ones I have now in hand and they must get finished this week. Therefore the whole matter has to suffer a delay for as many weeks as I need for the analytical completions; August will anyhow get a very busy time. I think the few weeks' delay will

not make any difference, I remember your last words: No hurry.

We are very much pleased at your plan to revisit Dresden and Hosterwith earlier than in autumn, and, I hope, accompanied by Francis it will give us great and hearty pleasure.

There is yet a business-matter that I must not forget to ask you. The agents in Bremen will need the address of any person in the Museum at Cambridge who receives the bills and cases. To there anyone of your assistants who could care for this, or is it sufficient to address: Botanical Museum, Prof. D. Goodale, Department, Cambridge etc, Care of Mr. E. A. Snow express-agent Boston? Please write me about this occasionally, at perhaps I have the pleasure to see you with us before end of August.

Why mother joins me in kindest regards and all cordial good wishes for Mrs. Goodale yourself and dear Francis, and, Au Revoir!

very sincerely yours

R. Blaschka

Dear Sir:

Your letter of the 14th inst. duly received. In reply thereto I beg to forward you typewritten statement of the cost, dimensions, etc. of the cases used for exhibits installed by this Institution.

These cases are all made of angle iron, not steel, and are made so that the sizes are interchangeable. They come to us from the Stow Flexible Shaft Co., 26th & Callowhill Streets, Phila, in the rough; in other words, not painted and with no glass in them. They are painted and the glass put in them at this Institution, the cost for all of which you will find on the enclosed statement, each itemized under its separate head.

In connection with this matter I desire to inform you that you can get little satisfaction from an explanation of this kind, but wish you would pay the Institution a visit when details could be explained and the cases seen, which in every way would prove more satisfactory.

The Wistar Institute of this city have exceptionally fine cases which you should see and which you no doubt could duplicate.

Very truly yours,

Avery N. Tevisoy

Da aber die Neubearbeitungen wegen der angestrebten Vollständigkeit viel Zeit erfordern, so dürften viele thatsächlich erst 45—20 Jahre nach dem Erscheinen der entsprechenden Bearbeitung in den genannten Werken in die Öffentlichkeit gelangen.

Bei dieser Art der Veröffentlichung fällt der Übelstand weg, dass der Druck einer fertig vorliegenden Bearbeitung durch das Ausbleiben einer anderen gehindert wird, welche dem System nach vorangehen müsste.

The crash was opened by our Electric company as I prophesied, paralyzing the last hope for our electric connection with the city, at least for next winter. But when a prominent credit bank of Dredden and the old solid Leipzig Bank had failed the general anxiety got epidemics. Even such first rate

institutions as the Dredner Bank and the Taxon bill-bank where we also have a deposit, had been rendered suspected by some incompetent news-paper and the consequence was a feverish run on those banks as it never as yet has taken place. Many people got so nervous, they neither would trust any bank nor company nor even the state. It is uncountable how many millions have got lost during the last weeks but the presumable amount is horrible. Those people with small savings who lost everything are really to regret. Fortunately we have not had any losses as the state-bonds are well situated, and I trust they will not crash! It is not without interest to watch the present disgustful stock-jotting. The stocks of the crashed companies f.i. the Electric hereabout were sold this week at the Dredner Exchange: Monday 100 Mark original value for 1 Mark, Tuesday for 1 Mark and a half, Wednesday for half a Mark, Thursday I Mark and a half, Friday for 2 Mark and a half, Saturday for 3 Marks, and so the play will renew this week until the final result after the concourse will come: presumably 100 Mark for nothing. It was with very sad feeling that my mother and I read in your good letter the sad news of the death of your dear cousin also. Hale. We are floared by the thought how cruelly fate rules life. The kind lady whom we loved after the short acquaintance has died four months later, nobody would have forbidden this! We regret sincerely the young ladies who have lost their dear mother so suddenly and far from home and we unite in sincere sympathy. Would you be so good to express it to them, and, we also symbolize sincerely with you and can feel what a terror loss it must be for you all.

I had indeed been anxious at not hearing from you for so long time as we had presumed it was owing to any serious recurrence of your sufferings. So I am very glad to hear you keep on feeling well and this pleasant result of your stay in Europe will give you comfort in the sad time. We both, my mother and I are not ailing. Dear Miss Ware,

Your valued letter of August 5, has reached me some weeks ago and I would have replied promptly unless I had been again in great sorrow at my dear mother's suffering. The enigmatic nephritis came again after a short pause and developed into a colic accompanied by fearful pains and fever. The doctors were quite puzzled at the unknown symptoms. At last one of the best specialists gave the diagnosis on Nephrolithiasis, a stone having pierced through the Peritoneum. However also this seemed to be untenable. My mother fortunately got better and she is now again pretty well and able to walk. I shall take her this week to a Dresden Roentgen-Laboratory and consult the most experienced physicians on purpose to investigate the cause of her suffering. It is dreadful to feel always in fear of such treacherous sufferings, but I hope we will find out the root of them.

If there are people missing information on methods therein you simply can refer to me. Moreover I know many Museum-guides of prominent collections of art, but they never contain such reports of processes, how their precious objects have been done, so it is not strange at all, the guide of a unique collection of scientific Botany does not inform on working-methods concerning its models. I am not afraid of cpiers, neither of Paris artists nor of others. Glass flowers have been made by other people long before my father's first studies, and yet nowadays, I always enjoy to see these productions, of course, owing to the fame of your collection, the coveting of cpiers is worked up to the highest degree. After the great world's expositions they rush on the matter like dogson a fat sausage and I can tell many a story of the sauciness of such undertakers. In short time the ardor is cccled. Here is the old rule as in every kind of art, it will prove hard to find anyone who can say and prove he is able to do a scientifically perfect model of every kind of plants in that way as we have done it and I do it. Ascetic devotion, indispensable for this, is usually not the habit of these cpiers. I think you will like to see the letter and so I try to mail it for the second time. It came unopened. As to the tenor I must now explain something. You can remember I told you in summer of my studies on the Genus Platanus. I had made a model after the Sycamores planted here and it got uncertain whether this is P. cccidentalis or orientalis. Gardens about here and descriptions in books could not clear up the matter and so I applied to Mr. Jackson Dawson of your Arboretum who sent to me in a very obligating way plenty of material, four sample packages, in August. By this I saw, the American Sycamore is entirely different from ours, and the latter has turned out a genuine orientalis. I am just about to finish a model of the American form, that I�Impossibly could omit, so the Platanaceae will be well represented in your collection by the two remarkable species, and the Platanus matter is now fixed up. I cannot get here the Samara-fruit of Acer rubrum. May 1th, 1908

Dear Doctor,

A few weeks ago I received a letter from you asking whether it would be possible to send over anything from our Museum to the Medical School, for the coming meeting of the American Medical Association. I replied immediately by special delivery letters forwarded to your home address and to the Medical School, saying that probably Professor Yarlow could send over a few things, and that I should be willing to send over a case containing four of the Blaschka models of plants, together with the medicinal preparations derived from those species, provided such exhibit would be thought desirable. Since I have not further heard from you or from any one else regarding the matter, I assume that the matter of such exhibit has been given up. It is perhaps better so, since it would have taken at least three weeks for us to have the tablets for mounting them constructed, and the time is now rather too short. I write now thinking that it is best to remove any possible misapprehension relative to the exhibit.

Hoping that the meeting of the Associetion may be a pronounced success in every way;

I remain,

Yours faithfully

George Lincoln Goodale,

My dear Friend,

As I have already told you, after my return from Cuba, I had a series of bad attacks of neuralgia, which with some feverishness, left me every day hardly well enough to do my College work. All of my correspondence had to be suspended. But now as the term is drawing to an end I feel somewhat better and therefore my first duty does to take up the broken thread of my correspondence with you. I hope that the Spring has been pleasant for you and your mother. Here we have had an "open" winter and now have a late spring to pay for it. Cold days are the common thing. Our plants are much behind last year, and it has been difficult to provide the students with enough material for their laboratory work. But all of the laboratory practices stop this week, just as the plants begin to come on in sufficient numbers.

The season is visiting Boston has fairly set in, and of course there is a great influx of visitors here. Everybody comes to see your handiwork. You and your mother would be delighted, I well know, to see and hear the many intelligent visitors admiring the collection. But you would find it hard to answer their innumerable questions, particularly since there are so many who desire to obtain facts which they can use in publication. All of them ask in a good spirit, but many of their inquiries are far beyond my power to answer. For instance, "how long does it take Mr. Blaschka to create this specimen?" "Is this a more difficult specimen to make than this" and so on. Mrs. Goodale and Francis are in fairly good health, and they both join with me in sending to you and your mother very kind wishes and sincere regards. Miss Ware has had a bad attack of Rheumatism but is better now.

Yours very faithfully George Lucothu Gootaly

Dear Miss Ware,

Your good letter came on monda and gave us delight to hear at last from you, though it met with our sincere sympathy to hear of all the hardship you have suffered during this year. Your check for 5000 Mark came safely and I simply can thank you for it though I did not reckon with it at all. I am pleased you show by this your will not to have stopped the development of your unique collection so soon. I however would have proceeded anyhow for some time. Unpleasant to me is that I have not yet forwarded the model and I can realize how impatiently you will look for it. However you cannot be more impatient than I and I assure you it would only have been in my interest if I could finish this troublesome consignment earlier. There was not an idea of vacation this year since you were with us and I can look back on the worst year of trouble since the beginning of this work. Only the peculiar thing that were to do and the way in which they were to do are the reason of the long delay, difficult tasks you will see soon enough. The plants are finished since June, there was however yet a lot of fucary detail work which is almost finished

at present. I have yet the last detail model for 2 Confiferae, Juniperus and a Bephalastane and for Casuarina in hand, no giant but very fuzzy things, and I trust to finish them about midst of next week. After this I shall mount the models and as soon as I get the boxes I shall send. More haste is impossible. I cannot sit up nights, it would ruin me. About the time when you receive this line you may think the term of forwarding of the consignment is near. I shall write again after this, more particular about the models today I have no time for it. Of course I must next some weeks after having sent off the models, though I feel strangely strong yet after this hard summer. My mother and I are very sorry to hear you have been so seriously ill and we hope and wish you will be perfectly well again at this time. We also were so sorry at the danger your country home has met with and the saving was very fortunate The loss of it would have very much afflicted you. Prof. Goodale has sent me a very kind letter this summer and invited us to visit America. However this is an impossible matter. We can fancy how lovely the whole collection must look in the fine arrangement, and all we heat about it gives us much pleasure. Now I must hasten to work again. Please accept our kindest wishes and regards and best thanks

very sincerely your

Well, I have studied and experimented a great deal, since I reflected after the renewed earnest broaching last year what there possibly yet would be done. I told you already in the early years of my Sunday Study To contrive new compositions of enamels to be used for flashed or annealed textures, well adhering together with harder kinds of glass such as can be used for these models. This can only be reached empirically. The result is visible in the analytical details that are all enamelled and annealed with the self-made material (except in the cut ripe fig that is painted in the old way). The sections, being a good experimental object, appear by this like as if cast of one piece. The Coniferae are all of self-prepared glass, nothing or almost nothing painted, and so on. Dear Mife Ware,

On Tuesday 23.Tnet. The

consignment, packed in 6 cases, has at last left for Bremen. It was impossible to finish it at an earlier date, and when I wrote you last, I did not guess before how much work was yet waiting for me. The sections had turned out to be not quite complete and here and there was yet something to do so it got late in September before I could start mounting. The consignment contains all species completed, as talked over last year, except the Cambridge small Nymphaea odorata minor. I want to do this directly from nature as soon as I can see the true form. The present Nymphaea are not quite satisfactory to me, there is too much variety in the garden. Specimens here, of Hybrid-forms of the European Nymphaea alba. Our little red maple was not as bright as last year this autumn, probably owing to the desolately miserable weather in August and all September. Only a few leaves showed the much-searched scarlet, reminding me of hard weeks of last autumn. You would have been surprised to see the half dozen red leaves, I had done while you were in Dresden, a few days later. Smashed, sealing, full of flavors they lay on the table. The process that had given pretty satisfactory results in the small berries of Daphne failed in the broad blades, a case, that often occurs. The cause was, that the German glass, annealed with my silac yellow, as fundamental, and the flashed upon ruby, made of my gold-purple and Bohemian enamel, developed in the thin blade a different coefficient of tension. That was

a vested question. The samples painted south oil had been unsatisfactory, and everything I bought and tried of china and glass-annealing paints was useless. It is curious, and an old experience with us, that renowned factory-productions, as those of Meijien, Solneberg etc., excellent enamel-paints for the china-industry, in most cases fail on the glass used for these models. They also prepare a scarlet for china, preparation kept secret, but this springs carefully and changes in sharp heat into yellow. Since I studied already for some years more thoroughly in ceramical chemistry I used the latter property of that enamel in search of the secret and was soon successful to find it. It is a preparation of the Nichromate, giving various shades of orange-scarlet, minimum scarlet and cinnabar-red. When I also had good success to prepare a useful enamel from the very fundamental matter, quartz and alcales, that adhered well together with my glass, I was so happy, and gladly underwent to do the maple leaves for the second time. This week I send by sample-post a few samples to you, The darker shades I now use to things over with gold. The property of the chromo-scarlet to get yellow by repeated annealing made it impossible to anneal on the red maple leaves the whitish cover beneath and the dark veins and veinlets, I was compelled to paint this with oil. This summer I also discovered a remedy for this, used in the magnified cut berries of Daphne and Taccus, the magnified red flowers. It factory in Nohemia brought this year as novelty, was et. for sale, of a very bright cinnabar-color, annealed on crystal-glass, it seems to be new, after research, however it is of no use for my work. I had lately acquired a glass-object of this. They keep it awfully secret. Since the enamels, I prepared from fundamental material had stood proof I tried to use them more extensively for features. The details also the sections are prepared by means of them. Cold painting is only a help in such cases as above mentioned if colors change by burning or even get colorless, as all the colors do, that are prepared of the oxidation of irons to the spots on the pitchers of Nopenthes Burtisii, and the ripening figs had much burnt away in the heat of the blow-flame, the brown-red iron-enamel-paint does not stand this high temperature, and so it must be helped after by oil-or varnish-painting. In general there is much ignorance about this work with the public who increasingly asky whether the colors are annealed, a question that I had more right to affirm than ever. The public knows of course the decorated glass-ware and thinks what there is painted and annealed must also be possible in these models. However there is a great difference. China and decorated glass get annealed in stoves, in square cases of thermotel. clay, called, muffles'. For china it is easy, it does change shape. In glass they must be very careful in heating, otherwise the objects get deformed by the heat. Therefore all these glass-vess etc. To be decorated by annealed enamel, are generally made of a hardly furtile glass, while again the paints must be very easily furtile. This kinds of hard glass are useless for our glassmodels, and if these paper-thin blades, as leaves, pitals etc. are burnt in muffles, the objects get easily shapeless. Dear Miss Ware,

Last week I sent over to you by sample post some scraps of plate-glass etc. annealed or enamelled with my preparations of scarlet. You had been so much interested in these studies last year, that I thought you would be glad to know the method. Some specially of the lighter shades represent another form of this process. The coloring enamel - mass appears like half-burnt and seemingly not in the degree fastened to the glass as the other enamels. This is done intentionally because this color is more fine-proof than the others, and in using it for the models I glaze it over by a smooth hyaline enamel. I consider these annealed scarlets by no means perfect; from these shades to the brilliance of a scarlet - Pelargonium there is yet a step, though it comes near in sunlight.

The steamer, Friedrich der Große having the models on board, is almost in America and perhaps you have the shipment ever this line reaches you.

My dear Friend Blaschka,

We have finished unpacking your marvellous creations, and we have found only very slight breakages, so slight and few as really to be hardly worth mentioning. The colors are surpassingly fine-and-and satisfactory. You have succeeded far beyond our expectations in the autumnal colors of the red maple. The great specimens of Nepenthes are beyond credibility. They must have demanded innumerable precautions and repetitions. All of the invoice is exceedingly beautiful and scientifically perfect. Especially important in our series are the Gymnosperms and the Casuarina. The Nymphaeas also fill a most important place. I congratulate you upon your increasing power to accomplish the impossible! Today I have had the great pleasure of showing the packing and the un-packing in the presence of Miss Ware, to the wife of our President. Dear Mifs Ware,

Your good letter of Van. II. has reached me yesterday and I thank you sincerely for it as well as for the enclosed draft for 5000 Mark. It is a noble act of yours to let me finish your unique collection, and certainly I shall be glad to do it. The 30 lacking families will be cared for in possible speed, though in some cases the fresh material is hard to get for and I shall be compelled for a representative of Bycadaceae, Amonaceae and Harcegraviaceae to apply to foreign gardens. Why mother and I also thank you heartily for your good christmas-greeting, the beautiful Tudubon-calendar, by which we get a glimpse of your birds-fame, and I am very glad to have already moving to your goodness, a small collection of these very instructive fine plates. We hope you will enjoy your stay on the coast and your cousin will be wholly recovering there. We sympathize heartily with it. Goodbye in his bereavement and I also shall write him a line today. I am happy to report that my mother is much better now and yesterday she could make again the first attempts of walking. I am always very anxious for her, in her increasing age, however I hope, spring will give her full strength again. I am a few days we have fearful winter with temperature.

of 5 to 12° below zero Fahrenheit. We are told by the papers that this sold blow just now came right from Russia. The new year has commenced rather crossly with us by a new big renovation in the garret-floor of our house. In about half of the wood-party not yet old, the wood-worms had melted in, and it was scientifically interesting to see their treacherous destructive work. Outside the boards and beams looked quite intact and new, inside they were filled with dust. To n't it funny, here sits the artist and carries on natural history, and above his head in the mean time the worms eat the house! I am now very glad to get all well in order, the matter will be finished next week. Of the stores I wrote you already too much enough, and if only remains to report, that the new laboratory has got finished this week, and the melting stove will be tried next week. What I chiefly am planning by this undertaking is a matter concerning my health. The continuous work of preparing for the larger leaves in the huge free lamp-flames is a tiring out and vacations matter, and so I want to try working of self-prepared glass fluidly melted in the stove. Perhaps it is possible and this would well pay, to be more protected against the direct heat, even for the short end- period in these models of plants. I undertook the whole matter using to my experience in the last shipment. To do it in earlier periods that really been impossible by many reasons. The process of doing the other delicate work of course remains all the same as it already is. I was about to write to Jamaica on account of some Stona-Blossoms when the news of the fearful catastrophe came. It is a saddening thought now of the beautiful country and of the person I got acquainted with there. Two wonderful places which I saw on my journey, Van Francisco and Kingston were destroyed by earthquakes! Good, that it was quiet when I was out there!

Now I renew my sincere thanks, and my mother joins me in all good wishes and kind regards to you.

Very sincerely yours

My dear Miss Ware,

Will you excuse a type-written letter? It is a little easier for me to write it than the other kind, today, after my tiresome lectures, - two this morning.

Answering your question of last evening, I will say that in my view, it would be best to see Mr. Elliot C. Lee first of all. His last letter to me was dated June 16th, 1906. He says, (enclosing a check from Mrs. Lee) "It certainly is devoutly to be hoped that we may get an endowment instead of this annual and perpetual uncertainty". I think that it would be a good plan to have a talk with him about the bare possibility of inducing his mother to give the whole amount of the wished-for increment to the fund. It cannot do harm: it may do good.

Next, if you should be able, through Mr. Elliot C. Clarke, to find out about the Lowells and their attitude to the fund called "the Lowell Fund for a Botanic Garden" you would be doing what none of the rest of us can do.

I am now to prepare my note to the Corporation asking permission in behalf of our Committee to try for a Fund. So I must now cut my letter short.

Dear Miss Ware,

Your good letter has reached me yesterday and I thank you sincerely for your kind opinion pronounced by it. I only had intended to state in my letter that it proves hard, may, impossible, to bring a faster pace into my work, which is now limited to certain families. Prof. Goodale can convince himself of this. I had too very please letters from Prof. Goodale. The was so very good to send to me right from the steamer a large set of beautiful photographs of our models, artistic reproduction

of high value, by which we were much delighted. I am sure this pleasure we owe in first line to you and I feel so much obliged to you for the fine set which I keep for a Fourvenin with many thanks. The pictures are so excellently done as to light and shade that none would believe they are taken from artificial things, and you could well use them for illustrating of a manual of Rotany. We are delighted to learn from Prof. Goodale's letters that we shall have the pleasure to see Abte, and Prof. Goodale here after midst of September, only sorry, we cannot see Francis who must

return in some weeks.

Consequently any matter of biology cannot be done after fancy, but only after careful study from life, and as I neither have descriptive papers on, nor living flowers of those. My dear Friend,

I have received a letter from Miss Ware, dated Paris, from which I learn that there has been a misunderstanding with respect to a few points relative to the Collection of Models. You will allow me to take up these points for consideration, one by one, and I will ask you to tell me what other course I should have pursued or what course I should pursue now, in order to meet your wishes. There have been certain persons who have not been friendly to our enterprise, and who would not be unwilling to make trouble in some way. Usually I have thought it best to ignore the ill-natured attacks, because I felt sure that such attacks would fail of their purpose. But besides these attacks, which have been annoying, there have been two intermeddlers who, with the best intentions in the world, have been made cats-paws, and they do a good deal of serious mischief. I will make a clear statement of present conditions, and will ask your friendly criti-cism.

(I) The unofficial guide prepared by Mr. Kent, is not sold at the Museum. As soon as it was discovered that the janitor had been induced by a few pennies to sell copies when called for, the sale was peremptorily stopped and none have been sold since the prohibition.

(2) The only official matter in print in the cases, besides the labels, is the German account written by the late Professor Fluckiger, and which received substantially your commendation, but I will withdraw this if you desire. There is a type-written account which is exactly as you returned it to me. I had supposed that this was satisfactory. It stands, word for word, just as you sent it corrected to me. I had thought it hardly possible to do to get to gratify an inquisitive public, and I am at loss to know what less could be said, explanatory.

(3) When we received the shipment of models after your lamented father's death, there was some question as to the proper inscription to be played on some of the labels. The one who transferred the models from the paste-board supports, had not carefully noted the name of the artist or artists. We deplore the fact that a few of the labels are marked L.&R.B. instead of R.B., and a list of all our models will be sent to you for immediate noting thereon, of the exact name or initial. If you will take the trouble to make such notation, a copy will be forwarded at once.

(4) On my resignation from my professorship and Directorship, the Corporation of the University appointed me Honorary Curator of the Botanical Museum, that is, a Curator without pay. By and by, when we find a Curator, to whom the charge can be entrusted, it is probable that he will be selected from among our graduates), he will be paid a small stipend for his work. But this is still in the future.

(5) Personally, I am to be placed on the Carnegie foundation, and not on any College pension.

(6) Unfortunately there is as yet no provision for providing for faithful University employees, other than the professors, and adequate pension. But it has been among my hopes that I could secure from friends of the University, a testimonial pension for you, after your final work for the University is done, and this has already been mentioned with a gratifying degree of success. I have hitherto been able to say that for twenty years, there had not been any unpleasant word pass between us, even during very

prolonged and complicated negotiations. I have not in my possession any letter from you which betrays impatience. In all doubtful cases, you had been willing to "give me the doubt-benefit", and thus we have succeeded admirably all these years. If, to Miss Ware, you have expressed any serious belief that I have been unfriendly, it was a belief based on a complete lack of correct information. Miss Ware has been conversant with my desire to advance not only the interests of the whole Museum, but especially, those of the Ware Collection of Blaschka Glass Models of Plants and Flowers. # REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE TO VISIT THE BOTANIC GARDEN

To THE BOARD OF OVERSEERS OF HARVARD COLLEGE:—

Your Committee to visit the Botanic Garden report as follows:—

It seems to us that this Department, in common with a great part of the College Departments, requires money. They wish to acquire five acres of land which it would be well to get for future needs.

At the same time your Committee think that the Bussey Institution and the Arnold Arboretum and the Botanic Garden should have some common head, or guiding power, who should direct what each Department should devote itself to, to prevent duplication of work and waste of time, money, and material. Neither one can be given up and consolidated with the other Departments, apparently. For instance, the Botanic Garden has been in existence for a great many years, and its close proximity to the College gives it increased importance in its usefulness to the College, and while its small area and the value of its property might tempt one to advise its sale, your Committee feel, after deliberation, that this would be very unwise, and that any attempt to consolidate it with other Departments would be a mistake. They do feel, however, that there should be some guiding man to direct each one of these Departments as to what it should devote its energies.

The greenhouses needed repair, one in particular, the palm house, being very much out of order. This has been torn down and greenhouses put up more adapted for work than for show. The cost of this work has been met by friends of the Garden, one of whom has been particularly generous.

Interesting experiments are being made in the Garden with reference to the gypsy and brown-tail moths. A germ has been found that has been very effective with the brown-tail moth, and your

Committee are in hopes that equally good results will be accomplished in the case of the gypsy moth.

The branch of the Botanic Garden in Cuba seems to be running with success.

STEPHEN M. WELD, Chairman,

WALTER HUNNEWELL,

OLIVER AMES,

ERNEST B. DANE,

EDWIN F. ATKINS,

DECEMBER 14, 1910.

ARTHUR F. ESTABROOK.

The Committee also present the following minority report: —

I cannot agree with the recommendation embodied in this report to the Board of Overseers of Harvard College in regard to a common head to guide the work of the Bussey Institution, the Arnold Arbore-tum and the Botanic Garden, for the reason that I think the interests of the Botanic Garden would inevitably suffer. Though the three departments may have some points in common, their work is carried on with very different objects in view. The Botanic Garden is small in area and endowment, but is very important in its own place, yet under a common head it would easily arouse less interest and demand less attention than the other two, and in my opinion would soon become extinct. For this reason I find myself unable to agree with the majority report.

(Signed) MARY LEE WARE.

The subject of the Botanical Museum Budget is of such importance that I have devoted to it a good deal of study and anxious consideration, and I can as yet offer only preliminary suggestions.

The absolutely necessary running expenses for our Museum appear to be the following,-

I. An assistant to the Curator, answering to the "DIENER" in German institutions, whose duties are numerous and responsible. (A) He is to be at the service of the Curator for personal errands which economise the time or strength of the Curator. (B) He is to familiarise himself with all of the material and appliances of the Museum, and especially acquaint himself with every method of preservation and installation of specimens. And he is to prepare such specimens as the Curator desires to have attended to. (C) He is to inspect all the material and specimens on exhibition, in order to ascertain what specimens require replacing on account of the Museum. (D) In the absence of the Curator he is to act as a guide to the Museum as occasion demands. Such service is accounted worth about eight hundred or one thousand dollars per annum, including about four weeks of vacation, that is to say, $66. to $83. per month. (Louis C. Bierweiler is now receiving $16. dollars a week, and should soon receive at least $18. per week, or about $936. per annum)

These items aggregate rather less than $2,300. a year of fifty-two weeks.

In some years, the total expense would be considerably less.

The above account does not include the purchase of books or pamphlets or the care of the library, but this is supposed to be otherwise provided for.

All of which is hesitatingly and doubtfully submitted.

My dear Friend Blaschka,

Mrs. Goodale and I are much indebted to you for the excellent postal-card view of Villa Blaschka, a souvenir of your early life. We know that you must have had a delightful wedding—journey in Bohemia, and we trust that you found your Mother well on your return. We are glad that you are to take your time this summer to complete the arduous task of the models representing the relations of plants to insects. Miss Ware told me the other day, when she was here, that she had in mind forwarding your Honorarium as usual, about July.

Today, I have had a delightful call in our Museum from a gentle-man who has examined your models of animals as well as of plants, and he seemed much pleased with them. He asked me as to the present condition of any contract or understanding with you about continuing to construct models for Harvard University. To his question I gave the following pro- visional answer, namely, that you were anxious to take a good rest after finishing the present shipment, and that you would probably desire to have a good part of a year for this purpose. I said that, so far as I was aware you had not yet made any arrangement with any institution for constructing zoological models, but that it would seem desirable to secure your services if possible, for the Museum of Comparative Zoology in Cambridge, since you were so fully identified with Harvard. He expressed a desire to be informed as to any arrangement which you would be willing to make with Harvard University or its representatives, to this end.

Therefore I write now, on my own responsibility, asking you to write me, at your leisure, whether you would be willing to undertake a series of models of marine invertebrata, from your fresh original studies, as soon as you have finished the plants, and have had sufficient rest, such models to be for this University, and if circumstances favor, without any replicas of the specimens for other institutions.

A second question would involve the amount of annual honorarium which you would consider adequate.

Thirdly, it would be likely that the subjects would be selected by our Curator-in-Chief, Mr. Samuel Henshaw, due regard being had to the supply of material available on the European coast.

Might I ask you to think this matter over, and let me know your views. We trust before you relinquish your activity, our University may be enriched by models replacing some of the earlier specimens which we have, and which your greater facility in exact reproduction would perhaps replace to your satisfaction.

Let us, at any rate, have the privilege of meeting your views, if we possibly can, and thus continuing your name in its pleasant and honorable connection with our University.

We were glad to learn of the excellent health of you all. I am glad to state that Mrs. Goodale's health continues to improve slowly, and she sees no reason for not going soon to our country home.

With every good wish to you all from us all,

Dear Miss Ware

On Thursday this week I received your good letter of Feb. 6th enclosing cheque for: 5000 Marks (Fiveth thousand Marks) The receipt of which amount I hereby acknowledge with thanks, placed it to your credit as advance-payment, which is amounting by this totally to 19000 Mark (Nineteenth thousand Marks). Of course I have already also a number of activa by models finished and in hand, and I could only wish in my interest, I had more. But these enlarged models of Anthesis of flowers and insects remain always a remarkably difficult matter not to compare with any plants formerly received from us, I'm cases f.i. the broom and when very rarely a viewer will have the slightest idea of the trouble applied in these things. This I state without any exaggeration as I have not the least interest in any way to

puff in these matters. I only wish you will be satisfied with the time in which I am able to perform these models and I wish you would receive them sometime as safely as the former ones as I don't like to do this work for a second time. It is quite in my own interest to see how I best get through this work and, as I wrote you in my letter of Feb. 3 your determinations are entirely free. I shall see how much I finished until about the end of this year.

We all are very glad to learn from your letter that you are well again. It's I already told you we all three were visited by heavy Bronschitis all January. While I got much better by the beginning of February, my poor ladies got serious relapses, that made me apprehensive for both. Fortunately they are now almost over it and the near spring will make it all right.

February was mild, no snow, almost like spring, vegetation with swelling buds, the taxels in our garden almost past bloom. Such early springs are not favorable here, better much snow and ice in February than later in April and May when we hate it. We read much in our papers of blizzards and hurricanes in America but I know these storms are as a rule more dreadfully raging in the printing-press than in truth. I can well understand what you write of the election in Boston and your mayor. I'm it curious, we live in a time of conflicts and sultry policy everywhere in the world. We read here with attention the reports of Russia's hasty arming, though I think our national papers use it for justifying the German arming contribution. But one thing is remarkable and gives to think: the severe order of abstinence. To think, Russia and no brandy! If strictly carried out, this state can get dangerous.

Today I also wrote a line to Prof. Goodale very late. Oiving to the various troubles with us it had been postponed.

We all unite in cordial good wishes and

kindest regards to you and with renewed

thanks, believe me,

very sincerely your

Rudolph Blaschka

The selection of species for illustration has been so carefully thought out and has so perfectly met Herr Blaschka's view and secured from him such full co-operation, that we have no important gaps in our systematic collection! It would be well to have about fifteen more, but although we have room for them, it will be almost impossible to get fresh material for their preparation.

We need about twenty more specimens to illustrate fully the subject of pollination. Since these are simple species,and easy to procure,they could be perhaps finished in one year.

(2) SUGGESTIONS.

From R. Blaschka's statement, it appears that he considers that he has in hand, and standing to Miss Ware's credit, the sum of 14,000 Reichsmark.

While this is plainly enough to remunerate him for the twenty specimens above referred to, it would be perhaps better, in this last year of his work on these models, to offer him another draft, say in July. This depends wholly upon the attitude of Miss Ware, since in my opinion, Blaschka does not feel like exacting any more than he has received. Blaschka's work and dealings have always been so satisfactory, that everything which we can do to show high appreciation, will be most gratefully received by him.

During this coming year, it will be the task of no small magnitude to transfer, under favorable conditions, Blaschka's activities to the Department of ZOOLOGY. And this is the task to which, if my health permits,

(2) The suggestion to remove the large specimens of Australian woods from the Economic room was made because (a) we need the space, and (b) nobody even looks at them twice, as they pass through the room. We should not miss them after a single day.

(3)The laboratory was removed to my house because I could not view with

composure the use of flame in it.I wanted to reduce the fire risk,although

it was almost negligible,to absolutely nothing. The laboratory is used

### for

University purposes just as much as ever, and its small expenses are in part defrayed from our assigned income. Since the University provides a part of the conveniences and the whole of the chemicals, and the service of the aids , (other than Louis), I have preferred to consider it as constructively a University matter, although I furnish the heating, gas , light, and give my entire services. Professor Sharples has investigated the rooms and reported to the Committee that they were well adapted to their purpose. He made some recommendations as to additional conveniences, and these will be probably furnished by a member of the Committee. So, you see, the laboratory is mine chiefly because I house it and run it: it is partly University, because the solicited funds are employed for some of the materials, etc.

Before making the suggested changes,I shall wait to hear from two members of the Committee who wish to think the matter over a little.

In these depressing days of reduced incomes, I am determined that the friends of the University shall not feel burdened by any requests of the Museum. I can economize in every way rather than have any such burden come on anybody's shoulders.

I hope that you have not been tired by my long explanations, and if there is any point left unexplained, please tell me when you come down.

Etta who is just going out for some shopping, asks to join in sending to you love and thanks and all good messages, and she expresses the hope that you will soon return to Cambridge, where we can talk over everything except the war.

1 Dec 1916

My dear Mr. Blaschka,

We still haven't heard from you or your family and it is very upsetting to us. We would so much like to know how you and your loved ones are. It appears that our letters to you and yours to us were stopped on their way, but I can't think of anything written in our letters that would have been objectionable for the censors of either country.

All of your friends here are doing well, although I was seriously ill with Glycosuria this summer. I had to follow a strict diet and am now doing much better. Mrs. Goodale is “Thank God,” in excellent health. On December 4 $ ^{th} $ we will celebrate our golden anniversary and we are thankful in our hearts that this great milestone finds us both in good health, but we see that we are nearing the end of our lives.

You will be glad to hear that the director of the zoological museum gave your models of invertebrate sea animals a place with much better light than they had previously. They make a magnificent exhibit and we are hoping that after the war more objects will follow these fine ones. Miss Ware is doing very well and would send all of you heartfelt greetings if she knew I was writing to you.

With our best wishes to you and your dear family for Christmas and the New Year

I remain your loyal friend,

GLG

Dear Miss Ware:

At last I am, after long delay, enabled to reply

to and to thank you for your good letters of June from Interlaken

and of August 20th from Tunbridge Wells. I had made up my mind

not to write before the shipment of models is on the way to America

which has taken place on Saturday, September 8th when 4 cases,

signed R. B. No. 1 to 4, were brought to Dresden station for Bremen.

The forwarding agents, Ehrhorn, Emden & Mayer, Bremen, will take

care for the shipping by next steamer to New York where the cases

go in bond to Boston, care of E. A. Snow, Customhouse broker and

forwarding agent, Boston, Mass., addressed to the University Museum,

Harvard University, Director Mr. Samuel Henshaw, Cambridge, Mass.

The models were finished exactly about the time when I wrote you

last in June, and after the work of mounting etc. it was on Monday,

July 16th, when I met the request of some friends to exhibit the

models for some afternoon hours in two rooms of my house. Only a

small circle was admitted, the mayor, the parson, some scientists

and their families, about 20 persons, who would witness to have

seen my work ready for sending at this day. In normal times the

shipment had long ago reached the Museum. However, it was not a

trifle to conquer the official obstacles. At first I had to

apply to one of the export offices at Berlin on account of the

export permission. I requested for the exemption from export tax

for these unique means of instruction and explained the difficult

case of the consignment of 1913-14, which had got into the

possession of the Harvard Museum by your prepayment of 19000 Marks

at that date and would have been sent at a time when the export

tax has not yet existed, unless the war had prevented shipping.

Owing to the abolition of the gold standard in Germany 1914 and the

government's decision that, Mark is Mark, I had actually with the

deposited amount only 19000 paper marks in my hands, a complete loss,

as it is the case with all our old bond fortunes. This was specially to state as the export tax is presently calculated after

valorization in gold marks. So my German invoice of August 5th

demanded by the authorities, gives the value in Marks as actually

received, 19000 Marks for the models of 1913-14, and 24831000 Marks

received for the grasses 1921-22. In the American consular invoice

however, the amounts are given in Dollars, the actual value for

America as paid, 4514 Dollars for the models of 1913-14 and

2000 Dollars for the grasses. The insurance is fixed after this

Dollar value. After a long delay the license came from Berlin on

September 3d, and a polite letter, the export office had not been

competent about exemption, they laid it before the Reichs-commissary

who again declared himself incompetent. The matter must go to the

Economic department and to the Financial department of Germany.

They charge an export tax on the shipment of 40 gold pennies

(= 516000 papermarks or a little less than 10 American cents) and

283000 extra charges and at a renewed applying I might get it

returned. Well, I paid this all, and don't care for farthur

claims as postage, paper and ink would cost more. The second and

most important obstacle and the most obvious reason why an earlier

shipping was impracticable was the strict paragraph of the exportorder-reglement that all export goods, before delivered to railroad,

must be brought to the next custom-house and unpacked and delivered there for revision. Exception was not admitted. As my delicate work would not stand this treatment I went to the Director of the Chief custom-house of Dresden and explained the matter, asking for an exception. He kindly agreed as an exceptional case to send 2 custom-house officers to Hosterwitz who came on 6th Inst. and I packed the models before their eyes. As the packer from Dresden could finish the case packing at the same time, the whole matter was finished in 9 hours. After this the officers put the official German custom seal on the cases, so they are safe on the road to America. It was a remarkable feeling with us when the 4 cases left the house, at least reached the aim after so long waiting, so many pains and all the experiences. The cost of the charges that I had to carry along on my own shoulders as I, curious, had not received even a cent this year from America, were considerable, though trifles in your money. The charges amounted to 30 to 40 times higher sums than I had pre-estimated in my German invoice. I had calculated at beginning of August for them 15 Millions 100000 Marks altogether, so that from the whole received sum of 24850000 Marks net amount of 9 Millions 750000 Marks remained for my models. But how badly this has changed! The custom house charges were actually 7842000 Marks, the packer charged 12 Millions for the afternoon, the carter 20000000 (twenty Millions) for cartage from Hosterwitz to Dresden, the American consulate's certificate charges are 150 Million Marks. There were still some more Millions extra to spend, a visit to Dresden in the electric car has cost, Hosterwitz to Dresden and return each person; last week 600000 Marks, (since

Wednesday this week it costs one Million and a half). If these charges should be calculated today on a bill in German money there would be left less than nothing for my work. The average index for daily life expense was this week five millions times higher than 1914, and as the prices rise rapidly to reach or surmount the Dollar parity, we have to except the 25 Millions fold in a few weeks. This is worse than in the worst times of Russia. I really did not know how to mobilize the huge sums for sending charges and there will still be a lot of subsequent taxes. It is a bad blow that the friends in America have left me in the briers this year, and they ought to be so kind now to think of me. I am at the end of my financial power. The materials, paraffine, etc. have risen to hundreds of millions so that I must be provided with money to be enabled to continue my work. What the late good Dr. Goodale would say who has offered me such a noble contract! I have read thank-fully your very kind offer in your letters. It is by no means difficult to remit money to here. Checks directly assigned to any bank or banker in Dresden go safely as the receiver must show his legitimation. There is also a much used manner to send money without draft only by the correspondence of the banks. This is the safest of all. The banker in America sends the money directly to a Dresden bank, who after receipt notifies me of it and I get the amount without deduction. The money is better sent in smaller amounts and always in Dollars, never in papermarks, which soon will be, hors de combat. We don't get now handed over bank remittances in Dollar bills except against a license of the financial state office. The state collects these valuable bills himself and gives gold mark

checks for it. There are many people here who have friends in America and receive of them now and then a dollar bill right within the letter. They wrap it in a piece of newspaper and put it between the lines. We have relatives here who have friends in America and never failed to receive their enclosures. Now I have still to say that the expenses of railroad freight, insurance and sea-charges are to pay by the consignee. The amounts are disbursed by the above called Lloyd-agents at Bremen and raised by reimbursement, as it always was the use. The models of 1913-14, chiefly packed in the cases No. 1 and 2, are adequate to the list I sent Prof. Goodale in November 1920, with the addition of Passiflora. The number of species with these models as well as with the grasses are not the measure to rate them. Most of the enlarged models don't range among the former, analytical details, they rather are adequate in rank and value to intricate plants. Everything of these matters is painful work.

We hope you have safely reached your home and feel happy in the reflection on your pleasant journey. We can understand how sad it was to miss your deal old friend Dr. Goodale. We know this feeling as we still miss our good mother at every turn. I thank you sincerely for your warm words of cordial sympathy in our bereavement and for the love and esteem you remember of her. She was so plain and modest, but by her noble gifts and the qualities of her mind she deserved the highest respect by the world. We feel we have lost our true friend for ever, but as to the dreadful times, we are compelled to live in, and what still is impending over us, it is a comfort to think she is happy.

My wife joins me in kindest regards and all good wishes for you. Very sincerely yours,

Rudolph Blaschka.

My dear Miss Ware:

On the assumption that you have returned from your trip to Europe, I am sending this letter to your home-address.

Your letter of June twenty-first has been often in my mind because of your suggestions regarding the very problematical status of my future relations to the Museum. I would have answered that letter long ago, if I had not been deterred from doing so by the length at which I should have had to write. It seemed wiser to await your return when a conference, should you desire one, would be a much better means than a lengthy letter of making my position clear.

The Museum has also been much in my mind because there seem to be many points of view regarding its future development. Aside from finan- cial details there is the very serious question of the policy to be adopted if you have any influence in shaping it. The financial details are truly elastic. At this time if only sufficient income is available to pay salaries, the question crops up, 'What will salaries purchase in the way of constructive progress? There is nothing really constructive in shifting the collections about to make them more attractive. But I imagine many changes might be suggested to somebody who found himself confronted by the necessity to make a show of activity.

Curator will be a museum-man with a strong leaning toward economic botany, or shall we say, plants in the service of man? At heart Dr. Goodale was an economic botanist. A reading of his reports on the departments under his direction will prove this beyond any cloud of doubt. In fact, he expressed himself significantly for us in that report to President Eliot in which he wrote: It seems no longer wise to withhold a declaration of the policy which I advocate in regard to the

Museum or Economic Botany. It is my wish to make the collection an authoritative cabinet of type specimens to be described in an illustrated series of studies. Goodale did not live in good health long enough to make this ambitious project take definite shape. Perhaps his enthusiasm and optimism prompted the declaration of a hope before he had reached that point in the acquirement of knowledge which made economic bot-any seem to great a subject for one man to handle.

As I think of the Museum I am a bit pleased by the thought that some young man might begin to carry through the task which Goodale hoped to begin. I would be pleased to co-operate with any candidate for the work, unofficially if neceassry, if my aid or advice were regarded worthy of consideration.

Just at present I do not believe that the question of a large endowment is very pressing. To me it seems that the policy for future research is important. To be perfectly frank with you, I am not sure that there is anybody in sight who would satisfy my tastes in the matter of the policy that should prevail. This letter will give you at last.

my matured views regarding the Museum. To pick up in a few words what I have tried to say:

I. Salaries for a Curator and one or more assistants.

II. A policy that will carry through Dr. Goodales strong interest in economic botany.

and I would add, lectures that should make the Museum of vital importance in the instruction offered to classes in botany in Harvard College.

Yours faithfully,

Oakes Amers,
