My dear Mr. Pingree:

In a letter addressed to Francis Goodale you were kind enough to inform him that you would be interested in any report I might wish to make regarding the Botanical Museum. At that time I was feeling my way in a new position and I did not think that I could speak with authority. Now I have had an opportunity to study the Museum and I am anxious to tell you something about what has been done and of what I propose to do.

There were difficulties in the way of carrying out Dr. Goodale's cherished scheme for a consolidation, in different rooms, of the several types of exhibition material, because the Blaschka models had encroached on the fourth floor where it was thought the economic collections, research laboratory and library of economic botany should be concentrated. The solution of the main problem was furnished by Miss Ware, who undertook to pay the bills for moving the heavy exhibition cases from the third floor stairhall to the gallery. This single change (a heroic one), made possible the bringing together of the entire collection of Blaschka models on the third floor of the Museum to form a comprehensive unit. The fourth floor gallery now presents a most attractive room, free for the display and systematic arrangement of those plants which take part in the service of the human race. Your thoughts will turn to the economic room on the third floor, between the botanical and zoological sections. I intend to assemble here the botanical raw products that enter commerce through the port of Boston, in attractive and thoroughly explained exhibits. This room will be conducted with special attention to the needs of the schools of Cambridge and Boston, and will form a unit, distinct as to conception and purpose from the main economic department.

My course in Applied Botany 15, will be given in the Museum. This means that my library and equipment now at the Bussey Institution will be moved to Cambridge and installed on the fourth floor of the Museum in the two delightful rooms known as 20 and 21a. These rooms are just about ready for use, having been painted and supplied with electric current. Room 20 is to be used as a laboratory and reference library. Room 21a will become my research laboratory. In this room my books of economic botany will be installed on the Museum.

ed, together with my extensive catalogues devoted to botanical

products, their source, history and bibliography. Here also, the growing rebarrium of economic plants will find a place. In these rooms the background of facts will be built up, against which the collections of the Museum are arranged.

One thing has been a source of keen delight to me. I refer to the extensive use of the collections by supervised classes from neighboring colleges and from the public schools. It is really pleasurable to see young people armed with note-books, attack their problems with a complete knowledge of the welcome that is extended to them. I intend to reach these young people through a series of bulletins just as soon as I can settle down to the task of doing this. Here is an opportunity to do a useful bit of Museum work.

We have sufficient space for our needs and an interesting diversity in the service we attempt to render, but to take a commanding position in our field of effort, we should concentrate our attention on the research work that is necessary to make the Museum an outstanding institution. Research is costly because it means labor of a highly technical kind. Until a research assistant is added to the Museum staff, the entire burden of investigation, fact-finding and fact-treasuring will devolve on the unpaid Curator.

The Museum is visited daily by the public with great crowds on Sunday. It can be said without danger of exaggeration, that the Botanical Museum through the Ware Collection, is the most attractive and most popular institution in the University. This being true, it is a wonder of wonders that until the Eliot C. Lee Fund with an income of $24. per annum was formed on December 24, 1923, this influential department of Harvard University which ought to be overwhelmed with opulence, has been for thirty-six years, without a dollar of endowment.

My dear Mr. Blaschka:

I was delighted to learn from your letter of the fourth February that my instructions reached you promptly, and I was overjoyed to learn from your reply that you have grasped my idea. I am sure that the new basis for operations will open up a most satisfactory opportunity for you to make your skill stand out and to allow your artistic temperament full sway. One word of caution: In making models of the diseases of plants, please confine yourself to the macroscopic details of the lower organisms; that is, to the appearance of the disease rather than to its microscopic details. The reason for this caution is this: there is always the danger of jealousy playing a part in universities, and if one department seems to take over the function of another department, trouble often arises. This has happened before when the phanerogamic botanist has attempted to exhibit materials that are properly in the province of the cryptogamic botanist. The other day during a conference with one of my colleagues, I remarked that the glass models were attracting to our University over one hundred thousand visitors a year. To this he replied that in Baedecker's Guide-Book, there were two stars against the Cistine Madonna.

This led to the suggestion that we ought to have a model maker on the spot. Of course, under the present conditions this is impossible, and the suggestion is only interesting. Then, Dr. Wheeler referred to the models at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and remarked that the man who makes the models for that museum is, in his estimation, more skilful than Blaschka. I find it hard to believe this, but I shall go to the New York Museum in the near future to check up. Perhaps, if you are in New York in the near future, it might be well for you to take the time to examine the models there from a comparative point of view.

Just at this time I am rendered unsettled in my mind by an invitation to go with Ham Rice and Dr. Strong to the Amazon this summer. Dr. Strong wishes to have me along to study poisonous plants. Nothing may come of this, but while it remains a probability, I shall be uneasy. A little hardship along the Amazon might result in collections of value for the Museum. So much for that.

Work is progressing at the Museum in a satisfactory way, and I

expect to drive the painters from the stairway before the middle of next week.

Yours faithfully,

Qakes Amess.

My dear Miss Ware:

John Waugh has arrived with material for the construction of the new cases. His promptness rather took my breath away, as I had been led to believe that he would need much time in which to secure the necessary stock. I am afraid that you are not ready to go on with the new cases at this time. If my understanding is right, undoubtedly I can weather the storm in some way. Please be very frank about this, and if you wish me to so, I shall attempt to raise funds to meet Waugh's bill when it is presented.

We are about ready to start on the distribution of the models. In fact, I think the autumn will see the collection properly named and distributed.

Biology 1 students are making daily use of the Museum and my economic library seems to be doing good work at last. This is what I hoped for and I am very well satisfied.

To-day a great strangling fig arrived from Horticultural Hall. This specimen was brought from Florida by Mr. Burrage for the great Orchid Show.

Attendance at the Museum is on the increase. About five thousand for May so far.

I lectured for half an hour to a class from me of the high schools. This experiment led me to believe that we might arrange for such lectures as a regular service of the Museum. It is a simple matter to arrange an attractive exhibit on one of the tables and then touch the high-spots of economic botany. We might make friends for the Museum in this way if we could from time to time get small groups of interested people to come to the laboratory lecture-rooms. Parents and children might come together in small groups.

Prof, Wheeler is making use of the insect models in connection with his course on entomology. This course is given on the fifth floor, in the laboratories assigned to the Bussey Institution.

A vacancy is about to be made by the removal of Mr. Webster from the Visiting Committee. Mr. Webster is no longer eligible for reappointment. I think Victor M. Cutter, Vice President of the United Fruit Company might be a good man for the Committee. If you have any suggestions as to other candidates, I wish you would give them to me.

I saw Dr. Gage on Monday. He did not think that another meeting of the Committee would be necessary until next year.

I have already had enquiries about my course in economic botany. It would seem that the Biology 1 students who come to my laboratory to read economic subjects in connection with their written reports have their interest stimulated in the broader significance of Botany and wish to go farther in the subject.

Please excuse this very scrappy and badly written

letter, I find that my mind becomes weary by night time.

My last orchid book was awarded a gold medal.

Yours faithfully,

(Signed) Oakes Ames.

My dear Miss Ware:

I realized when I wrote to you last, that the news of John Waugh's activities would disturb your equanimity. When I gave the order for the new cases, I was under the impression that John would be busy in Philadelphia for the greater part of the summer. What I thought, however, has nothing to do with the present situation. It is before me and I intend to master it. I have studied my budget carefully and I think I can see money enough to pay John's bill without having Mr. Mead take me to task. So much for that. It is the very least of my burdens.

The heavies burden in sight for me to carry is one that will

fill your soul with pure joy. I have just passed what might be termed an exclamatory morning. Something like witnessing a show of fireworks that begins with a

few Roman canfles, and ends with bombs that explode in succession and make the

most physical onlooker give audible expression to his feelings. At eleven o'clock

I met Professor Weston by appointment and together we went through the models of

the cryptogams. For the first time I saw this collection as a whole. The experience

both for Weston and myself was not only delightful but overwhelming. We agreed

that the necessity for exhibiting these models is a pressing one and we both felt

impatience for the day to arrive when the collection can be made available for

students and the public. But here comes the burden. A burden that is best expressed

in terms of space. We have not the cases in which to exhibit the cryptogams. Even

with the addition that Waugh is now making to our case equipment, we shall fall

far short of space enough for them. Then again, we must do some experimenting

with tablets, because Weston agrees with me that the delicate cell structures

constructed of white glass must be contrasted with black. It will take our combined

ingenuity to make the best of a beautiful collection. Weston gave vent to his

feelings by saying, "And these have been rotting here all these years!"

Our meeting this morning was for the purpose of weeding out

the poorer models. I think we came to the end of our task with less than four

models in the discard. To exhibit the models that were accepted would take more

case-room than is now given over to the insect-models. Yes, much more. And that

is a serious discovery. It may mean a row of tower cases along the wall to the

left of the stairs on the third floor where the ferns are now in position. If we

are able to mass the cryptogams as a unit, I am sure that we shall have an exhibit

that will call for three stars in Baedeker.

I agree with you as to Dr. Gage's attitude toward another meeting this year.

My impression is that he not aware of the importance of the work the Museum is doing for the University and for the public. How to awaken the interest of the Committee is a matter for serious consideration. I have enough faith in the Museum to give my time to it, and it seems to me that my efforts should meet with something more substantial than thanks or praise. I have reached that point in life where thanks and praise mean very little. I am more interested in results of a substantial and helpful kind. You and Miss Minns have made me very happy, but I am not willing to impose on you good people.

I find that the glass models are regarded by a captious critic of by gone days, as one of the really great achievements of Dr. Goodale's administration. This man has come to see that a museum must first attract and then educate. As Dr. Moore of the Missouri Botanic Garden put it to me at the Orchid Show on May 10th, "The glass models are the most attractive bait that exists anywhere against which to build a botanical museum." This change of front on the part of bot anists makes me anxious to have the whole collection of models tell its story at last. I expect to leave for North Easton by the end of next week. Through the summer I shall make trips to the Museum to keep the work moving smoothly.

Yours with best wishes,

Qakes Amess

##### No. 45

#### REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE TO VISIT THE BOTANICAL MUSEUM

To THE BOARD OF OVERSEERS OF HARVARD COLLEGE:—

The Committee to visit the Botanical Museum is pleased to report that very great progress has been made in the last few years in several directions:

1. Closer relations have been established between the Museum and the Botanical Department of the University. The Museum collections are now used for demonstrations in laboratories and lecture rooms, special exhibits have been set up in the lecture rooms to remain in place while a special topic is being developed, students in the elementary courses, Biology A and Botany 1, are conducted through the Museum to study certain groups of models to amplify observations made in the laboratory. The Museum, in other words, has become a living thing in botanical instruction in Harvard University.

2. It is now adequately lighted.

3. The Blaschka collection of models of cryptogams, after remaining in storage for more than twenty years, has been placed on exhibition and is used by the students under the direction of their instructors. This is the outstanding collection of its kind. In addition, all the Blaschka models have been reclassified in conformity with the Engler and Prantl system, which marks an outstanding accomplishment in museum technique. A valuable manuscript based on the Blaschka glass models is now ready for the press. In the course of this year over 200,000 visitors came to inspect these models.

4. A private laboratory has been created for the Curator in the basement of the building, where is deposited one of the priceless botanical treasures of the world,— a collection of plants used to supply information to the National Museum and to other large establishments in America and Europe.

5. A large collection of botanical raw products which has suffered seriously from inroads of time and insects has been thoroughly sterilized and transferred to museum bottles and is now available for study in connection with research work in industrial botany.

6. One of the most outstanding accomplishments of the Museum has been the making of a complete catalogue of its library, including the articles in current magazine literature, according to subjects and to illustrative plates. This catalogue is constantly used by the Museum staff, by the professors and students in the Botanical Department, and by investigators who come to the Museum for specialized information.

Too much credit cannot be given to Professor Oakes Ames for the progress indicated by the foregoing statements. It is not only a remarkable example of administrative efficiency, but is making the Museum a very valuable adjunct to the teaching of Botany. To keep this catalogue up to date and maintain the Museum at its present level of efficiency, an additional sum of $1300 per annum is needed to provide for the necessary clerical assistance. The accomplishments of the Museum certainly warrant this additional expenditure.

My dear Miss Ware.

It seems ages ago since my last letter to you was written, but there has been very little to write about except my own troubles. In February I went on a trip to the West Indies, planning to spend some time in Jamaica with Blanche for the purpose of assembling material for the Museum. When we reached Havana, word came that Pauline was very ill and needed her mother. There was nothing to do except obey the calls of home. Blanche made a quick get away and I went on with the baggage making the round trip via the Canal Zone and Costa Rica. The day I reached home I came down with grip and had to remain in bed for days. Recovery was slow after I got up and to make myself fit for duty, I went to Arizona and remained there among desert things until the first of May was coming along. Then I returned to Boston and began to pick up my work at the Museum and elsewhere. I have been busy almost every hour of the day since May first and while I have thought of you and the things that are of interest to you, I have really had no time in which to write, unless I used my stenographer, and that is not according to Hoyle.

Work on the Economic Room is progressing slowoy. It takes time to prepare the exhibits and to arrange them after they are prepared. But I am sure that the new arrangement will please you and be more useful.

Your letter about amber thrilled me of course, because I have a deep interest in this material and have a strong desire to assemble as many examples as possible of the different types including the rare Sicilian variety. What we already have makes a brave showing, but it is chiefly Baltic and a bit monotonous

from the point of view of a Museum collection. If you have succeeded in picking up some additions, your efforts will bring joy to my soul.

You have a very wrong idea of the book I have had prepared for the elucidation of the glass models. This book has very little to do with the Blaschkas and the history of the collection. It is rather a catalogue raisonné and not only deals with every species represented but uses each species as an excuse for bringing in allied species that are of economic importance. It is a book which will appeal to the student and will be a distinct addition to botanical literature. Once published it will make the Ware Collection a basis for the wider study of plants in the service of man. I am in no hurry to issue the book as I want first to receive the fruit models and include them. This is a wise delay.

You wrote that you would be willing to help the Museum in its 1927-28 budget. Of course you have done more than your share already and it seems unkind to look to you for additional funds. If you feel that you want to help, any assistance received before June 30th will be pure gold. I want the Committee to help this year as I have been far to liberal in running up bills against our slender and dadly inadequate income. I am afraid however that the members of the Committee, excepting the ever kind and interested Miss Minns, will not contribute very generously.

The collection of fossils displayed on the third floor landing, has been the source of much favorable comment and the palaeontologists from the other side of the Museum are coming to us for opportunities to study fossil plants. Each fossil has been provided with a lacquer red stand and the bright color helps the general appearance vastly.

We have nearly arrived at the million mark for the Arboretum Fund.

I have added one full professor to the staff with the title of Professor of Forest Pathology and now I am after a first rank plant breeder. Mr. Lowell is standing back of my enthusiasm and my one hope is that my efforts will please him.

This is a very anxious week for me as the General Education Board,

Rockefeller Foundation, has its meeting this week and will consider whether or not to grant three or four millions for Harvard Biology. The Chairman of the Board had lunch with a group of us a few Saturdays ago and I have a feeling of confidence in the result of the Board's meeting which takes place, I believe, on the 24th May. With several million dollars we could make a brave showing in matters biological. And I should have a feeling that I had had my finger in the pie.

Louis informed me a day or so ago that there was a rumor about that you might not return home this summer. I sincerely hope that there is no foundation for such a situation. We need encouragement and enthusiastic support in our work and we look to you as one of our staunch allies. Any way it was very fortunate that you were away this winter and that you have been able to escape this awful spring. Day after day of east wind and chilly nights.

I am really worried about Mr. Blaschka's work. The last shipment

came in before I was appointed Curator of the Museum. Surely there must be some completed work that could be forwarded to us for exhibition. I sometimes wonder if the poor man is really able to produce any more. At other times I have hoped that his product of these recent years will be outstanding even if limited in amount.

Just now I am looking forward to the end of administrative duties.

Vacation is coming along, and when it arrives, I can settle down to a little research and turn out some of the long delayed papers I have had in mind.

With the best of good wishes,

Miss May Lee Ware, Florence, Italy.

Faithfully yours,

Oakes Ames

My dear Miss Ware:

Your good letter of the seventeenth June was on my desk when I reached the Museum yesterday afternoon. It was most kind of you to have Mr. Ware send to me a check for current expenses of the Museum. Five hundred dollars came in before the end of the fiscal year and I found that this amount added to what I could spare, carried the accounts to an end without the blemish of a deficit and the threat of a criticism.

Two hundred and nineteen visitors came to see the Ware collection between May 1927 and May 1928. There seems to be no decrease in the interest which the collection arouses in the public.

I am indeed delighted with the success that has attended your efforts in the search for Roumanian and Sicilian amber. The specimens you have obtained will round out the resin collection in a most satisfactory way. Resins and ambers are about all I think about just now. When I began my studies of the varnish resins, the so-called copals, I found that the Museum collection was in a sorry mess systematically, although Dr. Goodale had given a great deal of attention to the group and was deeply interested in it. Most of the varnish resins are either fossils or semifossils and to identify them as to the yielding species is a patience-testing task. The difficulties of the subject have aroused my deepest interests and I just roam about thinking of copals and neglecting other important subjects. Alfred Rehder of the Arboretum is leaving for a tour of the European Herbaria and I have slipped into his hand a long list of the kinds of copals I want him to obtain from the Museums of botanical raw products. I don't suppose there is anything you can do in this line, but if you have an opportunity to visit

some one of the more important varnish resin importing houses in Germany or England or France or elsewhere, you might find amusement in an attempt to obtain for the Museum sample specimens of the different types of East African and West African can copals. You must understand that one of the chief reasons for my wanting material from a variety of sources is based on the fact that one must have an abundance of material in order to arrive at definitive conclusions. My present supply of material is too exasperatingly limited to lead me to safe conclusions. You may not find the slightest bit of interest in this hobby of mine, but if you need some pleasant work to occupy your mind, I can recommend an attack on the copals. The cost of copals is so reasonable that one does not have to think about prices. They cost so much a pound and the price is regulated by commercial demands. Some of the larger pieces of West African copal are really beautiful when they are properly prepared for exhibition purposes.

Pauline came through her troubles all right. She is here with us now for the summer vacation. Blanche is threatening to turn me out of my library as she wants it for a studio while painting a large portrait group of Mrs. Winthrop Ames and her two children.

I shall be busy this summer planning for the new biological building. Mr. Lowell has made me chairman of the Committee that is to have the new building in charge. By this I mean the planning of the distribution of space.

The painters are busy in the Mineralogical Exhibition Room.

Dr. Palachi has decided to use the same color scheme that now prevails in the Bot-anical and Zoological Sections.

I cannot tell you how deeply I appreciate your substantial coming interest in what we are doing. Your generous gift/at a time when I really felt discouraged about the budget for 1927-28 gave me a thrill of satisfaction and made me very happy.

My dear Miss Ware:

I received the specimen of Roumanian amber on Tuesday and immediately placed it in the amber collection. I lack the capacity to tell you how deeply I feel my indebtedness to you for your kindness. It was difficult to believe that a strong desire had at last been gratified. If you could realize what the acquisition of that amber specimen means to me you would be able to measure my gratitude and understand my feeling of obligation. And then there is the knowledge that the remaining gap is to be filled and that again I shall owe to you the feeling of satisfaction which comes when a long quest is successfully completed.

It might have been wise to secure the other pieces that were offered. But the specimen you chose has the distinct advantage of showing the amber in the natural matrix. For educational purposes I feel that you could not have done better.

Many times I have thought of you this summer and been thankful that you decided to remain abroad, because never has another summer like this come within my experience. When it has not rained, the sky has been masked by heavy clouds and the air has been constantly humid and without snap.

I expect to be busy all summer with biological development at the University. We are expected to have our plans ready for the new building before the autumn sets in as President Lowell wishes to complete the building before the end of 1930. My dear Miss Ware: Your very welcome letter of the Fourth July came in this morning and was read with a deep interest. When I arrived at your reference to Sussmann I was much amused. I hardly believed that he would go so far out of his beaten track as Florence is. Before he departed on his annual trip to the amber markets he called on me to borrow a camera. Of course I had to mention the fact that at last Sicilian and Roumanian amber were within my reach. Sussmann's first reaction was one of fear that you might be imposed on. He asked if there would be any harm in his calling on you and requested that in any case I should furnish him with your address. Down deep in his heart I am sure the conviction that if he could come in touch with somebody who had really found a source of genuine Sicilian amber he would obtain profitable information. I am sure Sussmann is honest and that he will see to it that your confidence is not abused. He is an amber crank of the first rank and has been very kind to me, turning over to my collection at rediculously low cost or even as gifts, specimens of Baltic amber that only a man with his trade relations is able to pick up. His own large collection of Baltic amber is at present on loan to the Mineralogical Museum. Recently I have heard rumors that it has been purchased by the Field Museum. In the meantime the Botanical Museum collection has been growing in strength and with your additions will be among the most instructive in this country.

Today I am sending a cable message to you which means that I would very much like to have a large, unpolished piece of Sicilian amber and the two hundred dollar piece of Roumanian amber to which you have made references in your letters. If you are able to obtain these pieces, please let me know at once

how you wish to be paid for money out. In my last letter I referred to this matter and I am simply awaiting instructions. In the meantime I am overwhelmed with pure joy in thinking about all you have done. At least I am in part satisfied because I am sure that you have found the spirit of the chase uplifting and worth while.

There is nothing of importance to report regarding the Museum. The Summer School course in Botany is being given there and the sight seeing busses are more numerous than ever.

Dear Professor Ames,

It seemed easiest in this very long letter to separate the de-scription of the glass work itself from the more personal part, so I have done this and now will tell you the rest to the best of my ability. I have been out alone, half an hour by auto, three of the four times that I have been to Hosterwitz and have passed the whole afternoon, along one, looking first at the models, it took two afternoons to see them, then looking over the work room and its contents, being shown all the gmat improvements made by them in the house since his marriage, and finally accepting their hospitality of tea and delicious cakes, a far better arrangement than the old time one of a whole day and two solid meals! Both Mr. and Mrs. Blaschka received me most cordially at the little garden gate and we looked at each other to see what time had done, and that first day I was daunted to see what seemed a little old man, with not strong legs, very rounded, stooping shoulders and a very white face. He must have dropped nearly two inches in height, his hands are somewhat out of shape from rheumatism and were very trembling. However, to at once correct that impression, I came to the conclusion that it was partly or largely excitement at seeing me again and anxiety as to what I should say to the models. When I was ready to leave and said aufwidersehn he drew himself up with quiet dignity and said, "Well, Miss Ware, are you satisfied?" I said, "Yes, Mr. Blaschka, I am more than satisfied and I do not see how anyone could feel otherwise." He looked intensely relieved at once, and the next time I went out his colour had returned and Miss Niklason thought he looked well and strong, barring the stoop which I suppose is inevitable with such sedentary work.

His eyes are simply marvelous, piercing, and yesterday in painting the leaf he worked most of the time without glasses, and he is seventy-one! He speaks freely of his age, of the work which can possibly still

be accomplished and that he is the only one in the world who can do

it, which I think is true. You would never find another man who combined the scientific knowledge of many years study in plant and animal

life; the study of glass, its component parts and its possibilities,

not merely book knowledge but derived from experiment as well, together

with the power of concentration, mental and moral, the artistic ideal

as a load-star which has enabled him to forego everything called pleasure except his wife. She is sweet and devoted to his ideal too, has

softened and broadened him, and so humanized him that he is much better

fitted to come in contact with the world than the Rudolph Blaschka who

came to America in 1896. He is just as modest and absolutely honorable

as he ever was, but he has a sense of his own worth, his own unusual

force of intellect and character, and there is everything to justify

that. I asked him one day whether he was still applied to for models to

be kept in Germany and he said, "Oh, yes; the Prof. Nevmann, to whom he

went for something at your suggestion, asked why he would not give them

some of his work. I asked what he replied. "Oh," he said, "I told him

that I worked for Harvard University, that I was a man of absolute

honor, made no change and was satisfied."

I found that Sunday was his one day of rest and suspecting, from previous knowledge, that he was not taking time for air and exercise and perhaps working late in the evening, I extracted the information that lately he had taken little or no time for fresh air and had been working evenings, sometimes till midnight. I remonstrated vigorously and told him he must not do so, but he only said Prof. Ames wanted the models and tho' him very slow--that it was impossible for him to do such work any faster, that no man could. It had evidently worried him much and I had to work hard to reassure him that you would not feel so if you know him and could see him at work, that I would explain to you and that he

absolutely must stop evening work and get the necessary air and relaxation to keep himself in good condition. I told him also that you

were only impatient to complete the exhibition cases in the half, and

that even if the finished models were not completed in group form

as yet, that he had so many finished, that he better send those at once

before the bad weather of winter. It will be quite enough for you to

take care of at once, he only regrets that each group of fungus, etc.

is not complete, but he has had to do them as he could and when he could

get the specimens, etc. etc. Dependent more or less on seasons, weather

etc. He hopes to send off by the middle of the month, I think it will

be nearer the end, but perhaps not, some twenty-five models, sprays or

plants with their sections, etc. I think this includes all the pears except the blossoms, and strawberries, whether more I do not know. Apples,

plums, apricots, peaches, cherries, are largely finished ready for the

sprays, and the leaves largely ready to paint, exquisite fruit blossoms

ready for the branches (that part of the pears too will not come). He

thinks the rest will be ready for shipment in the spring, some thirty

more. The fruits are not so beautiful to look at as the flowers are,

but they are marvellous and how our man can do their hour after hour, putting in the gossamer veinlets, or all the myriad little brown dots and

irregular brown patches to the Beurres (在), passes my understanding,

you would say that years could not do it, or a lifetime. If he hurried

or worked quickly he would be insane.

I sat and watched his movements as he worked, the tale is covered not only with implements but with trays of leaves, formed but not colored, bottles in which he could stand the glass stems with leaves while drying or cooling, specimens of fungus covered fruit or dried leaves for use as guides (for the most part he could study them without glasses) bottles with powdered glass as needed, and saucers for the enamel paints of

powdered glass. In spite of the slightly unsteady hand his movements were quiet, deft, soft in laying down or taking up where speed or a miscalculated movement might ruin the work of hours. It is breathless to watch.

The first afternoon I saw the pears in every stage of disease, sometimes the fruit only, sometimes leaves and branch too. The moulds were wonderful and I think you will be delighted with them all, but, of course, I know nothing of fungus, etc. He had magnified 250 times a section of mould which comes on bread--remarkable. The strawberries were fascinating, plants, fruit and moulds, also the result of frosts on the developing fruit. The apples etc. were good, the peaches in their present stage of development seemed to me less so, but the final varnish was not yet on and they all looked rather glassy. It all leaves you breathless that anyone can and will do such work. Mr. B's head and bearing are very expressive and I wished I could catch a photograph of his profile as he stood for a few moments, a plaque with a model lying on its held in both hands, and his whole expression of absorbed, concentrated study was worth keeping, had it been possible. His own garden is small but full of fruit trees from which he gets some of his material for work and more he gets from large fruit orchards near by. He also has books on the fungus, mushrooms, and is looking forward eagerly to the work for Prof. Weston. He says the lamellae will be very difficult but that he can make them. In view of his advancing years and the uncertainty of health, I would suggest that Professor Weston makes a list of those subjects which he wants most, which are most important, although on account of weather, season, and materials it may be impossible for Mr. Blaschka to follow the sequence exactly, still it would be a guide.

It troubles me very much that he and his wife cannot come over to see his life's work now that you have them so beautifully arranged and he looks so eager and pathetic when I describe the mise en scene. They are very simple and unaffected, dignified, and I hope sometime that I can manage it if I can only keep well when I come home. It seems cruel not to but of course they could not travel on what they have in our country. I find that he did not lose all his investments in real estate or mortgages, etc. but all government investments. One change in the character of his work and consequently in the time necessary to accomplish results since I was last here is very noteworthy. Then he bought most of his glass and was beginning to make some, and his finish was in paint. Now he makes himself a large part of the glass and all the enamels, which he powders himself to use as paint, which he considers practically indestructible except by force--that if we could come back in a thousand years we should find from and color as today. He has dozens and dozens of little bottles with colored powders and little boxes labeled with colored enamels which he makes himself and pollers for paint. The colored enamels are beautiful and fascinating. Some pieces he exposed on his roof or under the eaves for over a year, winter and summer, and it had not changed in any way!

I have been housed for two days with a slight cold but otherwise

am feeling so much stronger. Tomorrow I go out for my last visit and

stay to supper. I will keep this open for any last items. Harm dreadfully

sorry that you hurt your finger so badly and hope that it is well before you begin work. I had no idea that you were fifty-five and as to

lectures, if I could do it as well as you can, I should adore hearing

myself speak! You really ought to have a gallery for ladies, exempt

from exams! I have had much bad news from home this summer, the death

of my cousin, Miss Morse, came very close; notwithstanding I have been

I have been showing the results of the year and a half of Dr. Gigholi's work. He has been patient and I have tried to be. Now when the rheuma-tism is finished off, I hope to return to my native land. Alas, I have had to give up the poultry plant. Too many grain bills to carry, I could not send at once to Bucharest, but have done so now and asked them to send you a colored drawing of the big piece in case some generous soul should feel inspired. I have not heard from them, post connections there are slow, but you will doubtless receive it like the other by Government pouch. I hope Susman turns up duly and shall be most anxious to hear what you think of the pieces of amber.

October 6 - My last visit to Hosterwitz was made most happily, Miss Niklason went with me and enjoys it as much as I do. Supper was excellent and informal and pleasant, and I regaled them with all the Museum gossip that I could think up. Mr. Blaschka did some leaf work again and Miss N felt just as I do, that it is a great experience to watch that man at work, his whole head and hands are a study and he worked until it was almost dark without turning his electric light. She also felt that the work was enough to wear anyone's nerves to madness. The confined position and closed room being a part of it.

I told him that he must stop evening work with late hours, and must get out for air and exercise for a time every day, that it was not fair to his wife or himself and that it made no difference how long it took to complete the models and that I should tell you I had said so. She is 45 only and perfectly devoted to him but nobody can keep fresh without a little fun. She said they used to come in sometimes when first married but it was long since. I tried to get them in to supper and the opera but unfortunately had to give it up on account of a cold. I know it has given him a fresh start and fresh courage to see me, and I am sure that I accomplished what I came for in the five times that I have been out there.

The painting of one peach leaf affected by fungus:

Each leaf is formed of clear white glass, pulled and worked by simple instruments in the flame, and each point on the margin must be pulled out separately from the hot glass, to make the crenate edge to the degree characteristic of the species.

The leaf remains attached to the long stem of glass, 12 inches

perhaps, from which it has sprung, until the cloring is completed and

annealed, when it is separated and the fine wire, necessary for the

permanent stem, is attached, coated with glass and the leaf is ready

to be attached to the branch; this last I could not see as it took from

about three till half after five to odor three leaves and put in ribs

and veins to one, then anneal it.

A green leaf would be made of green glass, the method of coloring would be the same for both.

The colors are made in powdered glass mixed (moistened) with a few drops of turpentinemor ..... carefully administered to the powder in little china saucers and mixed with a fine camel's hair brush, which, finely pointed in the midst paint, administers the color to the leaf also.

The undulations of the leaf have already been made in the white glass so the buff or yellow paint is brushed on perfectly smooth, several times and before it has wholly dried, a strip of pointed whale bone marks the main vein down the centre, and the pointed quill of one of the canel's hair brushes is used to mark each rib. Then a little of the powdered glass is dusted on by a camel's hair brush, shaken off and dusted on again in spots. If the leaf is partially healthy faintly colored green glass is applied to the healthy parts. The camel's hair brushes, larger of finer, then are drawn down the vein and the ribs over and over and again to give the necessary strength to the vein of size and color and to emphasize, as needed, the ribs. Many, many times the delicate tip of

the brush only would touch tiny spots on the lines which needed a thought more of col $ \underset{\cdot}{a} $r.

Then with the most delicate touch of the finest pointed brush the cob-web veins were drawn in to the texture of the leaf, between and at the end of each rib, like fine etching perhaps, but almost more delicate, like a breath rather than a touch and absolutely exhausting to nerves and patience to continue, till the leaf was completed and ready to anneal.

Two wicks in two cups of parafine were started in front of him and the flames driven at each other horizontally, his face, nose and mouth, protected by a piece of asbestos.

He took the glass stem in his left hand and inserted the leaf between the flames, where they just met. The tip first, moving it constantly after it had become red hot till the whole leaf was finished. He

keeps his right hand free to manipulate the apparatus or to handle,

guide the leaf if necessary, as he turns and twists it in the flame.

Not infrequently the annealing starts a flaw in the glass and the leaf

breaks so that many are necessary to complete a branch. He says that

there is far more nervous strain and it is far slower and more difficult to make a leaf than to make flowers. The use of annealing the

powdered glass instead of simply painting, makes the process slower and

more dangerous, but the final result much more permanent, in fact, the

color cannot change and nothing but violence can destroy the model.

He can scratch and scrape a leaf with his penknife and it leaves not

a mark.

There is additional labor which I did not see. Annealing leaves the glass glittering and shining, and that look he destroys by the application of a certain varnish, and he applies this to the flowers aftast stamens and pistils are set.

I think he said that he no longer paints at all except with the powdered colored glass which he can anneal, and another complication is that only a certain kind of glass can be used for the foundation glass, as the others spring and destroy the coat of anneal. All this is now since I was here nearly twenty years ago. He told me then that he had not at all come to the end of the possibilities of glass work and these latest models show it to have been true.

The fruits are made over a fine but very strong wire and he says in some of them there is as much as a $ 1/2 $ lb or glass. That proves I have not seen, most of the fruits I think are done and quantities of leaves on their glass stems ready for painting are in drawers. Some of the fruits are blown but very few, for he dislikes blowing glass and the fruits are like eggshells, too perishable for transport. There are one or two sprays however with fruit of both kinds on them and you would never know the difference in their looks.

The large Beurre pears and large apples looked to me hopeless to transport for no wire could stay on them and no paper hold against their weight but he is confident that by pinning the stalk firmly above the fruit stem it will never move. He has ordered a very heavy weight for the card board boxes.

Boston Mass, January 18th, 1929.

My dear Miss Ware:

Your letter dated December 27th, 1928, arrived just after I had completed one

addressed to you. And then came your cablegram asking if the Roumanian amber had come through without delay. The first specimen of amber was report3d as being safe and in my letter to you dated July 15th. The Sicilian amber given to Mr. Sussmann for transference to me arrived shortly after the opening of the University. A few weeks ago the large piece of Roumanian amber was sent to me from Providence and was acknowledged at once in a letter written to the Consul. I am afraid I have been guilty of remissness on more than one occasion recently, and the pity of it is that you should have been the worst sufferer. I rarely sit down to write a letter now. I dictate almost entirely. And this being so I keep promising myself to devote a Sunday or so to those letters which are not supposed to be rattled off to a secretary. I sometimes wonder if I am not living in too much of a turmoil for peace and happiness. First one thing pulls and then another. This morning Tom Barbour informed me that if/did not go to Cuba in February to superintend the moving picture that is to be made of the Botanic Garden through the generosity of Mrs. Atkins, the whole thing would be a fiasco. I suppose I must plan to get away early in February. But first I have the delightful task of assembling the data for the different departments in the new biological building. President Lowell is anxious to have the Building Committee meet with him and the architect at the earliest possible date and for several days I have been at work on plans enlisting Loius's services as letterer. The fact that my lectures came to and end on Tuesday of this week does not mean by any means that I can settle down to do the things I want to do. If I were not in pretty good health and becoming a philosopher of sorts, I should be at the end of my endurance by this time.

I am most anxious to see what Blaschka is doing. There is a man at the American Museum of Natural History who weems to be doing extraodinary work in

glass. He has completed models that show aquatic life highly magnified. Pictures of these models were published in the Museum Journal. I had colored lantern slides made from these models and they look awfully good. I intend to look at the originals if I go to New York in February. They have a delicacy of treatment which seems to be lacking in Blaschka's magnified details. I wonder if Blaschka knows anything about the American Museum man. His name is Muller, I believe. The algae and protozoan life in a "drop of water" is an extraordinary production. The technique appears to me to be far in advance of the marine models on which the Blaschka made their reputation.

Two days of snow, and today a tough of spring that took all the snow, or the larger part of it away. Typical Boston slush is everywhere and the gutters are singing merrily. Italy at this time of year must be paradise indeed, if one has New England in mind as a place where mortals must live out a vile season of hard work.

I hope that your mind is at rest with regard to the amber. It was unpardonable of me to keep silent at a time when I should have been attempting to convince you that the delight of having dreams come true had come to me through your energy and kindness. I hope that your recovery will be so satisfactory by the coming of spring that you will turn your thoughts toward home and come back to discuss the collections and to approve or condemn what has been done during your long stay abroad.

With all good wishes for the New Year,

Faithfully yours,

Qakes Annus

Miss Mary Lee Ware.

Dear Professor,

At last I am enabled to redeem my promise given in my previous letter, my next line to you should inform you of the sending of the models to the Museum, 4 cases, R.B. N.I to 4, have gone to Bremen on 16th. Inst. and I just received the information that they have safely arrived there. I determined again the way of transportation by the route always used since 1888 as per Dr. Goodale's dispositions, by North German Lloyd-steamer to New York in bond to Boston. The forwarding firm Elkhorn, Emden & Mayer in Bremen who always were ordered for the forwarding, now probably other holders, tried to alter the route into direct steamer to Boston, as a somewhat cheaper way. However this would have made a lot of trouble, returning and new consular certificate of the invoice, at last long delay, so I decided that I insist on the usual way as already ordered, New York in bond to Boston. Dr. Goodale had a remarkable aversion against the direct route. Thus the cases will probably be shipped by Thursday 25 on the Lloydsteamer, München. I shall receive the bill of lading about end of this week. If you should prefer to receive the next consignment by the direct line to Boston I should ask you to let me know if occasionally sometime later. I have packed the models after the experience in the latest shipment, well bound up on framed plates in solid framed boxes. You shall not have trouble in unpacking, but your skilled Mr. Bierweiler can look forward to pretty much work when loosening the models for

North Easton, Massachusetts, July 15th, 1929.

My dear Mr. Blaschka:

You must have been puzzled by the long wait

you have had for a letter from me regarding the fruit models that arrived over a month ago. The truth is, I have given way to the let-down that came after a hard year of University work and I have neglected pretty much everything.

First of all you will be anxious to know in what condition the models reached their destination. With the exception of one or two slight breaks which Louis Bierweiler was able to mend, everything came through the long journey in prime condition.

I should say that this shipment was in far better shape than the last one.

I have arranged the models in temporary cases in my private laboratory where I can study them and think about the best method of presenting them to the public. I want you to know that the models make a delightful group and will offer an opportunity for making an outstanding educational exhibit. I shall devote much care to the preparation of the labels. The historical background with emphasis on the origin of our cultivated temperate climate fruits will tax my ingenuity to the limit because the opportunity for a worth while effort is at hand.

One thing we must bear in mind, when the cases were opened at the Museum, the official from the Custom House was much disturbed by the packing material. He informed me that under ordinary conditions the cases would not have been admitted to the country. In the warfare against introduced plant diseases, may be forbidden entrance at our ports. In future will you bear this in mind and use excelsior, or some similar material.

You will be pleased to know that the number of visitors, attracted to the Museum by the glass models, does not lessen. You will also be interested to learn that in the moving-picture film made to show the activities of Harvard University there is a showing of several of the models. The title which in-troduces the pictures of the models is rather good. It states that the number of visitors to the Museum in one year would fill the Harvard Stadium three times. To one who has attended a Harvard-Yale football game and has seen the sea of human faces surrounding the field this statement seems beyond reason. The Stadium holds about sixty thousand people.

Now I am looking forward to the "fruits of your present labor". I realize the difficulties of your work and I am amazed at the progress you have made. Please do not feel that I am pressing you for results. It would be unkind to hasten you or to say one word that would disturb your deserved tranquility.

It is to be regretted that you are unable to come here to see the collection that has issued from your studio. I think you would suffer from the thought that "all this is the work of just two men". It seems incredible that two men could do so much in the short span of human life. Indeed, the Blaschka models of plants are among the wonders of the world.

Faithfully yours,

Oakes Anner

Method of preparing the models for Transportation.

All of the glass-models, without exception, are constructed in the Studio at Hosterwitz, near Dresden.

When the models are ready for shipment, each model is fastened securely to a plate of firm cardboard and placed in a strong cardboard box. Every dependent part of the model is kept from shaking by means of a roll of crushed tissue paper, which holds it in place. The cardboard boxes are packed with great care in a pine-wood box of convenient size, with plenty of straw between them. Over the whole box is new wrapped a bale of straw, and covered with burlap, forming a very elastic bundle which can bear even a heavy shock. Such bundles arrive in Cambridge, after the ocean voyage with practically no parts broken. After the boxes have been opened in the Museum by the Custom-house Inspector, the models are removed from the cardboard supports to plaster-plaques. The plaster plaques are strong plates of Paster of Paris made after a method invented by Dr. H. F. Libby, of Boston. Each model is then placed in its proper case with a suitable label. Most of the critical determinations of the species have been made by Dr. Jesse M. Greenman, of Chicago, formerly of the Gray Herbarium,

Up to the present time, none of the models have appeared to undergo any marked change upon exposure to the light and air of our exhibition-cases.

Owing to the decreasing income of the University, it has been decided to close the Museum on certain days to save lighting bills and janitor service. My dear Merrill:

Your telegram regarding the sad loss to the Museum through the deathof Miss Ware, came in yesterday. I had already ordered a wreath sent in the name of the staff. In thinking over all of the conditions, I decided that it would be unwise for me to attempt to be present at the funeral.

Your letter of January 9, came in this morning. I

an indeed sorry to learn of Dr. Howe's passing. The New York Botanical Garden is surely having a hard time. So far as you are concerned it would be quizotic for you to reconsider your position.

I really feel that I am making progress here. The

orchids I want to study are not yet in flower, but I am pushing on with the Bardo Colorado Flora, writing very simple introductory chapters regarding structure, history, distribution, pollination etc. and in addition writing up the species and superintending the drawings. The madame has made some unusually good studies of the pollinia and I feel sure that the book, for that is what it is growing up to be, will meet a real need among collectors and biologists in general. There is really nothing in English that quite answers the needs of our people. Not that I have the ability to meet that need, but that I can make a strong effort to do so.

It is quite a task to illustrate the entire group of Barro Colorado stuff, but by the time I am ready to return home, If that fellow John L. Lewis keeps away from the artist, I expect to have a pretty complete gallery of genera and species.

I feel that I could not begin to do this job at home. There are too many distractions and I always want to be doing the thing I should'nt do. Here I can go out on the verrandah and get an inspiration; not one perhaps, that the captious critic will overlook, but something which, for the minute seems worth while. If one had some means of writing awhisper on the type-writer, I should at this point tell you that I may dump the whole thing in the Hali-fax River on the day I start north! That has been my system all my life. The ashes of my lectures have travelled farther than my fame!!

I am planning to stay here until April. An it is I seem to be at home already, because I am using this place as a distant office, keeping in touch with things and doing a better job than I might do if I were hating the cold and dreading the coming of snow; and eventually going to bed with a old.

January 14, 1937

My dear Tom:

Your letter of January 12 came in this morning. I heard promptly about Miss Ware's sad ending and ordered a wreath sent to her funeral from the staff of the Botanical Museum. I am sure it would have been dreadful for her/linger on after paralysis had set in, and I am glad her last days were free from pain. As you say "Now we shall see what we shall see."

The sample of cloth for the walls of the stair-hall in the botanical section seems to me just about right. I like the material and Blanche thinks the warmth of the color will go well with portraits and with the mahogany color of the cherry cases. Her only question is about how it will look as amass. Perhaps it will be best to wait until we get together after your return from the tropics before doing anything definite.

The weather here has been about perfect. Many showers, but a warm sun most of the time and delightly nights. Today is really hot. I have been sitting on the verrandah working on the introductory chapters to that damned flora of your Barro Colorado Island. I have chapters of sorts on structure, history, pollination, and (this is whispered) a chapter on the technique of herbaria. I am afraid I am a dismal failure as a writer and the stuff I have written strikes me as being unscientific and stranglerile. If it is not beyond redemption, I may bring it home for a final struggle. But the flora part and the drawings are coming along by gratifying degrees. Blanche

is giving me her mornings and has made some delightful pencil sketches of pollinia and other sexual parts for the chapeter on structure. These will have to be heliotype as they are in pencil. You see, there is nothing in English that really gives the poor planter's wife a chance when she becomes orchid-conscious. And I find that some of our Ph.D. fellows have no conception of what an orchid really can do. So, instead of limiting myself to keys, descriptions and pictures I am trying to do something that the tired biologist can read in the evening, after wearying of his bugs.

I suppose you will soon be off to

find sun and warmth.

With all good wishes,

Faithfully yours,

Caskin Cross

The article in yesterday's NEW YORK TIMES, relative to glass flowers, brings to my attention the fact that Mrs. Menken has a large collection which she has made or had made at great trouble and expense over a period of many years. There are a few of the common variety of flowers, but many of them are of the orchid or marine types. All have holders of the most perfect museum design. We had all these in a special apartment which we have given up, and they are now in storage.

Our son, Arthur von Briesen Menken, is a graduate of Harvard, as are Mrs. Menken's brothers, Hans and Fritz von Briesen.

I think it likely, if Mrs. Menken were urged to do so, she would be willing to give these flowers to your museum.

Having recently had a great deal to do with the contribution of additions to the Museum of Natural History in this City, I understand a little of the formality connected with these matters, and I know arrangements could be made with Mrs. Menken by which your representatives could see the articles. As I am going south, will you kindly write to her direct at the Hotel Ambassador, 51st Street and Park Avenue, New York.

Needless to say, I would not write you in this way unless I was convinced that the collection had definite value as well as public interest.

Yours very truly,

Stannwood Huttenf.

S. Stanwood Menken.

My dear Miss Ware,

Your welcome letter of the 11th December came in this morning. Aside from the references to your continued depression of health your letter was most gratifying. Mr. Blaschka's letter gave me the assurances I have so much wanted.

I have been to the Museum to-day to make plans for the changes that are to be made in the Economic Room. If I can find the money, I am going to alter the objectionable tower cases and free the middle of the room from obstructions to the view. John Waugh was with me for an hour estimating costs and as he feels sure that he can do the work for about one thousand dollars, I am inclined to push ahead with my plans. My reason for hurrying developments are found in my desire to co-operate with Barbour. Substantial changes are being made in the zoological division and it is necessary that the transition between our rooms and the zoological rooms shall be made psychologically attractive. At present there is no call to the visitor to leave our restful exhibition rooms and pass into the dark, forbidding precincts of zoology. If the Economic Room is made enticing, the step to Zoology will come naturally and the Museum will be made more influential.

On the mineralogical side, vast changes are being made. So, with my neighbours working to excel my quarters, it is natural that I should feel an irresistable inclination to keep a step in the lead.

I wrote a long letter to you some time ago: I am afraid you failed to receive it.

The University has started work to floor over the open space in the gallery. When this work is finished I shall have a delightful and spacious laboratory, informal lecture room, and students' collection for my museum work in Botany 15. The models have been protected from threats

of injury by means of a temporary floor and special coverings.

Really, things are moving rapidly. And each change means greater efficiency and more happiness.

It is needless to tell you that I am giving most of my time to administrative work. But I have many irons in the fire and I hope to get down to productive work again before the winter ends.

Blanche joins me in sending to you the best wishes we have, not only for your health, but for your happiness in the attractive surroundings you have chosen for your winter rest.

Faithfully yours

Oakes Ames.

My dear Miss Ware,

I am writing to you my first letter of the New Year.

Next Tuesday the finishing touches on the main exhibition room will be made by the painters. The white walls and ceiling make the models appear very precious. I wish you were here to enjoy with me the progress we are witnessing in the development of the entire Museum.

Next Tuesday, also, John Waugh will begin work on the Economic Room. The central tower cases are to be moved back against the wall. When the changes have been made I attend to rearrange and amplify the collections. I want this small room to be a model in its field.

For the amber collection I need specimens of Sicilian amber. I wonder if it would amuse you to try to obtain some. It would seem that from Florence, as a base of operations, you might be able to locate authentic pieces of Sicilian amber under expert guidance. We also pieces of Rumanian amber to complete the exhibit we plan to make in the group of fossil resins used commercially.

Day before yesterday I examined Professor Cheney's book (manuscript of course) which he prepared on the history and significance of the Ware Collection. I think the time has come when this book should be printed. It is a most valuable contribution and will be a very welcome contribution to botanical literature. I am planning to submit the manuscript to the Harvard University Press for an estimate of the cost of printing. I think we should insist on an attractive and distinguished volume. Would you be interested in helping financially in the undertaking?

Have you any objection to my plan to have picture post cards of a few of the models made? I think it would be worth while to attempt this form of publicity. I am sure that where would be a ready sale for these

post cards. We already have a series for the Arnold Arboretum. If you do not object to the post card idea, I intend to have some good photographer experiment with some of the outstanding models.

You must hasten the recovery of your good health. We are looking forward to your return. We are anxious to have you realize that real progress is being made and to have you see with your own eyes what has been done during your absence.

One thing more! I have been studying the forbidding entrance to the Museum with the hope that I may be able to find some way to make it change for the better. I know that Tom Barbour will welcome radical changes and I am sure that Palache will co-operate. Once we begin to remove the objectionable features of the entrance, it will be necessary to install beautiful exhibits on the stair landings. A beginning of this will be made at once, as I am planning for a large exhibition case on the second story stair landing.

Blanche sends to you her very best wishes; in this I join and remain

faithfully yours

Oakes Ames.

My dear Miss Ware,

Everybody is most enthusiastic over the changes that have been made in the main exhibition room. The freshness of the room, the delightful contrasts, the added preciousness which seems to characterize the models - all are felt by the Museum inmates and there is a real dignity about the plan that would, I know, delight your soul. It seems almost as if a new world had opened doors to the public. Yesterday a representative of the Harvard Alumni Bulletin arrived to get material from me for an article on the Arboretum. He was so carried away by the beauty of the Ware Collection, made conspicuous by the improved environment, that he began to take notes for an article. I kept him wandering up and down between the cases, for all the world like a man who had discovered something new in the realm of beau-tiful things. Tom Barbour and Ludlow Griscom, (a new acquisition in the Agassiz Museum staff) have been in several times to see what to copy from us to make their exhibition rooms attractive.

The Economic Room is going to be a gem, I think. - A memorial,

(in the minds of Louis, John Waugh and the Superior), to Dr. Goodale. I want to make the new room worthy of its purpose. If you find in your heart that you want to help me make this new effort, worthy of the purpose I have in mind, I shall be delighted. I am going to ask Miss Minns to help. She was at the Museum yesterday afternoon and expressed complete satisfaction with my plans. The centre cases have been removed; the result is astonishing. To the amazement of everybody the room has developed a feeling of spaciousness.

What I have done is this: (1) I have removed the tall case that contained the exhibition of woods. (This case will be installed on the second floor landing.)

(2) I have cut off the flat cases on one side of the central cases and made the assembled pieces into a low exhibition case for the first floor landing.

(3) I have removed the horrible case that contained the cottons and other fibres. (4) The central cases have been moved back against the wall. Result: (5) Both walls have cases that match, and the whole room is free between these cases. (6) The cases are being stained to match the Ware Collection cherry. (7) 14 ceiling lights are being installed. (8) The room is to be painted.

From the above outline you will readily understand that a vast change is taking place and that the Botanical Museum is being put in first class order.

Just at present my scheme for the new case on the first floor landing is a display of botanical books and plates beginning in 1300 and passing through the centuries down to date. This exhibit will illustrate the development of botanical books and seveal the progress of printing and binding from the days of manuscripts. I am most enthusiastic about this. It will be a most attractive unit in our exhibitions.

Day before yesterday I had a most attractive half hour with Mrs Goodale at 5. Berkeley Street. It was like old times to be in the rooms made dear to me by Dr. Goodale.

Blanche sends her best wiehes and I remain as always

Faithfully yours

Oakes Ames.

P.S.A short time ago President Lowell brought the Governor General of Canada to see the collections.

# Blaschka newspaper small report

Generated 2026-08-05 from public endpoints only; no LLM or paid API was used. Archive masters were unavailable, so archive alignment is explicitly provisional.
## 1. Corpus and coverage

- bna: 43 queries; 0 raw results; 0 normalized; A/B/C/X 0/0/0/0; failures 43.
- chronicling_america: 43 queries; 1270 raw results; 314 normalized; A/B/C/X 1/1/10/302; failures 0.
- deutsches_zeitungsportal: 43 queries; 0 raw results; 0 normalized; A/B/C/X 0/0/0/0; failures 0.

Coverage gaps include database OCR quality, incomplete digitisation, public-preview restrictions, and any failed public HTML responses. A database zero is not evidence of historical silence.
## 2. Direct Blaschka newspaper evidence

- BNP-000001 — 1900-12-09, the indianapolis journal (indianapolis [ind.]) 1867-1904, p. 0000000020. “LJ TÜE IlDMUArGLiO JOUIIITAL ßUiTDAY DLjjJlJLt 0 IC FLOWERS MADE OF GLASS THE nCMAItKAIlLE CRCATIOXS OP two nnisuix autists Secret rrocf Which IIa Inrlohed llnrvnrd Uotnntcal Mnseuin Wonderful Accuracy CAMBRIDGE Mass Dec” — https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn82015679/1900-12-09/ed-1/?sp=20&q=blaschka
- BNP-000010 — 1912-07-04, ottumwa tri-weekly courier (ottumwa, iowa) 1903-1916, p. 0000000007. “y A V1 Jiv JK K y 1 v If EXTRA AvK XtM 4 VMHN MUTT PUKCSO 1 1 s W In the University Museum of Har vard is a collection of plants modeled in glasB It is a wonderful collection both in size and in the beauty and ac curacy ” — https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn86061215/1912-07-04/ed-1/?sp=7&q=blaschka

## 3. Consignment-event dossiers

- PROVISIONAL-1891 (1891-07-01 provisional): provisional/no aligned hits. Sender: no newspaper voice located; carrier/customs: no newspaper voice located; receiver: no newspaper voice located. Gap: exact archive date and consignment identifiers unavailable.
- PROVISIONAL-1892 (1892-07-01 provisional): provisional/no aligned hits. Sender: no newspaper voice located; carrier/customs: no newspaper voice located; receiver: no newspaper voice located. Gap: exact archive date and consignment identifiers unavailable.

- PROVISIONAL-1932 (1932-07-01 provisional): provisional/no aligned hits. Sender: no newspaper voice located; carrier/customs: no newspaper voice located; receiver: no newspaper voice located. Gap: exact archive date and consignment identifiers unavailable.

## 4. Forms of handoff

Only forms explicitly present in the candidate rows are encoded in `handoff_stage` and the controlled term columns; no missing labels, lists, case numbers, invoices, customs categories, packing materials, unpacking instructions, or repair reports are inferred.
## 5. Forms of failure

Physical damage, customs difficulties, ambiguous breakage, repair, and feedback are reported only where a row contains matching source text. Candidate OCR requires image verification.
## 6. Negative evidence

Zero-result searches are retained in `search_log.csv`. They may reflect coverage, OCR, date, geography, indexing, or access limitations and must not be interpreted as proof that no report existed.
## 7. Implications for the Harvard digitisation request

Highest priority remains exact per-case lists, bills of lading, forwarding/customs papers, arrival and unpacking reports, and repair/feedback notes. Newspaper candidates can identify dates and public framings but cannot substitute for sender–carrier–receiver documentation.
## 8. Appendix

Complete machine-readable query logs, source coverage, candidate review, event clusters, and duplicate clusters accompany this report. Every candidate includes a local record ID and URL; archive record IDs are absent because the masters were unavailable.

Sensation: the action of perceiving external objects by means of the organs of Sense. —

To conceive the manner wherein Sensation is effected, observe by the way, that all the organs consist of little threads, or nerves; which have their origine in the middle of the Brain; [the nerves?] are diffused thence throughout all the members, [deleted words], which serve our sense and terminate in the exterior Parts of the Body; that when we are in health and awake, one End of these nerves cannot be agitated, or shaken, without shaking the other, by Reason they are always a little stretched, — as is the Case of a stretched Cord; one part of which cannot be stirr'd without a like motion of all the Rest.

Observe again, that as nerves may be agitated two ways; either by the End out of the Brain, or that in the Brain: In the [former?] they be agitated from without by the action of objects; [the lower continuation is lost or too fragmentary to read continuously].

The year 1736 was filled up with remarkable passages of providence towards the Country in general, but more especially towards our family — Some time the year before we heard of the throat distemper's proving very mortal at the Eastward and in the Winter 36 we frequently heard of its proceeding & raging exceedingly, which made our hearts to bleed for those so visited and to tremble, fearing what the ensuing year would bring on us — We were in expectation and did as it were wait for the Judgments of God — which seemed in some measure to solemnize the minds of people — it continued coming nearer and nearer till as it approached it lost some of its terror growing more mild and less mortal — In the Spring it reach't Wethersfield, Hartford and several Towns near us and appeared at its first coming in a terrible Shape. The next Summer & Autumn following it overspread this part of the Country; scarce any Town escaped, in some Towns proving very mortal & terrible and at others very gentle, and in the same Town to some very terrible and the effects awfull and to others light. As to our Family and myself in particular — I being under melancholy and Difficult circumstances ...

... the most Distrest condition — Worn out with grief and terror and with the great Burden which lay upon them for want of help (my mother and Sister Molly not being fully recovered from their own sickness) the Neighbours being frighted and almost as shy as if it had been the Small Pox —

My Sister Died August 21st on Saturday morning, at which time my Sister Nabby [that day?] as was feared at the point of death with the same Distemper; the next Tuesday morning I was seized with it and in less than a week's time was brought to Deaths Door; at which time on Saturday night, Sister Patty voluntarily was seized with the same distemper; and my Sister Nabby, tho better of her distemper, in the utmost distress, and Horror, in her mind and in a manner turned out of her Reason, which of itself, would have been a sore Affliction.

After Her Return from Springfield She writes thus [Lucy Wetmore Whittelsey, in smaller hand:] She did not return untill after her Sister was buried

On monday evening went to Lucy's grave & found it at Jerushas left hand, a place I had often laid out for myself. The next morning I awakt ill; & by noon was convinc'd it was with the same Distemper; and began to take care, to put things in such order, as were best to leave them — at night I grew very ill for the time, but was not under any amazement at all: but felt a Calmness that I cannot account for, which did not seem arise, from a Satisfaction, that my soul was safe; nor altogether, from Senselessness & Stupidity — But as my Distemper prevailed upon me, I was apt to be lost, & found it difficult to fix my thoughts; and I soon grew Delirious at times — but tho my Distemper was laid upon me, yet my Courage kept up; my Spirits seem'd generally in a pleasing posture — & always hoped for the best; my mind was much solemniz'd; I seem to be set at great distance from this world, & to have no concern with it. It then appear'd to me a vain Toilsome place & that the inhabitants were Strangely wander'd, Lost, & bewilder'd. transcription.full_diplomatic:
... consulted with myself about it & concluded it was in my imagination only, I thought of speaking of it to those about me but forbore lest that should abate the pleasure I took in it, or occasion the ideas to leave me; at times I endeavoured to give a close attention to it, discern the notes more particularly and then it would vanish from me when any body spoke to me or when I was talking I should loose the Ideas, but when I lay still again they would instantly Return. This held a day or two & then began to change to the Ringing & tolling of Bells, and at last against my will to the merriest notes of a violin, exceeding lively & distinct; & the finest of the sort I ever heard, but I strove against it. It seemed to raise my Spirits in a different manner & made me feel airy & light as if I could fly, which made me uneasy & afraid I should be so in Reality — then I was in some degree out of my head which made me talk of it to those about, and then it left me — this I think was on Saturday night —

but I held this confidence, or hope, some time, & when I was out of my head, & thought myself sick & Lost, or at a River Side, & among strangers that would not direct me home.
