transcription.full_diplomatic: We apprehend things very differently one from another & the same persons from themselves at different times. What brings misery to some is Happiness to others, and to the same person what he dreads & shrinks at one time, he counts a privilege at another when he views things in another light. Perhaps the man who is puff'd up with vanity; Prizes Honour & Popular applause as a great Happiness, but another Esteems it but vanity & prizes Obscurity before it — Labour, which is a grievous toil to some is Natural & pleasant to others. Sickness & Pain, Contempt & disgrace which are the most universally called afflictions, are vastly less so with some than with others — Things become great or small in our apprehension, by comparing them with other things, so the good that this world affords appears very valuable & of great importance to be obtain'd & while it is the best we have any Idea of it is the chief; but when our minds are enlarged with a Realizing sense of things infinitely Superiour, how do they vanish into nothing, & with what indifference or rather disdain do we look upon them, and then also do lesser Evils vanish before greater — Things are what they are made to us; what Children prise, grown persons despise and what youths are fond of is altogether Tasteless to old People.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
... an infinitely wise, and mercifull God, who knows your frailty, as well as your [perverseness] —

But if the World should Smile upon you, be upon your utmost watch, and guard, least you are ensnared. Let not your expectations, be Raised, or your Spirits Elate, with the flattering prospect it shews you; believe me it is for want of Wisdom & Experience —

[rule]

If you will place your Happiness in creatures, and have much dependence and Expectations from them, Cutting Disappointments, are like to be your Reward. If you would not be Shocked, with disappointments, you must be prepared to bear them — those that you think you may most surely, and safely, confide in, will fail you, like a Broken Tooth, or a foot out of Joint; Consider how extremely mutable are persons, & things, and have but little dependence upon them — if you will Lean upon an arm of Flesh, you must at least expect to have your hand pierced.

... the Happiness or uneasiness of others in so Lively a view, in so distinct a manner as they do their own? none Love their Neighbour Just in the same manner as themselves.

[rule]

I have somewhere seen it observ'd that we while in the world, are made more for action, than Speculation and so it seems, for the more we Speculate; the more we are confused; the more we endeavour to know, the more we are Lost, and bewilder'd, and plunge'd in unreconcilable difficulties — poor Broken impotent creatures, vastly ignorant, yet mighty pretenders to knowledge; always for wading beyond our depth — knowledge is too wonderfull for us in this Life — if we did more and inquired Less perhaps we Should keep more within our own sphere and be more profitably employed.

[rule]

Boldness and assuming confidence does not bespeak Wisdom; sure a wise man will see himself so dark and confused a Creature, that after his most painfull diligence, to inform himself, he is extremely prone to mistakes & errors, which one would think should make him cautious & carefull & unapt to be Boisterously Positive.

transcription.full_diplomatic: A single Life to people in years is somewhat vacant and Solitary, Especially to a woman, whose affairs Ly in a narrow Compass — they meet with but few new things to enliven, & entertain, them but little expectation to feed upon, Except they can fetch their expectations from another Life, and place their happiness in Religion and the improvement of their minds; they must needs wax dull & want motive for action — But if they can make Religion & knowledge their chief end — it is a Life of wonderfull advantage, and of Ease compared with wedlock, & if they can have Expectation enough, or their Lives can any ways be diversified enough, to keep their Spirits going — why is it not at least many times to be prefer'd? But we are such Creatures, we must be beguiled with vain hopes & expectations, to ease us along through the world. and when we have lived long & been so often defeated as to have done expecting for ourselves we want Children to expect for — Those that do not make Religion their Refuge, must [interlinear: live] upon Cheats or their Life would soon become a Burden.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
... enlivens us, & keeps our Spirits in a pleasing Posture, very much according to our prospects are our Spirits, low or high; and indeed our Happiness. tho we call it false Happiness, that arises from expectations that deceive us, & occasion our affliction by disappointment — such are the expectations from this world; as every one must Learn that lives Long in it.

[rule]

Mark the infinite goodness of God to man in that every thing is contrived for our good, and all the injunctions yt are laid upon us, are not to add to his infinite Happiness which is out of our power to disturb or increase, but it is to work about our own good, and tho God is pleased to seek the glorifying of his own Name; it is not because he is happified, as we are by such insignificant creatures adoration as man is; but because it is truth, & Just, & equal, that he should be treated as a Being infinitely more excellent than we can possibly comprehend. and our apprehending of his excellency is most Conducive to our Good.

[rule; smaller writing]

We are most prone to contentment when most severely Crost, so as to bow the will & make it give place and not oppose itself — it is the opposition of the will that makes so much discontent & tumult; and when it is too much indulged it Rises high, grows Strong and opposes much.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
Oh! that I had the wing of a dove, that I might fly away and be at Rest — but whether could I fly, Oh that I cou'd find some more sure & abiding good portion, and no longer be the sport of these alluring, deceiving enjoyments. I am weary with pursuing Shadows, where shall I find Real & substantial good — How long shall I wander from Mountain to Hill Seeking Rest and finding none — Oh that I could find the way but I cannot; could but find a rest for my foot. but I am Lost and bewildered and weary myself to find the way; but cannot. I am weary with my vain Life yet afraid to Die —

[rule]

I am plagued all my Life long with a Levity of mind, which flutters & tosses me, to & fro, from one vanity to another; till I am weary, & Heart sick, pursuing Shadows, & things, that I know are nothing — But when I am deeply afflicted, by some great Disappointment, or the loss of something dear unto me, it Poises my mind, & a little tames my Frenzy.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
... did not seem to be led into my mind by any thing as it were, but thrown in, abruptly and so strong that it made me cast in my mind, whether I had not some Reasons, to look upon it as Supernatural. but I consider'd I was very unable to Judge, of the power of imagination & that there were many operations, in my mind, to me as unaccountable as this, tho not so new — So I left my-self undetermined, or rather Determined, that I had no Reason to Conclude, it was any thing unnatural, But it made considerable impression on my mind; and led me to Reflect, what a vast hindrance the cares, & Business, of the World, is, to our making progress in Religion.

[rule]

How insipid a thing must Life needs become, to those who by long Experience, & multiplied disappointments, have Learned there is no Happifying portion here: and yet have no Realizing Sense of the things of another Life, nor no Hope nor Expectation from it to Support yt. It must needs be the dullest thing in the world; and I should think that such a one, would in short time, fall into the deepest melancholy — how it is Expectations enliven [text cut off].

transcription.full_diplomatic:
The year 1736 was filled up with Remarkable passages, of Providence towards the Country in general but more especially towards our family — Some time the year before we heard of the throat distemper's proving so very mortal at the Eastward and in the Winter 36 we frequently heard of its proceeding and Raging exceedingly, which made our hearts to Bleed for those so visited and to tremble fearing what the ensuing year would bring upon us — we were in expectation of and did as it were wait for the Judgments of God which seem'd in some measure to solemnize the minds of people — it continued to come nearer and nearer but as it approached it lost some of its Terror growing more mild and Less mortal. in the Spring it Reacht Wethersfield Hartford and Several Towns near us and appeared at its first Coming in a terrible shape. the next Summer and autumn following it overspread this part of the Country; Scarce any town escaped; in some towns very mortal and terrible and at others very gentle, and in the same town, to some very terrible and the effects awful and to others but slight —

as for our family and my self in particular — I being under Melancholy and Difficult Circumstances on some accounts it then occasioned me [to spend] great part of my time that spring and Summer at Springfield. I went first at the Beginning of april and return'd the beginning of May and found my Brother Ellsworth Dangerously Sick and in a few days his Child was also taken very ill. in about a weeks time I was obliged to return to Springfield again — Left my Brother and his Child both in a Doubtfull State tho' with hopes the worst was past with them. I went from home from prudential Considerations, but there with many Relentings and with a heavy heart I Left my friends — I had not been gone Long before I heard of my mother being laid up and Suffering much pain with the Rheumatism which made me very uneasy and more Long to go home but was as I thought providentially forbid. I was soon after Seized with the throat Distemper but it proved but a Slight visitation and soon past off — and after some time I heard of the amendment of my mother my Brother & his Child but was presently made sorrowfull by hearing my sister Backus was dangerously Sick of the throat Distemper and had Lost her infant Child. transcription.full_diplomatic:
... she had a settled weakness and pain in her Breast; it was very unnatural to me to be absent from home at such a time; my soul did long after my fathers House & felt as if I was Banished, for some circumstances Relating to [blank] forbid my going home. But took care to ease my sister of the Burthen of Business that lay upon her and I soon heard she had Recovered her health and the Rest of friends were better — but in the mean time Mr Hopkins and his eldest Daughter were taken with a very bad fever and ague which held them till three days of sister Lucy's sickness, three Days before her Death — and Just about that time Mr Hopkins family were taken with the throat Distemper and five of them had it and some of them considerably bad, and at the time of sister's Sickness and after our family were in the most distrest Condition, worn out with grief and terror and with a great Burden which lay upon them for want of help (my mother and sister Molly not being fully recovered from their own Sickness) the neighbors being frightened and almost as shy as if it had been the small Pox. My sister Died August 21th on Saturday morning, at which time my sister Nabby Lay as was feared at the point of Death with the same throat Distemper; the next tuesday morning I was seiz'd with it, and in less than a weeks time was brought to Deaths Door. at which time on Saturday night sister Patty [voluntarily?] was seized with the same Distemper and my sister Nabby tho better of her Distemper in the utmost Distress and Horror in her mind and in a manner turned out of her Reason which of itself wou'd have been a sore affliction.

transcription.full_diplomatic: I Remember the Summer before my sister Jerusha's Death about nine years ago (I was all that Summer in great hurry and making stays was then my Business) I was one evening walking Just below my fathers orchard (after I had taken up many Resolutions to make Religion and the concerns of my Soul my Business and after I had often set my Self to it and pray'd for and labour'd after an awakening Sense of my miserable Condition: and finding I yet Remained very insensible) I thought with a great Deal of Concern about growing so old in Sin and Remaining so insensible and Negligent Notwithstanding so many means and Resolutions; and as I was leaning over the south fence and thinking after this manner, that I was never more Likely to be sensible than now; what sho'd I do where sho'd I go &c. instantly without any one Chain of thought I saw a Bible open before me — or at least I had as lively and sensible an image of it in my mind as if I had seen it with eyes, which a little surprised me but I attempted to Read but did as sensibly seem to be hindered by a piece of stays intercepting and covering the page. this Representation was exceeding Lively and sensible and did not seem to be led into my mind by any thing, but as it were thrown in abruptly and so strong that it made me cast in my mind whether I had not some Reason to Look upon it as Supernatural, but I consider'd I was very unable to Judge of the power of imagination and that there were many operations in my mind to me as unaccountable as this tho' not so new. transcription.full_diplomatic:
[Earlier administrative or tax text, heavily cancelled:] To [illegible], one of the [Collectors?] of the said Town of Middletown in the County of Hartford, Greeting. [Name], you are hereby Commanded to Levy and Collect of the Persons Named in the Rate Bill herewith committed unto you Each one [his proportion] as therein set down of the sum total of [illegible].

1763 January 10. And they all with one consent began to make Excuse.

Mr Whittelsey the first said I have bought a piece of ground & must needs go & see it I pray thee have me Excused, & another said I have bought five yoke of oxen I go to prove them I pray thee have me Excused another said I have married wife; therefore I cannot come. Luke Chap xiv ver 18, 19, 20.

[rule]

what a Strange proneness is there in Man, to Slight and neglect the great concern of religion and these immortal Souls; every trivial Excuse serves & they all with one consent began to make Excuse — but how vain are their Excuses; in what Stead will it Stand them at the Last Day? Before the Judge of all the earth. What service to every one according to their works — [damaged lines] it will not avail them; then nothing [but an interest] in that Saviour (whose invitations they have so often Slighted & made light of) can save them.

Jan 17 forenoon Mr Judson [or Julson?] — and ye will not come unto me that ye might have Life. John Chap fifth ver 40. afternoon — therefore we conclude that a Man is justified by faith without the deeds of the Law. Rom third 28.

Jan 29 Mr Strong — who hath saved us & called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose & grace which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began. 2 Timothy Chap first ver 9.

Feb 13 Mr Noah [or Noad?] Ryssel [or Russell?] — those that seek me early shall find me. Proverbs Chap VIII ver 17.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
Jan 1763 [day uncertain] Except ye be born again, ye cannot see the Kingdom of God. John 3.

wherein four things came under consideration — viz first the nature & Appendages of such a change; secondly the efficient author of it; thirdly the importance of it; and fourthly the nature of Obedience — which was considered from these words Genesis Chap xvii ver 1: I am the Almighty God: walk before me & be thou perfect; & I will make my Covenant between me & thee.

from whence it was considered first that God is an Almighty being & in respect to [illegible] an almighty & an all-sufficient portion, to those that put their trust in him; thirdly they that would have God for their portion, must walk before him and be perfect.

March 20th Be ye therefore perfect as your father which is perfect in heaven is perfect. Matthew 5 ver 48. forgetting the things that are behind and pressing forward toward the mark of the prize of the high calling in Christ Jesus.

[rule]

March 29 forenoon, Mr Whittelsey Come unto me all ye that Labour, and are heavy laden & I will give you rest. Matthew XI.

[damaged section] I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand in the latter day upon the Earth. Job 19th 25.

[damaged section] and the voice said cry; & he said what shall I cry? all flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof as the flower of the field. Isaiah Chap 40th ver 6th.

The discourse from these words was occasioned by the death of two remarkable youths, cut down in the prime & vigour of manhood; the one the week past the other a fortnight since. we have been Solemnly Exhorted to a serious consideration of the vanity & Shortness of human Life; & have had that Solemn truth once more inculcated that man at his best Estate is altogether vanity; whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed before the moth. May this consideration have its proper effect, namely Solemnize, to lay up my treasure in heaven where moth nor rust doth corrupt nor thieves break through & Steal; may it excite me to give all heed & diligence to make my calling & Election sure that I may have a portion secure; when all that this vain world can afford shall perish, & be no more.

afternoon Mr Whittelsey concluded the Sermon began the Last Sabbath.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
Mr Whittelsey text June 176[?]

For Bodily exercise profiteth little: but Godliness is profitable to all things, having promise of this life, & of that which is to come. 1 Tim. Chap 4 ver 8.

Godliness is profitable to all things: is profitable both to the life that now is and that which is to come. what advantage then hath the Saint over the Sinner? The advantage is great Surely, very great; what tho the godly suffer persecution in this life as well as Sinners perhaps; Nay it is what we are told to Expect, that in the world might be tribulation; & exchange the light of God's Countenance, that Calamity, that Serenity of mind which arises from a consciousness of having acted justly — who would wish to Exchange it for the love [of the world?] and fleeting external pleasures of the Senses? uncertainties — who enjoys not himself in this world, nor has any Expectations from another; who continually Suffering from the bitter Remorse of his own Conscience & that to be dread[ed] still lives in hopeless Despair, while on the other hand the Saint if he even burns only in regard to this life hath a very great advantage.

[rule]

afternoon Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea we Establish the law. Romans the 3d ver 31.

March 19 1769 Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea we Establish the law. Preacht by Mr Hallock of [Lebanon?], afternoon [illegible]. [illegible short scripture text]

July For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God. 1 Peter Chap 3d ver 18th.

Behold what manner of love the father hath bestowed upon us that we should be called, and made heirs with the Children of God; not from any Righteousness of our own did he this, but Christ suffered the just for the unjust. how can we enough admire and adore the gracious author of our Salvation; can we enough be humbled before him? how ought we to lament and bewail our transgressions before him. Considering when we consider how his great his unexpressible Suffering on our account. O amazing love, love mysterious, love ye beyond compare. 1 Pet. Chap hath suffered the just for the unjust that he might bring us to God.

June 19th [scripture heading partly illegible] How shall the Righteous Shine forth as the Sun in the Kingdom of their father — father! what unexpressible condescension is this.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
May 1769 For we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also that sleep in Jesus will God bring with him. 1 Thessalonians IV Ch. 14 ver.

Hence we may derive Consolation to Assuage our grief on the death of a dear friend, to whom we have been near and dear; for those only afflicted are those who at the Separation of the nearest of friends, or the tenderest Relation, ought not a Consideration of the happiness they now enjoy, and the hopes their sorrowing surviving friends have once conceived but now ascended Redeemer, ought not [this consideration] to sooth and comfort one. Let us remind them as oft flat of our selves & in Such let us be excited to Stir up ourselves to him our Saviour and follow their example that we be not denied at Last, that we be not Separated in Heaven from those we so dearly loved on Earth.

[rule]

May 18th 1767 My little Children these things write I unto you that ye sin not, and if any man sin, we have an Advocate with the Father; Jesus Christ the Righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. 1 John Chap 2d ver 1 & 2.

what Comfort, what Consolation for the Children of God; if any man Sin we have an Advocate with the father; a great & glorious Advocate one that is touched with the feeling of our infirmities; one who fulfils our weakness & is able to save to the uttermost all those that come unto God by him — one that was tempted on all points like as we are yet without Sin — how may Christians joy and rejoice in the God of their Salvation; what reason have they to go on their way rejoicing chearfully; may they Submit themselves to all the Misfortunes of life; they may laugh at Calamity, nor fear nor even Destruction cometh; being assured of this one thing, that their Redeemer liveth, who is the propitiation for Sin.

[rule]

text Rev. Mr White — June the 9th 1767 because the carnal mind is Enmity against God: for it is not Subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. Romans Chap 8th ver 7.

O most mercifull God; give me grace I beseech thee humbly to acquiesce in thy Sovereign dealings with mankind; Save me from mean and unjust thoughts of thee & the methods of Salvation by grace.

[rule]

whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises, that by these you might be partakers of the Divine Nature, having Escaped the corruption that is in the world through Lust. 2 Peter Chap 1st ver 4.

Consider O my Soul these great these precious promises & may they excite thee to an interest in them; give all Diligence may I add to faith virtue; to virtue knowledge; & to knowledge temperance; & to temperance patience; & to patience godliness; & to godliness brotherly kindness; to brotherly kindness Charity.

[upside-down note at foot:] Mr Whittelsey Communion Aug 1767.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
Fortune has been too often adverse to you; The various Changing of your Advantage be now useful to make your self capable of Supporting her frowns, as well as her smiles. for the vicissitudes of Prosperity are much more severe than those of adversity, because we yield to the one, and resist the other. Although you should preserve your virtue, yet all those near you will lose theirs. Flattery will take the place of truth and interest that of affection, to which they are poison and Venom.

[rule]

teach me the Number of my days, that I may apply my heart to true Understanding — how vain are the Expectations of man, how narrow his Comprehension, how unbounded his Wishes, never arriving at the thing perhaps, but differing endlessly in the attempt. Freedom & virtue (or what is wrongly called by that Name) not may that is no ways Consistent; this daily or Eever in pursuit of Something beyond his reach; Seeking happiness where it is not to be found — happiness is no where to be found but in the paths of Virtue; peace of mind that the Richest blessing that is to be attained in this life, is not to be purchased with gold nor Silver, neither is it the fruit of riches or honors, but the reward of a virtuous life.

[large blank interval]

September the 13th Mr Tully Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. 1 John Chap 2d ver 15.

here is a command as prohibitive as we ought to Seek very much every heart and Stir us up to great Diligence and watchfulness that we suffer not the world, nor the things that are in the world, too much to Engage our attention and that we place not our affections too much on things of time and Sense. I assure love the world the love of the father is not in him; but alas how oft is man fallen and Depraved, mean to forget that they cannot Serve God and Mammon and to think that the love of the world is consistent with the love of the father; how oft are we to Set our heart upon the world, as tho it were our abiding place, but ought not a consideration of the shortness and vanity of human life to excite us to Seek a happiness more lasting, one Substantial than any that this world can afford.

July 1767
Luke the 23d, 28, 29, 30, 31.

And there followed him a great Company of people, and Women who bewailed and lamented him.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
July 1767 Luke the 23d, 28, 29, 30, 31.

And there followed him a great Company of people, and Women who bewailed and lamented him. but Jesus turned unto them and said, Daughters of Jerusalem weep not for me, but weep for yourselves and for your Children — For behold the days are coming in the which they shall say, blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bare, and the paps which never gave suck — then shall they begin to say to the mountains, fall on us; and to the hills, cover us. For if they do these things, in a green tree what shall be done in the Dry?

If they do these things in a green tree what shall be done in a Dry? If these were done to the holy Jesus, to the Eternal Son of God; what may the Sinner Expect. Surely the most aggravated Misery will be the portion of all Such, as reject the gracious offers of grace & what do they not Deserve that trample under foot the blood of Jesus.

[rule]

July 1767 And the Spirit and the bride say, come, and let him that heareth say come, and let him that is athirst come; and whosoever will let him take the water of life freely. Revelations 22 ver 17.

August 1767 Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my thoughts and see if there be any wicked way in me and lead me in the way Everlasting. Psalm cxxxix ver 23 & 24.

August the 9th Acquaint now thy self with him, and be at peace: thereby good shall come unto thee. Job Chap 22 ver 21. [small note:] Preacht again by Mr Huntington, March 12th 1769.

August 23 Grace be with all them that love our Lord Jesus Christ in Sincerity. Amen. Ephesians Chap 6th ver 24.

Likewise reckon ye yourselves to be dead indeed unto Sin; but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Romans Chap 6th ver 11.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
February 6th 1768 [A crossed heading, partly legible: A Sacrament ... next Thursday.]

Sabbath morning this day is set for renewing our Covenant with God in the ordinance of the Lords supper.

And here O most gracious God I desire once more to offer up my self to thee in & through thy beloved son; Resolving by grace that I will live to thee & for thee & to none other. I desire to dedicate myself to thee & to present my body a living Sacrifice holy & acceptable to thee which is but my only reasonable service.

may this solemn transaction which I have so often renew'd be with proper weight upon my mind that I keep myself from all sin; may I constantly fear offending one whom I am sure will not [illegible] but that I am resolved by my own voluntary act to be from whose right I am & to whose glory I have consented to be.

Many are the Snares & temptations that beset me here in this evil world; many are my incentives to forget God; surrounded on all sides with the pleasures & vanities of life create by my youthful companions, withheld by those I love & naturally inclined to pursue the world and the enjoyments of it. I find that I am too apt to forget the more important concerns of Soul & the things that tend to the Glory of my great possessor and redeemer.

July 9th 1768 O Sinfull dust & ashes, that I am, who shall deliver from the body of this death. [deleted passage] the treachery & deceitfulness of which betray me into a thousand Snares & temptations. Oh the depravity of my nature — weak are my resolutions & depraved my inclinations; how alas I discover from those that I have made even when I had the greatest reason to think would be of lasting Effect — but Examine O my Soul whether these Resolutions have not been made too much in thy own strength & without that dependence upon the only all-sufficient Saviour, which is required. how I have had that constant dependence that becomes a creature on her Creator; have I not been wanting out a righteousness for myself that will stand me in no Stead — instead of casting myself at my Saviours feet & bemoaning my hard Heart to be cleansed — have I not been trying to make it better myself & thereby adding Sin to Sin — Oh God thou enough; cleanse thou me from Secret faults; lead me out of thy Law, & lead in the way Everlasting.

September the 4th This day attended on the Sacrament of the Lords Supper with some peculiar delight and satisfaction when I reflected on the great things done for sinners; the riches of free grace in the provision made for fallen man; the all-sufficiency, & the willingness of Christ to save all that come unto God by him; who come bearing & heavy laden with their sins ... [end damaged].

transcription.full_diplomatic:
July 15th 176[?] on the eleventh of this month departed this life after an illness of nineteen days Capt Joseph Gleason an intimate friend and acquaintance of our family — an Instance of the truth of the Scripture that Man at his best Estate is all together vanity. he was in health, a well Man of a fine Constitution and in the prime of life; he has left an afflicted and Disconsolate Widow and an only Child bereaved of the best of Comforts, the tenderest and most indulgent of parents.

may this Instance of the frailty and uncertainty of all earthly enjoyments excite me to seek a happiness that is not to be found in this short lived world of trouble and Sorrow & may I in particular be taught to Remember my Creator in the days of my youth & be and may all my Affections be devoted to my Creator and Redeemer that I place them not on the world nor the things therein.

August 2 1767 Repaired to the house of God, attended upon the administration of the word with a heart far from God I fear; but a little more considerate than sometimes. how is it possible for a Creature upon the brink of Eternity to be so thoughtless & so inattentive to the things that concern my Everlasting welfare — I have this Day been told & charged to accustom my Self to stand still an hour every day in the great Duty of Self Examination and to seek the Assistance of divine grace that I might be enabled to perform it aright.

I think to resolve by the divine grace to come into the practice. It Seems to me Absolutely Necessary that my mind be more employ'd with a sense of the importance of living well than it is in general; and this I am Sure of, that it is owing to my own Slothfull wicked Disposition and that I labor so much under Darkness of mind & who can tell but that if I Set myself Seriously to Examine my self and go on in this prudent way, make it a means of awakening me & making me more Diligent in the ways of my duty.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
August the 9th 1767 what a black account Should I have drawn up against myself had I only but every Sabbath night Recollected and Set down the past actions of the day — but consider Oh my Soul that every transaction of thy life is Registered in the great book of accounts; that all thy sins are had in remembrance before that God before whom thou must appear. Consider O my Soul thy to hide me from that God whose mercy I have so oft abused, whose gracious offers I have so often slighted; hide me underneath thy wings, Oh thou that Suffered on the cross, that did to save Sinners, even the chief of them.

August the 23 this day renewed by and Solemnly given my self up to God by a Solemn Dedication of my self to him in and through Christ freely and without Reserve have I done it, Resolving through grace to keep gods commandments, considering myself to be not my own nor have I a right to Dispose of my Self or my time or whatsoever I possess; but as God directs, Submitting and Resigning my self to him. I am so weak before him with humility and a godly fear. may this make a lasting impression on my mind, and be with more weight upon my mind; and may I be Enabled thereby to guard against Sin and watchfully that I keep myself from all sin — but alas! how frequent have been my Resolutions yet how often have I swerved from them, but —

Look forward, Oh my Soul, take one view of Eternity ere thou turnest; Stop & pause a moment before it be too late. Consider well what thy being and Existence Take a view of what thou art now, & what thy State will be the thousand years hence — It is true that I Exist now, and is it not as true that I shall Exist then & for an Eternity of ages to follow — What then Oh my Soul what is Life & the enjoyments of it that I should set my Heart upon it. What are all the vain amusements of this momentary Scene; it is but a gilded Scene of Pleasure that continueth but for a day & is gone. [deleted line] Set not your Heart on the World nor Things that are in the world.

transcription.full_diplomatic:
January 1st 1769 Sunday

Oh that my Head were waters & mine eyes Fountains of tears, that I might weep Day & Night for the sin of my transgressions. Oh the wickedness of my Life & conversation! awake my soul; why Sleepest thou on the brink of Destruction; awake from this awfull Stupidity ere it be too late; awake awake thou that art Dead in trespasses & sins & Christ shall give thee Light.

This day begins another year anew & what improvements or advances in the Divine Life have I made the year past? Four years and Eighteen days have now past since I made Solemn Dedication of my self to the Lord & bound myself to him in a perpetual covenant never to be forgotten. And have I not reason to be greatly ashamed to lament & bewail the innumerable and aggravated sins I have been guilty of; the many breaches of covenant vows and obligations.

[rule]

Oh most Holy God pardon me Sinfull Dust & ashes. I presume to come unto thy Holy presence, and once more to make the most solemn Dedication of myself to thee. [one full line heavily deleted]

Who O Lord or what am I or what is my House? what is my Nature or Descent, my Character and Desert that I Should speak of this & desire that I may once be a party in a Covenant, where thou the King of Kings and Lord of Lords art the other — Trembling might Justly take hold of me when I Sinfull worm of dust presume to appear in thy Sacred Presence. But O God great as is thy Majesty, so also great is thy Mercy. To thee therefore would I come invited by the Name of thy Son, & trusting in his Righteousness & Grace — Laying myself at thy feet with Shame & Confusion of face & smiting on my Breast, I would cry with the humble Publican, God be mercifull to me a sinner & with the deepest humility bewail before thee irregular propensities of my Nature together with Practical wickedness of my Life.

pages.transcription:
Sarah Bradstreet
MS Am 1007
Bradstreet Mrs. Anne (Dudley)
meditations divine
and morall.

The following are
the excellent sayings
& performances, of
Lady Ann Bradstreet,
Consort of Governor
Bradstreet; designed
for her son, Simon
Bradstreet, afterwards
the worthy Minister
of Charlestown, and
father of the late

vinerable Simon,
Bradstreet, of
Marblehead:
never before in
print.

For my Dear Son
Simon Bradstreet.

Parents perpetuate their Sins in their
posterity, and their maners in their im-
itation, Children do naturaly rather
follow the failings, then the vertues of
their predecessors, but I am persuaded
better things of you - you once desired
me to leave some-thing for you in writ-
ing, that you might look upon, when
you should see me no more. I could
think of nothing more fit for you nor
of more ease to myself, then these short
meditations following, such as they are
I bequeath to you, small legacys are
accepted by true friends, much more
by dutyfull children, I have avoided
incroaching upon others conception
because I would leave you nothing but
my own, though in value they fall

short of all in this kind, yet I presume
they will be better pris'd by you for
the Authors sake. The Lord bless
you with grace here, and crown you
with glory hereafter, that I may meet
you with rejoyceing at that great day
of appearing, which is the continual
prayer of

your affectionate Mother
Ann Bradstreet

March 20
1664

Meditations Divine
and Morall

1

There is no object that we see, no
action that we doe, no good that we
injoy, no evill that we feel, or fear,
but we may make some spiritual
advantage of all, and he that makes
such improvement is wise as well
as pious. 鈥揬n

2

Many can speak well, but few can
do well. we are better Scholars in
the Theory, then the praticque part, but
he is a true Christian that is a pro-
ficient in both.

3

Youth is the time of getting, middle
age of improveing, and old age of spen-
ding; a negligent youth is usualy atten-
ded by an ignorant middle age, and
both by an empty old age, he that hath
nothing to feed on but vanity and lyes
must needs lie down in the Bed of
Sorrow.

4

A ship that bears much sail and
little or no ballast, is easily overset, and
that Man whose head hath great abilities
and his heart little or no grace, is in dan-
ger of foundering.

5

It is reported of the Peacock that
prideing himself in his gay feathers
he russels them up, but spying his

My dear Children,

I knowing by experience that exhortations
of parents take most effect when the
speaker leaves to speak, and those especially
sink deepest which are spoke latest, and
being ignorant whether on my death Bed
I shall have opportunity to speak to any
of you, much less to all, thought it the
best whilst I was able to compose some
short matters (for what else to call them I
know not) and bequeath to you, that when
I am no more with you, yet I may be
dayly in your remembrance (although that
is the least of my aim in what I now doe)
but that you may gain Spirit, and

The former it had been perhaps better
pleasing to you, but being the last is the best

I will observe shall be this, I will begin with
Gods dealing with me from my childhood to
this day.  --- In my young years I began
to make course of my wayes and what I
knew was sinfull as lying, disobedience to
parents.  that I avoided, if at any time I was
overtaken with the like evils it was a great
Trouble, and I could not obtain rest till by
prayer I had confesst it unto God.  I was also
troubled at the neglect of private dutyes tho'
too often tardy that way.  I also found much
comfort in reading the scriptures, Especially
places I thought most concerned my condition,
and as I grew to have more understanding,
so the more solace I took in them.

In a long fitt of sickness which I had
on my bed I often comuned with my heart,
and made my supplications. to the most
High who sett me free from that affliction.
But as I grew up to be about 14 or 15 years
I found my heart more carnall and sitting
loose from God, vanity and the follyes of
Youth took hold of me.

When I was about 16 the Lord laid his hand
sore upon me and smote me with the
small pox, when I was in my affliction.
I besought the Lord, and confessed my
pride and vanity and he was intreated
of me, and again restore'd me.  But I
rendered not to him according to his
benefitt; receive'd.

After a short time I changed my condition
and was marryed, and came into this Country

Where I found a new World and new
manners at which my heart rose, But
after I was convinced it was the way
of God, I submitted to it and joined to
the Church at Boston. ---  After some time
I fell into a lingering sickness like a con-
sumption together with a lameness - which cor-
rection I saw the lord sent to humble me
and do me good: and it was not altogether
ineffectual.  It pleased God to keep me
a long time without a child which was
a great grief to me, and cost me many
prayers and tears before I obtained one
The first was a Son, and after him many
more, of whom I now take the care, that
as I have brought you into the world, and
with great pain, weakness, cares and fears
brought you (to) this, I now travil in birth

again of you. till christ be formed in you.
Among all my experiences of Gods gratious
dealings with me, I have constantly observed
this, that he hath never suffered me long
to sit loose from him, but by one affliction
or other hath made me look home, and
search what was amiss -- so usualy there is
sometimes grief within me, that I have
no sooner felt my heart out of order,
but I have expected, correction for it,
which most comonly hath been upon
my own person, in sickness weakness
and pains, sometimes on my Soul in
doubts, and fears of Gods displeasure,
and my sincerity towards him.  Sometimes
he hath smote a Child with sickness,
sometimes, chastne'd by losses in Estate,
and these times, (there is great mercy)

hath been the times, of my greatest
getting and Advantage, yea I have found
them the times when the Lord hath
Manifested the most love to me, then
have I gone to searching and have said
with David, Lord search me and try me
see what ways of wickedness are in me
and lead me in the way everlasting:
and seldom or never but I have found
either some sin I lay under which God
would have reformd, or some duty ne-
glected which he would have perform'd
and by his help I have lay'd vows and
Bonds upon my Lord to perform his
righteous commands. 鈥揬n
If at any time you are chastned
of God take it as thankfully and

Joyfully as his greatest mercyes, for
if you be his, you shall reape the
greatest benefits by it; it hath been
no small Support to me in times of
darkness when the Almighty hath hid
his face from me, that yet I have had
abundance of sweetness and refreshment
after affliction, and more circumspection
in my walking after I have been afflicted
I have been within like an untoward child,
that no longer then the rod has been on
my back (or at least in sight) but I have
been apt to forget him and myself too.
Before I was afflicted I went astray, but
now I keep thy statutes.  I have had great
experience of Gods hearing my prayer,
and returning comfortable answers to me.
either in granting the thing I prayed for

or else in satisfying my mind without
it, and I have been confident it hath
been from him, because I have found
my heart through his goodness enlarged
in thankfulness to him.

I have often been perplexed that I have
not found that joy in my pilgrimage
and refreshing which I supposed most
of the Servants of God have, although
he hath not left me altogether without
the witness of his holy spirit, who hath
oft given me his word and sett to
his Seal, that it shall be well with me,
I have sometimes tasted of the hidden
Manna that the world knows not
and have sett up my Ebenezer and have
resolved with myself 鈥揬nthat against such a promise, such taps

of sweetness the gates of Hell shall never
prevail; though have I many times sinkings
and dropings, and not enjoyed that fe-
licity that I should have done, but when
I have been in darkness and seen no light,
yet have I desired to stay myself upon
the Lord, and when I have desired in
sickness and pain I have thought if
the Lord would but lift up the light
of his countenance upon me, although
he ground me to powder it would be
but light to me, yea oft have I thought
were I in Hell itself, and could there find
the love of God towards me, it would be
a Heaven.  And could I have been in
Heaven without the love of God, it
would have been a Hell to me, for in
Truth it is the absence and presence

of God that makes Heaven of Hell.
Many times hath Satan troubled me
concerning the verity of the Scriptures,
many times by Atheism, and how I could
know weither there was a God, I never saw
any miracles to confirm me, and those
which I read of, how did I know but they
were fiegned.  That there is a God my
reason would tell me, by the wonderous
works that I see, the vast frame of the
Heavens and Earth, the order of all things
Night and Day, Summer and Winter, Spring
and Autumn, the dayly providing for this
great househould upon the earth, the pre-
serving and directing of all to its proper
End.  The consideration of these things would
with amazement certainly, resolve me,
that there is an eternal Being.

But should I know he is such a God
as I worship in Trinity, and such
a Saviour as I rely upon tho: this hath
thousands of times been suggested to me,
yet God hath helped me over.  I have
argued this with myself, that there
is a God I see, if ever this God hath
revealed himself it must be in his
word, and this must be it or none.
Have I not found that operations by it,
that no humane invention can work
upon the Soul, hath not judgments
befallen diverse who have scornd and
contem'd it, hath it not been preserved
though All ages maugre all the heathen
Tyrants and the enemys that have

how the worst came to be as we see, do

The consideration of these things and

But some new Troubles I have had since

Now to the King Imortall Eternall and

occasion to read this hereafter, and
to others that shall read it when I shall
possess that I now hope for, that so they

August 28. 1656

After much weakness and sickness when
my spirits were worn out, and many
times my faith weak, likewise the
Lord was pleased to uphold my drooping
heart, and to manifest his Love to me,
and this is that which stayes my Soul,
that this condition that I am in, is the
best for me, for God doth not afflict will-
ingly, nor take delight in greiveing the children
of Men, he hath no benefit by my adversity,
nor is he the better for my prosperity, but
he doth it for my advantage, and that I may
be a gainer by it. And if he knows that
weakness and a frail body is the best to make
me a vessell fitt for his use, why should I
not bare it, not only willingly but joyfully,
The Lord knows I dare not desire that health
that Sometimes I have had, least my heart

should be drawn from him, and sett upon the
world.   --  How can I wait, looking every day
when my Saviour shall call for me. Lord grant
that while I live I may do that service I am able
in this frail body, and be in continual ex-
pectation of my change, and let me never
forget thy great love to my Soul so lately
expressed, when I could lye down and bequeath
my Soul to thee and Death seem'd no terrible
Thing. O let me ever see them that Art
invisible, and I shall not be unwilling to
come, tho' by so rough a Messenger.

May 11.1657

I had a Sore Sickness, and weakness took hold
of me, which hath by fitts lasted all this
Spring, till this 11th of May, but my God
hath given me many a respite and some
ability to perform the dutyes I owe to him
and the work of my family.

Many refreshments have I found in this
my weary Pilgrimage, and in this valy of
Baca, many pools of water, that which
now I have chiefly labour'd for is a con-
tented thankfull heart under my affliction
and weakness, Seeing it is the will of God
it should be thus. who am I that I should
repine at his pleasure espescialy: seeing
it is for my spiritual advantage, for I
hope my Soul shall flourish while my
body decays, and the weakness of this
outward man shall be a means to strengthen
my inner-man.   --  Yet a little while,
and he that shall come, will come, and
will not tarry.

May 13. 1657

As Sprng the Winter doth succeed
And leaves the naked Trees doe dress
The earth all black is cloth'd in green
At Sunshine each their joy express.

My Suns returne'd with healing wings
My Soul and body doth rejoice
My heart exults and praises sings
To him that heard my wailing voice.

My Wnters past my Storms are gone
And former Clouds seem now all fled
But if they must eclipse again
I'll run where I was succoured.

I have Shelter from the storm
A Shadow from the fainting heat
I have access unto his throne,
Who is God so wonderous great.

O hast thou made my pilgrimage
Thus pleasant fair and good
Bless'd me in youth and elder age
My Baca made a springing flood.

I studious am what I shall doe,
To share my duty with delight.
All I can give, is but thine own,
And at the most a Simple mite.

Sept. 30. 1657

It pleased God to visit me with my old
distemper of weakness and fainting, but
not in that manner that sometimes he
hath.  I desire not only willingly but thank-
fully to submit to him for I trust it is
out of his abundant Love to my straying
Soul which in prosperity is too much in
Love with the world.  I have found by
Experience. I can no more live without
correction then without food.  Lord with
correction give instruction and amendment,
and then thy stroaks shall be welcome,
I have not been refined in the furnace
of affliction as some have been, but have
rather been preserved with Sugar than
Brine, yet will he preserve me to his
heavenly Kingdom.

Thus (Dear Children) have you seen the
many Sicknesses and weaknesses that I
have passed thro! to the end that if you
meet with the like, you may have recourse
to the same God who hath heard and
delivered me, and will do the like for
you if you trust in him; And when
he shall deliver you out of distress, forget
not to give him thanks, but to walk
more closely with him then before, this
is the desire of your Loveing Mother.

A.B.

Unless thou help, what can I doe
But still my frailty show
If thou assist me Lord I shall
Return thee what I owe.

In thankfull acknowledgment for
the Letters I received, from my Husband
out of England.   ------

O thou that hear'st the prayers of thine
And 'mongst them hast regarded Mine,
Hast heard my cry's, and seen my Tears
Hast known my doubts and all my fears
Thou hast releived my fainting heart
Nor pay'd me after my desart.

Thou hast to Showe him Safely brought
For whom I thee so oft besought
Thou wast the Piolott to the ship
And rais'd him up when he was Sick
And hope thou'st given of good Success
In this his Buisness and Addresse
And that, there will return him back
Whose presence I so much doe lack
For all these mercyes I thee praise
And so desire Ev'n all my dayes.

In thankfull Remembrance for my
dear Husbands safe Arrivall. Sep't. 3: 1662

What shall I render to thy Name
Or how thy praises speak
My thanks how shall I testify
O Lord thou know'st I am weak.

I owe so much so little can
Return unto thy Name
Confusion rests upon my Soul
And I am fill'd with shame.

O thou that hearest prayers Lord
To thee shall come all flesh
Thou hast me heard and answered
My 'plaints have had accesse --

What did I ask for but thou gave'st
What could I more desire
But thankfulness even all my dayes
I humbly this Require.

Thy mercyes Lord have been so great
In number, numberless
Impossible for to recount
Or any way Express.

O help thy Saints that sought thy face
To Return unto thee praise
And walk before thee as they ought
In strict and upright wayes.

Here follows some verses upon the
Burning of our House, July. 10. 1666:

In silent night when rest I took
For sorrow neer I did not look,
I wakend was with thundering nois
And piteous shrieks of dreadfull voice
That fearful sound of fire and fire
Let no Man know is my desire
I starting up the light did spye
And to my God my heart did cry
To strengthen me in my distress
And not to leave me comfortless.
Then coming out behold a space
The flames consume my dwelling place.
And when I could no longer look
I blest his Name that gave and took.
That lay'd my goods low in the dust
Yea so it was , and so, twas just.
It was his own it was not mine
Far be it that I should repine

He might of all justly bereft
But yet sufficient for us left.
When by the Ruins oft I past,
My sorrowing eyes aside did cast,
And here and there that place did spye
When oft I sate, and long did lye,
There stood that Trunk, and there that chest
There lay that store I counted best.
My pleasant things in Ashes lye
And them behold no more shall I.
Under thy roof no guest shall sitt
Nor at thy Table eat a bitt
No pleasant tale shall ere be told
Nor things recounted done of old.
No Candle 'ere shall shine in thee
Nor bridegrooms Voice ere heard shall be
In silence ever shalt thou lye
Adeiu, Adeiu, all's Vanity.
Then streight I 'gin my heart to chide
And did thy wealth on Earth abide.

Did fix thy hope on mouldering dust,
The arm of flesh did'st make thy trust.
Raise up thy thoughts above the skye,
That dunghill mist away may flie.
Thou hast an house on high erect,
Fram'd by that mighty Architect.
With glory richly furnished,
Stands permanant tho: this be fled.
I'ts purchased and paid for too,
By him who hath enough to doe.
A price so vast as is unknown,
Yet by his gift is made thine own.
Ther's wealth enough I need no more
Farewell my pelf, farewell my Store.
The world no longer let me Love
My hope and treasure lyes Above.

AB

A Pilgrim

As weary Pilgrim, now at rest,
Hugs with delight his Silent nest.
His wasted limbes, now lye full soft
That merry steps, have troden oft
Blesses himself, to think upon
His dangers past, and travils done.
The burning Sun no more shall heat
Nor stormy rains, on him shall beat.
The Bryars and thorns no more shall scratch
Nor hungry wolves at him shall catch.
The erring pathes no more shall tread
Nor wild fruits eat, instead of bread
For waters cold he doth not Long
For thirst no more shall parch his tongue
No ragged stones his feet shall gaule
Nor stumps nor rocks cause him to fall
All cares and fears. he bids farewell
And means in Safety now to dwell.

A Pilgrim I on Earth, perplext
With sins with cares and sorrows vext
By age and pains brought to decay,
And my clay house mouldering away.
Oh how I long to be at rest
And soar on high among the blest.
This body shall in silence sleep
Thine eyes no more shall ever weep
No fainting fitts shall me assail
Nor grinding pains, my body frail.
With cares and fears  ne'r cumbred be,
Nor losses know, nor sorrow's see.
What tho my flesh shall there consume,
It is the bed Christ did perfume.
And when a few years shall be gone,
This mortall shall be cloth'd upon.
A corrupt carcasse downe it lyes
A glorious body it shall rise.

In weakness and dishonour Sown -
In power 'tis rais'd by Christ alone.
Then soul and body shall unite,
And of their maker have the Sight.
Such lasting joyes, shall there behold
As ear 'ner heard, nor tongue 'ner told
Lord make me ready for that day,
Then come dear bridegroom come away.

AB

Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka Collection, Circa 1730-1981 - Page 3 - Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka Collection, Circa 1730-1981. MS 0013. The Rakow Research Library, The Corning Museum of Glass, Corning, New York. Preferred Citation: Collection materials are in and .German English Language of Materials: 80.4 Linear Feet (10 Hollinger boxes, 6 half Hollinger box, 7 card file boxes, 31 flat boxes, and 21 oversize folders) Physical Description: Majority of material found within Circa 1820-1939Date [bulk]: Circa 1730-1981Date [inclusive]: /repositories/3/resources/21ID [aspace_uri]: MS-0013ID: Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka CollectionTitle: Blaschka, Rudolf, 1857-1939Creator Blaschka, Leopold, 1822-1895Creator The Rakow Research Library Manuscript CollectionRepository: Summary Information Return to Table of Contents Biographical / Historical Leopold (1822 – 1895) and Rudolf Blaschka (1857 – 1939), father and son glassmakers from Bohemia, now the Czech Republic, are known for their highly-accurate, three-dimensional marine invertebrate and botanical glass models created for study in institutions worldwide. While other craftsmen in the mid-19th century were fabricating educational study models out of materials such as such as wax, papier–mâché and wire, the Blaschkas were the first to create these models from glass. Leopold was born in 1822 in Aicha, Bohemia (now Český Dub in the Czech Republic) into a family of glassworkers who traced their glassworking lineage back to 15th century Venice. As a young man, he worked for a short time as an apprentice goldsmith and gem-cutter before joining the family’s metal and glass business making flame-worked costume jewelry and luxury goods for an expanding export market. Rudolf was born in 1857 to Leopold and his second wife Karolina Blaschka (née Reigel) also in Aicha, Bohemia. The company moved to Dresden in 1863, and in the 1870s Rudolf joined the studio. In the early 1860s, Leopold began creating glass models of tropical flowers based on botanical drawings. Prince Camille de Rohan (1800 – 1892) of Prague discovered Leopold’s

Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka Collection, Circa 1730-1981 - Page 4 - In the early 1860s, Leopold began creating glass models of tropical flowers based on botanical drawings. Prince Camille de Rohan (1800 – 1892) of Prague discovered Leopold’s work and became a patron, commissioning 100 models of exotic flowers for his private collection, and supporting Leopold’s further botanical study. The Prince introduced Leopold to Ludwig Reichenbach (1793 – 1879), director of The Natural History Museum and Botanical Garden in Dresden; in 1863, Reichenbach arranged an exhibition of Leopold’s glass flowers. Soon Leopold began working almost exclusively in glass, and by the 1870s the studio focused production on human and animal eyes, models and dishes. Order records from this period reflect several commissions for glass animals; in particular, artificial glass sea anemones for aquariums. In the mid-19th century, the study of natural history through observation and empirical evidence flourished, well-positioning the Blaschkas’ model-making to grow into a business. Glass models were ideal, as they held their color and shape, unlike dried plant specimens, or marine invertebrates preserved in alcohol or formaldehyde. Additionally, an interest in aquariums, popularized by British naturalist Philip Henry Gosse (1810 – 1888), undoubtedly spurred the market for marine models. Gosse’s drawings inspired the Blaschkas’ early marine invertebrate models which were reproduced from the marine animal drawings in Gosse’s book Actinologia Britannica: A , in three-dimensional detail depicted in theirHistory of the British Anemones and Corals natural habitats. A later influence on the Blaschkas’ work were the scientific descriptions and interpretations of Ernst Haeckel (1834 – 1919). Haeckel, an artist and zoologist, described thousands of new invertebrate species, producing several monographs in his career. Correspondence indicates that the Blaschkas and Haeckel shared books, and most likely visited one another. Eventually, the Blaschkas worked from an aquarium of their own, populating it with live specimens shipped to them in wet seaweed. By the 1880s, glass models were the main product of the Blaschka studio. Their models held a certain prestige, and they supplied universities, museums and schools around the world, including Ireland, India, Japan and the United States. In 1886, George Lincoln Goodale, professor of botany at Harvard University saw Leopold and Rudolf’s work at the Boston Society of Natural History Museum and visited the Blaschkas in Dresden to commission models for Harvard’s Botanical Museum. Although Leopold was initially hesitant, this visit marked the beginning of a long relationship between the Blaschka studio and the university. From 1887 to 1890, the Blaschkas divided their time between producing botanical models for Harvard and marine invertebrate models for other institutions. However, in 1890 the Blaschkas signed a 10-year contract to work exclusively on creating glass botanical models for Harvard. Shortly after meeting the Blaschkas in 1886, Goodale sought funding from wealthy Boston philanthropists Elizabeth and Mary Lee Ware to create a collection of botanical models. Mary, a former student of Goodale’s with a passion for botany, was able to convince her mother to support the project after seeing an initial set of models, despite heavy damage caused in transit. As a result, the collection was named the Ware Collection of Blaschka Glass Models of Plants in memory of their late husband and father Charles E. Ware. After her mother’s death in 1898, Mary remained the primary sponsor of the collection for nearly forty years. In 1892, Rudolf traveled to the United States and Jamaica to obtain reference materials for new models. While staying with Goodale in Boston, Rudolf visited the Botanical Museum and saw the models on exhibit for the first time. Rudolf traveled to the United States a second time in 1895, intending to study plants in the Southeast of the United States before

Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka Collection, Circa 1730-1981 - Page 5 - and saw the models on exhibit for the first time. Rudolf traveled to the United States a second time in 1895, intending to study plants in the Southeast of the United States before continuing to Mexico, but his trip was cut short by the death of his father, prompting an early return to Germany. Following his father’s death, Rudolf continued to supply botanical models to Harvard until 1936. He died in 1939. Today, the Ware Collection of Blaschka Glass Models of Plants at the Harvard Museum of Natural History contains over 4,000 botanical works. Cornell University employed the Blaschkas as well, beginning in 1885, and has 400 marine invertebrate models among its holdings. Other Blaschka model collections, both of marine invertebrates and botanicals, exist in numerous institutions around the world. Bibliography: The Archives of Rudolf and Leopold Blaschka and the Ware Collection of Blaschka Glass Models of Plants, 1886-2020: A Guide. Whitehouse, D., (1991). The Blaschka Animals. Glass, no. 44, 36 – 41. Return to Table of Contents Scope and Contents The Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka Collection represents the life and work of the father and son glassmakers who created thousands of botanical and marine invertebrate study models in the late 1800s and 1900s, supplying institutions around the world. The collection is divided into six series. (1) Drawings, Circa 1863-1930 (2) Correspondence, Circa 1863-1981 (3) Photographs, Circa 1864-1937 (4) Business Files, Circa 1864-1936 (5) Research Material, Circa 1849-1889 (6) Personal, Circa 1730-1935 Return to Table of Contents Administrative Information Publication Statement

Researchers must make an appointment to view this collection. Immediate Source of Acquisition Received from Gertrud Pones via Gerhard Walther and Renate Albrecht between 1979 and 1982, Phyllis Montgomery in 1981, and the Botanical Museum of Harvard University via Susan Rossi-Wilcox in 1993. Physical Characteristics and Technical Requirements Boxes 23 and 24 of Series 01, Sub-Series 04 (Sketchbooks), Box 26 of Series 02 (Correspondence), Boxes 33 and 42 of Series 04 (Business Files), and Box 41 of Series 05 (Research Material) contain notebooks and sketchbooks with fragile bindings and should be handled with care. In Series 03 (Photographs), Boxes 29-31 contain photo albums with loose photos that can easily fall out and should be handled with care. Researchers should also use book cradles when looking at the photo albums, as the bindings and pages are fragile. In Series 05 (Research Material), Box 43 contains a portfolio of dried grass specimens affixed to cardboard pages and should be handled with care to avoid dislodging any of the specimens. The books in Boxes 44, 46, and 47 of Series 06, Sub-Series 02 (Travel) and Boxes 48-54 of Series 06, Sub-Series 04 (Books and Ephemera) also have fragile bindings. Use of a book cradle is recommended. Some materials in the collection have received conservation assessment and treatment. Processing Information Processed by Kylie McKenna in 2025. Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka Collection, Circa 1730-1981 - Page 8 - 122937Identifier folder 01box 10 32.3 Linear Feet (18 flat boxes and 6 oversize folders) Physical Description Sub-Series 01Identifier 60.1 Linear Feet (3 Hollinger boxes, 3 half Hollinger boxes, 18 flat boxes, and 20 oversize folders) Physical Description Series 01Identifier Drawings, Circa 1863-1930 Scope and Contents This series is composed of sketches and drawings of marine invertebrates, botanicals, and insects by Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka in watercolor, pen, ink, and crayon on paper, along with prints from a variety of sources that the Blaschkas likely used as design inspiration. The series is divided into four sub-series. (1) Marine Invertebrates, Circa 1863-1890 (2) Botanicals, Circa 1890-1930 (3) Insects, 1890-1913 (4) Sketchbooks, Circa 1881-1892, Undated Title/Description Instances Marine Invertebrates, Circa 1863-1890 Scope and Contents This sub-series contains preparatory sketches and drawings of marine invertebrates by Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka for their three-dimensional glass models. The drawings were derived from a variety of sources including published illustrations by Philip Henry Gosse and Ernst Haeckel and, later, the Blaschkas’ own in-studio aquarium populated with live specimens sent to them wrapped in wet seaweed. This sub-series also includes some of the illustrations used by the Blaschkas to create their drawings and models. The sub-series is arranged alphabetically. Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka Collection, Circa 1730-1981 - Page 100 - folder 01box 25 0.7 Linear Feet (1 Hollinger box and 1 half Hollinger box) Physical Description Series 02Identifier 97763Identifier folder 02box 24 95869Identifier folder 01box 24 95865Identifier folder 03box 23 87384Identifier folder 02box 23 Rudolf Blaschka Sketchbook, Circa 1892 Sketchbook, Undated Sketchbook, Undated Sketches from , UndatedZoologia Danica Correspondence, Circa 1863-1981 Scope and Contents This series is composed of personal and business correspondence in both English and German, either exchanged by or relating to Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka. It includes two notebooks containing drafts of business correspondence, a letter from Leopold to Rudolf, and sympathy cards sent after Leopold’s death in 1895 to his wife, Karolina. The series also features correspondence with Ludwig Reichenbach, who arranged the first exhibition of Leopold’s work in Dresden; George Lincoln Goodale, the founding director of Harvard’s Botanical Museum; Mary Lee Ware, the principal sponsor of the Blaschkas’ botanical models for Harvard; and Joseph William Blankinship, Rudolf’s assistant during his second trip to the United States in 1895. Correspondence with Rudolf’s wife, Martha Frieda Blaschka, mainly pertains to the disposition of Rudolf’s pension after his death in 1939. Additionally, there is a small amount of correspondence that does not involve a member of the Blaschka family; in these instances, both the sender and recipient are noted. The series is arranged alphabetically by correspondent, and chronologically when the correspondent could not be identified. Title/Description Instances Anders, Wilhelmina, 1939

#!/usr/bin/env python3 Corning Alma SRU probe and harvester, v1.4

This uses Alma's SRU search endpoint rather than Primo's guest search endpoint. SRU supports startRecord pagination and is not subject to Primo VE's 250-result guest offset restriction.

Probe: python corning_alma_sru_harvester.py --probe

Full harvest: python corning_alma_sru_harvester.py --all

Outputs: Corning_Blaschka_SRU/ probe.xml raw_sru_pages/ records.jsonl records.csv summary.json

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse import csv import json import logging import re import sys import time import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET from pathlib import Path from typing import Any

try: import requests except ImportError: print("Install requests with: python -m pip install requests", file=sys.stderr) raise SystemExit(2)

BASE = "https://na02.alma.exlibrisgroup.com/view/sru/01CORNING_INST" QUERY = "alma.all_for_ui=blaschka" NS = { "sru": "http://www.loc.gov/zing/srw/", "marc": "http://www.loc.gov/MARC21/slim", "diag": "http://www.loc.gov/zing/srw/diagnostic/", USER_AGENT = "AcademicResearchHarvester/1.4 (Corning Blaschka catalogue audit)"

def request_xml( session: requests.Session, start_record: int, maximum_records: int, timeout: int, attempts: int = 5, ) -> str: params = { "version": "1.2", "operation": "searchRetrieve", "recordSchema": "marcxml", "query": QUERY, "maximumRecords": maximum_records, "startRecord": start_record,

last_error: Exception | None = None for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1): try: response = session.get(BASE, params=params, timeout=timeout) response.raise_for_status() text = response.text ET.fromstring(text) return text except (requests.RequestException, ET.ParseError) as exc: last_error = exc if attempt == attempts: break wait = min(60, 5 * attempt) logging.warning( "Request failed %s/%s: %s; sleeping %ss", attempt, attempts, exc, wait, time.sleep(wait)

raise RuntimeError(f"SRU request failed: {last_error}")

def number_of_records(root: ET.Element) -> int: node = root.find("sru:numberOfRecords", NS) if node is None or node.text is None: diagnostics = [] for diagnostic in root.findall(".//diag:diagnostic", NS): uri = diagnostic.findtext("diag:uri", default="", namespaces=NS) message = diagnostic.findtext("diag:message", default="", namespaces=NS) details = diagnostic.findtext("diag:details", default="", namespaces=NS) diagnostics.append(f"{uri} | {message} | {details}") raise RuntimeError( "SRU response had no numberOfRecords. Diagnostics: " + ("; ".join(diagnostics) if diagnostics else "(none)") return int(node.text)

def subfields(record: ET.Element, tag: str, code: str | None = None) -> list[str]: values: list[str] = [] for field in record.findall(f"marc:datafield[@tag='{tag}']", NS): for subfield in field.findall("marc:subfield", NS): if code is None or subfield.attrib.get("code") == code: if subfield.text: values.append(subfield.text.strip()) return values

def controlfield(record: ET.Element, tag: str) -> str: node = record.find(f"marc:controlfield[@tag='{tag}']", NS) return node.text.strip() if node is not None and node.text else ""

def record_to_dict(record: ET.Element) -> dict[str, Any]: title_parts = subfields(record, "245") title = " ".join(title_parts).strip(" /:;") creators = ( subfields(record, "100") + subfields(record, "110") + subfields(record, "700") + subfields(record, "710") dates = ( subfields(record, "260", "c") + subfields(record, "264", "c") physical = subfields(record, "300") notes = [] for tag in ("500", "505", "520", "545", "561", "506", "540", "590"): notes.extend(subfields(record, tag)) subjects = [] for tag in ("600", "610", "650", "651", "655"): subjects.extend(subfields(record, tag)) urls = subfields(record, "856", "u")

return { "mms_id": controlfield(record, "001"), "title": title, "creators": " | ".join(creators), "dates": " | ".join(dates), "physical_description": " | ".join(physical), "notes": " | ".join(notes), "subjects": " | ".join(subjects), "urls": " | ".join(urls), "marcxml": ET.tostring(record, encoding="unicode"),

def parse_records(root: ET.Element) -> list[dict[str, Any]]: result = [] for record in root.findall(".//marc:record", NS): result.append(record_to_dict(record)) return result

def write_text(path: Path, text: str) -> None: path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) temp = path.with_suffix(path.suffix + ".tmp") temp.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8") temp.replace(path)

def write_json(path: Path, value: Any) -> None: write_text(path, json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))

def probe(outdir: Path, timeout: int) -> int: session = requests.Session() session.headers.update({"User-Agent": USER_AGENT, "Accept": "application/xml,text/xml,*/*"})

text = request_xml( session, start_record=1, maximum_records=10, timeout=timeout, write_text(outdir / "probe.xml", text)

root = ET.fromstring(text) total = number_of_records(root) records = parse_records(root)

print(f"SRU endpoint: {BASE}") print(f"Query: {QUERY}") print(f"Total: {total:,}") print(f"Returned: {len(records)}") for index, record in enumerate(records, start=1): print( f"{index:>2}. {record['mms_id'] or '(no MMS)'} | " f"{record['title'] or '(untitled)'}"

write_json( outdir / "probe_summary.json", "endpoint": BASE, "query": QUERY, "total": total, "returned": len(records), "records": [ "mms_id": item["mms_id"], "title": item["title"], for item in records return total

def harvest(outdir: Path, timeout: int, delay: float, force: bool) -> None: session = requests.Session() session.headers.update({"User-Agent": USER_AGENT, "Accept": "application/xml,text/xml,*/*"})

raw_dir = outdir / "raw_sru_pages" raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

records: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {} total: int | None = None start_record = 1 page_size = 50

while total is None or start_record <= total: path = raw_dir / f"start_{start_record:06d}.xml"

# Corning Blaschka Primo harvester

## First run

Open PowerShell in this folder and execute:

```powershell Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass .\run_probe.ps1

The probe should report a result count close to the catalogue's current `blaschka` search total.

## Full catalogue harvest

```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe .\corning_primo_harvester.py --all --verbose

Outputs are written to `Corning_Blaschka_Primo`:

- `raw_search_pages/`: every API page, unchanged - `blaschka_primo_records.jsonl`: one lossless record per line - `blaschka_primo_records.csv`: normalized audit table - `summary.json`: counts and resource-type distribution

The script is resumable. Re-run the same command after interruption.

## Full PNX enrichment

Only after the first-stage harvest succeeds:

```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe .\corning_primo_harvester.py --all --enrich --verbose

This makes roughly one additional request per catalogue record and stores the responses under `raw_full_pnx/`.

## Current boundary

This version inventories catalogue records and exposed links. It does not yet bulk-download PDFs or page JPGs. The catalogue often presents one object as both one PDF and many JPG page images, so file downloading should be designed after the delivery metadata has been audited.
