content.title: Blaschka Fondazione Scienza e Tecnica Florence: Pietro Marchi's multi-purchase systematic teaching collection, 118 original / 111 surviving models, 1891 Tubipora hemprichi for 10 lire, complete MFST Cat. I 1–118 register, Opificio delle Pietre Dure technical conservation, and 3D/public-display renewal
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass-model collection inherited by the Fondazione Scienza e Tecnica (FST) in Florence from the nineteenth-century Istituto Tecnico di Firenze / Istituto Tecnico Toscano teaching collections. The module reconstructs Pietro Marchi's deliberate multi-purchase programme, preserves the complete local historical sequence MFST Catalogo I nos. 1–118, distinguishes the 118-object original corpus from the 111 surviving models reported in 2017, and records the last certain item-level transaction: Tubipora hemprichi, MFST Cat. I no. 85 / Inventario I no. 245, acquired in 1891 from a Florentine dealer for 10 lire. It also captures the full conservation-science layer: Opificio delle Pietre Dure radiography and FTIR, documented binders and pigments, cleaning/consolidation/colour fixing/re-adhesion, and the explicit decision not to reconstruct missing portions. Finally it records the 2017 3D-documentation project, the 2017 exact display subset of seven objects, the 2023 reinstallation/preview of rooms containing Blaschka marine animals, and the current 2026 institutional continuity while leaving the exact present display count unresolved.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 43 only after Santiago de Chile, Rio de Janeiro and Montevideo were screened under module 42's Latin-American promotion rule and failed to produce a completed transaction, locally identified surviving object, or explicit Blaschka physical collection. Florence emerged from the same global screening with much stronger closure: a peer-reviewed local-museum study documents 118 original objects, 111 surviving, a complete local sequence, a named museum-side collector/selector, a certain 1891 price and inventory crosswalk, whole-collection restoration, and later 3D/public-display work. Duplicate audit of active 06 v3 found no Florence/FST/Pietro Marchi node.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: Active 06 v3 contains no occurrence of Fondazione Scienza e Tecnica, Istituto Tecnico di Firenze, Pietro Marchi, Firenze or Florence as a standalone Blaschka node. Pisa remains a separate Italian collection already captured.
merge_policy.institutional_identity_guard: The present FST museum preserves and valorizes the historical scientific patrimony of the nineteenth-century Istituto Tecnico Toscano / Istituto Tecnico di Firenze. Institutional succession is used for collection provenance without implying that every museum object followed an identical administrative history.
merge_policy.118_vs_111_guard: 118 is the original local catalogue corpus. Faustini & Lotti state that seven of the 118 original objects are missing and that the extant series consists of 111 models. FST's 2017 public 3D article informally says the collection 'vanta 118 esemplari'; this is treated as nominal/historical collection size, not as a competing current survival count.
merge_policy.missing_seven_guard: The 2017 publication does not identify the seven missing MFST Cat. I numbers in the recovered text/table. No missing-object identities are inferred by subtracting from display status or other secondary sources.
merge_policy.acquisition_window_guard: The same 2017 paper uses two slightly different formulations: the abstract says the collection was acquired in the last twenty years of the nineteenth century, while the body places Marchi's programme in the last thirty years. The module does not synthesize a false exact start date. It records multiple acquisitions in the late nineteenth century, with 1891 as the last certain item-level acquisition currently published.
merge_policy.Marchi_role_guard: Pietro Marchi is treated as the museum-side architect of the collection and selector of catalogue models. No claim is made that he personally executed every payment or received every package.
merge_policy.multiple_dealers_guard: The local study says acquisitions were made through multiple scientific-material dealers. The exact dealer chain for each model remains unresolved; dealer identity is not generalized from the 1891 Florentine seller.
merge_policy.1891_transaction_guard: The final certain datum is Tubipora hemprichi, MFST Cat. I no. 85 / Inventario I no. 245, entering in 1891 for 10 lire from a Florentine dealer. This price and inventory number apply to that object only.
merge_policy.MFST_catalogue_number_guard: MFST Cat. I nos. 1–118 are the Florence museum's preserved historical sequence. They are not silently equated with Blaschka's or Ward's commercial catalogue numbers.
merge_policy.original_name_guard: The 118 names in the 2017 table are preserved as historical collection nomenclature, including authors' explicit [sic] corrections. Modern taxonomy is not substituted silently.
merge_policy.table_survival_guard: The 2017 paper prints the complete original 1–118 sequence while separately stating that only 111 survive. Appearance in Table 1 therefore does not by itself prove 2017 survival of a specific non-displayed number.
merge_policy.2017_display_guard: The paper explicitly identifies seven objects then visible to the public: MFST Cat. I nos. 1–5, 10 and 102. That seven-object display count is historical to the 2017 publication and is not projected into 2026.
merge_policy.2023_display_guard: A City of Florence cultural-news item reports a 2023 preview of three reinstalled first-floor rooms including Blaschka marine animals. It does not publish an exact number or object list, so no current count is inferred.
merge_policy.2026_display_guard: FST's current website confirms the museum and its natural-science patrimony remain active, but the exact 2026 number of Blaschka models on view is not stated in the recovered current pages. Current display count remains unresolved.
merge_policy.restoration_scope_guard: Faustini & Lotti state that the entire collection underwent restoration with technical/professional contribution from the Opificio delle Pietre Dure. Specific analytical results are not assumed to apply identically to every model unless the source says so; radiography and FTIR were conducted on selected objects/materials.
merge_policy.OPD_identifier_guard: OPD Sch. S 1087.2 is the radiographic investigation record; OPD Sch. S 1087.1 is the FTIR/material-analysis record. These are conservation-document identifiers, not museum object numbers.
merge_policy.material_analysis_guard: The published FTIR results identify binders including glues, egg white, casein and drying oils, with silicate material in especially thick pigments. These findings are preserved as analytical results from sampled material, not as a universal recipe for all Blaschka models.
merge_policy.treatment_ethics_guard: The conservation treatment included cleaning, consolidation, colour fixing and re-adhesion of detached/broken parts. Missing portions were deliberately not reconstructed, prioritizing historical-scientific documentary value.
merge_policy.3D_count_guard: FST's 2017 public report says about fifteen glass objects were documented in 3D during 13–17 February 2017. The project intended eventual full-collection documentation; no claim is made here that all 111 survivors were completed in 3D.
merge_policy.university_Florence_small_lot_guard: FST's 2017 3D article also mentions a small analogous lot from the Zoology Section of the University of Florence Natural History Museum. That lot is a separate institutional collection and is not merged into the 118/111 FST count.
merge_policy.Bunodes_drawing_guard: The Bunodes gemmacea no. 49 note about direct live observation and a corresponding Blaschka drawing at Corning is a design-source relationship cited through Reiling; it is not an acquisition transaction.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No commercial catalogue number, accession number for objects other than the explicitly published 1891 Tubipora, missing-object identifier, shipment mark or dealer invoice number is invented.

summary.key_result: Florence is an unusually closed teaching-collection node. Pietro Marchi did not assemble a random assortment: he selected across sales catalogues to construct a systematic representation of European marine invertebrates. The original 118-object local sequence survives as an archival catalogue, 111 physical models were still present in 2017, and the final certain purchase can be tied to a year, price and dual local identifier. The collection's later history is equally unusually legible because the entire surviving corpus underwent conservation supported by radiography and FTIR, followed by 3D documentation and renewed public-display work. The main gaps are now narrow: the identities of the seven lost catalogue numbers, the earlier dealer-by-dealer acquisition chronology, and exact 2026 object/display status.

network_implications.procurement_value: Florence shows collection formation as deliberate syllabus construction: Marchi selected across catalogues to build systematic coverage rather than purchasing a single preassembled set.
network_implications.price_value: The 1891 Tubipora record supplies a rare locally preserved nineteenth-century retail price in lire and an explicit dealer-mediated transaction outside the better-known Ward/Frič networks.
network_implications.conservation_value: FST is unusually important for technical material history because conservation science documents internal armatures and organic/mineral surface media, while treatment philosophy explicitly preserved losses rather than cosmetically reconstructing them.
network_implications.survival_value: The 118→111 ratio is unusually legible, but the seven missing identities remain open; this makes Florence a strong site for studying attrition at the level of an almost-complete original local catalogue.
network_implications.next_institutional_action: Return to the large-museum screen after Florence. Santiago de Chile remains a catalogue-contact/teaching-model lead but is below promotion threshold. For module 44 prioritize a major uncaptured institution where a current or historical physical Blaschka collection can be joined to transaction evidence; strong candidates include UW–Madison for a named purchaser and active preservation project, or another national museum emerging from the Rakow recipient lists. Do not promote Leiden/Stockholm/Copenhagen solely from catalogue-contact evidence.

content.title: Blaschka Muséum d’histoire naturelle de Genève: 1888 117-object acquisition, 94 survivors, 512-mark shipment to Godefroy Lunel, long display history, 2008 restoration and dedicated room, MHNG inventory anchors, and 2024–2026 vibration-controlled rehousing
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass-model collection at the Muséum d’histoire naturelle de Genève (MHNG). The module separates the reported 1888 acquisition of 117 objects and the last exact published survival figure of 94 from approximate current public summaries; preserves the 512-mark shipment-cost breakdown and 20 February dispatch to director Godefroy Lunel as a locally published documentary reconstruction; records evidence of public display at the Bastions and Malagnou sites; captures Isabelle Pirotte’s verified 2008 conservation-restoration work and the opening of a dedicated Blaschka room on 12 June 2008; registers two public MHNG inventory identifiers; and follows the collection into the current renovation cycle, during which it was boxed and moved to municipal heritage storage to protect it from construction vibration, with further consolidation/restoration and vibration-, climate- and light-adapted showcases planned before its return.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after Field Museum because module 34 explicitly identified Geneva as the strongest next European target after duplicate audit. The active backend contained only cross-references to Isabelle Pirotte’s Geneva restoration work, not a standalone Geneva institutional node. Geneva is unusually valuable because the public evidence spans the full lifecycle: a quantified 1888 acquisition, a named museum director and shipment date, a survival count, long-term display, a documented modern restoration campaign, dedicated exhibition design, public local inventory numbers, and a current preventive-conservation move prompted by building vibration risk.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Geneva/MHNG institutional module was found in the active 06-through-34 sequence. Existing references to Geneva in the Liège restoration network and comparative model-location table remain cross-references rather than duplicate nodes.
merge_policy.117_count_guard: 117 is the reported number of objects in the 1888 Geneva order/acquisition. It is a historical acquisition count, not a present display count or a count of components within compound models.
merge_policy.94_count_guard: 94 is the last exact published survival/conservation count recovered in this pass. Mirabilia later summarizes the collection as about one hundred objects. The module does not silently convert 94 into a guaranteed 2026 inventory count without a current object export.
merge_policy.512_marks_guard: 512 marks is reported as the total value of the order including listed packing/logistics charges: 15 marks for two large crates, 26.50 marks for cartons, and 12 marks for packing and transport to the railway station. No model-only price is asserted.
merge_policy.shipment_date_guard: The locally published reconstruction states that the crates were sent to Godefroy Lunel on 20 February; the exact manufacture dates and exact date on which the order was placed remain unknown in that same source. The year is interpreted in the context of the stated 1888 acquisition but should be verified against the original accompanying letter/register before item-level chronology is treated as closed.
merge_policy.direct_route_guard: A Leopold Blaschka accompanying letter and shipment addressed to Lunel support a workshop-to-museum shipping route. No separate dealer is inserted into the transaction without documentary evidence.
merge_policy.uninsured_guard: The locally published reconstruction reports Leopold Blaschka saying that the shipment had to be sent uninsured and asking to be informed quickly about safe arrival. This is retained as a documentary claim pending recovery of the original letter image or museum register.
merge_policy.display_continuity_guard: A local historical account says the objects were probably always at least partly on public display, with examples at the Bastions and about forty at Malagnou from 1965. The word 'probably' is preserved; uninterrupted continuous display is not asserted.
merge_policy.2008_restoration_guard: The MHNG 2008 annual report directly verifies that Isabelle Pirotte carried out restoration of the Blaschka objects and that the dedicated space opened on 12 June 2008. Public summaries saying about half the collection was fully restored are treated as approximate, not an exact treatment count.
merge_policy.display_remounting_guard: A museum-engaged didactic-model study describes the 2008 display as separating models from their bases and lighting them from below. This is encoded as observed/scenographic practice, not as proof that every one of the 94 surviving objects was detached from an original base.
merge_policy.inventory_identifier_guard: Mirabilia, a collaborative collections platform of City of Geneva cultural institutions, publishes MHNG-INVE-79252 and MHNG-INVE-79257 for 'Méduses des Blaschka'. These are genuine public local identifiers, but no taxon-level identity is inferred from the grouped web record alone.
merge_policy.half_restored_guard: Mirabilia states that about half of the approximately one hundred marine-invertebrate models had been fully restored. This is a rounded public summary and is not converted into 47, 50, or any other exact number.
merge_policy.current_storage_guard: PR-1648 states that the Blaschka collection had already been boxed and transported to City heritage storage to protect it from vibrations from the Ambre construction project. This is collection-level preventive-conservation evidence; no individual packing unit, crate number or object movement date is invented.
merge_policy.current_treatment_guard: PR-1648 says consolidation and restoration work is to be planned because the collection remains very fragile. This is a planned/current renovation-phase intervention, distinct from Pirotte’s 2008 campaign, and is not treated as completed unless later treatment records confirm completion.
merge_policy.future_showcase_guard: PR-1648 specifies adapted conditions for vibration, climate and lighting, and a second-floor plan labels the Blaschka showcase as anti-vibration and sealed. These are renovation design commitments/plans, not evidence that the new case is already commissioned and populated as of 7 August 2026.
merge_policy.reopening_guard: An official City press release of 20 March 2025 moved the progressive public reopening to September 2026; a 2026 financial-plan document similarly refers to reopening at the start of the 2026 academic/autumn season, while gallery renewal extends beyond that point. Because PR-1648 calls the return of the fragile Blaschka collection the last milestone of gallery renovation, this module does not assume the Blaschka room will be accessible on the first day of progressive reopening.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: The National Museum Wales/Meechan comparative 'Model Locations' spreadsheet is external cross-collection research. Rows naming Geneva are catalogue-type candidates only; NMW accession numbers, Cardiff condition notes and Cardiff display histories are never transferred to Geneva objects.
merge_policy.catalogue_crosswalk_guard: A matching taxon and Blaschka/Ward catalogue number in the comparative table does not assign that number to a specific MHNG physical model unless a Geneva label, register, object file or photograph supplies a local crosswalk.
merge_policy.image_guard: Visitor and press images are useful display evidence but are not treated as inventory records unless accompanied by MHNG metadata.

summary.key_result: Geneva is one of the cleanest full-lifecycle nodes in the global project. A quantified 1888 shipment can be followed from crates and railway-station transport through long-term public display, object loss/survival, specialist restoration, a purpose-built 2008 gallery, public MHNG inventory identifiers, and then back into boxes and heritage storage because the museum itself became a physical risk environment. PR-1648 makes the conservation logic unusually explicit: vibration from construction prompted removal, and return depends on consolidation/restoration plus a case engineered around vibration, climate and light. The decisive remaining gap is the original 1888 order/letter/register and a current 94-object-level MHNG export connecting local IDs to Blaschka catalogue numbers, treatment histories and post-renovation locations.

content.title: Blaschka Glasgow Museums: Philip Brookes Mason private collection, 300-model sale notice, 1909 £275 municipal purchase, 1909.66 numbered objects and current multi-taxon holdings
content.scope: Deep capture of the Blaschka glass-model holdings of Glasgow Museums, emphasizing the secondary-market transition from the private natural-history museum of Philip Brookes Mason (1842–1903) to his widow and then to Glasgow Museums in 1909. The module separates the 1904 advertised quantity of 300 Blaschka invertebrate models from the exact but still unrecovered 1909 accession quantity, records the £275 purchase price, captures two current local-numbered physical-object anchors in the 1909.66 accession series, registers current official collection-level Blaschka holdings across molluscs, annelids and echinoderms, and builds a controlled cross-institutional candidate register from the National Museum Wales/Meechan comparative spreadsheet.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after a parallel audit of Guernsey, Leicester and Glasgow/Hunterian because Glasgow exposes the strongest combination of provenance, price and local identifiers. Corning's global-collection research documents a 1904 sale announcement for 300 Blaschka models and a 1909 sale by Mason's widow to Glasgow Museums for £275; current sources expose accession numbers 1909.66.ca and 1909.66.js, while Glasgow Museums' own database confirms surviving Blaschka groups in annelids and echinoderms.

merge_policy.Glasgow_Museums_vs_Hunterian_guard: Municipal Glasgow Museums / Art Gallery & Museum holdings are kept separate from the Hunterian Museum, University of Glasgow. The NMW comparative spreadsheet lists both institutions in some rows; shared city does not imply shared custody or provenance.
merge_policy.Science_Museum_origin_guard: The earlier Science Museum 1925–1927 recipient audit found no evidence that Glasgow Museums received Blaschka models in that dispersal. The Mason 1909 private-to-municipal acquisition is an independent provenance chain and must not be conflated with South Kensington transfers.
merge_policy.300_advertised_vs_1909_received_guard: The Museums Journal notice reproduced by Corning advertises 300 Blaschka invertebrate models from Dr Philip B. Mason's estate in December 1904. Corning states that Mrs Mason eventually sold her husband's models to Glasgow Museums in 1909 for £275. Until the 1909 accession register is transcribed, 300 is not asserted as the exact number accessioned by Glasgow.
merge_policy.current_count_guard: Neither the 300 advertised models nor any 1909 accession-series pattern is treated as the present-day surviving count. No complete current Glasgow Blaschka inventory total was recovered.
merge_policy.1909_66_series_guard: The local identifiers 1909.66.ca and 1909.66.js strongly indicate membership in the same 1909 accession group. No synthetic suffix range, series size, or unseen 1909.66 child identifier is created.
merge_policy.Mason_provenance_scope_guard: Glasgow Museums explicitly identifies several annelid Blaschka models as from the Mason collection. The exact Mason provenance of each separately published Glasgow object or taxonomic-group page remains object-file/accession-register dependent unless the local record states it.
merge_policy.photo_asset_guard: Glasgow Life Photo Library search/result counts are not physical-object counts. The media asset 1909.66.ca_01 is tied to physical object 1909.66.ca; other search assets are not counted without object-level metadata.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: NMW/Meechan Model Locations rows are cross-collection research evidence, not Glasgow accession records. They are captured as candidate model types only; NMW accession numbers, NMW condition statements and NMW display histories remain Cardiff evidence.
merge_policy.catalogue_crosswalk_guard: A matching taxon and external Blaschka catalogue number does not automatically assign that catalogue number to a Glasgow physical object. Candidate crosswalks for Aurelia aurita (224) and Loligopsis/Chiroteuthis veranii (564) remain explicitly provisional until a Glasgow label, register, object file or photograph confirms them.
merge_policy.maker_name_guard: Current sources vary between 'Blaschka of Dresden' and 'Leopold and Rudolph Blaschka'. Those raw maker strings are retained per object/source rather than normalized into stronger personal authorship claims.
merge_policy.current_location_guard: Glasgow Museums' mollusc collection is primarily stored at Glasgow Museums Resource Centre with a small number of molluscs on display at Kelvingrove, but this does not establish the present display/store location of any particular Blaschka object.
merge_policy.incorporated_shell_guard: The mollusc collection page says some Glasgow Blaschka mollusc models incorporate real shells. This is not assigned to the 1909.66.js squid unless the object record specifically documents a shell component.

active_backend_recommendation.statement: Among the newly generated catalogue and network files, keep only this 06 master. The 01A–05B backend remains external and unchanged.

consolidation_policy.losslessness: The latest Boston network master, UCL capture, and ISIS audit are embedded as complete parsed JSON objects without field normalization.
consolidation_policy.dependency_collapse: The Boston network master already embeds the Harvard, Ireland, Otago, Canterbury, Cornell finding-aid, and Cornell pilot stages. Those intermediate masters are not embedded again.
consolidation_policy.duplicates: Exact duplicate '(1)' copies are identified by SHA-256 and are not duplicated inside the active modules.
consolidation_policy.conflicts: All uncertainty markers, count conflicts, candidate corrections, and unresolved provenance links from the source masters remain unchanged.
consolidation_policy.external_binary_policy: The ISIS primary-excerpts PDF remains an external image companion. Its hash and size are registered because embedding binary page images in JSON would inflate the backend and would not improve text search.

Haast considered duplicating Hutton's Otago order; Leopold could not reconstruct its details and encouraged a new selection.
The order was placed in 1882; the original order list no longer survives.
Leopold reported substitutions and additional free 'worms and corals' intended for a later catalogue.
The models arrived in October 1883 and were displayed in the Technological Room.
Echinoderms and cuttlefish in spirits were displayed with Blaschka models.
The Technological Room had been dismantled and the models were integrated among zoological displays.
Some models required conservation following the Canterbury earthquake.
The collection was photographed and published as a comprehensive illustrated catalogue.

verified_public_claims: The collection contains approximately 430 models of marine and terrestrial invertebrates.
Models were purchased during the 1870s and 1880s.
The majority were acquired through Henry Augustus Ward.
Ward's 1878 catalogue offered approximately 630 models priced from $0.30 to $6.50.
The models use glass, pigments, glues, animal hide, and wire.
Around 1900 many were removed from their original cardboard trays and wired to white plaster plates.
The permanent exhibition Sea Creatures in Glass opened in May 2014 and rotates approximately 60 models.

direct_records.source: Verzeichniss der Mitglieder der Gesellschaft ISIS in Dresden zu Anfang des Jahres 1880
direct_records.transcription: 14. Blaschka, Rudolf, Glasmodelleur, aufgen. 1880, Kaulbachstr. 11, I.
interpretive_value: Rudolf was institutionally classified by occupation as Glasmodelleur.
The list records his admission in 1880 and gives a Dresden address.
Leopold is not listed on this page; the immediate institutional affiliation is Rudolf's.

direct_records.author: Rudolf Blaschka
direct_records.key_transcription: Redner legt der Gesellschaft unter specieller Erläuterung eine Sammlung von 131 Arten von ihm unter Leitung seines Vaters hergestellter Glasmodelle von Seenacktschnecken vor, welche das Museum der Natural History Society in Boston bestellt und angekauft hat. Ferner zeigt er auch verschiedene Spirituspräparate von meist mediterranen Arten aus der eigenen Sammlung.
evidence_claims: The displayed series comprised 131 species of sea-slug glass models.
Rudolf stated that he made the models under his father's direction.
The Boston Natural History Society museum had commissioned and purchased the series.
The lecture juxtaposed glass models with spirit specimens, mostly Mediterranean, from the Blaschkas' own collection.
interpretive_value: This fixes a workshop hierarchy rather than an undifferentiated father-and-son authorship.
The models functioned inside a comparative zoological apparatus alongside preserved specimens and taxonomic exposition.
The Boston order was publicly cited as part of the scientific authority and material scale of the presentation.

direct_records.speaker: Rudolf Blaschka

key_transcriptions.text: Hierauf hält Herr Glasmodelleur Rudolf Blaschka folgenden, im Auszug wiedergegebenen Vortrag über: ‘Hydroidquallen oder Craspedoten’. (Den Vortrag erläuterten eine Anzahl Blaschka’scher Glasmodelle und viele Alkoholpräparate aus der Sammlung des Vortragenden.)

Diese Mittheilungen über das Meeresleuchten entstammen den Beobachtungen des Vaters des Vortragenden, des Herrn Leopold Blaschka, welche derselbe im Mai 1853 auf einer Reise von Bremen nach Nordamerika angestellt hat. Das Segelschiff, die Bremer Brigg ‘Pauline’, hatte im atlantischen Ocean lange andauernde Windstille. Wirbellose Thiere fanden sich dort in grosser Menge, und Herr L. Blaschka, welcher sich besonders für die Quallen (unter denen sich auch Craspedoten befanden) ihres glasartigen Aussehens wegen interessirte, hatte durch die Freundlichkeit des Kapitäns Henry Coster aus Bremen und des Steuermannes J. de Haan Gelegenheit, diese Beobachtungen anzustellen.
Neu aufgenommene wirkliche Mitglieder: 1. Herr Glasmodelleur Rudolf Blaschka, aufgen. am 29. Jan. 1880.

evidence_claims: The lecture was materially demonstrated with Blaschka glass models and numerous alcohol specimens from Rudolf's collection.
Rudolf explicitly embedded Leopold's May 1853 Bremen-to-North-America voyage in the lecture's evidentiary genealogy.
Leopold's interest in jellyfish was linked to their glass-like appearance.
The record names the ship Pauline, Captain Henry Coster, and mate J. de Haan as conditions enabling observation.
The proceedings separately record Rudolf's admission as a full member on 29 January 1880.
interpretive_value: The Atlantic voyage appears as a site of observation that later entered a public scientific argument.
Model-making was anchored in an intergenerational chain of travel observation, preserved specimens, glass models, and society presentation.
The material resemblance between jellyfish and glass was an actor's category, not merely a later historian's analogy.
The society meeting created a local validation site for knowledge that was simultaneously being commercialised transatlantically.

direct_records.source: Harvard/Corning-derived Blaschka archive OCR corpus, source 017
safe_metadata: 017:419 is on Naturwissenschaftliche Gesellschaft ISIS zu Dresden letterhead, naming its Bibliothek und Archiv and Prof. Dr. Rudolph Zaunick, dated 7 January 1944.
017:422 appears to be a reply from Rudolf Blaschka in Hosterwitz dated 17 January 1944 and addressed to Professor Zaunick.
direct_records.restriction: The current OCR is too corrupt to support a reliable account of the letter's substantive claims. Image-level retranscription is required before asserting what papers, estate materials, or transfers were discussed.
direct_records.confidence: high for metadata; low for body text

first_order_sequence: maintenance of an in-house collection of alcohol or spirit specimens
Rudolf's fabrication of glass models under Leopold's direction
demonstration of models and preserved specimens in the ISIS zoological section
institutional recognition of Rudolf as Glasmodelleur and full member
transatlantic commission and purchase by the Boston Natural History Society

research_assessment.strongest_contribution: The ISIS materials close the gap between workshop production and public zoological knowledge. They show the same objects moving through observation, preservation, fabrication, demonstration, classification, and purchase.
research_assessment.relevance_to_transport_argument: The strongest transport evidence here concerns the movement that generated knowledge: Leopold's 1853 Atlantic voyage became an inherited evidentiary resource in Rudolf's 1880 lecture. The source does not yet document the packing or damage of finished models in transit.
research_assessment.relevance_to_design_argument: Glass models were designed and evaluated within a mixed apparatus of wet specimens, taxonomic distinctions, developmental sequences, and institutional orders. The material's glass-like relation to marine animals was explicitly articulated by Rudolf through Leopold's observations.
limits: The selected run concentrates on 1880 and the 1944 correspondence node, not every ISIS volume from 1846 to 1940.
No reliable packing, repair, breakage, adhesive, or crate evidence was found in these selected ISIS records.
The 1944 letter bodies require fresh transcription from scans.
The Boston institution is named in the source as the Natural History Society; its precise corporate naming should follow the original wording when quoted.

content.title: Blaschka Great North Museum: Hancock / Natural History Society of Northumbria: historic marine-invertebrate collection, c.50 sea-anemone subset candidate, 2008 National Glass Centre loan, 2013 jellyfish X-ray, and 2025 Imitating Life exhibition
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka glass marine-invertebrate models associated with the Natural History Society of Northumbria (NHSN), the historic Hancock Museum, and the present Great North Museum: Hancock in Newcastle upon Tyne. The module preserves the current institutional/ownership complexity: the nineteenth-century museum was built by NHSN for its natural-history collections; the present museum is managed by North East Museums on behalf of Newcastle University; NHSN still owns the building and many collections. A 2008–2009 NHSN report describes the Society's collection of Blaschka glass sea anemones as having been displayed at the National Glass Centre, while the Great North Museum's official 2025 Imitating Life exhibition describes the museum's broader collection of Blaschka glass marine invertebrate models. A secondary 2015 collection-visit account reports approximately 50 sea-anemone models, but because the collection also includes at least a Blaschka jellyfish used in 2013 X-ray imaging, c.50 is retained only as a sea-anemone-subset candidate and never promoted to an exact total collection count. No purchase invoice, donor record, accession sequence, exact acquisition year, local object identifier, or complete object list was recovered in this pass.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 44 after a large-museum screen. UW–Madison and University of Galway were excluded because they are already deeply captured elsewhere; Leiden, Stockholm, Copenhagen, Santiago, Rio and Montevideo remained below promotion threshold; Liverpool and Carnegie Museum of Natural History yielded physical-object/loan evidence but not enough collection-level closure. Great North Museum: Hancock qualifies because its own official 2025 exhibition explicitly used the museum's Blaschka collection, a Newcastle University research record documents technical X-ray imaging of a Blaschka jellyfish, and the collection has a traceable NHSN/Hancock institutional custody context. The acquisition transaction remains a deliberate open field rather than being reconstructed from comparative-location lists.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Great North Museum: Hancock / Hancock Museum / Natural History Society of Northumbria Blaschka institutional node was found in the active consolidated 06 v3 backend through module 40 or in standalone modules 41–43.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: The NMW comparative spreadsheet lists 'Hancock Museum, Newcastle, U.K.' under Model Locations for numerous Blaschka types. Those rows are external comparative occurrence candidates only. NMW accession numbers, condition notes, labels, repairs and local metadata must never be transferred to Newcastle.
merge_policy.institutional_identity_guard: The nineteenth-century New Museum of Natural History opened in 1884 and was later known as the Hancock Museum; the redeveloped Great North Museum: Hancock opened in 2009. Historical and current names are retained by date.
merge_policy.ownership_management_guard: Current institutional sources state that Great North Museum: Hancock is managed by North East Museums on behalf of Newcastle University, while NHSN owns the building and many of the collections. A 2008–2009 NHSN report calls the Blaschka glass sea-anemone material 'The Society's collection'. This supports a strong NHSN ownership/custody association, but exact present legal title for every Blaschka object should be verified from the collections register.
merge_policy.2008_pdf_access_guard: The NHSN 2008–2009 Transactions PDF was discoverable through indexed text, but the runtime could not open the PDF itself because the host returned an anti-bot verification page. Its Blaschka statement is therefore retained with an explicit verification flag and should be checked against the original PDF/page 12 before diplomatic quotation.
merge_policy.fifty_count_guard: A secondary 2015 collection-visit account reports 50 models of sea anemones. This is not an official current inventory count. Because official/research sources also document broader marine-invertebrate material including a jellyfish, 50 is encoded only as an approximate sea-anemone-subset candidate, not as total Blaschka holdings.
merge_policy.whole_collection_count_guard: The exact historical acquisition count, exact 2025 exhibition count and exact 2026 survival count remain null. No synthetic total is created by combining the c.50 sea-anemone subset with separately documented non-anemone objects.
merge_policy.acquisition_guard: No purchase, gift, dealer, invoice, order letter or accession-book entry was recovered. The models are therefore not assigned to Ward, Frič, a direct Dresden order, Albany Hancock, John Hancock or another purchaser without evidence.
merge_policy.late_nineteenth_century_guard: The secondary 2015 account describes the sea-anemone models as late nineteenth century. This is used only as a broad object-date context and not as an acquisition date.
merge_policy.Albany_Hancock_guard: Albany Hancock's importance to Newcastle marine-invertebrate zoology and the survival of his nudibranch watercolours provide local scientific context. No claim is made that he personally purchased, selected or commissioned the Blaschka models.
merge_policy.2013_xray_guard: Newcastle University records an X-ray image of a Blaschka glass jellyfish shown at the Hancock Museum in 2013 and states that imaging in different forms of light aimed to recover aspects of the Blaschkas' construction technique. The recovered page does not provide a local object/accession number, species identification, X-ray file identifier, or confirmation that the image was newly made in 2013.
merge_policy.jellyfish_scope_guard: The 2013 jellyfish evidence prevents treating the collection as exclusively sea anemones. It does not establish how many non-anemone Blaschka models are present.
merge_policy.2008_loan_guard: Indexed NHSN text states that the Society's glass sea-anemone collection was displayed at the National Glass Centre in Sunderland in 2008. The exact number loaned, checklist, dates of each object, and conservation condition are unresolved.
merge_policy.2025_exhibition_guard: The official Imitating Life page states that the exhibition featured the museum's collection of Blaschka glass marine invertebrate models and ran until 21 September 2025. It does not publish a complete object checklist or exact count.
merge_policy.current_2026_display_guard: Imitating Life is explicitly marked as a historic/ended exhibition. No current 2026 Blaschka display page was recovered, so the present on-display count is null rather than projected from 2025.
merge_policy.resource_centre_guard: Newcastle University states that reserve natural-science collections not on public display are housed at the Great North Museum Resource Centre at Discovery Museum. No claim is made that any specific Blaschka model is currently stored there until an object-location record is recovered.
merge_policy.object_identifier_guard: No Newcastle local accession, catalogue, loan, case, X-ray, conservation or digital-asset identifier is invented.
merge_policy.commercial_catalogue_crosswalk_guard: No Blaschka/Ward catalogue number is assigned to a Newcastle object solely from taxon or comparative Model Locations.

content.title: Blaschka Indian Museum Calcutta/Kolkata: catalogue-listed purchaser, 1883 Lieferungs-Buch shipment, Superintendent orders, Hamburg route, 1894 Invertebrate Gallery glass-model display, and current ZSI survival gap
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass-model relationship with the Indian Museum, Calcutta (now Kolkata). The module triangulates four independent evidence layers: Leopold Blaschka’s 1878 and 1885 catalogue-preface customer lists naming the Indian Museum in Calcutta; Corning/Rakow archive metadata for the 1883–1893 Lieferungs-Buch explicitly identifying 1883 shipments to the Indian Museum and stating that the book records the specific model numbers sent; a circa-1880–1885 business-correspondence notebook explicitly containing orders from the Superintendent of the Indian Museum, Calcutta, plus a later workshop statement that former Calcutta model shipments normally went via Hamburg either directly or through London; and the Indian Museum’s own 1894 guide, which documents extensive glass-model teaching displays in named cases and taxa throughout the Invertebrate Gallery. The 1894 guide does not print the Blaschka name, so object-level maker attribution remains guarded even though collection-level identification is exceptionally strong. Current Zoological Survey of India documentation confirms continuity of an Invertebrate Gallery in the Indian Museum complex, now holding 548 models/exhibits in 16 showcases, but no current Blaschka-specific object record or survival count was recovered.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected immediately after Jeypore/Jaipur. Module 37 revealed a workshop-side retrospective statement that previous model shipments to Calcutta had used Hamburg, independently upgrading Calcutta from a printed customer-list node to a proven shipment destination. A renewed archive audit then located Corning catalogue metadata for the Lieferungs-Buch identifying an 1883 shipment specifically to the Indian Museum in Calcutta, and a separate business-correspondence notebook containing orders from its Superintendent. The Indian Museum’s 1894 official Invertebrate Gallery guide supplies the missing receiving/display layer, with numerous glass-model taxa and case locations. No standalone Calcutta institutional module existed in the active backend through module 37.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Indian Museum Calcutta/Kolkata Blaschka institutional module was found in the active consolidated backend through module 31 or in standalone modules 32–37.
merge_policy.institution_identity_guard: The historical phrase 'Indian Museum in Calcutta' is normalized to the Indian Museum, Kolkata, while preserving Calcutta/Kolkata as chronological place-name layers. Current zoological galleries in the Indian Museum complex are maintained by the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), whose institutional genesis lies in the Zoological Section of the Indian Museum.
merge_policy.catalogue_customer_guard: Corning states that the prefaces to Blaschka catalogues published in 1878 and 1885 list the Indian Museum in Calcutta among institutions that purchased models. This proves purchaser/client status by 1878 but does not identify every order date, price, quantity or species.
merge_policy.lieferungsbuch_guard: The Corning/Rakow catalogue record for the Lieferungs-Buch (1883–1893) states that it is a record of filled orders with the specific numbers of models sent and explicitly includes 1883 shipments to the Indian Museum in Calcutta. The current research pass has not recovered a reliable diplomatic transcription of the Calcutta model-number row(s), so exact numbers and count remain pending rather than reconstructed from noisy OCR.
merge_policy.possible_may27_entry_guard: PaddleOCR of one ledger/calendar-like page has a May heading and a line resembling '27 ... Indian Museum in Calcutta ...', but surrounding numbers and words are too corrupt to determine date, amount, model count or catalogue numbers confidently. This is retained only as an OCR target for image-level verification and is not promoted into the transaction timeline as a closed date.
merge_policy.business_drafts_guard: Corning catalogue metadata for a circa-1880–1885 notebook of business-letter drafts explicitly says it includes orders from the Superintendent of the Indian Museum, Calcutta. This proves direct order correspondence at institutional level but does not yet supply the Superintendent’s name, exact dates or complete order contents in this module.
merge_policy.workshop_route_guard: In later correspondence concerning Jeypore, Blaschka says that when he previously sent models to Calcutta he normally forwarded them via Hamburg, with transshipment either by direct Hamburg steamer or via London. This proves prior workshop-to-Calcutta shipping practice. Taken alone, the statement does not identify the recipient; combined with the independent Lieferungs-Buch and customer-list evidence, the Indian Museum is the securely documented institutional Calcutta purchaser.
merge_policy.1883_vs_1878_guard: The Indian Museum was already listed as a purchaser in the 1878 catalogue preface, while the Lieferungs-Buch specifically records an 1883 shipment. These are treated as evidence of at least two chronological purchase/shipment layers or continuing customer status, not automatically as one order repeated in later documentation.
merge_policy.1894_maker_name_guard: The 1894 Indian Museum guide repeatedly documents 'glass models', 'enlarged glass-models', 'life-sized models' and 'the usual glass models', including many taxa known from the Blaschka catalogue, but it does not name Blaschka or Dresden. The module therefore treats the gallery-level identification as high-confidence triangulated attribution rather than direct maker inscription within the 1894 text.
merge_policy.1894_count_guard: No total number of Blaschka models is printed in the 1894 guide. Phrases such as 'numerous examples', 'series of models', 'usual glass models' and 'some glass models' are qualitative and are not converted into counts.
merge_policy.case_number_guard: Case 3, Case 7, Case 47, Cases 170–171 and other numbers in the 1894 guide are gallery/display-case locations, not accession numbers or Blaschka catalogue numbers.
merge_policy.life_size_guard: The statement that different zooids are lettered on 'life-sized models in Case 3' documents pedagogical model use but does not establish the maker or exact number of those models independently of the broader triangulation.
merge_policy.argonauta_guard: The 1894 guide refers to a 'model of Argonauta' and later to life-size cephalopod models, but the cited passage does not explicitly call the Argonauta object glass. It is therefore retained as a model/display anchor, not automatically counted as a glass-model anchor.
merge_policy.catalogue_crosswalk_guard: External Blaschka catalogue numbers derived from Cornell, Berlin or other authenticated collections are retained as taxon-level candidate mappings only. No catalogue number is assigned to an Indian Museum physical object without a Calcutta delivery-book row, label, accession register or object file.
merge_policy.carmarina_guard: The Indian Museum guide says only 'series of models of Carmarina hastata'. External Blaschka records distinguish multiple Carmarina hastata catalogue types, so the candidate set is retained without selecting one number.
merge_policy.halistemma_guard: The 1894 guide names Halistemma only at genus level in its glass-model list. The external catalogue match Halistemma punctatum no. 207 is therefore a possible type candidate, not an object-level identification.
merge_policy.apolemia_guard: The 1894 guide names Apolemia only at genus level. Catalogue no. 201 corresponds to Apolemia uvaria in an authenticated Cornell record, but the Indian Museum model is not silently normalized to that species.
merge_policy.current_548_guard: ZSI currently reports 548 'models/Exhibits' in 16 showcases in the Invertebrate Gallery. This is a gallery-wide total across many phyla and object/material types; it is not a Blaschka count.
merge_policy.current_survival_guard: No current Indian Museum or ZSI object record recovered in this pass explicitly identifies a surviving Blaschka model. Historical presence is not projected forward into a 2026 survival figure.
merge_policy.gallery_continuity_guard: The continued existence of an Invertebrate Gallery in the same institutional complex demonstrates institutional and display-function continuity but not continuous survival, continuous display or unchanged location of any individual nineteenth-century glass model.
merge_policy.zsi_genesis_guard: ZSI states that it grew from the Zoological Section of the Indian Museum, established in 1875. This institutional genealogy supports custodial investigation but does not by itself prove formal transfer of every nineteenth-century model into a present ZSI inventory.
merge_policy.historical_taxonomy_guard: Taxon names and spellings are preserved at the source layer. Modern synonyms are not substituted silently.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No modern local object identifiers, accession numbers, shipping marks or model counts are invented.

summary.key_result: Calcutta is now a high-confidence end-to-end institutional node rather than a customer-list footnote. The Indian Museum is named as a Blaschka purchaser in 1878 and 1885, Corning’s Lieferungs-Buch catalogue record explicitly identifies an 1883 shipment to the Museum and says the book records the exact model numbers sent, and a separate correspondence notebook contains orders from the Museum Superintendent. Workshop correspondence independently preserves the normal Hamburg/direct-or-London freight route used for earlier Calcutta shipments. content.title: Blaschka Jeypore Museum / Albert Hall Jaipur: 1886–1887 Hendley order, Damon mediation, 640-mark model value, LB 285–286 Trieste–Bombay shipment, numbered 1895 Natural History display, tropical teaching rationale and present survival gap
content.scope: Deep institutional and transaction capture of the Blaschka invertebrate glass-model collection ordered for the Jeypore Museum in Rajputana in 1886–1887 and documented in Thomas Holbein Hendley’s 1895 Handbook to the Jeypore Museum. The module reconstructs the order from Blaschka-side correspondence preserved in the Corning/Rakow notebook OCR, including Hendley’s amended order, Robert Damon’s financial/intermediary role, manufacture from new because the workshop had no stock, price and prepayment evidence, route negotiation between Hamburg/London and Trieste, shipment as packages LB 285–286 by rail to Trieste and Austro-Hungarian Lloyd to Bombay, forwarding through Grindlay & Groom, and final balance settlement. It then connects that commercial/transport chain to the museum’s 1895 Natural History and Educational display, where Hendley explicitly identifies the Blaschka series, explains its pedagogical and tropical-material advantages, and lists numerous local museum numbers. Current public sources confirm institutional continuity as the Albert Hall / Government Central Museum but do not yet establish which Blaschka objects survive, their present local identifiers, condition, or display status after the 2020 flood and subsequent collection-wide conservation/documentation programme.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after Rostock and after screening weaker or incomplete candidates including Leipzig, Manchester/Leicester, Utrecht and Calcutta. Jeypore is unusually strong because both sides of the historical lifecycle are documented: workshop correspondence preserves ordering, finance and international freight decisions, while Hendley’s 1895 museum handbook proves arrival, installation, pedagogical use and local numbering. The Jeypore correspondence also independently upgrades Calcutta from a catalogue-listed customer to a workshop-confirmed previous Indian shipping destination, making the node strategically important for the wider imperial circulation network.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Jeypore Museum / Albert Hall Museum Blaschka institutional module was found in the active consolidated backend through module 31 or in standalone modules 32–36.
merge_policy.institution_identity_guard: The nineteenth-century Jeypore Museum collections were transferred at the close of 1886 to the Albert Hall and formally inaugurated there on 21 February 1887. The present Albert Hall Museum / Government Central Museum in Jaipur is treated as the institutional successor/custodial continuity, without assuming that every nineteenth-century object remains there.
merge_policy.spelling_guard: Historical sources use Jeypore; current usage is Jaipur. Both are retained as chronological name layers.
merge_policy.Hendley_name_guard: Corning OCR variably renders the Honorary Secretary’s surname as Handley, Hraugley, Handling or similar. Thomas Holbein Hendley is normalized as the person because the 1895 museum handbook identifies him as Honorary Secretary and the historical context matches. Raw OCR variants remain evidence-quality warnings.
merge_policy.order_date_guard: The workshop letter explicitly refers to Hendley’s postcard of 19 October and letter/amended order of 8 November; a reproduced image independently dates the acknowledgment to 12 December 1886. Manufacture then begins around the turn of 1886–1887. Exact date of the first order and every subsequent workshop letter should be checked against the original notebook images before diplomatic transcription.
merge_policy.manufacture_guard: The workshop states that it had nothing in stock and would make the Jeypore models for the order. This supports made-to-order production at collection level but does not prove every object in Hendley’s later 1895 Blaschka display belonged to only one invoice or manufacture batch.
merge_policy.640_marks_guard: A workshop-side letter states that the models in the Jeypore order amounted to 640 Marks and estimates that two large cases would bring the total above 700 Marks. The 640 figure is treated as model value at that stage, not a final all-inclusive invoice total.
merge_policy.final_total_guard: Later OCR records a prepayment of about 698 Marks and a final Jeypore balance of 61.50 Marks, yielding an arithmetic candidate of 759.50 Marks. The dispatch-page OCR of the invoice total is corrupt and appears as '260' or an incomplete/incorrect reading. 759.50 Marks is therefore stored as a reconstructed accounting candidate, not as a closed invoice transcription.
merge_policy.Damon_guard: Robert Damon of Weymouth is documented as the financial/commercial intermediary with whom Blaschka arranged the order and payments. He is not automatically treated as the museum’s legal vendor, sole agent, or physical carrier without further invoice evidence.
merge_policy.package_guard: LB 285 and LB 286 are shipping/package marks recorded in the workshop correspondence. They are not museum accession numbers or Blaschka catalogue/model numbers.
merge_policy.route_guard: The correspondence documents route deliberation and subsequent dispatch by rail to Trieste, delivery to the Austro-Hungarian Lloyd, direct sea shipment to Bombay, and forwarding via Grindlay & Groom to Jeypore. The precise ships, sailing dates, customs entries and inland rail legs remain open archive targets.
merge_policy.Calcutta_route_guard: Blaschka says that earlier models sent to Calcutta normally went via Hamburg, by direct Hamburg steamer or via London. This proves a prior Calcutta shipping practice at workshop level but does not by itself identify the exact Calcutta institution, quantities or surviving objects.
merge_policy.1895_number_guard: The numbers printed beside Blaschka examples in Hendley’s 1895 Handbook are Jeypore Museum display/catalogue identifiers embedded in the museum’s Natural History educational sequence. They are not Blaschka/Ward/Frič catalogue numbers.
merge_policy.one_number_one_model_guard: Several Hendley entries explicitly contain two forms, living/dissected states, multiple developmental stages or a group. A local number or number range therefore cannot automatically be converted into a count of individual physical glass components.
merge_policy.jellyfish_range_guard: Hendley assigns Nos. 1116–1138 to glass jellyfish and a sea-anemone group in Case 110. The inclusive range contains 23 local catalogue numbers, but this is not automatically a count of 23 physical models because grouping and cataloguing practice require verification.
merge_policy.tropical_material_guard: Hendley’s comparison of glass models with spirit preparations and wax is treated as the museum’s explicit pedagogical/material rationale. It demonstrates the value assigned to colour retention and tropical display suitability; it is not generalized to every Blaschka purchaser.
merge_policy.current_survival_guard: No current Albert Hall public object record recovered in this pass explicitly identifies a Blaschka model. Nineteenth-century catalogue presence is therefore not projected forward into a 2026 survival count.
merge_policy.current_collection_category_guard: Current Albert Hall public descriptions emphasize art, craft, archaeology and related categories. Their silence about the Blaschka Natural History teaching series is not evidence that the models were destroyed, deaccessioned or transferred.
merge_policy.2020_flood_guard: Government of India sources state that the Albert Hall collection and documentation suffered heavy damage during the August 2020 Jaipur flood and that a 20,000-object documentation/conservation/verification programme followed. No source recovered here identifies Blaschka objects among the damaged or treated material, so flood exposure and present condition remain unresolved.
merge_policy.post_flood_numbers_guard: Collection-wide figures for digitization, documentation and conservation after the flood must not be read as Blaschka-specific counts.
merge_policy.historical_taxonomy_guard: Taxon names and spellings in the 1895 Handbook are preserved as historical museum terminology. Modern synonymy is not silently substituted.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No new object identifiers are invented. Historical Jeypore numbers and shipping package marks remain in separate namespaces.

summary.key_result: Jeypore/Jaipur is a rare end-to-end imperial museum transaction node. The Blaschka workshop records the museum’s amended order, made-to-order manufacture, 640-Mark model value, Damon-mediated payment, competing India freight routes, two marked packages and the final Trieste–Bombay forwarding chain. Hendley’s 1895 handbook then proves institutional arrival and embeds the models in a numbered Natural History curriculum. Its most distinctive historical claim is material and environmental: glass preserved visible colour and remained suitable for tropical exhibition where spirit specimens and wax were judged deficient. The largest unresolved layer is the present fate of the numbered nineteenth-century series, especially after later collection reconfiguration and the 2020 flood.

content.title: Blaschka Leeds City Museum: 1865 Frič sale, 64 European Actineae, LEEDM.C.1865.23, 27 extant in 1995, wartime damage and restoration
content.scope: Deep capture of the early Blaschka sea-anemone collection acquired by the Leeds Philosophical and Literary Society in the 1865/66 session and now associated with Leeds City Museum. The module separates the historical acquisition wording attributing 64 European Actineae models to 'Wenzel Fric, of Prague' from later identification of Václav Frič as dealer and Leopold Blaschka as workshop maker; records the group catalogue identifier LEEDM.C.1865.23; preserves the 1995 survival count of 27 without projecting it to 2026; reconstructs the 1921 municipal transfer, 1941 bombing context, 1959 salvage/restoration and 1991-1995 Corning/curatorial identification history; and quarantines NMW comparative-location rows as candidate Leeds early-set types rather than local inventory records.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after Oxford because Reiling's Frič research identifies the Leeds 1865 transaction as the earliest known sale of Blaschka glass models by Václav Frič, while a Leeds curatorial article independently preserves the local 1865/66 acquisition record, a stable group identifier, a historical quantity of 64, a 1995 extant count of 27, wartime and restoration history, and a directly illustrated Aiptasia Couchii model. This yields a stronger dealer-to-institution transaction chain than Oxford.

merge_policy.group_identifier_guard: LEEDM.C.1865.23 is treated as the catalogue/accession identifier for the 64-model acquisition group. No synthetic child identifiers such as LEEDM.C.1865.23.1–64 are created.
merge_policy.historic_attribution_guard: The 1865/66 acquisition list attributes the 64 models to 'Wenzel Fric, of Prague'. Modern research reported in 1991/1995 identified this as Václav Frič, natural-history dealer, and the models as products of Leopold Blaschka's workshop. Raw historical attribution and modern maker/dealer interpretation are retained as separate layers.
merge_policy.first_known_sale_guard: Reiling 2002 characterizes the 1865 Leeds transaction as the first known sale of Blaschka glass models by Frič. This is a published historiographic state-of-knowledge claim, not proof that no earlier Frič transaction will ever be found.
merge_policy.maker_guard: The 1865 group is attributed to Leopold Blaschka / the early Blaschka workshop. Rudolf is not silently added as co-maker because the acquisition predates his later formal role in the business.
merge_policy.date_guard: The local annual report covers the 1865/66 session and the group identifier contains 1865; Reiling dates the sale to 1865. The exact day/month of purchase and delivery remain unresolved.
merge_policy.64_count_guard: The historical acquisition quantity is 64 European Actineae models. This is retained as an acquisition-unit count and is not silently converted into a claim about current physical components.
merge_policy.27_count_guard: Adrian Norris reported 27 models still extant in 1995, some damaged. This is a 1995 survival count only; no 2026 current survival total is inferred.
merge_policy.loss_arithmetic_guard: 64 minus 27 equals 37 arithmetically, but 37 is not treated as a documented number destroyed by the 1941 bombing. Norris states that time and bomb damage took a toll without itemizing the fate of every absent model.
merge_policy.bomb_damage_guard: The 1941 bombing of Philosophical Hall is independently documented and the Leeds curatorial article connects bomb damage to the collection. No individual model is assigned a bomb-loss fate without an object-level record.
merge_policy.restoration_guard: John Armitage salvaged and performed some restoration on the models in 1959. No treatment count, materials, techniques or individual object assignments are invented.
merge_policy.photo_anchor_guard: Aiptasia Couchii is directly illustrated and captioned in Norris 1995 as a Leopold Blaschka glass sea-anemone of c.1865. No early-set glass numeral, later catalogue number or individual Leeds accession is assigned without direct evidence.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: NMW Chris Meechan spreadsheet rows listing 'Leeds City Museum, U.K. (1865)' are retained only as comparative-location candidates. They are not Leeds accession records and do not prove current survival.
merge_policy.Cardiff_field_guard: NMW accession numbers, Cardiff condition fields and Cardiff mounting notes describe Cardiff physical objects and are not transferred to Leeds candidates.
merge_policy.Foraminifera_guard: The 1865/66 Leeds report also mentions enlarged plaster Foraminifera models obtained from Prague. These are contextual co-procurement evidence only and are not included in the 64 glass Actineae or attributed to Blaschka without further evidence.
merge_policy.current_location_guard: Leeds Museums & Galleries currently manages major natural-science holdings across Leeds City Museum and Leeds Discovery Centre, but no source recovered here identifies the present display/store location of each surviving Blaschka model.

content.title: Blaschka Milwaukee Public Museum: 70 Ward-supplied invertebrate models, 1883–1884 acquisition hypothesis, Glaucilla briareus anchor, Jass 1987 catalogue study, archival reopening and 2027 museum move
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Milwaukee Public Museum (MPM) Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass-model collection. The module preserves the official institutional statement that MPM purchased 70 invertebrate glass models offered through Ward's Natural Science Establishment; separates that verified transaction layer from a secondary historical account of a $12,000 public-subscription purchase of a large Ward natural-history collection in late 1883 for display in May 1884; records a recently published MPM object/media anchor, Glaucilla briareus; connects that taxon cautiously to Blaschka catalogue no. 446 through an independent Corning catalogue/drawing record; registers Joan P. Jass's 1987 MPM-specific comparison against Ward's 1888 catalogue as the strongest known but unrecovered item-list source; and captures 2024 comparative archive research plus the ongoing 2026 collections move toward the Nature & Culture Museum of Wisconsin.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after Redpath/McGill because it extends the North American Ward-distribution network with a larger institutional purchase and a concrete historical count of 70. Milwaukee also provides an unusually useful combination of museum-opening acquisition context, an MPM-specific Ward catalogue study by curator Joan P. Jass, a recent named object image, a 2024 museum-and-archives research visit by the UW–Madison Blaschka project, and an active 2026–2027 collections migration.

merge_policy.official_70_count_guard: The figure 70 is the number of Blaschka invertebrate glass models MPM states that it purchased. It is a historical acquisition count, not a current survival, display, component, or accession-row count.
merge_policy.Ward_route_guard: MPM explicitly states that the 70 models were offered for sale through Ward's Natural Science Establishment, Inc. The module therefore treats dealer mediation as verified, while leaving exact invoice date, price, shipment and item list unresolved.
merge_policy.1883_1884_Ward_collection_guard: A secondary institutional/business history states that MPM officials saw a large Ward natural-history collection in late 1883, raised $12,000 by public subscription to buy it, and displayed it in May 1884. No source recovered in this pass explicitly states that the 70 Blaschka models were included in that $12,000 acquisition. The relationship is therefore encoded as a high-value acquisition hypothesis, not as a closed provenance fact.
merge_policy.12000_price_guard: $12,000 applies to the large Ward natural-history collection described in the secondary history. It is not assigned as the price of the 70 Blaschka models.
merge_policy.museum_opening_guard: MPM opened to the public on 24 May 1884. The Ward collection reportedly went on display in May 1884, but the module does not assert that the 70 Blaschka models were necessarily on public display at opening without a direct checklist or annual-report entry.
merge_policy.public_catalog_NA_guard: The current MPM 'Blaschka Glass Works' collection-highlight page displays 'Catalog Number: N/A'. This is a property of the public highlight record and is not interpreted as proof that all 70 physical models lack internal MPM catalogue/accession numbers.
merge_policy.Glaucilla_anchor_guard: MPM's 2023–2024 annual report identifies a photographed Blaschka glass figurine as Glaucilla briareus. This establishes a recently recognized physical/media anchor but supplies no visible local object number in the recovered public text.
merge_policy.Glaucilla_446_guard: A Corning Blaschka design-drawing catalogue record independently maps 'Glaucilla briareus, Reinhardt' to Blaschka catalogue no. 446. Because no MPM label, accession record, Jass list, or photograph bearing 446 was recovered, the Milwaukee object-to-446 mapping remains a strong candidate rather than a verified local crosswalk.
merge_policy.taxonomic_normalization_guard: The historical/display name Glaucilla briareus is preserved as MPM wording. Modern taxonomic literature has treated the name inconsistently, including as a nomen dubium; no modern synonym is substituted into the historical object identity.
merge_policy.Jass_1987_guard: The bibliographic record for Joan P. Jass, 'Milwaukee Public Museum Blaschka glass models, per Ward's "Catalogue..." of 1888,' demonstrates that an MPM-specific catalogue concordance was published. The full article/table was not recovered in this pass, so its item rows, counts and identifications are not reconstructed from title alone.

content.title: Blaschka Musée Zoologique de Strasbourg: 1890 Goette order, 58/53 count conflict, numbered Sepia, last European commission, conservation and complete 2025 display
content.scope: Deep capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass-model collection at the Musée Zoologique de Strasbourg. The module separates the 1890 order/receipt unit ('58 models or series'), later statements about survival and display, individual physical objects and developmental series, public image records, the fully numbered Sepia officinalis anatomical model MZS Mod65, collection-wide diagnosis and restoration campaigns, environmental/display controls, and the collection's pedagogical role in anatomy and embryology.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after duplicate audit showed that University of Vienna had already been deeply captured. Strasbourg is a high-yield uncaptured node: a dated 1890 institutional order by Alexander Goette, a documentary total of 58 models or series, a current official claim that all 58 are displayed together, an older official 53-of-58 survival statement, a locally numbered and technically studied Sepia model, a collection-wide 2022 condition diagnosis, a 2023-2025 restoration/display funding chain, and a 48-file public photographic register.

merge_policy.count_ontology_guard: The 1890 University source describes '58 models or series of models', some series containing up to six development stages. The current museum uses the simpler wording '58 models'. Neither figure is automatically a count of individual physical glass components.
merge_policy.53_58_conflict_guard: A 2017 University of Strasbourg article states that 53 of the 58 ordered models remained. Current 2025-2026 official museum pages state that all 58 models are presented in their entirety. The module preserves both claims and does not convert the 2017 wording into five documented losses, nor the current wording into proof of uninterrupted survival.
merge_policy.restoration_reconstruction_guard: The Sepia officinalis model MZS Mod65 was encountered as forty loose fragments and restored to formal unity. Fragments are not counted as forty museum objects.
merge_policy.last_european_order_guard: The 'last European commission/order' characterization is supported by the INP conservation thesis and a 2022 Musées de Strasbourg interview. It is retained as a published expert/institutional characterization, not independently reconstructed from the complete Blaschka order book in this module.
merge_policy.inventory_guard: Only one local museum inventory number, MZS Mod65, is securely recovered. Dimensions or taxa published in museum figures without local identifiers are retained as identified physical/display records but are not assigned synthetic numbers.
merge_policy.commons_guard: The Wikimedia Commons category contains 48 files, including multiple views, grouped objects and six photographs of a developmental series. Forty-eight media files are not treated as forty-eight physical objects.
merge_policy.media_taxon_guard: Scientific names in public image titles are retained as media-level identifications. Common-name-only files such as 'Calmar commun', 'Poulpe commun' and 'Limace arborescente' are not silently normalized to a species.
merge_policy.catalogue_crosswalk_guard: Comparative catalogue numbers appearing in other institutional inventories, including the Cardiff concordance, are not assigned to Strasbourg models unless a Strasbourg label, order list, catalogue, or museum record establishes the link.
merge_policy.current_display_guard: Current official wording that 58 models are shown 'in their entirety' is treated as a display statement. It does not by itself resolve whether a documentary 'model/series' contains multiple separately mounted stages.
merge_policy.conservation_scope_guard: Collection-wide diagnosis in September 2022 and a later restoration campaign are documented. Detailed treatment status for each of the 58 documentary units is not public and is therefore not inferred.
