content.title: Blaschka Museo Nacional de México → Museo Nacional de Historia Natural / El Chopo → UNAM Instituto de Biología + MHNCA: 1885 catalogue contact, 1895 physical display, institutional fission, and surviving glass-animal anchors
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Mexico City national-museum Blaschka node. The module separates four evidential layers: (1) a workshop-side catalogue-mailing list, in a July 1885 sequence, containing the OCR string 'Musical nacional Mexico', interpreted cautiously as Museo Nacional Mexico; (2) Frank Collins Baker's 1895 published eyewitness description of a 'very good collection of glass models, by Blaschka' in the national museum's Mollusca/lower-invertebrate hall, including sea-cucumbers and sea-anemones; (3) the institutional redistribution of the Museo Nacional's natural-history collections into the Museo Nacional de Historia Natural at El Chopo, then through the Dirección de Estudios Biológicos and UNAM's Instituto de Biología; and (4) present or recent successor evidence: the Instituto de Biología publicly identifies a Colección de Animales de Cristal Blaschka, while the current Museo de Historia Natural y Cultura Ambiental lists a historical glass argonaut and glass jellyfish from the former Chopo museum, and a UNAM cultural-history article identifies those two as Argonauta argo and Pelagia noctiluca within the Blaschka tradition. No original purchase invoice, exact historical quantity, local accession number, or item-level transfer chain has yet been recovered.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 42 after a duplicate audit of the active 06 v3 backend showed no Mexico / Museo Nacional / UNAM / Chopo standalone Blaschka node. Mexico City meets the project's large-institution threshold because physical Blaschka display is independently documented by 1895 and multiple successor institutions still preserve Blaschka or Blaschka-linked glass-animal material. The case also introduces a new Latin American national-museum succession problem rather than another catalogue-contact-only node.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Mexico City / Museo Nacional de México / Museo Nacional de Historia Natural / UNAM Instituto de Biología / MHNCA Blaschka module was found in the active 06 v3 backend through module 40. Module 41 Auckland is separate and remains external to that consolidated v3 master.
merge_policy.workshop_raw_OCR_guard: The Rakow notebook OCR reads 'Musical nacional Mexico'. The normalized interpretation 'Museo Nacional Mexico' is contextually strong because it appears in a global institutional catalogue-mailing list, but the raw OCR is preserved and the original notebook image remains the authority.
merge_policy.catalogue_contact_not_order_guard: The workshop list proves catalogue/contact activity only. It does not prove a purchase, shipment, payment, model quantity, catalogue selection, or acquisition date.
merge_policy.catalogue_date_guard: Adjacent catalogue-mailing pages carry July date markers (14, 15, 16, 20, 21 July), and a nearby Damon letter belongs to the June 1885 new-catalogue context. Mexico is therefore placed in a July 1885 mailing sequence. No exact day is assigned to the Mexico row because the OCR does not preserve a secure row-to-date alignment.
merge_policy.1885_to_1895_guard: Workshop catalogue contact in 1885 and Baker's physical display evidence published in 1895 create a bounded contact-to-presence sequence, but they do not prove that the displayed collection resulted from that particular catalogue mailing or that acquisition occurred in 1885.
merge_policy.1895_display_guard: Baker's 1895 publication explicitly reports a collection of Blaschka glass models in a museum case and names sea-cucumbers and sea-anemones among its contents. This establishes physical presence and public display by the time of publication, but gives neither quantity, accession numbers, prices nor acquisition route.
merge_policy.1895_institution_name_guard: The module uses 'Museo Nacional de México / national museum natural-history galleries' for the 1895 display layer. It does not retroactively call that 1895 gallery the later formal Museo Nacional de Historia Natural at El Chopo.
merge_policy.1909_split_guard: Mexican institutional histories state that the Museo Nacional was reorganized in 1909 and the natural-history collections were separated into the new Museo Nacional de Historia Natural. This supports a collection-level succession route, not an item-level Blaschka transfer unless a register is recovered.
merge_policy.1913_chopo_guard: The Museo Nacional de Historia Natural opened at the Palacio de Cristal / El Chopo in December 1913. No surviving 1913 Blaschka packing list or transfer schedule has yet been recovered.
merge_policy.1915_DEB_guard: UNAM collection histories state that in 1915 the Museo Nacional de Historia Natural passed into the Dirección de Estudios Biológicos founded by Alfonso L. Herrera, or that the DEB integrated the museum and other biological institutions. This is institutional custody evidence, not a model-by-model inventory.
merge_policy.1929_UNAM_guard: UNAM histories document the 1929 creation of the Instituto de Biología and receipt of historical Chopo collections. The present Instituto de Biología also publicly acknowledges a Blaschka glass-animal collection. The module does not assume that every 1895 Blaschka model passed intact into the Instituto de Biología.
merge_policy.historical_loss_guard: UNAM and museum histories describe deterioration, closure, damage and losses in the old Chopo museum. No loss count or Blaschka-specific destruction mechanism is inferred.
merge_policy.1964_MHNCA_guard: The current MHNCA states that some Chopo collections were preserved when the Chapultepec museum opened in 1964, while many other holdings were acquired specifically for the new museum. Therefore present MHNCA custody alone does not establish uninterrupted possession from the 1895 national-museum case.
merge_policy.institutional_fission_guard: Two successor endpoints are currently documented: UNAM Instituto de Biología has a named Animales de Cristal Blaschka collection, and MHNCA has two named Chopo-derived glass-animal display anchors linked to Blaschka by UNAM cultural history. This strongly motivates an institutional-fission hypothesis, but the exact date and administrative logic of the split, and the item-level relationship of either endpoint to Baker's 1895 collection, remain unresolved.
merge_policy.UNAM_IB_count_guard: The 2023 Gaceta UNAM article confirms the existence of a Colección de Animales de Cristal Blaschka but provides no model count, local object identifiers, taxonomic list, condition register or exact display/storage location for that collection.
merge_policy.UNAM_IB_display_guard: The 2023 documentary discussed collections located both at Instituto de Biología facilities and in some Pabellón Nacional de la Biodiversidad spaces. The module does not infer that the Blaschka collection itself is currently displayed at the Pabellón.
merge_policy.2014_didactic_collection_guard: The 2014 UNAM institutional-history book identifies Radiolaria sp. and Aurelia aurita as Blaschka glass models in its reconstruction/illustration of the Museo Nacional de Historia Natural didactic collection. Publication identity is verified through UNAM; the exact page text was recovered from a digitized mirror. These taxa are treated as historical didactic-collection anchors, not as automatically verified current Instituto de Biología survivors.
merge_policy.MHNCA_two_object_guard: The current MHNCA exhibition-collection page lists 'El argonauta y la medusa de cristal' as historical pieces from the former Museo del Chopo. A UNAM cultural-history article identifies the two as Argonauta argo and Pelagia noctiluca and discusses them in the context of Herrera's appreciation of Blaschka models. No public local inventory numbers were recovered.
merge_policy.nineteenth_twentieth_century_date_confli: The current official MHNCA page says the argonaut and glass jellyfish date from the nineteenth century. The 2020 Revista de la Universidad de México image captions call Pelagia noctiluca and Argonauta argo 'réplica de cristal del siglo XX'. The conflict is preserved unresolved; neither source is silently corrected.
merge_policy.Baker_to_current_objects_guard: No present object is equated directly with a specific model seen by Baker in the 1895 case. The historical national-museum collection may have been larger, altered, dispersed, damaged, re-registered or partly replaced.
merge_policy.Herrera_guard: Antonio Lazcano's UNAM article states that Alfonso L. Herrera and his disciples recognized the didactic and aesthetic value of Blaschka models. This supports a later interpretive/museographic context; it does not prove Herrera purchased the original nineteenth-century national-museum collection.
merge_policy.Aurelia_catalogue_guard: Authenticated comparative records map Aurelia aurita adult to Blaschka no. 224 and developmental stages to no. 225. The Mexico historical Aurelia is not assigned to either without local label, morphology or inventory evidence.
merge_policy.Pelagia_catalogue_guard: Cornell's digital collection contains two Pelagia noctiluca model types, nos. 234 and 235, under different historical Blaschka species-name layers. The MHNCA Pelagia cannot be assigned from modern taxon name alone.
merge_policy.Argonauta_catalogue_guard: Authenticated comparative records map Argonauta argo female to no. 549 and male developmental stages to no. 550. The MHNCA object is not assigned a number from its display image or modern taxon name alone.
merge_policy.Radiolaria_catalogue_guard: The generic label Radiolaria sp. is insufficient for a Blaschka catalogue-number crosswalk. No number is proposed.
merge_policy.current_MHNCA_display_guard: The current official MHNCA webpage places the argonaut and glass jellyfish among representative examples of the Colección de exhibición, a collection defined as pieces exhibited in vitrines and dioramas. This supports current exhibition-collection status, but no specific gallery/case number or same-day visual verification is claimed.
merge_policy.current_total_guard: The project does not sum the two MHNCA anchors with an unknown-size Instituto de Biología collection to create a synthetic Mexico total.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No Mexican local accession number, old Museo Nacional number, Chopo inventory number, UNAM number, MHNCA number, Blaschka catalogue number, invoice number or transfer number is invented.

summary.key_result: Mexico City is a genuine large-museum Blaschka lifecycle node. A workshop catalogue was directed to the national museum in an 1885 global mailing sequence, and Baker's 1895 account independently proves a substantial physical Blaschka display. The natural-history collections were later separated from the Museo Nacional and institutionalized at El Chopo, then entered the 1915 Dirección de Estudios Biológicos / 1929 UNAM biological-collection system. Today, the Instituto de Biología publicly acknowledges a Blaschka glass-animal collection, while MHNCA preserves two named Chopo-derived glass-animal anchors, Argonauta argo and Pelagia noctiluca. The unresolved core is item-level fission: which parts of the 1895 national collection went to UNAM scientific collections, which went to the 1964 Chapultepec museum, and which were lost, damaged, replaced or re-registered.

content.title: Blaschka National Museum Prague: 1884 four-model gift, Frič mediation, catalogue numbers, wartime loss, surviving Eledone and conservation
content.scope: Deep capture of the National Museum Prague Blaschka node, centered on the 8 November 1884 gift of four catalogue-numbered glass models sent with a Václav Frič business shipment; museum accession-book confirmation; survival and loss histories; identification of later replacement/non-Blaschka comparison objects; the surviving Eledone moschata object's materials, construction, damage and conservation; and the node's connection to Frič's wider Austria-Hungary and international natural-history trade.
content.target_selection_reason: After the UK Science Museum dispersal audit, a global rather than UK-only scan identified Prague as a higher-yield uncaptured node. It supplies an unusually closed object-level chain: dated workshop letter draft, intermediary, recipient, four exact Blaschka catalogue numbers and taxa, accession-book confirmation, one confirmed surviving object, one documented wartime loss, two unresolved originals, and a modern technical conservation study.

merge_policy.wartime_loss_guard: The 2025 Vesmír account explicitly states that the Aurelia aurita displayed with the octopus from 1908 was destroyed during shelling/bombardment in May 1945. This is retained as the current best fate statement for the 1884 Blaschka Aurelia, while noting that Reiling 2002 also documented other Aurelia models at the museum attributable to an unknown glass worker.
merge_policy.technical_material_guard: Materials and construction below apply to the surviving Prague Eledone model as reported by Rydlová and Kopecká 2016, not generically to all Blaschka models.

content.title: Blaschka National Museum of Victoria / Museums Victoria: nine surviving models, McCoy–Ward acquisition hypothesis, Royal Exhibition Aquarium alternative, 1944 glass-model display, 1953 fire survival problem, and Rudolf Blaschka's Melbourne Radiolaria memory
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass models now held by Museums Victoria. The module records the complete current public collection of nine locally numbered models, including a four-object Sycon raphanus developmental series, and separates that secure current inventory from two competing acquisition hypotheses published by Museums Victoria: purchase by National Museum founder Frederick McCoy through Henry Ward, or original purchase for the Royal Exhibition Aquarium. It strengthens the McCoy–Ward hypothesis with independent 1881 Ward correspondence documenting McCoy's substantial purchase of Ward fossil casts in Melbourne, without converting that different transaction into a Blaschka invoice. It follows the aquarium hypothesis through the aquarium's 1885 opening, its museum collections, a Museums Victoria statement that 'glass models of the lower forms of marine life' were on display there in 1944, and the 28 January 1953 fire. It also preserves Rudolf Blaschka's later recollection that some later marine/Radiolaria models reached 'the Museum in Melbourne, Australia'. Because the nine present objects contain no confirmed Radiolaria, that recollection is treated as evidence for a possible additional historical Melbourne tranche rather than as direct provenance for the present nine. Exact purchase date, original quantity, original prices, movement into or out of the aquarium, fire exposure, and any lost or dispersed Melbourne models remain unresolved.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after the Tokyo Educational Museum module, whose next-action audit identified Melbourne as the strongest uncaptured non-European node. Melbourne is unusually valuable because current Museums Victoria records expose every surviving object by local specimen number while the institution itself openly preserves uncertainty over the acquisition route. The node therefore combines unusually strong present-day object control with unusually weak nineteenth-century transaction provenance, plus a documented aquarium/fire lifecycle and a workshop-side memory of Melbourne holdings.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone National Museum of Victoria / Museums Victoria Blaschka institutional module was found in the active consolidated backend through module 31 or in standalone modules 32–39.
merge_policy.nine_count_guard: Nine is the complete current Museums Victoria Blaschka Model Collection count stated by the institution and represented by nine public specimen records. It is a current surviving collection count, not the original historical acquisition count.
merge_policy.four_sponge_guard: Museums Victoria states that four of the nine models form a developmental series of a sponge. The four local specimen records are distinct physical models/stages; their relationship to a single Blaschka catalogue-series number does not collapse them into one physical object.
merge_policy.acquisition_route_guard: Museums Victoria explicitly states that exactly how the collection was acquired is unknown. The McCoy–Ward route and Royal Exhibition Aquarium route are maintained as competing institutional hypotheses, not merged into one synthetic provenance.
merge_policy.McCoy_Ward_guard: Museums Victoria says Frederick McCoy regularly bought items from Henry Ward. Independent Ward correspondence from 1881 records McCoy taking a large lot of Ward's fossil casts in Melbourne. This independently demonstrates an active McCoy–Ward purchasing channel but does not prove that the Blaschka models were part of that fossil-cast purchase or any specific Ward invoice.
merge_policy.Ward_1881_visit_guard: Henry A. Ward's 1881 Melbourne presence and McCoy purchase are evidence of dealer access and purchasing practice, not a Blaschka shipment date.
merge_policy.aquarium_route_guard: Museums Victoria says it is possible that the Blaschka models were originally bought for the Royal Exhibition aquarium. No acquisition ledger, invoice or transfer record has yet been recovered to prove this route.
merge_policy.aquarium_institution_guard: The Royal Exhibition Aquarium and the National Museum of Victoria were distinct institutions/administrative collections. A model's presence in the aquarium would require a transfer, loan, purchase or shared-custody event before it can be identified with the present Museums Victoria objects.
merge_policy.1944_display_guard: Museums Victoria reports that in 1944 'glass models of the lower forms of marine life', possibly the present Blaschka models, were displayed in the Melbourne Aquarium. The institution itself uses 'possibly'; the module does not upgrade this to certain object identity.
merge_policy.1953_fire_guard: The Melbourne Aquarium burned on 28 January 1953. Current survival of nine Blaschka models does not prove that they were physically inside the aquarium during the fire, nor that they survived the blaze in situ. They may have been removed earlier, transferred, stored elsewhere, or otherwise escaped exposure.
merge_policy.1953_survivor_wording_guard: A Museums Victoria handbook record says only three seals and a Japanese salamander survived the blaze. This is treated as a summary of the aquarium complex/living collection, not as an exhaustive inventory statement proving the destruction of every museum object.
merge_policy.Rudolf_1920_Melbourne_guard: Rudolf Blaschka's later correspondence remembers some later marine/Radiolaria models reaching 'the Museum in Melbourne, Australia'. The surrounding OCR is corrupt and the statement occurs in a discussion of Radiolaria and related later series. None of the nine current Museums Victoria objects is presently identified as Radiolaria. The recollection therefore may refer to an additional historical Melbourne tranche now lost, dispersed, unrecognized or held elsewhere; it is not direct object-level provenance for the current nine.
merge_policy.historical_original_count_guard: Because Rudolf's Melbourne recollection may concern objects beyond the nine now catalogued, the historical Melbourne Blaschka total must remain unknown rather than being set to nine.
merge_policy.catalogue_mailing_guard: A workshop catalogue-mailing list includes 'Melbourne 1'. This confirms commercial/catalogue contact only and is not treated as an order, shipment, model count or invoice.
merge_policy.catalogue_crosswalk_guard: Blaschka catalogue numbers derived from Cornell, Canterbury, Tübingen, Prague or other authenticated collections are model-type candidates only. No number is assigned as a local Melbourne object identifier unless confirmed by a Museums Victoria label, historical register, invoice or object file.
merge_policy.Chrysaora_guard: Cornell records expose at least two Blaschka catalogue types associated with the modern name Chrysaora hysoscella / historical Chrysaora hyocella: nos. 227 and 232. The Melbourne F 83578 object cannot be assigned to either number from taxon name alone.
merge_policy.Sycon_647_guard: External authenticated teaching-collection records connect Sycandra/Sycon raphanus developmental stages with Blaschka catalogue no. 647. Melbourne's four stages are retained as four physical objects and one guarded catalogue-series candidate; no stage-to-subnumber reconstruction is invented.
merge_policy.Lucernaria_128_guard: Cornell maps Lucernaria quadricornis to Blaschka no. 128. This is a strong type candidate for F 83577 but is not a locally verified Melbourne crosswalk.
merge_policy.Veretillum_17_guard: Cornell maps Veretillum cynomorium to Blaschka no. 17. This is a strong type candidate for F 82018 but is not a locally verified Melbourne crosswalk.
merge_policy.Serpula_343_guard: Cornell maps Serpula vermicularis to Blaschka no. 343. This is a strong type candidate for F 238817 but is not a locally verified Melbourne crosswalk.
merge_policy.Eledone_553_guard: Cornell maps Eledone moschata / historical Eledone moschatus to Blaschka no. 553. This is a strong type candidate for F 238818 but is not a locally verified Melbourne crosswalk.
merge_policy.maker_attribution_guard: Museums Victoria object pages vary between attributing models to Leopold Blaschka alone and to Leopold and Rudolf together. Source-specific wording is preserved rather than forcing an artificial reconciliation.
merge_policy.current_storage_guard: All nine public specimen records are currently marked 'Not on display / Currently in storage'. This is a 7 August 2026 public-database status and may change.
merge_policy.current_display_count_guard: Current display count is therefore recorded as zero for the nine public records, not as a permanent statement that Museums Victoria never displays them.
merge_policy.museum_succession_guard: The National Museum of Victoria and present Museums Victoria are historically connected institutional entities. Institutional succession does not by itself prove uninterrupted custody through every move; the current local specimen records establish present custody, while intermediate movement remains an archival question.
merge_policy.1899_move_guard: The National Museum moved to the Public Library building in 1899 with more than 510,000 items. No claim is made that the Blaschka models were definitely among those moved unless the acquisition route is first resolved.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No local accession number, Blaschka number, aquarium number, Ward invoice number, historical case number or lost-object identifier is invented.

summary.key_result: Melbourne is a rare case in which the present object inventory is essentially complete while the original transaction is not. Museums Victoria exposes nine numbered surviving models, all currently in storage, but explicitly leaves acquisition unresolved between a McCoy–Ward purchase route and a Royal Exhibition Aquarium route. The 1944 aquarium display reference and the 1953 fire create a concrete mid-century survival problem. Rudolf Blaschka's separate memory of models, apparently including later Radiolaria, reaching a Melbourne museum suggests that the historical Melbourne corpus may have been larger than the nine now recognized. The decisive archival task is therefore not object discovery alone but reconciliation of current specimen numbers with McCoy accounts, Ward correspondence, Exhibition Aquarium records and any fire-era transfer documentation.

historical_context: Museum of Natural History opened in Melbourne in 1854.
Collection moved to the University of Melbourne in 1856 and became known as the National Museum of Victoria.
Frederick McCoy became director in 1858 and actively sourced natural-history material overseas.
A separate Royal Exhibition Aquarium opened at the Exhibition Buildings in February 1885.
National Museum moved to the Public Library building in 1899.
The Royal Exhibition Aquarium complex burned in January 1953.
National Museum of Victoria and Science Museum of Victoria collections merged in 1983 to form the Museum of Victoria, predecessor of current Museums Victoria.

First screen South Australian Museum / Adelaide and Queensland Museum / Brisbane because workshop catalogue-mailing evidence names both Australian cities, but promote either to module 41 only if an institutional purchase, surviving object, or archival transaction can be recovered. conservation_sequence.description: Broken pieces were laid out, assessed and matched to original locations.
A wax former was shaped, pierced for tentacles and formed to receive the original circular glass lid.
A two-part silicone mould was created from the wax former and cured.
Epoxy was poured into the silicone mould, cured, removed and refined.
The replacement support was colour matched and given a final gelled-epoxy layer.
Support structure, tentacles and original glass top were bonded into place.

content.title: Blaschka Nottingham Natural History Museum / University College Nottingham → Wollaton Hall: John Wesley Carr, 1887 workshop account and Damon agency restriction, municipal collection continuity, published local object INV 2000, and current Endangered Planet display
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass models in the Nottingham municipal natural-history collection, historically housed with University College Nottingham in the Shakespeare Street civic complex and now held by Nottingham Natural History Museum at Wollaton Hall. Two independent workshop-side records close an 1887 Nottingham transaction at collection level without establishing an exact model count. First, the Blaschka account notebook contains an 1887 entry OCR-read 'Museum Nottingham Nodelle [Modelle] 356'; the annual account closes on the following page with 'Summa pro 1887 mark 4963', making 356 a strong monetary-value candidate in Marks, but the missing column structure and OCR quality prevent treating it as a definitive invoice amount until the original page image is checked. It must never be read as 356 models. Second, a separate workshop letter is addressed to J. W. Carr of the Museum of Natural History, University College Nottingham and explains the Blaschkas' English agency arrangement: Damon had to prepay large sums for multiple orders, and the workshop had promised Damon that it would not undertake direct commissions for England, so Carr's wish for direct dealing could not be fulfilled. The Carr letter belongs to the late-1886/early-1887 correspondence sequence and follows a reference to Carr's or an adjacent correspondent's 13 December communication; no exact letter date is imposed. A £13 6s 6d / 268-Mark payment paragraph immediately above the Carr heading belongs to a separate preceding correspondence block and is explicitly excluded from Nottingham accounting. Institutionally, the Nottingham Natural History Museum was a municipal collection housed in the same Shakespeare Street complex as University College; John Wesley Carr served as its director while also teaching biology/natural sciences at the College. The natural-history collection later moved to Wollaton Hall, opened as Nottingham's Natural History Museum in 1926, and remains a Nottingham City Council museum collection. Current Nottingham Museums evidence supplies a local object anchor, a Blaschka octopus published as 'INV 2000', while a 2025 Endangered Planet gallery resource explicitly includes a selection of Blaschka glass models of sea invertebrates. The exact historic order count, the definitive reading/unit of the 356 account entry, the complete current Blaschka object list, object-level 1887-to-Wollaton crosswalk, and exact August 2026 survival/display counts remain unresolved.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 48 after a global major-institution screen following module 47. Carnegie Museum of Natural History again remained below promotion threshold because public evidence still supplied only surviving/loaned objects without a Blaschka-specific acquisition record, exact collection count, or local object register. Nottingham crossed the threshold because primary Rakow workshop OCR names both 'Museum Nottingham' in the 1887 annual account and J. W. Carr at the Museum of Natural History, University College Nottingham in correspondence explaining the Damon English agency structure. On the receiving side, Nottingham's municipal collection history provides a defensible institutional continuity into Wollaton Hall, and current Nottingham Museums sources provide both a published local identifier (INV 2000) and plural current/recent display evidence. Duplicate audit of active 06 v3 and standalone modules 41–47 found no Nottingham / Wollaton / John Wesley Carr Blaschka node.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Nottingham Natural History Museum / University College Nottingham / Wollaton Hall / John Wesley Carr Blaschka node occurs in the mounted active 06 v3 backend or standalone modules 41–47.
merge_policy.institutional_identity_guard: University College Nottingham and the municipal Natural History Museum shared the Shakespeare Street civic complex, but the museum was a Nottingham Corporation municipal collection rather than simply a university departmental collection. Current Wollaton holdings are therefore traced through the civic museum collection, not by assuming that all University College scientific property became University of Nottingham property.
merge_policy.Carr_identity_guard: The workshop OCR renders the addressee approximately as 'W. J. W. Carr' with a corrupt role word. Independent sources identify John Wesley Carr (1862–1939) as the Nottingham Natural History Museum director and University College natural-sciences/biology teacher, and an 1894 Natural History Museum London archive record independently places 'J W Carr' at University College Nottingham. The normalization to John Wesley Carr is therefore high confidence; the exact wording of his title in the Blaschka letter remains unverified.
merge_policy.Carr_role_guard: Carr is a verified museum director/curator and university teacher. The workshop correspondence shows him engaging the Blaschka commercial network, but the surviving OCR does not establish that he personally paid every invoice or legally owned the models.
merge_policy.Carr_letter_date_guard: The Carr correspondence appears in a late-1886/early-1887 sequence: adjacent pages discuss the 1886 Jeypore order, New Year wishes, a Damon '26 Decbr' context, and later 1887 orders. The Carr block follows reference to a communication dated 13 December. No exact day or even a silently normalized January date is assigned without image-level verification.
merge_policy.Damon_agency_guard: The Carr letter states that the Damon agency in England had been instituted for the Blaschkas' commissions, that Damon had to prepay large sums on diverse orders, and that the workshop had promised not to undertake direct commissions for England. This establishes a commercial-policy constraint on Carr's attempted direct dealing. It does not by itself prove the exact identity of the Damon family member responsible for the Nottingham transaction.
merge_policy.Damon_exclusivity_scope_guard: The English-agency promise is preserved as the workshop's statement in this correspondence context. It should not be generalized into an invariant rule for every British transaction across the entire Blaschka business without date-specific evidence.
merge_policy.Carr_direct_order_guard: Because the workshop says it cannot fulfill Carr's wish 'in this respect' while keeping its word to Damon, the letter is not treated as evidence that Carr successfully placed a direct Dresden commission. The later Nottingham account entry proves a museum transaction at collection level, while the exact intermediary chain still requires invoice/receipt evidence.
merge_policy.preceding_payment_block_guard: The £13 6s 6d bill of exchange and OCR-read 268 Marks occur in a separate text block immediately before the explicit Carr heading. They are not assigned to Nottingham. Earlier exploratory reading considered a possible connection, but page/block structure shows that doing so would be unsafe.
merge_policy.1887_account_guard: The Rakow account notebook contains the raw OCR '5. S.d. Museum Nottingham Nodelle 356' and the account sequence ends with 'Summa pro 1887 mark 4963'. This securely places a Museum Nottingham model entry in the 1887 annual account.
merge_policy.356_guard: 356 is never a model count. The account context strongly suggests that it is a monetary amount, likely Marks, because nearby model entries carry monetary figures and the annual total is explicitly in Marks. However OCR has lost the original column structure. The module therefore stores 356 only as an account-value candidate pending image verification.
merge_policy.356_invoice_guard: Even if image verification confirms 356 Marks, this need not equal a final all-inclusive invoice; it may represent an account posting, model value, balance, payment, or another ledger category. No packing, freight, insurance, commission, or tax component is invented.
merge_policy.dense_number_list_guard: A dense page of apparent Blaschka catalogue numbers immediately before the Nottingham account page is not assigned to Nottingham. The preceding account page contains a Prof. Chun/Königsberg model entry, so the number list may belong to another order. No Nottingham model list or count is reconstructed from page adjacency.
merge_policy.1887_transaction_to_INV2000_guard: The current Nottingham object INV 2000 is not asserted to be part of the 1887 transaction. The public object page gives a general/model date statement of 1890, while the workshop account proves Nottingham activity in 1887. Without accession/register crosswalks, these could represent approximate dating, later acquisition, multiple order strata, or cataloguing convention.
merge_policy.1890_object_page_guard: Nottingham Museums' INV 2000 page says glass sea-invertebrate models 'like this one' were made in the Dresden studio in 1890. This is preserved as the current museum's published date layer, not used to overwrite the independently documented 1887 transaction.
merge_policy.INV2000_guard: INV 2000 is the local identifier printed on Nottingham Museums' Blaschka octopus page. It is treated as a published Nottingham inventory/object identifier. It is not a Blaschka commercial catalogue number, shipment number, or proof of an original 1887 accession.
merge_policy.octopus_taxon_guard: The current Nottingham page describes the object generically as a Blaschka model of an octopus and does not print a species name or Blaschka catalogue number. No commercial catalogue number is inferred from morphology or comparative collections.
merge_policy.municipal_continuity_guard: Nottingham City Council's Picture Nottingham describes the Shakespeare Street complex as housing University College and the Natural History Museum, notes municipal control by Nottingham Corporation, and identifies that Natural History Museum as the one now at Wollaton Hall. This supports collection-level civic continuity; it does not prove that every nineteenth-century object survived the move.
merge_policy.1926_move_guard: Wollaton Hall opened as Nottingham's Natural History Museum in 1926. Historical accounts state that the civic natural-science collections were moved there from the Shakespeare Street/University College museum and associated temporary storage. No Blaschka-specific packing list for the 1926 move has yet been recovered.
merge_policy.current_service_guard: Wollaton Hall remains Nottingham's Natural History Museum in 2026 and Nottingham Museums remains a Nottingham City Council service. This establishes current institutional custody framework but not exact legal title to each individual Blaschka model without CMS records.
merge_policy.current_display_guard: The Nottingham Museums 2025 Endangered Planet teaching/gallery resource explicitly includes a selection of Blaschka glass models of sea invertebrates. This supports plural current/recent display at Wollaton Hall; it does not state the exact number, taxa, or local IDs displayed.
merge_policy.2026_display_projection_guard: Endangered Planet material remains an active Wollaton teaching resource and Wollaton is actively celebrating its Natural History Museum centenary in 2026, but the exact same-day August 2026 Blaschka display count is not published. The module records current/recent display presence and leaves exact 2026 display count null.
merge_policy.current_total_guard: No exact current Nottingham Blaschka total has been recovered. The fact that a current gallery displays a 'selection' proves plurality but cannot be converted into a collection size.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: The NMW comparative spreadsheet lists Wollaton Hall as a model location for multiple types including Lucernaria, Porpita, Idyia, Pleurobrachia and Aurelia. These are external comparative-location candidates only. NMW accession numbers, condition notes and Cardiff object metadata must never be transferred to Nottingham.
merge_policy.commercial_catalogue_crosswalk_guard: Comparative catalogue numbers such as 127, 217, 224, 245 and 248 are not assigned to Nottingham physical objects without a local label, museum register, photograph or authenticated Nottingham catalogue crosswalk.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No Nottingham accession number beyond published INV 2000, Blaschka catalogue number, exact model count, Damon invoice, shipment mark, packing charge, transfer number, missing-object number or 1926 movement identifier is invented.

Workshop records show a Museum Nottingham model account entry in 1887 and separately record John Wesley Carr being told that English direct commissions could not bypass Damon. The receiving institution was not merely a university collection: the Natural History Museum was part of Nottingham's civic museum structure, co-located with University College, and its natural-science collection later moved to Wollaton Hall. network_implications.British_agency_value: Nottingham gives direct workshop evidence for the practical effect of the Damon English agency: a museum-side curator sought a form of direct dealing and the workshop explicitly invoked its promise not to accept direct English commissions.
network_implications.transaction_account_value: The 1887 annual ledger independently records 'Museum Nottingham' and models, demonstrating that the agency-policy correspondence was not merely hypothetical interest. The unresolved 356 field is therefore a high-value image-verification target.
network_implications.municipal_university_value: Nottingham cautions against classifying nineteenth-century museum holdings by the later university name alone. University College and the Natural History Museum were institutionally intertwined in one municipal complex, while the natural-history objects followed the civic museum into Wollaton Hall instead of following University College to its later university campus.
network_implications.continuity_value: Unlike nodes where a historic university teaching collection disappears into an unknown successor, Nottingham has a defensible collection-level route from the Shakespeare Street Natural History Museum to the current municipal museum at Wollaton Hall.
network_implications.dating_strata_value: The 1887 workshop transaction and current INV 2000 page's 1890 date layer should remain separate until object-level accession work shows whether Nottingham acquired multiple batches or whether the current date is approximate.
network_implications.current_register_value: INV 2000 demonstrates that local identifiers are publicly recoverable even though the complete register is not indexed. A direct CMS export from Nottingham could therefore turn this node rapidly from collection-level to full object-level provenance.
network_implications.next_institutional_action: For module 49 continue the global large-museum screen rather than defaulting to Carnegie. Promote only a node with a dated acquisition/transfer plus surviving local objects, or a sufficiently complete local object register. Keep Carnegie pending until its Blaschka-specific purchase/donation/count or accession layer can be separated from general Ward collection history.

content.title: Blaschka Oxford University Museum: 1867 British sea-anemone series, Gosse 68-model numbered-set system, Anthea cereus anchor and catalogue gap
content.scope: Deep capture of the early Blaschka sea-anemone holdings at Oxford University Museum of Natural History (OUMNH). The module separates the Oxford physical collection from the broader early numbered-set design system, reconstructs the documented relationship to Philip Henry Gosse's 1860 British sea-anemone illustrations, records the 1867 acquisition date and one directly documented Oxford physical-object anchor (Anthea cereus), and quarantines cross-institutional location notes from the National Museum Wales comparative spreadsheet as candidates rather than Oxford inventory records.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after the Strasbourg conservation module because Strasbourg restorer Agathe Petit explicitly identified Oxford as the key comparative collection for early sea-anemone models. Oxford is unusually early (1867), tightly tied to Gosse's illustrations and the pre-1870 glass-numeral numbering system, but its public object catalogue remains incomplete. The resulting module therefore focuses on an early design/order ontology rather than inventing unavailable local IDs.

merge_policy.68_set_vs_Oxford_count_guard: Chris Meechan's 1995 reconstruction states that Leopold made numbered sets of 68 models based almost entirely on Gosse. The number 68 is a design/set-system count and is NOT treated as Oxford's original acquisition count or present-day count.
merge_policy.glass_numeral_guard: The glass numerals attached to early models belong to the pre-later-catalogue numbered-set system. They must not be silently equated with later Blaschka catalogue numbers appearing in 1871/1874/1878/1888 catalogues.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: The National Museum Wales Chris Meechan spreadsheet contains cross-collection 'Model Locations' notes including Oxford and early-set numbers. These rows are retained only as comparative-location candidates. They are not OUMNH inventory records, do not prove present survival, and do not supply Oxford local accession numbers.
merge_policy.Cardiff_condition_guard: Condition fields in the National Museum Wales spreadsheet describe Cardiff/NMW objects, not Oxford objects. No Cardiff condition statement is transferred to an Oxford candidate.
merge_policy.Anthea_cereus_guard: Sigwart 2008 directly documents an Oxford Blaschka model identified as 'Anthea cereus', acquired 1867 and based on Gosse plate 5. This physical-object anchor is not automatically equated with later Anthea/Anemonia variants or with any later catalogue number unless an Oxford label or inventory record establishes the concordance.
merge_policy.maker_attribution_guard: The 1867 group belongs to Leopold Blaschka's early marine-model phase, before Rudolf formally joined the business. Modern OUMNH pages may use the family/Blaschka plural generically; the module does not use that wording to assert Rudolf's personal manufacture of the 1867 Oxford models.
merge_policy.Gosse_match_guard: OUMNH states that many models can be recognized as species and even individual animals illustrated by Gosse. Only Anthea cereus is recorded here as a specific plate-to-Oxford-object match because it is explicitly published.
merge_policy.catalogue_gap_guard: OUMNH states that most of its non-specimen object collection has not been catalogued. Web searches did not surface Oxford Blaschka object IDs. This is treated as a public-catalogue gap, not evidence that internal inventory records do not exist.
merge_policy.current_count_guard: OUMNH's 2016 institutional blog says the only Blaschka models at the Museum today form a series of British anemones, but gives no numerical current count. No count is inferred from photographs, the 68-set design, or comparative spreadsheets.
merge_policy.current_display_guard: Institutional images and museum-memory material document the models in museum/display contexts, but an exact current display count, case number and displayed-versus-store split were not recovered.
merge_policy.Hope_collection_guard: A recent doctoral thesis states that the early sea-anemones came with the Hope collection. This is retained as a secondary research lead only until an OUMNH accession or bequest record independently confirms the exact transfer.

oxford_1867_british_sea_anemone_series.next_institutional_action: Prioritize Leeds City Museum next. Reiling's Prague/Frič research identifies a surviving 1865 Leeds acquisition as the earliest known Frič-mediated Blaschka sale, while the NMW comparative spreadsheet independently lists Leeds (1865) against multiple early-set sea-anemone types. object_records.description_raw: This is an example of a glass model of a sea creature which was made for natural history museums all over the world by the Blaschkas. Leopold (1822-1895) and Rudolph (1857-1939), his son, had a workshop in Dresden, Germany which operated from the 1870's to 1930's. Both skilled glassworkers they used clear and coloured glass, wire and glue to create life like models of sea creatures such as this jellyfish. This model is one of a series of fourteen models showing the different life stages of the jellyfish. The set of models was bought from the Blaschkas by the Perthshire Natural History Museum in the 1880s.

content.title: Blaschka Redpath Museum / McGill University: 31 models, probable two acquisition strata, Ward route, six early sea anemones, tubeworm remains, teaching damage, Reiling examination and 2010 exhibition
content.scope: Deep capture of the Blaschka glass-model collection at the Redpath Museum, McGill University, Montreal. The module separates McGill's umbrella statement that 31 models were acquired around 1878 from its more specific hypothesis that the collection contains a later group of 24 models probably made between 1878 and 1890, an earlier set of six sea anemones probably made before 1877, and the remains of a tubeworm model circa 1877. It captures Ward-mediated procurement, the museum-opening context, teaching use, severe damage and later paint/adhesive residues, Henri Reiling's 2001 examination, 2008 scholarly presentation, the 2010 Nature in Glass exhibition, current public-display uncertainty, McGill archival routes, and a controlled external comparative catalogue register.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected globally after University of Liège. File Library duplicate audit found no standalone Redpath institutional module in the active 06–31 sequence. Redpath has unusually dense provenance and lifecycle evidence for a relatively small collection: a published total of 31, probable internal acquisition strata, a Ward dealer route linked to preparations for the 1882 museum opening, a potentially very early North American subset, documented long-term teaching use and severe damage, universal traces of twentieth-century repair materials, direct Henri Reiling examination, later conference presentation and a dated temporary exhibition.

merge_policy.31_count_guard: 31 is the McGill collection total reported in 2010. The internal arithmetic 24 + 6 + 1 remnant = 31 is preserved as the source's proposed structure, but the tubeworm is explicitly a remnant rather than necessarily an intact model.
merge_policy.two_sets_guard: McGill says the collection was 'probably acquired in two separate sets'. This is a published institutional hypothesis, not a closed two-invoice provenance.
merge_policy.chronology_conflict_guard: The same McGill account says the 31-model collection was acquired around 1878, while 24 models were likely made during 1878–1890 and the models were purchased from Ward in a context congruent with preparations for the museum's 1882 opening. These claims are retained together as a chronology problem; no single exact accession date is imposed.
merge_policy.early_subset_guard: Six sea anemones are said to have probably been created before 1877, and those six plus the tubeworm remains could possibly be the oldest known Blaschka models in North America. This is a qualified institutional significance claim, not proof of manufacture date or absolute continental priority.
merge_policy.tubeworm_guard: McGill's image caption dates tubeworms to circa 1877, while the collection narrative speaks of the 'remains of a tubeworm model'. The object is therefore encoded as a damaged/remnant physical anchor, not as a complete surviving model.
merge_policy.Ward_name_guard: McGill's 2010 page uses the supplier label 'Ward’s Scientific' and calls the dealer 'Augustus Ward'. Archival and historical authority records identify Henry Augustus Ward and Ward's Natural Science Establishment. The raw McGill wording is preserved, while the normalized dealer entity is Henry Augustus Ward / Ward's Natural Science Establishment.
merge_policy.exclusive_agent_guard: McGill's statement that Ward was the Blaschkas' North American agent is retained as institutional wording. It is not generalized into an absolute monopoly claim beyond the context documented in this module.
merge_policy.damage_guard: McGill states that the models suffered severe damage that cannot be adequately repaired. No count of damaged, broken or lost models is invented; the statement applies collection-wide at the level of the 2010 account.
merge_policy.repair_residue_guard: Residues of twentieth-century paint and adhesives are reported on all models. These are encoded as evidence of historic interventions/repairs, not as a documented professional conservation campaign.
merge_policy.current_display_guard: The 2010 temporary exhibition is securely dated. Current 2026 Redpath public permanent-display and collections pages do not surface a Blaschka display, so current Blaschka display status remains unresolved rather than being asserted absent.
merge_policy.local_identifier_guard: No Redpath local inventory/accession number was recovered publicly. No synthetic child numbers are created for the 31 models.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: National Museum Wales / Meechan model-location rows listing Redpath are external comparative research. They are not McGill accession records and do not establish current survival, condition or acquisition stratum.
merge_policy.Cardiff_field_guard: NMW accession numbers, Cardiff conditions, Cardiff repairs and Science Museum transfer fields belong to Cardiff physical objects and are never transferred to Redpath.
merge_policy.catalogue_crosswalk_guard: Comparative Blaschka catalogue numbers are retained as candidates only. A taxon-level match does not assign a catalogue number to a Redpath physical object without a Redpath label, register or object file.
merge_policy.Argonauta_guard: A 2010 press review independently describes an Argonauta / paper nautilus in the Redpath exhibition, while the NMW comparative spreadsheet lists Redpath for Argonauta argo, catalogue no. 549. This is a strong cross-source candidate but still lacks a Redpath local identifier.
merge_policy.Ilyanthus_guard: A 2010 press review names an early anemone as Ilyanthus mitchelli. This observational identification is retained as a secondary exhibition anchor; no early glass numeral or later Blaschka catalogue number is assigned.
merge_policy.museum_opening_guard: Redpath Museum opened in 1882. McGill links the Ward purchase to other natural-history display material procured for that opening, but this contextual statement does not prove every Blaschka model arrived in 1882.

content.title: Blaschka Science Museum Group / South Kensington: 1877 registration cohort, 1888 order layer, and 1925–1927 institutional and market dispersal transaction hub
content.scope: Transaction-hub reconstruction of the Blaschka zoological models associated with the South Kensington science collections and later Science Museum: upstream 1876/1877 chronology, separate 1888 order layer, surviving Science Museum identifiers, 1925–1927 deaccession, institutional transfers, private-market dispersal, corporate-archive register targets, and downstream recipient nodes.
content.target_selection_reason: Module 20 converted the Cardiff branch of the Science Museum dispersal into object-level identifier chains. The highest-yield next move is therefore the hub itself, because one disposal register can potentially connect multiple present collections and explain why adjacent 1877 inventory numbers now survive in different institutional and private pathways.

merge_policy.hub_not_collection_guard: This module models a transaction and custody hub. It does not assert that the Science Museum currently retains a Blaschka zoological collection.
merge_policy.chronology_guard: Primary workshop evidence places an order for two complete zoological collections in 1876. UCL and later provenance records describe Science Museum-derived objects as ordered/acquired in 1877. These may represent order, fulfilment, registration, or distinct transactions and remain separate.
merge_policy.secondary_count_guard: A Frieze article describes a bulk order of around 500 models in 1877. This is retained as a secondary approximate statement only; no exact Science Museum 1877 physical count is assigned.
merge_policy.institutional_recipient_guard: UCL says models were transferred to UCL and six other institutions. Only UCL and Cardiff are concretely identified in this pass; five other institutional recipients remain unresolved.
merge_policy.imperial_recipient_guard: Imperial is a related South Kensington/Royal College of Science custody branch but is not counted as one of the six other 1925–1927 recipient institutions without direct transfer evidence.
merge_policy.market_path_guard: The 1925–1927 deaccession was not exclusively an inter-museum transfer. At least three 1877 Science Museum objects later entered the private market and were auctioned in 2019.
merge_policy.seven_institutions_not_total_dispersal_g: The UCL statement about seven institutional recipients is therefore not treated as a complete enumeration of every deaccessioned object or destination.
merge_policy.identifier_guard: Science Museum inventory/register numbers, E.-numbers, transfer shorthand, recipient accessions and Ward/Blaschka catalogue numbers are distinct identifier systems.
merge_policy.deaccession_date_guard: 1925–1927 is a window; an exact removal date is not assigned to an individual object without a disposal record.
merge_policy.auction_provenance_guard: Auction provenance establishes Science Museum acquisition/deaccession and a 2019 market appearance. Intermediate private ownership is left blank unless documented.
merge_policy.current_catalogue_guard: Failure to locate Blaschka zoological objects in the current Science Museum Group public object search is not evidence that no retained or uncatalogued material exists.
merge_policy.adjacency_guard: Adjacent register numbers surviving through different pathways are evidence of a shared historical registration neighbourhood, not by themselves proof of identical disposal dates or destinations.

content.title: Blaschka Stift Kremsmünster: Frič–Eggerth provenance, 263/253/226 count conflict, wartime damage, research audit and exhibition loans
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka zoological glass-model collection in the natural-history collections of the Sternwarte, Benediktinerstift Kremsmünster, Austria. The module distinguishes historical collection counts, modern surviving-count statements, dealer/donor provenance, wartime damage, research and catalogue-copy events, exhibition loans, current display status, and a public photographic object record. It does not invent local inventory numbers or reconcile contradictory counts.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected in a global rather than UK-only pass because Kremsmünster combines a large documented surviving collection with a strong Prague dealer chain (Blaschka workshop → Václav Frič → Karl Eggerth senior → Sternwarte Kremsmünster), explicit historical and modern counts, a documented wartime damage episode, research access, and later loan/display histories.

merge_policy.count_ontology_guard: The published figures 263, formerly 253, and 226 are retained as distinct documentary claims. No attempt is made to force them into one historical total.
merge_policy.loss_arithmetic_guard: 263−226=37 and 253−226=27 are arithmetic differences only. Neither figure is treated as a documented number of destroyed, lost, or deaccessioned objects.
merge_policy.wartime_damage_guard: The wartime source states only that part of the very rare glass models of marine animals was severely damaged during postwar/reoccupation rearrangement. It does not provide an item count and cannot by itself explain either numerical discrepancy.
merge_policy.donor_identity_guard: Karl Eggerth senior (1834–1888), not Karl Eggerth junior, is retained as the donor/buyer associated with the Frič provenance, following the explicit correction in the geological-history source.
merge_policy.loan_overlap_guard: The six jellyfish loaned in 1998 and six cnidarians loaned in 2015 are separate documented loan events. They may overlap physically; the module does not count them as twelve unique objects.
merge_policy.early_date_guard: The ca. 1865 date applies to the six objects described in the 2015 loan context, not to the entire collection.
merge_policy.taxonomic_media_guard: The public 2022 photograph reports a local/display identification of Cotylorhiza tuberculata but the uploader explicitly disputes that identification. The true taxon is therefore left unresolved.
merge_policy.catalogue_identifier_guard: No Kremsmünster museum inventory number or Blaschka workshop catalogue number was recovered for an individual physical object in this pass. None is inferred from appearance.
merge_policy.network_guard: The shared Frič dealer route links Kremsmünster to the Prague and Australian nodes as a commercial network only; it does not imply shared physical objects or a shared shipment.

content.title: Blaschka Stift Seitenstetten: 61-model rediscovered teaching collection, Frič catalogue context, conservation project and inventory gap
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka glass-model holdings in the natural-history and teaching collections of the Benedictine Abbey of Seitenstetten, Lower Austria. This module prioritizes the 2024 rediscovery statement, the 2026 project-level count of 61 Blaschka models, the historical teaching-collection setting of the Stiftsgymnasium, the relationship of sea-anemone models to Václav Frič's commercial offerings, ongoing documentation and conservation work, and the still-open acquisition, inventory-number and object-list questions.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as the next global node after Prague and Kremsmünster because it extends the Frič/teaching-collection network into a previously under-documented monastic school collection. A 2024 collections-science report described recently rediscovered Blaschka sea-anemone models, while a March 2026 specialist meeting subsequently reported a concrete collection total of 61 Blaschka glass models and active conservation/restoration preparation.

merge_policy.fric_offer_guard: Published research states that Frič offered Blaschka models in combinations of 5, 7 and 60 pieces. No Seitenstetten invoice, order list, dealer label, accession entry or catalogue concordance was recovered that proves the abbey bought any one of those standard combinations.
merge_policy.acquisition_guard: The collection's historical relationship to Frič is commercial-context evidence, not yet a closed transaction chain. No purchaser/donor, purchase date, invoice, price, case/shipment record or exact accession date is asserted.
merge_policy.count_guard: The figure 61 is retained as a 2026 project/conference count. It is not automatically interpreted as 61 surviving originals, 61 catalogued inventory units, or 61 sea-anemone models unless future project documentation explicitly defines the ontology.
merge_policy.taxonomic_scope_guard: The 2024 report specifically highlights sea-anemone models as rediscovered early Blaschka products. The 2026 statement refers more broadly to 61 Blaschka glass models. It is therefore not assumed that all 61 are sea anemones.
merge_policy.maker_date_guard: The phrase 'early products' applies to the rediscovered sea-anemone subset. No exact production year is assigned to all 61 models.
merge_policy.school_collection_guard: The natural-history holdings partly derive from teaching collections connected with the Stiftsgymnasium founded in 1814. This does not prove that every Blaschka model was originally purchased by the school rather than the abbey's museum or a private donor.
merge_policy.inventory_guard: No public Seitenstetten inventory numbers, Blaschka catalogue numbers, full taxon list, dimensions or individual condition records were recovered in this pass. These fields remain null rather than being inferred from comparative collections.
merge_policy.conservation_guard: The 2026 conference report documents preparatory work for conservation/restoration of Blaschka sea-anemone models. It does not publish treatment dates, treatment materials, object-by-object condition states or completed-treatment counts.
merge_policy.project_status_guard: The collection-research project runs from 1 March 2025 to 28 February 2027. The module therefore treats current inventory and conservation information as an active, potentially changing research state rather than a final catalogue.

content.title: Blaschka Tokyo Educational Museum / National Museum of Nature and Science: 1883 Tagima/Tejima shipment and curator orders, 1884 1000-Mark account, probable 1885 1846/846 settlement structure, Meiji teaching-object network, 1889–1890 Tensanbu transfer fork, 1923 earthquake and 1925 return pathway
content.scope: Deep institutional and transaction capture of Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass models ordered for the Educational Department / Tokyo Educational Museum in Tokyo during the early 1880s. The module triangulates Corning/Rakow metadata for an 1883 filled shipment 'for Mr. Tagima', business-letter drafts containing orders from the curator of the Tokio Educational Museum, a Blaschka account page recording 1000 Marks for the Tokyo educational recipient in 1884, and a following 1885 account row containing the figures 1846 and 846. The arithmetic relation 1000 + 846 = 1846 strongly suggests a multi-year payment/final-account structure but the exact 1885 wording remains OCR-corrupt and is not treated as a diplomatic transcription. Japanese institutional sources identify Seiichi Tejima, director of the Tokyo Educational Museum from 1881 and contemporary English 'S. Tegima', as the highly probable person behind the Tagima/Mitigima/Legima variants. The module then reconstructs the key custodial fork created by the museum's 1888 contraction: many natural-history specimens were transferred in 1889–1890 to the Imperial Museum's natural-products collection, while all facilities and specimens still held by the Tokyo Museum were destroyed in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. In 1925, animal, plant and mineral holdings of the Imperial Museum were transferred back to the Tokyo Museum. No Blaschka-specific transfer row or current object record has yet been recovered, so the models cannot be assigned either to the 1923 destruction or to the surviving/returned Tensanbu pathway without ledger-level evidence.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected immediately after Indian Museum Calcutta/Kolkata. The active backend had no standalone Tokyo Educational Museum / Kahaku node. Tokyo adds a new East Asian institutional route and is unusually strong because workshop-side evidence spans direct curator orders, a filled 1883 shipment and two consecutive annual financial records. Japanese sources also preserve unusually detailed institutional genealogies and historical natural-history ledgers, making it possible in principle to test the physical fate of the models across the 1889–1890 Imperial Museum transfer and the 1923 earthquake rather than simply declaring them lost.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Tokyo Educational Museum / National Museum of Nature and Science Blaschka institutional module was found in the active consolidated backend through module 31 or in standalone modules 32–38.
merge_policy.institution_identity_guard: The historical Educational Museum / Tokyo Educational Museum is an institutional predecessor of the present National Museum of Nature and Science (Kahaku), as confirmed by Kahaku's official history. Institutional succession does not imply uninterrupted custody of every nineteenth-century object.
merge_policy.tokio_spelling_guard: Workshop and Corning records use Tokio; Japanese and current sources use Tokyo. Both are preserved as chronological/linguistic variants.
merge_policy.Tejima_identification_guard: Corning metadata names 'Mr. Tagima'; OCR elsewhere produces Mitigima and Legima; Nature in 1884 calls the curator 'Mr. S. Tegima'. National Diet Library identifies Seiichi Tejima as director of the Tokyo Educational Museum from 1881 and as a participant in the 1884 London International Health Exhibition. These converging role, place and date signals make Tejima the high-confidence normalized person entity, but raw archival spellings are retained and no corrupted text is silently rewritten.
merge_policy.1883_shipment_guard: Corning's catalogue record for the Lieferungs-Buch explicitly states that the book records filled orders, including the specific numbers of models sent, and that 1883 shipments included the Educational Department in Tokio, Japan, for Mr. Tagima. Exact Tokyo catalogue numbers and physical model count were not reliably transcribed in this pass and remain pending original-page review.
merge_policy.business_correspondence_guard: Corning's catalogue record for the circa-1880–1885 business-letter drafts explicitly says the notebook includes orders from the curator of the Tokio Educational Museum. This establishes direct order correspondence but not the full content, exact date or item list of each order.
merge_policy.1884_1000_guard: The 1884 workshop account page records a Tokyo educational recipient with the amount 1000. On the same page the three preceding amounts are 9, 10 and 5 and the page subtotal is 1024; 9 + 10 + 5 + 1000 = 1024 exactly. The following page gives the 1884 annual total as 5442.95 Marks. The 1000 is therefore securely a monetary ledger amount rather than a quantity of models.
merge_policy.1884_raw_text_guard: The recipient/description OCR on the 1884 row is corrupt ('For Mitigima, Educational Abweern in Tokio, Japan forlize Sachen'). No diplomatic German or English phrase is reconstructed from this wording without the image.
merge_policy.1885_1846_846_guard: The 1885 account OCR reads approximately 'Educational Department Tohio / Japan nach Schulprechmann/1846 846'. Because 1000 + 846 = 1846 and because the entry sits within the 1885 annual account sequence, 1846 is a strong candidate for a full/cumulative or final-account total and 846 for an additional payment/balance following the 1884 1000-Mark entry. The exact column semantics and the corrupt phrase before 1846 require the original page and are encoded as an accounting reconstruction, not a closed invoice transcription.
merge_policy.1885_year_guard: The surrounding sequence culminates in 'Summa 1885' and an annual total of 4663 Marks, securely placing the 1846/846 row within the 1885 account.
merge_policy.1846_total_guard: The module never states that 1846 Marks is definitively the purchase price of the entire Tokyo Blaschka collection. It is the strongest current reconstruction of the account relationship and remains provisional pending image verification.
merge_policy.catalogue_mailing_guard: A separate OCR list records 'Mr. Legima, Tokio 3' under catalogues sent. Because the exact date/context of the list has not been closed, it is treated only as corroborating evidence of repeated workshop contact with the Tokyo recipient.
merge_policy.1884_London_guard: Tejima attended the 1884 International Health Exhibition in London and supervised the Japanese Educational Section according to contemporary Nature and NDL. This is relevant procurement context but no source yet proves that the Blaschka transaction was ordered, negotiated or paid in London.
merge_policy.1881_catalogue_guard: The 1881 'Educational Museum catalogue, Animal section' has the parallel English title 'Classified catalogue of the specimens of vertebrates...'. It predates the documented 1883 Blaschka shipment and covers vertebrates, so absence of marine-invertebrate glass models from that catalogue would have no negative evidential value.
merge_policy.educational_infrastructure_guard: Modern scholarship documents the Tokyo Educational Museum's 1880s role in distributing scientific apparatus and specimens for object-based teaching. This provides institutional context for the Blaschka order, but it does not prove a specific downstream school distribution of the imported glass models.
merge_policy.1889_1890_transfer_guard: Kahaku's official fish-collection history states that after the museum was reduced in 1888 many natural-history specimens, including fish, were transferred to the Imperial Museum in 1889–1890. Separate official and scholarly evidence shows Tokyo Educational Museum materials entering the Imperial Museum/Tokyo Imperial Household Museum natural-products (Tensanbu) system. No Blaschka-specific transfer entry has yet been recovered; the models are therefore only candidates for this pathway.
merge_policy.Tensanbu_ledger_guard: Published provenance research demonstrates that Tensanbu ledgers can preserve explicit transfer wording such as '二十三年東京教育博物舘引継' and that the ledger itself is held by the National Museum of Nature and Science. This proves the archival mechanism needed to test the Blaschka case, not that a Blaschka row has already been found.
merge_policy.1923_destruction_guard: Kahaku's official history says all facilities and specimens then held by the Tokyo Museum were lost in the September 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. The statement cannot automatically be applied to the Blaschka models because their custody after the 1889–1890 natural-history transfer has not been resolved.
merge_policy.1925_return_guard: Tokyo National Museum states that in 1925 the Imperial Museum's animal, plant and mineral collections were transferred to the Tokyo Museum, and the natural-products department was closed. Some material originally from the Educational Museum could therefore have escaped the 1923 destruction and later returned. No Blaschka-specific return record has yet been recovered.
merge_policy.current_survival_guard: No current public Kahaku object record explicitly identifying a Blaschka model was recovered in this pass. Kahaku itself warns that its public integrated database represents only part of its holdings. Public search silence is therefore not evidence of absence.
merge_policy.2017_exhibition_guard: Kahaku displayed Blaschka glass models in the 2017 British Natural History Museum exhibition, but the exhibition explicitly consisted of treasures selected from London's Natural History Museum. Those displayed objects are loan evidence and must not be used as proof that Kahaku's nineteenth-century Tokyo models survive.
merge_policy.radiolaria_guard: A 1920 Rudolf Blaschka letter says, in the specific context of the later Radiolaria series, that 'The Japanese Museum has none of them.' This is negative evidence for Radiolaria only and cannot be expanded into a statement that Japan or the Tokyo Educational Museum possessed no other Blaschka invertebrate models.
merge_policy.model_count_guard: No exact number of models in the Tokyo order is currently recovered. Monetary amounts, delivery-book references and catalogue-mailing quantities are never converted into physical model counts.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No modern object identifier, accession number, Blaschka catalogue number, shipping mark or local museum number is invented.

summary.key_result: Tokyo is now a strong transaction node and an unusually precise provenance problem. Workshop-side evidence proves direct curator orders and an 1883 filled shipment, while the 1884 account fixes a 1000-Mark monetary entry and the 1885 row probably closes or advances the same account through the numerically exact relation 1000 + 846 = 1846. The principal research problem is no longer whether Blaschka models went to Tokyo, but which side of the 1889–1890 custody fork they entered. That fork determines whether the models were destroyed with the Tokyo Museum in 1923 or potentially survived in the Imperial Museum/Tensanbu system and moved again after the earthquake.

tokyo_educational_museum_kahaku_blaschka.institution_current: National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo
historical_context: Educational Museum established under that name in Ueno in 1877.
Renamed Tokyo Educational Museum in 1881.
The museum combined educational objects, scientific apparatus, specimens and public/teacher-oriented instructional functions.
Museum scale was reduced in 1888; many natural-history specimens were transferred to the Imperial Museum in 1889–1890.
The institution moved to Yushima and became attached to the Higher Normal School in 1889.
The later Tokyo Museum lost all facilities and specimens then in its custody in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake.
Natural-history collections from the Imperial Museum were transferred to the Tokyo Museum in 1925.
The institutional line ultimately became the National Museum of Nature and Science.

network_implications.transaction_pattern: Unlike dealer-mediated Ward/Frič nodes, Tokyo currently appears as a direct educational-institution/client relationship with a named museum-side official and workshop-side accounts.

comparison_with_India.Calcutta: direct institutional purchaser + 1883 delivery-book shipment + Superintendent orders + Hamburg route
comparison_with_India.Jeypore: Hendley/Damon order + made-to-order production + Trieste–Bombay freight + numbered 1895 display
comparison_with_India.Tokyo: curator orders + 1883 filled shipment + 1884/1885 multi-year financial account + later state collection reorganization
comparison_with_India.interpretive_value: The three Asian nodes expose different administrative and logistical mechanisms by which the same Dresden workshop entered colonial and national educational-museum systems.

network_implications.Meiji_educational_object_significance: Tokyo places Blaschka models inside a museum explicitly involved in the national diffusion of scientific apparatus and specimens during the shift toward object-based teaching.
network_implications.custodial_significance: The Tokyo case is especially valuable for distinguishing institutional lineage from physical object lineage: the modern museum descends from the purchaser, but nineteenth-century natural-history objects may have crossed to another museum before returning or being dispersed.
network_implications.next_institutional_action: After duplicate audit, prioritize the historical National Museum of Victoria / Melbourne node. Rudolf Blaschka's later correspondence explicitly remembers models reaching a museum in Melbourne, and a Melbourne module would extend the non-European network while testing whether a direct workshop shipment can be joined to surviving Museums Victoria records.
