content.title: Blaschka Tufts University / Barnum Museum of Natural History: P. T. Barnum's 1885 purchase, 1962–1965 Corning loan correspondence, flood-and-fire false-loss history, 10-model 2007 return, 2008 Dana Biology Lab rediscovery, conservation, and the 22/24 current-count conflict
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka glass marine-invertebrate models at Tufts University, historically associated with the Barnum Museum of Natural History and now held by the Tufts Archival Research Center (TARC). Current TARC research states that some Blaschka sea creatures came to Tufts in 1885, purchased by P. T. Barnum for exhibition in the Barnum Museum. The later custody history is unusually well documented: Tufts/Corning correspondence began by 1962 and includes a 1965 letter from Barnum Museum curator Russell Carpenter asking the Corning Museum of Glass to take Tufts' Blaschka models on loan. Corning's 1972 flood damaged both documentation and some stored objects, while the 1975 Barnum Hall fire caused the models remaining at Tufts to be presumed destroyed. In 2006 Andrew McClellan rediscovered the archival correspondence; in 2007 Tufts requested the return of 10 loaned models, Corning located all 10, conserved them, and hand-delivered them to Tufts in December. In 2008 additional Blaschka invertebrates surfaced in a Dana Biology Lab supply closet and were transferred to the archives; Stephen Koob also cleaned/restored these. Tufts reported roughly two dozen models in 2009, exactly 24 in a 2022 Tufts Now article, and exactly 22 in TARC's July 2025 institutional account. This module preserves that 24-to-22 public-count conflict unresolved rather than inferring loss, deaccession, reclassification, counting-method changes, or error. The exact original 1885 order count, vendor route, invoice, model list, local accession/object numbers, and exact 2026 count remain open.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 46 after a post-Liverpool global large-museum screen. Carnegie Museum of Natural History was again confirmed to hold/loan Blaschka models, but the public record still did not isolate a Blaschka acquisition transaction, exact count, or local object identifiers. Tufts crossed the promotion threshold much more strongly: a current institutional archive gives an 1885 named purchaser and purpose; Corning independently documents a 10-object loan-return/conservation event; Tufts preserves the 1965 archival letter and 2006 rediscovery; the Dana Biology Lab contributes a separate surviving subset; and TARC provides a recent exact holdings count. Duplicate audit of the mounted active 06 v3 and standalone modules 41–45 found no Tufts/Barnum Museum Blaschka node.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No Tufts University / Barnum Museum of Natural History / Tufts Archival Research Center Blaschka standalone node was found in the mounted active 06 v3 or standalone modules 41–45.
merge_policy.institutional_identity_guard: The historical museum was the Barnum Museum of Natural History at Tufts College; the building became Barnum Hall and was destroyed by fire in 1975. The present Blaschka custodial endpoint captured here is Tufts Archival Research Center (TARC), with a secondary historical custody strand through the Department of Biology / Dana Laboratory.
merge_policy.1885_purchase_guard: TARC's 2025 institutional article explicitly states that some Blaschka sea creatures came to Tufts in 1885 and were purchased by P. T. Barnum for exhibition in the Barnum Museum of Natural History. This closes purchaser, year and purpose at collection level.
merge_policy.original_count_guard: No recovered source states the exact number of Blaschka models in Barnum's 1885 purchase. The later figures 10, ~24, 24 and 22 must not be back-projected as the original order count.
merge_policy.Barnum_direct_order_guard: P. T. Barnum is a verified purchaser/benefactor, but no recovered invoice or order letter establishes whether the Blaschka models were purchased directly from Dresden, through Ward's Natural Science Establishment, another dealer, or a mixed museum-supply order.
merge_policy.Ward_context_guard: Ward had a documented role in building the broader Barnum Museum zoological collection and was a North American agent for European suppliers including the Blaschkas in this period, but the Tufts Blaschka transaction is not assigned to Ward without a dedicated invoice/order record.
merge_policy.Barnum_employment_guard: Barnum's 1885 purchase must not be converted into a claim that Leopold or Rudolf Blaschka personally worked for P. T. Barnum or his circus.
merge_policy.taxon_examples_guard: TARC names a Portuguese man o' war, snail, cuttlefish and sea cucumber as examples. These are representative anchors, not a complete 1885 or current catalogue.
merge_policy.Physalia_name_guard: TARC's 2025 image caption uses 'Physalia pelagica' for the Portuguese Man of War; Corning's 2016 article identifies the returned/displayed object as Physalia physalis. Both published name layers are preserved and no silent taxonomic correction is imposed.
merge_policy.1962_1965_loan_guard: Corning states that the Carpenter–Perrot correspondence documenting the permanent-loan transition dates back to 1962; TARC and the 2009 Tufts Journal focus on a 1965 Carpenter letter asking Corning to take the models. The safest reconstruction is loan correspondence beginning by 1962 with a clearly documented 1965 letter. Exact physical transfer date remains unresolved unless registrar paperwork is recovered.
merge_policy.permanent_loan_guard: Corning describes the arrangement as a 'permanent loan'. This is historical terminology for custody and does not transfer ownership from Tufts.
merge_policy.loan_count_guard: In 2007 Tufts explicitly requested return of 10 Blaschka models. Corning located nine in storage and identified the tenth, a Portuguese Man O' War, as already on gallery display. All 10 were returned. This proves the size of the Corning-loan subset recovered in 2007, not the total Tufts collection.
merge_policy.1972_flood_guard: Corning's 1972 flood damaged loan documentation and reached the second floor of the offsite storage facility holding the Tufts models. Corning reports repair of pieces affected by the flood. No model-specific flood-damage list or loss count is inferred.
merge_policy.1975_fire_guard: The Blaschka models returned from Corning did not literally survive the 1975 Barnum Hall fire in situ: they were off site at Corning. The fire instead erased institutional memory/documentation and led Tufts to presume the collection destroyed.
merge_policy.false_loss_guard: The post-1975 belief that the Blaschka collection had burned is treated as an archival/custodial misidentification, not evidence of physical destruction.
merge_policy.2006_rediscovery_guard: Andrew McClellan's 2006 discovery was documentary: he found archival correspondence pointing to Corning custody. It was not the physical discovery of the models themselves.
merge_policy.2007_return_guard: Corning independently documents a Tufts request for 10 models in 2007 and a complete 10-model return after identification and conservation; the 2009 Tufts Journal dates the hand-delivery to December 2007.
merge_policy.2008_Dana_guard: Additional Blaschka invertebrates were found in a Dana Biology Lab supply closet in 2008 and transferred to the archives. The recovered public sources do not state an exact Dana-subset count; no arithmetic subtraction from later total counts is used to create one.
merge_policy.conservation_guard: Stephen Koob/Corning conserved the 10 Corning-return models and also worked on the Dana Laboratory discoveries. Published treatment discussion includes repair, careful dry cleaning, and sensitivity to natural glues and painted surfaces; it is not converted into identical treatment histories for every object.
merge_policy.natural_glue_guard: Koob's 2009 explanation describes animal, fish and rabbit-skin glues as examples of period natural adhesives and explains age-related brittleness. This is a technical interpretation of the Tufts pieces, not a universal recipe assignment to every Blaschka model.
merge_policy.2009_count_guard: The 2009 Tufts Journal describes 'some two dozen' objects. This is approximate and does not establish an exact 24-object count.
merge_policy.2022_24_guard: Tufts Now explicitly states 24 glass marine-invertebrate models in 2022. It is a dated institutional count and is not silently overwritten.
merge_policy.2025_22_guard: TARC explicitly states 22 glass invertebrates in July 2025. This is the latest exact institutional count recovered and is used as the latest count layer, not as a guaranteed August 2026 physical inventory.
merge_policy.24_to_22_conflict_guard: The reduction from the published 24 in 2022 to 22 in TARC's 2025 account remains unexplained. No claim is made that two models were lost, broken, deaccessioned, reclassified, excluded from a revised count, or double-counted previously.
merge_policy.current_2026_guard: The TARC page remains a current institutional source, but its exact count statement is dated July 2025. Exact August 2026 survival count is therefore null; 22 is stored as the last exact institutionally stated count recovered.
merge_policy.storage_guard: TARC states that the 22 models are in climate-controlled storage and only rarely brought out because of fragility. This supports current custodial/storage practice at the time of the 2025 article, not permanent non-display.
merge_policy.2009_display_guard: The reunited Tufts collection was publicly displayed in the Tisch Library main lobby through 11 March 2009. That historical display does not imply current display.
merge_policy.TARC_archival_object_path_guard: The 2025 TARC article links the Portuguese Man of War and snail to ArchivesSpace archival-object paths 16763 and 16770 within the Department of Biology Records. These are archive-database page identifiers, not Blaschka commercial catalogue numbers or physical-object accession numbers.
merge_policy.local_object_id_guard: No Tufts physical-object accession/registration numbers, Blaschka catalogue numbers, Ward catalogue numbers, box numbers for individual models, or 1885 invoice numbers are invented.

summary.key_result: Tufts is an unusually complete custodial-survival node even though its original 1885 invoice remains missing. A named benefactor purchased the models for a named museum purpose; a later curator deliberately externalized custody to a specialist glass museum when the objects had lost teaching utility and Barnum Hall was considered unsafe; that off-site custody meant the Corning subset was absent when Barnum Hall burned in 1975. Corning's own 1972 flood then damaged records and some models, creating a second provenance rupture, but registrar copies and conservation work allowed all 10 loaned objects to be identified and returned in 2007. A second Tufts subset surfaced independently in Dana Laboratory in 2008. The principal remaining first-order problems are the exact 1885 order route/count and the unexplained institutional count shift from 24 in 2022 to 22 in 2025.

network_implications.Barnum_museum_value: Tufts connects Blaschka procurement to P. T. Barnum's attempt to build a systematic teaching museum rather than a spectacle-only collection.
network_implications.custody_value: The node demonstrates that custody transfer can itself be a preservation mechanism: specialist off-site storage removed the 10-model subset from the building that later burned.
network_implications.provenance_failure_value: The same custody move also generated provenance failure. Fire erased Tufts' institutional memory of the loan while Corning's flood damaged the counterpart paperwork, producing decades in which ownership and object identity were effectively invisible.
network_implications.disaster_comparison_value: Tufts offers an unusually precise contrast to museums where fire is treated only as a possible loss mechanism: here the fire created a false-loss narrative, while the physically relevant disaster for the loaned models was Corning's flood.
network_implications.teaching_to_archive_value: The models moved from active biology teaching to obsolete/historical objects, then to specialist glass-museum custody, and finally to archival climate-controlled preservation with occasional research/display use.
network_implications.count_method_value: The 24-to-22 institutional count shift makes Tufts a useful reminder that even recent 'current count' figures require dated source layers and cannot be flattened into a single timeless survival number.
network_implications.next_institutional_action: For module 47 resume the global major-institution screen. Carnegie Museum of Natural History remains verified but should still wait for a Blaschka-specific acquisition/count/local-ID breakthrough. Prefer another uncaptured institution with an exact transaction or current object register; alternatively use the 1880s Ward/Barnum network to test another university museum only when a completed Blaschka acquisition can be separated from the broader Ward zoological supply.

content.title: Blaschka UCL Grant Museum: Lankester 1890 catalogue layer, Science Museum 1925–1927 transfer layer, numbered objects, teaching use and current display
content.scope: Deep capture of the Grant Museum Blaschka collection with strict separation of the Lankester-era 1890 catalogue layer and the later Science Museum deaccession-transfer layer, preservation of UCL accession and alternative numbers, eight publicly named accession anchors, model descriptions, teaching-use evidence, exhibition/display history, cautious Ward/Blaschka model-type crosswalks, and explicit catalogue/export gaps.
content.target_selection_reason: Module 21 identified UCL as one of only two concretely named institutional recipients in the Science Museum 1925–1927 dispersal. UCL also has an independent Lankester-era Blaschka layer, making it essential to distinguish repeated commercial model types from actual transferred physical objects.

merge_policy.lankester_catalogue_guard: UCL states that twenty models appear in the 1890 printed catalogue and suggests Lankester ordered them for teaching. A separate UCL institutional-history article warns that Lankester's catalogue can include labels for specimens he wanted to acquire as well as specimens that actually existed. Therefore '20' is retained as a catalogue-appearance count, not silently promoted to an exact acquisition or survival count.
merge_policy.remaining_models_guard: UCL says the remaining models entered from the Science Museum during 1925–1927, but the number of remaining models is not published on the current highlight page.
merge_policy.shared_model_type_guard: A UCL and Cardiff object can represent the same Blaschka commercial model type while having completely different physical provenance. Model-type equivalence is never converted into an object-transfer claim.
merge_policy.alternative_number_scheme_guard: UCL Alternative Number values such as 10846, D524, 15219, D502 and 438 are preserved raw. None is interpreted as a Ward/Blaschka catalogue number unless UCL or another primary source explicitly identifies its scheme.
merge_policy.current_display_guard: The current UCL highlight page supplies a collection-level display location; it does not identify every displayed accession.
merge_policy.teaching_evidence_guard: Collection-level claims that models were acquired for teaching are separated from object-level evidence such as the 1911 notebook illustration of LDUCZ-C182.
merge_policy.public_catalogue_guard: UCL Collections Online is described as ongoing/not comprehensive. Failure to recover a full export is not evidence that records do not exist.

content.title: Blaschka University of Liège / Aquarium-Muséum: 1886 order of 77, 1926 register 58, 1990 register 49, restoration cohort 37, TréZOOr display and protected heritage
content.scope: Deep capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass-model collection of the Université de Liège / Aquarium-Muséum. The module reconstructs Édouard Van Beneden's 1886 direct workshop order of 77 models selected from the 1885 Blaschka catalogue; the exact protected-heritage chronology from order on 24 September 1886 to delivery on 26 May 1887; later register checkpoints of 58 pieces in 1926 and 49 in 1990; the conservation campaign in which 37 pieces were reported as restorable; IRPA analysis of glass, adhesives and pigments; the transition from teaching aid to protected museum heritage; current TréZOOr exhibition conditions; one direct local inventory anchor R.E. 11215 (Renilla muelleri); and controlled external comparative catalogue candidates.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after a parallel global audit of Guernsey, Leicester, the Hunterian and non-UK nodes. A tempting Wisconsin node was rejected after File Library duplicate audit showed it had already been deeply captured. Liège was then selected because it exposes an unusually complete institutional lifecycle: named purchaser, exact order and delivery dates, original catalogue-based quantity, two later register counts, a defined restoration cohort, scientific materials analysis, a local inventory number, a legally protected 49-object ensemble and a current purpose-built permanent display.

merge_policy.count_ontology_guard: 77 (1886 order), 58 (1926 register), 49 (1990 register / 2017 protected ensemble / current official display claim), 37 (restoration cohort reported in 2012), and 39 (displayable/visible claim around 2014–2017) are distinct documentary quantities and must not be silently reconciled.
merge_policy.loss_arithmetic_guard: 77−58=19, 58−49=9, and 77−49=28 are arithmetic differences only. No difference is converted into a documented loss event or cause.
merge_policy.restoration_count_guard: The 2012 ULiège account explicitly says 37 of the 49 remaining pieces were restored and describes the others as irreparably damaged. A 2026 ULiège biography more generally says the 49 displayed examples 'have been restored'. The later wording is preserved as a current display statement and is not used to invent an undocumented second campaign or to erase the explicit 37-object treatment cohort.
merge_policy.39_display_guard: A 2014 public account and a June 2017 ULiège cultural feature state that 39 were visible / in condition to be exhibited. This is a displayability checkpoint, not a survival total and not a legal collection count.
merge_policy.49_heritage_guard: The Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles protected movable-heritage inventory and 7 June 2017 classification define the protected treasure as an ensemble of 49 glass models. This is a legal heritage-unit count and does not by itself prove that all 49 had identical conservation status.
merge_policy.order_vs_delivery_guard: 24 September 1886 is the official protected-heritage order date; 26 May 1887 is the delivery date. Generic sources saying 'acquired in 1886' are retained as shorthand but do not override the exact two-date chronology.
merge_policy.1885_catalogue_guard: The current ULiège Van Beneden biography states that the 77 models were selected from the Blaschka catalogue of 1885. External catalogue numbers from the NMW/Meechan spreadsheet are candidate concordances only unless matched to a Liège inventory/register row.
merge_policy.direct_order_guard: Official ULiège sources say Van Beneden ordered the models from the Blaschka workshops. No Frič, Ward or other dealer is inserted into the 1886 Liège transaction without direct evidence.
merge_policy.renilla_identity_guard: Current official ULiège identifies R.E. 11215 as Renilla muelleri. An external comparative spreadsheet lists Liège for Renilla violacea, Blaschka catalogue no. 12. These records are kept separate unless a Liège catalogue or label explicitly establishes synonymy/object identity.
merge_policy.named_media_guard: Bougainvillia, Porpita, Physalia and Renilla are direct named photographic subjects on the 2012 ULiège collection-history page. Only Renilla has a public local inventory number in the sources recovered here.
merge_policy.IRPA_scope_guard: IRPA analyses are recorded at collection/project level: glass, adhesives and pigments were analyzed to guide conservation. No exact analytical composition, sample number or object-to-sample mapping is invented from summaries.
merge_policy.environmental_display_guard: Current ULiège describes hermetically sealed cases with LED and fibre-optic lighting to limit heat. No relative-humidity or temperature setpoint is inferred.
merge_policy.comparative_spreadsheet_guard: NMW/Meechan Model Locations rows are comparative research notes, not Liège accession records. NMW accession numbers, Cardiff condition fields, Science Museum provenance and Cardiff display histories are not transferred to Liège.
merge_policy.current_inventory_guard: One public Liège inventory number is recovered. The full 49-object protected-ensemble inventory and the original 77-order row list are not publicly reconstructed in this pass.

content.title: Blaschka University of Michigan / Museum of Natural History / Museum of Zoology: 1890s teaching-model stratum, 1928 Harvard University gift, approximately 78 fragmentary marine invertebrates, 2017 Museum of Vitreous Ecology reunification, Object Lessons 16-object checklist, and post-Ruthven custody gap
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the University of Michigan Blaschka glass marine-invertebrate collection. The strongest U-M source sequence now distinguishes at least two acquisition strata. An official 2017 Object Lessons checklist states that some Blaschka glass creatures came to U-M in the 1890s as teaching models, while others were gifted to the Museum of Zoology by Harvard University on the occasion of the opening of the Ruthven Museums Building in 1928. A separate 2017 curatorial account describes the collection as approximately 78 marine-invertebrate models, many surviving only as fragments, and says the first group supported the scientific apparatus and teaching of biology while a second set arrived for the inaugural exhibition in the new University Museums building. That account further advances a broader curatorial hypothesis that the specimens seem to derive from the Harvard Museum of Comparative Zoology / Louis Agassiz Blaschka collection; this hypothesis is preserved without collapsing the two acquisition strata or treating Louis Agassiz as the 1928 donor. The formal 1928 donor named by the U-M exhibition checklist is Harvard University. In spring 2017, The Museum of Vitreous Ecology brought into one temporary display all remaining Michigan glass models that were not then on permanent display, emphasizing their fragmentary state. Later that year, Object Lessons, the final public exhibition in the Ruthven Museums Building before its December 2017 closure, displayed a named 16-object Blaschka teaching-model selection. The old Ruthven display state cannot be projected into the current Biological Sciences Building museum, which opened in 2019; no current U-M page recovered in this pass gives an exact 2026 survival count, complete object register, local accession numbers, or current display/storage distribution.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 47 after the module-46 instruction to resume the global major-institution screen without promoting Carnegie Museum of Natural History absent a stronger transaction/count/local-ID breakthrough. Michigan crossed the threshold because its own 2017 research gives a collection-scale count, physical-condition statement, two acquisition strata, a named 1928 intermuseum donor/recipient relationship, and two substantial exhibition/documentation events. The Object Lessons checklist adds 16 named physical exhibition anchors. Duplicate audit of the mounted active 06 v3 and standalone modules 41–46 found no Ann Arbor / University of Michigan Blaschka institutional node.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone University of Michigan / Ann Arbor / Museum of Natural History / Museum of Zoology Blaschka node was found in active 06 v3 or standalone modules 41–46. Generic occurrences of 'Museum of Zoology' elsewhere in the backend do not constitute a Michigan Blaschka node.
merge_policy.institutional_identity_guard: The pre-1913 natural-history museum, the post-1913 Museum of Zoology, the post-1956 public Exhibit Museum, and the present University of Michigan Museum of Natural History are related but administratively distinct layers. The 1928 gift is explicitly to the Museum of Zoology; 2017 exhibition labels attribute the Blaschka material to the Museum of Natural History. The exact administrative transfer between research-museum and public-exhibit custody is not silently reconstructed.
merge_policy.two_strata_guard: The best 2017 U-M checklist explicitly distinguishes some models arriving in the 1890s as teaching models from others gifted by Harvard University in 1928. These strata are preserved separately. Neither stratum's exact quantity is known.
merge_policy.2016_preliminary_history_guard: A 2016 U-M faculty-research notice summarized the models as acquired by Michigan from Harvard in 1928. The later 2017 curatorial work refines this into an earlier 1890s teaching-model group plus a 1928 Harvard gift. The 2016 statement is retained as a preliminary research state rather than used to erase the earlier stratum.
merge_policy.1890s_guard: The Object Lessons checklist says '1890s'; no exact year is assigned. The separate 2017 phrase that the creatures first came to Michigan about 125 years earlier is treated as rounded exhibition prose and is not converted arithmetically into 1892.
merge_policy.1890s_route_guard: No purchase invoice, donor name, dealer, direct Dresden order, Ward record, price, model list, or Museum accession entry has yet been recovered for the 1890s teaching-model stratum. It is therefore not automatically assigned to Harvard.
merge_policy.1928_Harvard_gift_guard: The official Object Lessons checklist states that a second group was gifted to the Museum of Zoology by Harvard University on the occasion of the opening of the Ruthven Museums Building in 1928. This is strong receiving-side evidence for an interinstitutional transfer; exact transfer date, object count, outgoing Harvard numbers, and incoming Michigan numbers remain unresolved.
merge_policy.1928_opening_guard: U-M history states that the University Museums Building was formally opened on 14 June 1928, while exhibits opened to the public in winter 1929. The Blaschka gift is associated with the 1928 building-opening occasion, but no exact receipt date or claim that the models were physically exhibited on 14 June is made.
merge_policy.Louis_Agassiz_wording_guard: The Museum of Vitreous Ecology text says all specimens 'seem' to have been bestowed from 'Louis Agassiz’s Blaschka collection' at Harvard MCZ. This is preserved as a curatorial provenance hypothesis/collection-lineage formulation. It is not converted into a claim that Louis Agassiz personally executed the 1928 gift. The formal donor in the Object Lessons checklist is Harvard University.
merge_policy.Harvard_MCZ_origin_guard: Harvard MCZ's current institutional history confirms a large Blaschka invertebrate collection acquired in the 1870s and 1880s, mostly through Henry Ward. That history provides a plausible source collection for the 1928 gift but does not publicly identify which MCZ objects left for Michigan. No Harvard current model number is transferred into Michigan.
merge_policy.all_from_Harvard_hypothesis_guard: The 2017 Museum of Vitreous Ecology broad hypothesis that all Michigan specimens seem to derive from the Harvard/Agassiz collection is kept distinct from the stronger Object Lessons statement that only 'others'—contrasted with the 1890s teaching models—were gifted by Harvard in 1928. The earlier stratum's Harvard provenance remains unproven.
merge_policy.approx_78_guard: Approximately 78 is the 2017 U-M collection-scale count. It is not an exact object inventory and is not projected as the 2026 total.
merge_policy.fragment_guard: U-M states that many of the approximately 78 models survived only in fragments. A fragmentary object may not map one-to-one to an original model, and no intact-versus-fragment count is synthesized.
merge_policy.model_component_guard: Physical model, broken component, fragment cluster, exhibition unit, commercial catalogue type, and museum registration record are kept separate. No current total is generated by counting individual glass fragments.
merge_policy.Vitreous_Ecology_scope_guard: The Museum of Vitreous Ecology, 24 March–15 May 2017, is described by its curators as exhibiting all remaining Michigan glass models not then on permanent display. The exact temporary-exhibition count is not stated and is not calculated as approximately 78 minus an unknown permanent-display subset.
merge_policy.2017_permanent_display_guard: The March 2017 curatorial account states that some Blaschka models remained in the Ruthven Museum of Natural History evolution display and were intermixed with plastic models without being marked as historical artifacts. This is a dated 2017 Ruthven-building status only.
merge_policy.Object_Lessons_16_guard: The official Object Lessons teaching-model checklist names 16 Blaschka exhibition entries. Sixteen is the checklist selection for that exhibition section, not the total Michigan holdings, the 1928 gift count, or the 1890s stratum count.
merge_policy.Object_Lessons_position_code_guard: Codes 03n through 03ü are exhibit/checklist position codes. They are not Michigan accession numbers, UMMZ catalogue numbers, Harvard MCZ numbers, Blaschka commercial catalogue numbers, or evidence of original order sequence.
merge_policy.Object_Lessons_taxon_guard: Taxon spellings and identifications are preserved as printed in the U-M checklist, including unidentified entries and historical or possibly outdated spellings. Modern taxonomy is not silently substituted.
merge_policy.maker_date_guard: The Object Lessons checklist labels the group 'Leopold & Rudolph Blaschka, 1880s'. This is an exhibition-level production-date label and is not converted into individual manufacture years for the 16 models.
merge_policy.2017_object_identity_guard: The 16 Object Lessons names are secure exhibition anchors, but no public local accession numbers were printed. They are not automatically cross-walked to Harvard MCZ records or Blaschka catalogue numbers by taxon alone.
merge_policy.late_twentieth_century_storage_guard: The 2017 curatorial account states that newer visualization/learning technologies displaced most glass miniatures into storage. No exact withdrawal year, storage location, or count is inferred.
merge_policy.2017_Ruthven_closure_guard: Object Lessons ran 13 October–30 December 2017 as the final public exhibition in the Ruthven Museums Building. The old Museum of Natural History closed to the public at the end of December 2017 before its move.
merge_policy.2019_move_guard: The present U-M Museum of Natural History opened in the Biological Sciences Building on 14 April 2019. The module does not assume that the 2017 Blaschka display configuration, or every object then associated with UMMNH, transferred into the new permanent galleries.
merge_policy.current_2026_guard: Current U-M pages establish the Museum of Natural History's active Biological Sciences Building home but the current exhibit pages recovered in this pass do not give a Blaschka total or explicit current Blaschka display statement. Therefore exact 2026 total, display count, storage count, and owning/registration unit remain unresolved.
merge_policy.local_identifier_guard: No Michigan physical-object accession/registration number is invented. The recovered public sources provide exhibition codes and taxon names, not collection-management identifiers.
merge_policy.commercial_catalogue_guard: No Blaschka/Ward catalogue number is assigned to a Michigan object solely from taxon resemblance or Harvard comparative records.

summary.key_result: Michigan is a major intermuseum-transfer and teaching-technology node. Its collection was not formed in a single transaction: U-M's own mature 2017 account distinguishes nineteenth-century teaching models from a 1928 Harvard University gift to the Museum of Zoology. Approximately 78 models or fragmentary model remains were recognized in 2017, and two exhibitions then converted obsolete teaching apparatus into explicitly historical objects. The main remaining gaps are unusually precise: the provenance of the 1890s stratum, the model-by-model Harvard-to-Michigan 1928 transfer list, Michigan local accession numbers, and the post-2017 custody/display state after the move from Ruthven to the Biological Sciences Building.

historical_context: The University of Michigan's natural-history collections originated with the university's nineteenth-century Cabinet/Museum of Natural History.
The Museum of Natural History was formally renamed the Museum of Zoology in 1913 after zoological collections had become dominant.
The new University Museums Building was completed and formally opened in 1928; it housed Zoology, Herbarium, Anthropology and Paleontology plus exhibition space.
The building later became known as the Alexander G. Ruthven Museums Building.
The public Exhibit Museum was formally created in 1956 and later renamed the University of Michigan Museum of Natural History.
The Ruthven Museum of Natural History closed to the public at the end of December 2017.
The Museum of Natural History opened in the Biological Sciences Building on 14 April 2019.

content.title: Blaschka University of Rostock Zoological Collection: Franz Eilhard Schulze acquisition, probable 1865–1873 window, nine surviving models from a formerly larger group, named object anchors and later public exhibition
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka glass-model holdings in the Zoological Collection of the University of Rostock. The module records the University’s attribution of procurement to Franz Eilhard Schulze, constrains the likely acquisition to Schulze’s Rostock zoological tenure without converting that inference into an exact transaction date, preserves the current count of nine surviving Blaschka models against the statement that the original group was substantially larger, captures eight named photographed model anchors, and records later teaching/public exhibition contexts. Exact order date, original quantity, invoice, catalogue crosswalk and local inventory numbers remain unresolved.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected after Utrecht was excluded by prior project work and after a duplicate audit showed that Vienna had already been treated as a substantive node in earlier backend logic. Rostock is a genuinely distinct uncaptured institutional node. It is especially valuable because the University itself identifies Franz Eilhard Schulze as the purchaser/procurer, while an independent scientific-collections register reports nine survivors from an originally much larger group. Schulze’s Rostock tenure creates a plausible early 1865–1873 acquisition window, potentially placing the collection among the earlier German university purchases.

merge_policy.Schulze_procurer_guard: The University of Rostock explicitly states that F. E. Schulze procured Blaschka animal models. This is treated as collection-level provenance.
merge_policy.acquisition_window_guard: Franz Eilhard Schulze worked in Rostock from 1864/1865 to 1873 and founded the Zoological Institute in 1871. Because the current collection history attributes procurement to him, 1865–1873 is encoded as a probable acquisition window only. No exact purchase year is imposed without invoice, accession register or correspondence.
merge_policy.nine_survivor_guard: The German scientific-collections portal states that nine Blaschka glass models survive and that there were originally 'weit mehr' (far more). Nine is therefore a current/recent surviving-object count, not the original acquisition count.
merge_policy.original_count_guard: No original Blaschka quantity is recovered. The phrase 'originally far more' is preserved qualitatively and is not converted into an estimated number.
merge_policy.named_media_guard: Eight named models are documented through the Wikimedia Commons category for the Rostock collection. These are media/object anchors only; they do not establish local inventory numbers, acquisition batch or condition.
merge_policy.display_guard: The 2017 university/zoo exhibition and 2001 collection presentation establish later public interpretation of the Blaschka material. They do not prove continuous permanent display.
merge_policy.current_access_guard: The Zoological Collection remains a teaching/research collection with parts accessible to the public. No claim is made that all nine Blaschka models are currently on permanent display.
merge_policy.local_identifier_guard: No public Rostock inventory/accession identifiers for individual Blaschka objects were recovered in this pass. Synthetic identifiers are not created.
merge_policy.taxon_spelling_guard: Historical or media-source taxon spellings are preserved as found. Modern taxonomic synonymy is not silently substituted.
merge_policy.cross_institution_guard: Schulze’s later careers in Graz and Berlin, and his broader relationship with marine zoology, are not used to transfer Rostock objects or transactions into those institutions.

content.title: Blaschka Vassar College Natural History Museum / Biology Department: 1887 purchase, William Buck Dwight-era teaching collection, Stephen Koob conservation, Swift Hall renovation rescue, Jelly Fish no. 229, 2016 science-art re-display, and archival purchase-register targets
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of Vassar College's Blaschka glass invertebrate models. Vassar's own Warthin Museum newsletter states that the Biology Department's Blaschka invertebrate models were purchased in 1887 as part of the college's natural-history collection and records an arrangement with Stephen Koob of the Corning Museum of Glass to repair and restore them. The purchase falls within William Buck Dwight's tenure as Professor of Natural History and curator of the Vassar College Museum of Natural History, but no recovered source yet names Dwight as purchaser or selector. A 2013 Vassar student-newspaper account of the Vassar College Artifacts Project reports that glass replicas of jellyfish and other organisms by the Blaschkas were saved during the renovation of Swift Hall. In 2016 Vassar's official Art at Vassar publication reproduced a physical model captioned 'Jelly Fish no. 229', glass on metal mount, 'Purchased for Vassar College, 1887'. The number 229 is retained as a published historical/model number, not a Vassar accession number; an independent Cornell authenticated Blaschka register identifies commercial Blaschka no. 229 as Cotylorhiza borbonica, now Cotylorhiza tuberculata, but the Vassar object is not silently assigned that taxon without confirmation of the numbering namespace or local label. A 2018 Vassar institutional invitation still states that Vassar has a collection of invertebrates created by the Blaschkas. The exact original 1887 model count, vendor or dealer, price, invoice, complete taxon list, local accession/registration numbers, Koob treatment list, and exact August 2026 survival/display/storage count remain unresolved. Vassar's current archival finding aids make the acquisition unusually recoverable: the College Archives explicitly preserve Natural History Department reports for 1887–1891, a cabinet catalogue with agreements/documents/correspondence, and separate Natural History Museum records containing inventories, specimen/model descriptions, purchase records, and later invertebrate inventories.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 49 after module 48 required another uncaptured node with a dated acquisition or transfer plus surviving physical objects, rather than promoting Carnegie Museum of Natural History without a Blaschka-specific transaction/count/local-ID breakthrough. Vassar crossed the threshold because the college itself supplies the exact purchase year 1887, modern conservation evidence, modern physical survival, a named/numbered 2016 model, and a 2018 plural collection statement. The Vassar archive additionally preserves precisely dated Natural History Department reports spanning 1887 and collection/cabinet records likely capable of closing the remaining transaction fields. Duplicate searches of the active 06 v3 backend and standalone modules through 48 returned no Vassar Blaschka node.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Vassar College / Poughkeepsie Blaschka institutional node was found in the active 06 v3 backend or standalone modules 41–48. Vassar appears in broader Henry A. Ward museum-building history but not as a previously captured Blaschka collection.
merge_policy.institutional_identity_guard: The historical collection is the Vassar College Museum of Natural History / Natural History Department collection. Later objects and records became distributed across Biology, the Warthin Museum of Geology and Natural History, the Vassar College Artifacts Project, and other campus custodial contexts. These are related Vassar collection layers, not assumed to be one unchanged administrative unit.
merge_policy.1887_purchase_guard: Vassar's 2010 Warthin Museum newsletter explicitly states that the Biology Department's Blaschka invertebrate models were purchased in 1887 as part of the college's natural-history collection. This closes purchase year and institutional purpose at collection level.
merge_policy.original_count_guard: No recovered Vassar source gives the exact number of models purchased in 1887. Plural wording cannot be converted into an object count.
merge_policy.William_Buck_Dwight_guard: William Buck Dwight was Professor of Natural History and curator of the museum from 1878 to 1906, therefore the 1887 acquisition occurred during his curatorship. No source recovered in this pass explicitly says that Dwight selected, ordered, paid for, or received the Blaschka models; those roles remain open.
merge_policy.Ward_route_guard: Henry Augustus Ward had created Vassar's original natural-history cabinet in the 1860s, Vassar retained a long institutional relationship with Ward, and Ward later acted as a U.S. agent for European suppliers including the Blaschkas. These facts make Ward a strong route candidate, but no 1887 Vassar Blaschka invoice, Ward letter, delivery book row, or receipt was recovered. The 1887 transaction is therefore not assigned to Ward.
merge_policy.direct_Dresden_guard: No evidence recovered shows that Vassar ordered directly from Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka in Dresden. Direct workshop purchase and dealer-mediated purchase remain alternative hypotheses.
merge_policy.price_guard: No price, currency, packing charge, freight charge, insurance amount, or payment date for the 1887 Vassar purchase is reconstructed from other U.S. institutions.
merge_policy.Koob_project_guard: The Spring 2010 Warthin Museum newsletter says the museum facilitated an arrangement with Stephen Koob of the Corning Museum of Glass to repair and restore the Blaschka invertebrate models in Biology. The wording securely documents a conservation/restoration project or arrangement, but does not provide a model-by-model treatment list, exact treatment dates, count, condition grades, or confirmation that every Vassar model received treatment.
merge_policy.Koob_affiliation_guard: Stephen Koob is identified by the Vassar source as a glass restoration expert from the Corning Museum of Glass. No Corning accession or ownership of the Vassar models is implied.
merge_policy.2013_student_source_guard: The 2013 Miscellany News article is a Vassar student-newspaper source rather than a registrar record. It is used as evidence for the Vassar College Artifacts Project's rescue/preservation activity and the presence of Blaschka glass replicas during Swift Hall renovation, not for exact object counts, manufacture dates, or formal custody.
merge_policy.2013_date_error_guard: The 2013 student article describes the replicas as crafted in the 'early 20th century'. This conflicts with Vassar's own 1887 purchase statement and the 2016 model caption. The article's date phrase is treated as imprecise secondary description and is not used to redatethe historical acquisition.
merge_policy.Swift_Hall_guard: The 2013 article says Blaschka glass replicas were saved from renovation of Swift Hall. It does not establish how long the models had been in Swift Hall, whether all Vassar Blaschkas were there, or whether Swift was their formal registered storage location.
merge_policy.2016_model_guard: Vassar's official 2016 Art at Vassar publication physically illustrates and captions one model as 'Jelly Fish no. 229', glass on metal mount, purchased for Vassar College in 1887. This is a secure modern physical-object anchor.
merge_policy.229_namespace_guard: The caption's 'no. 229' is not called a Vassar accession number. Its numerical match to authenticated Blaschka commercial no. 229 makes the commercial/model-number interpretation strong, but the module retains the namespace as 'published historical/model number; likely Blaschka commercial number' pending local label or catalogue confirmation.
merge_policy.229_taxon_guard: Cornell's authenticated digital collection identifies Blaschka no. 229 as historical Cotylorhiza borbonica, current Cotylorhiza tuberculata, Fried Egg Jellyfish. The Vassar object is not assigned that identification solely from the number until Vassar documentation or morphology confirms that its 'no. 229' uses the Blaschka catalogue namespace.
merge_policy.229_local_ID_guard: No Vassar accession, registration, artifact-project, Biology, Warthin Museum, or Special Collections identifier for the 2016 jellyfish was printed in the recovered source. '229' must not be stored as a Vassar local accession number.
merge_policy.metal_mount_guard: The 2016 source explicitly describes the jellyfish as glass on metal mount. The mount is part of the published physical description; no inference is made about whether it is original, restored, or replacement.
merge_policy.2016_display_guard: The model appears in Vassar's 2016 science/art program and is associated with the campus-wide Vassar Sources / Integrated Science Commons context. This proves public institutional use in 2016, not permanent display after 2016.
merge_policy.2018_collection_guard: A Vassar institutional event invitation states that 'Vassar has a collection of invertebrates created by the Blaschkas.' This is a plural collection-level survival statement in 2018 but gives no count or custody location.
merge_policy.current_2026_guard: No current 2026 Vassar page recovered in this pass publishes an exact Blaschka count, complete register, condition survey, or current display/storage distribution. The latest explicit institutional collection-level statement recovered is 2018; exact August 2026 survival and display counts remain null.
merge_policy.1979_museum_phaseout_guard: Vassar's Natural History Museum records state that the museum began being phased out in 1979 and remaining collections were distributed among various institutions, with what remained moved to Ely Hall in 1992. This is a collection-wide history. No Blaschka transfer out of Vassar is inferred; modern Vassar evidence independently proves at least a subset remained.
merge_policy.1992_Ely_guard: The move of what remained of the Natural History Museum to Ely Hall in 1992 does not prove that every surviving Blaschka model moved there, especially because later Blaschka material is documented in Biology/Swift Hall contexts.
merge_policy.archive_finding_aid_guard: Vassar's finding aids identify highly relevant record groups but do not themselves state that a specific folder contains a Blaschka invoice. Archive targets are treated as prospective sources until the documents are inspected.
merge_policy.Natural_History_4_82_guard: Box 6, Folder 4.82 contains Natural History Department reports, 1887–1891. Its date overlap makes it the highest-priority receiving-side target, but no Blaschka-specific content is claimed before examination.
merge_policy.Natural_History_4_83_guard: Box 6, Folder 4.83 contains the Natural History Department catalog of cabinet, agreements, documents and correspondence. It is a likely provenance source but not assumed to contain the 1887 Blaschka order.
merge_policy.Ward_4_84_guard: Box 6, Folder 4.84 contains Natural History Department cabinet/mineralogy material and correspondence with Henry A. Ward, dated 1873. It demonstrates preserved Ward correspondence but predates the 1887 Blaschka purchase and cannot establish the 1887 route by itself.
merge_policy.later_museum_records_guard: The separately processed Vassar College Natural History Museum Records, 1866–1969, preserve vendors/collectors correspondence, inventories, descriptions of anatomical/biological specimens and models, loans and purchases, and an invertebrate inventory. These are archive opportunities, not evidence that every listed record concerns Blaschka.
merge_policy.invertebrate_inventory_guard: Folder 29 is described as 'Inventories of shells and other invertebrates, 1866, undated'. The undated component could be relevant to Blaschka objects but no item-level match is assumed.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No Vassar accession number, Ward invoice number, Blaschka number beyond the published 229 layer, local catalogue number, price, shipment mark, conservation treatment number, lost-object identifier, or current location is invented.

summary.key_result: Vassar is a strong acquisition-to-survival college-museum node. The purchase year is institutionally explicit (1887), physical models survived into the twenty-first century, Corning expertise was brought in for conservation, models were rescued during campus renovation, and Vassar publicly illustrated an 1887-purchased jellyfish numbered 229 in 2016 before reaffirming a plural Blaschka invertebrate collection in 2018. The remaining transaction gap is narrow and archival rather than structural: Vassar's own 1887–1891 Natural History reports and cabinet records are already identified.

historical_context: Vassar's trustees commissioned Henry Augustus Ward in 1862 to construct the college's foundational cabinet of natural history.
The Vassar College Museum of Natural History formally opened in 1875 after the collection moved from Main Building.
William Buck Dwight served as Professor of Natural History and curator from 1878 to 1906.
Vassar's Blaschka invertebrate models were purchased in 1887 as part of the natural-history collection.
In 1918 the Natural History Museum moved to the New England Building.
In 1973 Biology combined physiology, zoology and plant sciences in Olmsted Hall, creating new custodial pathways for older teaching collections.
The Natural History Museum began being phased out in 1979; remaining collections were dispersed, while a residual museum collection later moved to Ely Hall and reopened as the Warthin Museum in 2006.
Modern evidence proves that at least part of the Blaschka corpus remained at Vassar despite the broader museum dispersal.

network_implications.dated_US_college_purchase_value: Vassar adds another securely dated U.S. college purchase in 1887, but unlike Cornell or institutions with published Ward invoices, its intermediary route remains open. That makes it useful for testing whether Ward's U.S. agency was universal, merely common, or institution-specific by the late 1880s.
network_implications.Ward_relationship_without_transaction_va: Vassar had one of the oldest institutional relationships with Henry Ward in the United States. The absence so far of a Vassar-specific 1887 Ward document is methodologically useful: long-standing supplier relationships must not be converted automatically into provenance for later object classes.
network_implications.women_science_teaching_value: The models entered an institution whose Natural History Museum had explicitly been designed around first-hand scientific observation for women's higher education. The Blaschkas therefore sit inside a long Vassar material-teaching program, not only an aesthetic or museum-display history.
network_implications.dispersal_survival_value: The late-twentieth-century dismantling and dispersal of Vassar's Natural History Museum did not erase the whole Blaschka collection. Modern survival through Biology, renovation rescue and the Artifacts Project shows how teaching collections can persist across administrative dissolution through distributed campus custody.
network_implications.conservation_network_value: Stephen Koob's involvement links Vassar's local teaching collection to Corning's specialist glass-conservation network, creating a modern circulation of expertise even where the objects themselves apparently remained Vassar property.
network_implications.number_229_value: The published no. 229 creates an unusually promising object-level bridge. If the Vassar label confirms the Blaschka commercial namespace, one surviving object can be tied directly to the international catalogue system without inventing a local accession.
network_implications.archive_recoverability_value: Vassar is unusually tractable because the exact 1887 acquisition window overlaps a named archival folder. The next research step is document retrieval, not speculative network reconstruction.
network_implications.next_institutional_action: For module 50 resume the global major-museum screen and favor a node outside the recently dense U.S./UK college sequence. Promote a continental European, Latin American, Asian, or other major museum only if it yields a completed acquisition/transfer plus current physical holdings/local identifiers or a quantified surviving collection. Carnegie remains pending under the same threshold.

content.title: Blaschka World Museum Liverpool / Free Public Museum: 1887 Damon–Higgins order, manufacture, I.B.268 Hamburg shipment, 247/268-Mark accounting layers, sea-anemone rediscovery, and surviving Blaschka catalogue no. 93
content.scope: Deep institutional capture of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate glass models ordered for the Liverpool Museum, the nineteenth-century Free Public Museum of Liverpool and present World Museum / National Museums Liverpool. The module joins a workshop-side 1887 commercial/logistical sequence to modern physical survival. On 11 October 1887 the workshop told its British intermediary that work on 'the models for Liverpool' would begin the following week. A 23 November account layer states that 247 Marks represented the Liverpool models alone and asks for roughly 50 additional Marks toward packing. A December dispatch letter records one freight case, I.B. 268, containing the models for Liverpool Museum, routed through M. O. W. Möller in Hamburg for onward delivery to a Higgins in Liverpool; the enclosed-invoice total is OCR-read as 268 Marks. The same account also mentions a £25 remittance converted by the Bank of Dresden to 506 Reichsmarks and a larger prepaid-account figure of £53, but these are retained as intermediary accounting layers rather than assigned to Liverpool alone. The recipient is contextually normalized as Rev. Henry H. Higgins, who had long organized the Free Public Museum's invertebrate collections and chaired its Museum Sub-Committee, while preserving the OCR uncertainty in the recipient line. Modern evidence independently closes physical survival: a 2017 Manchester exhibition report describes a trove of Blaschka sea anemones rediscovered in a drawer at World Museum Liverpool, and a 2019 NatSCA record photographs a World Museum Liverpool specimen identified as Blaschka catalogue no. 93. The exact original object count, exact surviving count, local Liverpool accession numbers, receipt date, and current 2026 display/storage status remain unresolved.
content.target_selection_reason: Selected as module 45 after module 44 left World Museum Liverpool and Carnegie Museum of Natural History as large-museum candidates requiring stronger acquisition/count closure. Liverpool crossed the promotion threshold when primary Corning/Rakow workshop OCR yielded a complete manufacture-to-dispatch chain for an 1887 Liverpool Museum order, including a models-only value, a packing estimate, a marked freight case, Hamburg forwarding instructions, and an enclosed invoice total. Modern sources then supply plural physical survival and a commercial-catalogue object anchor. Duplicate audit found no standalone Liverpool Blaschka node in active 06 v3 or standalone modules 41–44.

merge_policy.duplicate_node_audit: No standalone Liverpool Museum / Free Public Museum of Liverpool / World Museum / National Museums Liverpool Blaschka node was found in active 06 v3 through module 40 or standalone modules 41–44.
merge_policy.historical_institution_guard: Workshop correspondence uses 'Liverpool Museum'. For the 1887 institutional layer this module uses Liverpool Museum / Free Public Museum of Liverpool. Present custodial continuity is World Museum, National Museums Liverpool. Historical naming is not silently back-projected.
merge_policy.Damon_identity_guard: The 11 October 1887 page is addressed to 'Mr. Damon' and belongs to the British dealer/agency sequence. Robert Damon and Robert Ferris Damon worked in the same natural-history dealership. The module treats 'Damon / Damon firm' as the commercial intermediary context and does not assign every Liverpool letter to father or son without image-level verification.
merge_policy.Higgins_identity_guard: The dispatch OCR renders the Liverpool recipient corruptly as something like '... Higgins'. Rev. Henry H. Higgins is a strong contextual normalization because his 1880 published Synopsis identifies him as a long-serving Liverpool museum committee member, Chairman of the Museum Sub-Committee, and organizer of the Free Public Museum's invertebrate arrangement. Exact recipient wording must still be checked against the original notebook image.
merge_policy.Higgins_role_guard: Henry H. Higgins is treated as the likely museum-side receiving/administrative figure and an established organizer of the invertebrate collection. He is not automatically called the legal purchaser, payer, selector of every model, or private owner.
merge_policy.11_October_manufacture_guard: The 11 October 1887 workshop letter says the Liverpool models would be commenced the following week and sent as soon as ready. This is direct manufacture/order evidence, not a completed shipment on 11 October.
merge_policy.247_mark_models_only_guard: The 23 November 1887 OCR states that 247 Marks represented the Liverpool models only. This is retained as a pre-dispatch models-only accounting figure, not silently treated as the final all-inclusive invoice.
merge_policy.approx_50_mark_packing_guard: The same November account asks for approximately 50 additional Marks toward packing. This is an estimate/request before final dispatch, not a verified final packing charge.
merge_policy.268_mark_invoice_guard: The December dispatch OCR reads the enclosed invoice's whole amount as 268 Marks. Because OCR/account context may be imperfect, 268 is preserved as the dispatch-letter invoice transcription rather than reconstructed into model/packing/freight components.
merge_policy.247_vs_268_guard: The November models-only figure is 247 Marks while the later dispatch-letter invoice OCR is 268 Marks. The arithmetic difference is 21 Marks, but the module does not infer that 21 Marks equals packing, insurance, freight or any other specific charge. The earlier packing estimate was about 50 Marks, so the original invoice is required to resolve the accounting layers.
merge_policy.twenty_one_mark_non_inference_guard: No field labels the 21-Mark arithmetic difference as a historical charge. It is only a modern arithmetic observation.
merge_policy.package_mark_guard: I.B. 268 is a freight-case/package mark from the workshop correspondence. It is not a Liverpool accession number, Blaschka commercial catalogue number, object count, or model number.
merge_policy.single_case_count_guard: One freight case does not imply one physical model. No model quantity is inferred from case I.B. 268.
merge_policy.Hamburg_route_guard: The dispatch letter routes the case to M. O. W. Möller in Hamburg for immediate onward dispatch to Liverpool. The exact steamer, carrier after Hamburg, customs process and Liverpool delivery receipt remain unresolved.
merge_policy.shipment_date_guard: The dispatch is placed in December 1887 because the letter refers to Christmas-season congestion and hoped-for arrival before the 16th, within the contiguous October–November–December 1887 order sequence. The OCR reads 'Monday the 2th Inst'. Calendar logic makes 12 December 1887 a plausible candidate, but the exact day is not promoted to fact without image verification.
merge_policy.insurance_guard: The insurance figure in the dispatch OCR is corrupt ('2% Marks' or similar). No insurance amount is asserted.
merge_policy.25_gbp_remittance_guard: The dispatch letter says a £25 draft was converted by the Bank of Dresden to 506 Reichsmarks/Marks. This belongs to the Damon intermediary account context and is not declared to be Liverpool Museum's purchase price or a Liverpool-only payment.
merge_policy.53_gbp_prepaid_guard: The OCR also refers to a total prepaid account of £53 and a remaining credit applied toward Galway/Cardiff orders. This is a multi-order intermediary account layer and is not allocated wholly to Liverpool.
merge_policy.Galway_Cardiff_account_guard: The Liverpool dispatch letter immediately rolls remaining credit into Galway and Cardiff orders. This demonstrates a dealer-side running account across institutions and is why remittance/prepayment figures cannot safely be treated as single-institution invoices.
merge_policy.2017_trove_guard: Apollo's 2017 account describes a 'trove of Blaschka sea anemones' discovered in the back of a drawer at World Museum Liverpool and used in Manchester Museum's Object Lessons exhibition. This proves plural surviving Liverpool Blaschka sea-anemone material by 2017, but supplies no exact count, local IDs or guarantee that the rediscovered subset is the entire 1887 shipment.
merge_policy.Object_Lessons_guard: Manchester University's 2017 exhibition record confirms models from World Museum Liverpool were displayed alongside Manchester Museum and George Loudon material. It does not by itself itemize which World Museum models were Blaschka; the Apollo account supplies the specific sea-anemone attribution.
merge_policy.catalogue_93_guard: NatSCA's 2019 page captions a World Museum Liverpool specimen as 'Sagartia coccinia [sic] Blaschka catalogue Nr. 93'. The commercial catalogue number is therefore a published object-level Blaschka anchor. No Liverpool local accession number is supplied.
merge_policy.historical_taxon_guard: The NatSCA caption spelling 'Sagartia coccinia [sic]' is preserved as published. Modern taxonomy is not silently substituted in this module.
merge_policy.commercial_vs_local_identifier_guard: Blaschka catalogue no. 93 is a workshop/commercial identifier, not a World Museum Liverpool accession or registration number.
merge_policy.1887_to_2019_identity_guard: The 2019 catalogue-no.93 object and 2017 sea-anemone trove are consistent with survival from the 1887 order, but no local receipt/accession register has yet been recovered to prove that specific present model no.93 was inside case I.B. 268. The shipment-to-survivor bridge remains collection-level rather than item-level.
merge_policy.WWII_loss_guard: Liverpool Museum suffered catastrophic wartime destruction in 1941, but this module does not infer any Blaschka-specific loss count or damage mechanism without an object/register comparison.
merge_policy.current_2026_guard: Current National Museums Liverpool sources confirm World Museum's natural-science/zoology custodial framework, but no 2026 page recovered in this pass gives an exact Blaschka survival count, complete taxon list, current storage location, or current display status.
merge_policy.comparative_location_guard: Comparative institution spreadsheets or other museums' location lists may suggest Liverpool holdings but cannot transfer their accession numbers, condition notes, labels, repairs or catalogue crosswalks into Liverpool.
merge_policy.synthetic_identifier_guard: No Liverpool accession number, original museum receipt number, local catalogue number, insurance value, exact shipment day, model count or missing-object identifier is invented.

summary.key_result: Liverpool is a rare transaction-to-survival node. The workshop sequence documents an active 1887 order moving through manufacture, dealer-side account settlement, packing and a marked freight case routed through Hamburg to a named Liverpool museum receiving context. Modern evidence independently establishes that a plural sea-anemone corpus survived into 2017 and that at least one World Museum object was still identifiable to Blaschka commercial catalogue no. 93 in 2019. The most important remaining gap is the local accession bridge: the 1887 museum receipt/inventory and a current collection-management export are needed to prove which surviving models descend from case I.B. 268.

network_implications.Damon_batch_network: Liverpool sits in a tightly documented 1887 Damon-mediated British/Irish order sequence alongside Marlborough, Perth, Galway and Cardiff. The correspondence shows the workshop scheduling manufacture serially while the intermediary account carried credit across institutions.
network_implications.running_account_value: Liverpool demonstrates why institutional price history cannot be reconstructed by assigning every remittance in a dealer letter to the nearest named museum. The same account immediately reuses credit for Galway and Cardiff.
network_implications.museum_programme_value: Higgins had already formalized a systematic invertebrate display programme before the 1887 order, providing a strong institutional context for the models' didactic use.
network_implications.survival_value: The modern sea-anemone trove and catalogue no.93 object turn a workshop dispatch into a surviving-collection node, even though the item-level accession bridge is still missing.
network_implications.comparison_with_Newcastle: Liverpool complements module 44 Newcastle: Newcastle has strong modern collection/exhibition evidence but no recovered nineteenth-century transaction, whereas Liverpool now has a workshop-side commercial shipment plus modern survival, with the local accession register as the remaining bottleneck.
network_implications.next_institutional_action: For module 46 return to the global major-museum screen. Carnegie Museum of Natural History remains a verified physical-holding/loan candidate but should be promoted only if count, acquisition route or local identifiers can be recovered. Prefer an uncaptured institution with a dated transaction, complete local object register or a comparable workshop-to-survivor bridge rather than promoting catalogue-contact-only nodes.

The Botanical Models (1886-1936) Susan M. Rossi-Wilcox, Administrator for the Glass Flowers Collection and Curatorial Associate in the Botanical Museum-Harvard University Herbaria TROPICAL and temperate plants continuously bloom in their Victorian cherry wood vitrines as visitors to the Harvard Museum of Natural History marvel at their favorite flowers and the most noxious weeds. These nearly 4,300 botanical models represent roughly 840 species and 170 plant families in an incomparable collection popularly known as the Glass Flowers. Commissioned in 1886 by Prof. George Lincoln Goodale (Fig. 1), then director of the Harvard Botanic Garden, the exhibition was inspired by his desire to represent the full glory of the plant kingdom in the natural history museums that were then being developed at Harvard. This display would also help to supplement botanical courses because the numerous planted beds and greenhouses that Goodale oversaw at the Botanic Garden were subject to New England winters that limited the selection of teaching materials during the academic year. Goodale searched for something that would be aesthetically pleasing, scientifically accurate, and much appreciated by both botany students and the general public. While peacocks can be stuffed and minerals can be meticulously polished, presenting plants as attractive displays is more problematic. Although lovely botanical models fashioned from wax-covered silk or papier-mâché were available as teaching aids, Goodale was impressed by the idea of using glass after he saw the zoological models in the Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard, which housed detailed glass models made by Leopold Blaschka and his son, Rudolf. This allowed members of Harvard's faculty to use replicas of organisms to easily point out morphological features during lectures. Goodale realized that the fragile zoological creatures were much like fresh fruits and flowers that quickly decay and could never hold up as an exhibition. He also knew that dried, pressed herbarium specimens and color plates from botanical texts had a limited appeal. In 1886, Goodale traveled to Dresden, Germany, where the Blaschka family lived. Despite their initial resistance, Goodale ultimately persuaded the glass artists to accept a commission for a few plant models. The first shipment of these models was badly damaged by customs inspectors who hastily unpacked them, but the wafer-thin petals and leaves were convincingly lifelike. Goodale and his former Radcliffe College students, including Mary Lee Ware, believed that the Blaschkas' skilled hands and extensive botanical knowledge could create a most remarkable exhibition. Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka agreed to a part-time, three-year contract. When it was time to renew the agreement in 1890, Goodale convinced Elizabeth Ware (Fig. 2) and her daughter, Mary (Fig. 3), who had become the benefactors of the Glass Flowers collection, Acknowledgments. In this project, there are many colleagues to thank. Chief among them are Rosemarie Starlinger, who provided most of the transcriptions of the 1892 letters; Ulrich Jordis, who translated some of the 1892 letters; Hubertus von Posern, who translated the 1895 letters and other documents; and especially Laura E. Lukas, who translated the bulk of the 1892 transcriptions, including mine. All of the letters are housed in the Blaschka archives of the Botanical Museum-Harvard University Herbaria holdings. The notes on the drawings were translated by Erich Moraine, a flameworker, and Laura E. Lukas completed three other sets of notes. David E. Boufford and Gustavo A. Romero reviewed the captions for the drawings, and Richard W. Stratton provided a careful reading of the manuscript. Lisa DeCesare, Gustavo Romero, Sylvie Laborde, Jill Thomas- Clark, and Gail P. erworts; insects and pollination; and blighted apples, pears, and other fruits. Visitors to the exhibition, particularly gardeners, often ask about the basis of the Blaschkas' models. Over the years, Goodale brought the artists a wide variety of seeds, cuttings, and plants from Cambridge. Since the climate of Saxony is similar to that of New England, the plants grew well. Although there are only a few contemporaneous written accounts of the Blaschkas' activities, 19th-century photographs of their home reveal the extent of the cultivation on their property. Reference specimens were also obtained from important gardens nearby, such as the Pilnitz Castle gardens and the Royal Dresden Botanic Garden, and from other state arboretums and botanical gardens in Germany. The Blaschkas' neighbor, the grand duchess of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, parted with a mature branch of her fig tree. Male and female flowering branches of the maidenhair tree (Ginkgo biloba L.) were obtained from the Grand Ducal Gardens in Karlsruhe (Baden). By mid-1890, after they had made models of several hundred species to represent the major plant families, the Blaschkas had begun to exhaust their European sources. Although Rudolf was interested in undertaking a field expedition in North America, Goodale noted: "It seems worthwhile to induce young Mr. Blaschka to try his hand at reproduction of models from dryspecimens, exactly as the botanical artists do. He would have to be shown how this sort of work is done, and if the experiment is a success, there will be no limit to the material at command, for we can procure the dried specimens in every stage of development."1 This implies that the Blaschkas were used to, and preferred to have, living reference material. It also suggests the complications involved in adding exotic or difficult-to-cultivate species to the collection. Judging from some of the flat-looking models, relying on herbarium specimens must have worked for a while. But it later became evident that Rudolf's request would have to be considered seriously. This is indicated in a letter from Goodale to Elizabeth Ware on April 15, 1890, that outlined the conditions of the newly written contract. The Blaschkas offered to save enough money for Rudolf "to make a voyage to America in the winter of 1891-1892 in order to repair our broken models and make fresh studies." But Goodale told them "that when the time came for his voyage I would see that he had enough for his expenses. He is anxious to visit South America and study some of [the] plants of great interest in their native forests, which are known to Science only by poor drawings." Colored pencils and drawing paper were carefully tucked into his luggage when Rudolf Blaschka left the cozy villa he shared with his parents in Hosterwitz, Germany (the family had moved there in 1888), to begin a journey to study the flora of the West Indies and North America. The northwest trip to Bremen on February 1, 1892, was pleasant until he reached Hanover, where the wagon "shook worse than a stagecoach on a rocky country road. ... One could hardly balance oneself on one's seat." He sailed the next day from the northern coastal town of Bremerhaven. Like his fellow passengers, Rudolf endured a southwesterly storm. It blew in as he was enjoying the fresh air on deck, and it continued while he was in the lounge practicing his English, and later when he was ensconced in a luxurious private room. "I took Father's advice and didn't participate in the six-o'clock supper," he recalled in a letter dated February 14, and he was among the few who fared well enough to emerge for breakfast. They walked to the Botanical Museum, where, for the first time, Rudolf saw the dazzling exhibition of more than 250 sets of the models that he and his father had created, handsomely displayed in cherry wood vitrines (Fig. 4). Receiving the hospitality of Boston society and Cambridge academics alike, Rudolf quickly acclimated to life at Harvard. The island's varied terrain, including sandy beaches, lush riverbanks, marshlands, forests, and mountains, offers ecosystems supporting tropical, subtropical, and temperate plant communities. The rich flora and fauna had been observed by Europeans from the time that Christopher Columbus returned to Spain with descriptions of the paradise's diversity. Jamaica sustains more than 3,000 flowering plants, of which a third are endemic. These include hundreds of orchids, which were nurtured by early botanical gardens. In 1862, Castleton Gardens (Fig. 6), located in the parish of Saint Mary, was planted with material that had been rescued from the frequently flooded Bath Botanical Garden in Saint Thomas, the second-oldest garden in the Western Hemisphere. Rudolf studied these species, particularly those of the Croton, Bougainvillaea, and Jacaranda (Figs. 7 and 8). In 1892, Castleton Gardens was being developed into one of the most significant collections on the island. Hope Gardens in Kingston, Jamaica, which was renamed the Royal Botanical Garden in the 1950s, was founded as a public garden on the Hope family estate. It had been established only two decades before Rudolf Blaschka's visit. In a letter dated March 6, he related: Hope Garden [sic], where I am now staying, is still newly planted, as just four years ago thick forest was in this place, but there are still many old trees and useful plants that greatly interest me. So I could study many flowers and fruits of tropical bananas, for example, the coco tree, mango (Mangifer indica), the star apple (Chrysophyllum), and both of the coffee varieties [that] are grown in Jamaica, Coffea arabica and liberica. Today I had the pleasure of seeing the flowers of the cinnamon tree, Cinnamomum officinale [see drawing on page 103], which grow almost wild here.
